artigo.texto: SAN DIEGO (CNS) — The county Board of Supervisors unanimously backed a solar energy and battery storage project Wednesday to be built near the southeastern community of Boulevard. After hearing from more than 60 people, including many area residents opposed to the project, supervisors voted to adopt the major use permit, various environmental findings and a report for the Starlight Solar Project. The 588-acre project site, on land owned by the Haagen Company, is one mile south of Interstate 8 and Old Highway 80, and one mile north of U.S.- Mexico border.

artigo.texto: State Rep. Phillip Ensler says his record of working across the aisle and focus on pocketbook issues can help him reach Alabama voters who might not typically consider a Democrat in a statewide race. Ensler, a Montgomery Democrat and candidate for lieutenant governor, pointed to his legislative work on taxes, mental health and public safety as he makes his case to voters ahead of the November election. “The case is that I’ve been in the Legislature, I’ve gotten things done,” Ensler told 256 Today. “I have sponsored legislation to cut people’s taxes. I have my efforts to expand access to mental health services, so I know what it takes to get things done.” Ensler said affordability is at the center of his campaign, including eliminating the remaining state sales tax on groceries, cutting income taxes for working- and middle-class Alabamians and restoring an exemption on overtime pay. “The biggest thing is putting more money in people’s pockets, and there are a lot of ways we can do that,” he said. His other priorities include expanding access to health care and mental health services, investing in public safety and increasing support for public education. Ensler said Medicaid expansion could provide additional support to hospitals, particularly those serving rural communities. On education, he called for teacher pay raises, expanded access to literacy coaches and additional college and career counseling. Data centers and Flock cameras Ensler has also called for a moratorium on new data centers until Alabama establishes additional protections addressing their effects on surrounding communities. “I’m all for technology and data centers are something that we need to have, but put more guardrails in place to make sure that it’s not hurting people’s electrical rates, their water and noise pollution,” he said. Ensler said he has heard concerns in rural communities about noise, wildlife and other potential effects of large data center developments. “People who live in rural areas, they have chosen to live there for a reason, and they don’t necessarily want the noise pollution,” he said. “They don’t want it hurting the wildlife there.” He also raised concerns about nondisclosure agreements involving local officials during the recruitment of data center projects. “I’m not opposed to having them entirely, but at least having more parameters in place,” Ensler said. “The fact that local officials are signing non-disclosure agreements where they’re then keeping things secret, I mean, that’s crazy. If you want to be an elected official, you have to respond. You have to give information to your constituents.” Ensler said he favors a similar guardrail approach to Flock license plate reader cameras. While he cited concerns about misuse of the technology and the handling of data by private companies, Ensler said license plate readers have also proven useful to law enforcement in cases involving kidnappings and other serious crimes. “It is a helpful tool for law enforcement,” Ensler said. “So similar to data centers, we should have guardrails in place. The Legislature should pass legislation that regulates them more, but doesn’t completely ban them.” “The biggest thing for me is that hearing from law enforcement who have or are using it in the right ways, I wouldn’t want to take the tool completely away from them,” he added. “But people do have very real legitimate concerns, and we have to do better than what it is right now.” Working across the aisle Ensler is facing Republican John Wahl in the lieutenant governor’s race. While the two agree on eliminating the remaining state grocery tax, Ensler pointed to his experience as a public school teacher, attorney and state legislator and said he feels Wahl lacks the experience needed for the office. “I’ve worked on legislation for years, have been in the Legislature where I’ve gotten things done for people,” Ensler said. “You know, I love butterflies. They’re beautiful creatures,” he said. “But being a butterfly farmer is not necessarily relevant experience to get things done in the Legislature,” Ensler said, referring to Wahl’s background as a professional butterfly farmer in western Limestone County. With Republicans holding large majorities in the Alabama Legislature, Ensler said relationships he has developed across party lines would be central to advancing his priorities as lieutenant governor. He pointed to his work with Republican lawmakers on Bo’s Law, dealing with animal cruelty, and legislation banning Glock switches. “I have the relationships on the Republican side and definitely with Minority Leader Bobby Singleton and rank and file,” Ensler said. “I would go in, not even on day one in January, but November 4th, be ready to hit the ground running because I have those relationships on both sides of the aisle.” Ensler also said he believes increased Democratic engagement in Alabama this year will carry into the general election. He said his campaign is traveling to all 67 counties and trying to reach voters across party lines. “I get everywhere I go, I hear from Republicans who say, ‘I voted for Donald Trump. I had to vote Republican, but I am going to cross over and vote for you,’” Ensler said. He said data centers and utility costs are among the issues he hears about from those voters. “People are hurting. They’re having a hard time,” Ensler said. “They’re tired of things that aren’t working in their favor.” Got a tip for OTR? artigo.texto: List Of All The Data Centers In South Dakota You might not think of South Dakota as a major data-center destination, but there are quite a few facilities scattered around the state and more projects are being proposed. The tricky part is that there isn't one official statewide list, and different data-center directories count facilities differently. One current directory identifies 11 data centers in South Dakota, while another independently verified directory lists 9 facilities. The differences can come from whether a directory counts individual buildings, telecommunications facilities, planned projects or entire campuses. Here are facilities and projects currently appearing in South Dakota data-center directories: 1. TierPoint Sioux Falls: East — Sioux Falls 2. TierPoint Sioux Falls: West — Sioux Falls 3. Midco Sioux Falls: Sioux Falls 4. SDN Communications La Mesa Data Center: Sioux Falls 5. SDN Communications Campus: Sioux Falls 6. Midco Yankton: Yankton 7. Golden West Rapid City Facility: Rapid City 8. Sequitor Edge Rapid City Data Center: Rapid City 9. ADP South Dakota: Minnehaha County 10. Sioux Falls Technology Park / Gemini Data Center: Brandon area 11. South Dakota State University Research Cyberinfrastructure: Brookings There are also proposed or developing projects that could significantly expand South Dakota's data-center footprint. These include a proposed Leola Data Center in McPherson County and a planned Gemini Data Center project in the Sioux Falls area. A proposed Sequitor Edge facility has also been reported for Rapid City. South Dakota's Biggest Free Playground Is Open And Awesome! Gallery Credit: Jacobson Plaza Sioux Falls-Ben Davis

artigo.texto: LOS ANGELES (CNS) -- Los Angeles County's planning director Thursday ordered an immediate prohibition on the development of large-scale data centers that power artificial intelligence in unincorporated areas of the county. Department of Regional Planning Director Amy Bodek issued the directive in a memorandum Thursday, saying it is intended to serve as interim guidance for planning staff while the county moves toward codifying the prohibition in its zoning regulations. Los Angeles County Board Chair and First District Supervisor Hilda Solis said she introduced a motion in April addressing public health and environmental concerns surrounding data centers. The motion was unanimously approved by the Board of Supervisors. "I introduced it in response to concerns raised by San Gabriel Valley residents who were understandably concerned about the effects of data centers in their communities, concerns that have since been reflected nationwide," Solis said in a statement Thursday. "As a necessary next step to address these concerns, the county's report back on that motion identified zoning changes that would prohibit these facilities. The need for such a ban has only been further underscored by alarming developments from the AI sector on catastrophic impacts the technology may have on humanity," Solis added. Solis said she intends to bring additional actions before the Board of Supervisors to implement recommendations from the departments of Regional Planning and Public Health to amend the county's zoning code and prohibit data centers powering artificial intelligence in unincorporated areas. In the meantime, the Department of Regional Planning's guidance will prohibit such facilities while the zoning amendment process moves forward, Solis said. She thanked county departments, residents and other stakeholders who raised concerns about data centers and said she remains committed to ensuring technological growth does not come at the expense of public health, environmental protections or residents' quality of life. In January, a group of Monterey Park residents participated in a community meeting hosted by San Gabriel Valley Progressive Action, which bills itself as a "grassroots, community-driven organization focused on environmental justice, transparency, and equitable development in the San Gabriel Valley." The organization says it is not affiliated with any political party, according to its website. At the time, the group and residents criticized a proposal to build a massive data center by SDCF Monterey Park, LLC, as reported by LA Public Press. The project was introduced in 2024. The applicant proposed to demolish vacant commercial buildings at 1977 Saturn St. and construct a 218,400 square foot single-story data center on 15.8 acres of land. Residents had shared environmental concerns about living next to a data center, such as the potential pollution of air, land and water. Ultimately, in response to concerns from residents, the Monterey Park City Council imposed a 45-day moratorium on data centers and later extended it while city staff worked to codify planning and zoning codes to ban data centers outright. In June, Monterey Park voters approved Measure NDC, amending the land use element to prohibit all data centers unless repealed by future voters. Monterey Park's measure to ban data centers was a first of its kind in California. The City Council of neighboring Industry unanimously approved a change in zoning laws in February, allowing the construction of a battery storage site. The action sparked criticisms from city residents and people living nearby in La Puente and the unincorporated communities of Rowland Heights, Avocado Heights, Hacienda Heights and South San Jose Hills. Concerned residents expressed concerns that Industry was creating a pathway for a new data center that would take over its mostly vacant Puente Hills Mall. The No Data Centers SGV coalition opposed the project, which consists of members from the San Gabriel Valley Progressive Action, Avocado Heights Vaquer@s, Puente Hills Community Preservation Society, SGVoices, Party for Socialism and Liberation and No Data Center Monterey Park. In late April, the city councils of El Monte and Baldwin Park also voted to implement a yearlong ban on data centers proposed within their city limits. Data centers have existed in the country before, and the construction of them has increased in recent years. These facilities run AI technology and California has at least 287 data centers. In 2024, data centers provided more than 665,000 jobs in the state and generated $14.1 billion in state and local taxes, according to a report from The Data Center Coalition, which bills itself as "the trade association for the data center industry with members that own data centers operate and maintain data center infrastructure both nationally and globally."

artigo.texto: Lais Carregosa, Marisa Wanzeller e Geraldo Campos Jr., da Agência iNFRA Grandes consumidores, em especial data centers, têm procurado as redes de distribuição para se conectar ao sistema elétrico e evitar a competição por margem de escoamento na transmissão, em uma espécie de “drible” no ONS (Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico), afirmaram fontes à Agência iNFRA. Com esse movimento, os agentes conseguem evitar o pagamento de garantias prévias antes da certeza de que conseguirão espaço na rede elétrica. O aumento dos casos tem chamado a atenção do operador e do planejamento, por meio da EPE (Empresa de Pesquisa Energética), que relataram a situação à ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica). A suspeita é que haja também um movimento especulativo, em que os agentes reservam capacidade na rede de distribuição, sem garantia de que os projetos de fato se viabilizarão. O ONS e a EPE defendem a compatibilização da conexão na distribuição com a transmissão, que tem uma política de acesso própria, a Pnast (Política Nacional de Acesso ao Sistema de Transmissão) – criada em dezembro de 2025. Nesse caso, seria preciso alterar as regras dos procedimentos de rede, o Prodist, o que exige atuação da ANEEL. Gargalos Do ponto de vista dos agentes, o movimento é uma consequência direta da criação de uma política pública estabelecida sem conversar com o setor da economia afetado. Para Luciano Fialho, vice-presidente da Scala Data Center, essa falta de diálogo levou a uma “solução que não resolve nada”. Com isso, os empreendedores estão buscando formas de solucionar os problemas que enfrentam. Ele aponta que a Pnast impõe dois grandes gargalos aos projetos de data center: 1) aportes milionários de garantias prévias, sem a certeza de conexão dos empreendimentos; 2) poucas janelas para solicitar conexão ao sistema, as chamadas temporadas de acesso, que não acompanham a celeridade necessária para o setor digital. Fialho destaca ainda que nem todos os empreendimentos têm a possibilidade de se conectar às distribuidoras, sendo uma alternativa apenas para cargas menores. Além disso, ele reforça que as próprias distribuidoras podem negar a conexão se o ONS constatar que não tem espaço na rede de transmissão. Assim, a solução passaria por acelerar as obras e entregar mais linhas de transmissão, aponta. Para João Carlos Mello, CEO da Thymos, “o todo não está bem desenhado” e é necessária uma costura mais efetiva das regras de conexão, com participação “mais efetiva” da EPE. Ele aponta que a transição do modelo de conexão antigo para a Pnast foi “muito abrupta” e causou estranhamento no setor. “Ninguém tem espaço infinito na rede para as cargas entrarem, mas acho que tinha que dar uma melhorada nesse protocolo. O que era antes organizado pelo MME [Ministério de Minas e Energia], ONS, ANEEL e EPE, agora ficou só com o ONS”, pondera. Capacidade limitada A entrada de grandes cargas na distribuição depende da capacidade contratada, já que as concessionárias de distribuição também celebram CUSTs (Contratos de Uso do Sistema de Transmissão). Segundo as regras, as distribuidoras não precisam competir por margem, tendo o acesso assegurado. No entanto, como destaca o CEO da PSR, Luiz Barroso, à Agência iNFRA, já há casos de negativas de aumento dos montantes de capacidade contratados por falta de margem no sistema. “Muita carga se conectando diretamente nas distribuidoras faz com que elas necessitem solicitar ao ONS aumentar o sua contrato de uso do sistema de transmissão, o que pode ser um problema”, ressaltou Barroso. “O tradeoff entre conectar na distribuição ou na transmissão é bem relevante e economicamente importante para as cargas e o sistema”. Um interlocutor com conhecimento do assunto afirma que, com o aumento de carga na rede de distribuição, as concessionárias estão tendo que pagar penalidades de ultrapassagem do montante contratado junto às transmissoras. O executivo destaca que, por conta dessas restrições, grandes cargas podem ter o seu pedido de acesso na distribuição negado. Regulação A ANEEL disse que tem trabalhado em aprimoramentos regulatórios a fim de dar “sinais adequados para que os consumidores optem por determinado sistema de acesso considerando seus diferentes requisitos”. Em nota enviada à Agência iNFRA, a reguladora aponta que as mudanças também visam garantir a efetiva implantação dos empreendimentos para dar previsibilidade ao planejamento do setor e evitar ocupação ineficiente da capacidade das redes. O tema está na Agenda Regulatória 2026-2027 e tem sido tratado em diferentes processos, também passando por tomada de subsídios. A agência destacou que está acompanhando as discussões setoriais sobre o tema e que, até o momento, tem sido pautada pela análise dos casos concretos, “considerando que o atendimento por redes de distribuição continua sujeito a limitações técnicas, critérios regulatórios de conexão e, quando aplicável, à participação financeira do acessante nas obras necessárias”. Trabalho duplo O presidente da EPE, Thiago Prado, defendeu a necessidade de compatibilização de acesso em evento no Rio de Janeiro na última semana. Ele destacou que a quantidade de pedidos de conexão de data centers na distribuição tem se aproximado dos números do sistema de transmissão. Isso leva as distribuidoras a procurar a EPE solicitando estudos de expansão, o que, segundo Thiago, causa um trabalho “duplo” do planejamento. “Posso estar trabalhando duas vezes porque vou estar trabalhando para expandir a transmissão, […] mas esses estudos estão concorrendo com os estudos de expansão [solicitados pela] distribuidora, porque ela celebra esses acordos de acesso, mas sem necessariamente ter uma garantia financeira”, afirmou.

Ele aponta que a transição do modelo de conexão antigo para a Pnast foi “muito abrupta” e causou estranhamento no setor. “Ninguém tem espaço infinito na rede para as cargas entrarem, mas acho que tinha que dar uma melhorada nesse protocolo. O que era antes organizado pelo MME [Ministério de Minas e Energia], ONS, ANEEL e EPE, agora ficou só com o ONS”, pondera. Capacidade limitada A entrada de grandes cargas na distribuição depende da capacidade contratada, já que as concessionárias de distribuição também celebram CUSTs (Contratos de Uso do Sistema de Transmissão). Segundo as regras, as distribuidoras não precisam competir por margem, tendo o acesso assegurado. No entanto, como destaca o CEO da PSR, Luiz Barroso, à Agência iNFRA, já há casos de negativas de aumento dos montantes de capacidade contratados por falta de margem no sistema. “Muita carga se conectando diretamente nas distribuidoras faz com que elas necessitem solicitar ao ONS aumentar o sua contrato de uso do sistema de transmissão, o que pode ser um problema”, ressaltou Barroso. “O tradeoff entre conectar na distribuição ou na transmissão é bem relevante e economicamente importante para as cargas e o sistema”. Um interlocutor com conhecimento do assunto afirma que, com o aumento de carga na rede de distribuição, as concessionárias estão tendo que pagar penalidades de ultrapassagem do montante contratado junto às transmissoras. O executivo destaca que, por conta dessas restrições, grandes cargas podem ter o seu pedido de acesso na distribuição negado. Regulação A ANEEL disse que tem trabalhado em aprimoramentos regulatórios a fim de dar “sinais adequados para que os consumidores optem por determinado sistema de acesso considerando seus diferentes requisitos”. Em nota enviada à Agência iNFRA, a reguladora aponta que as mudanças também visam garantir a efetiva implantação dos empreendimentos para dar previsibilidade ao planejamento do setor e evitar ocupação ineficiente da capacidade das redes. O tema está na Agenda Regulatória 2026-2027 e tem sido tratado em diferentes processos, também passando por tomada de subsídios. A agência destacou que está acompanhando as discussões setoriais sobre o tema e que, até o momento, tem sido pautada pela análise dos casos concretos, “considerando que o atendimento por redes de distribuição continua sujeito a limitações técnicas, critérios regulatórios de conexão e, quando aplicável, à participação financeira do acessante nas obras necessárias”. Trabalho duplo O presidente da EPE, Thiago Prado, defendeu a necessidade de compatibilização de acesso em evento no Rio de Janeiro na última semana. Ele destacou que a quantidade de pedidos de conexão de data centers na distribuição tem se aproximado dos números do sistema de transmissão. Isso leva as distribuidoras a procurar a EPE solicitando estudos de expansão, o que, segundo Thiago, causa um trabalho “duplo” do planejamento. “Posso estar trabalhando duas vezes porque vou estar trabalhando para expandir a transmissão, […] mas esses estudos estão concorrendo com os estudos de expansão [solicitados pela] distribuidora, porque ela celebra esses acordos de acesso, mas sem necessariamente ter uma garantia financeira”, afirmou.

artigo.texto: Keeping Up with Data Centers From the Western Ag Network, I’m Bob Larson. More data centers are bringing new challenges for utilities across rural America. Jim Matheson, CEO of the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association, says as electricity demand continues to rise, utilities will need both new and existing resources to maintain reliability … MATHESON … “It’s going up, and it's going up a lot, and it requires a significant amount of new generating capacity to meet that need. It also requires us to stop shutting down power plants that still have useful life, which public policy has been encouraging over the last few years in this country, and we've got to stop doing that because we need to make sure we can keep the lights on at an affordable price." Despite the growing debate around data centers, Matheson says the issue is not whether or not communities should support data centers, because that’s not the right question … MATHESON … “But what we are for is making sure that our utilities have the ability to make the decision that's right for them in their local community. We don't like one-size-fits-all mandates on data centers or any other policy, quite frankly, that's out there. Because different geographic locations have different characteristics, different capacities, different needs, and different challenges. And the extent that you can maintain that autonomy and local control in making decisions from an electric cooperative standpoint, that drives through all of our policy advocacy that we do.” Jim Matheson, CEO of the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association.

artigo.texto: Georgia governor’s race: Where Bottoms and Jackson stand on data centers Where do Georgia's candidates for governor stand on data centers? Metro Atlanta leads the nation in new data center construction, but Georgia lawmakers have yet to pass major regulations governing the industry's growth. Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms supports pausing new data center development while the state studies the industry's economic, environmental and infrastructure impacts. Republican Rick Jackson says local governments, not the state, should decide whether data center projects move forward in their communities, while adding guardrails such as greater transparency and requiring facilities to cover their utility costs. For their complete positions and more in-depth analysis on data center development, growth and regulation, follow our "Where They Stand" series on AJC.com as we break down the candidates' views on the issues shaping Georgia's future. artigo.texto: CLARENCE, N.Y. (WBEN) - Not that there is one in its economic development pipeline, but Clarence would likely shoot down any data center project - should one arise. Clarence is like many municipalities both regionally and across the country that are not welcoming the development of a data center. The issue continues to be an economic development talking point with the City of Buffalo later this month expected to see its Common Council back a two-year moratorium on data center-anchored projects. "These projects make more noise than the Buffalo airport," said Clarence Supervisor Pat Casilio. In July, Gov. Kathy Hochul issued a one year statewide moratorium on data center projects. Data center developments remain key discussion points in the Town of Tonawanda and City of Niagara Falls - among other municipalities. Casilio said no developer has ever approached Clarence about a data center and there are none on its development log. Casilio said there is a proper location for data centers - just not in his town. The supervisor said rock quarries might make a good location because of environmental issues like noise and water usage. In fact, environmental issues are key reasons why Casilio thinks data centers would be a bad fit for Clarence. Chief among his concerns: noise, electrical and water usage. ""We don't have enough power to support one," Casilio said. "And, I do have concerns about the noise." But, data center advocates say the buildings can produce large scale tax dollars to aid financially ailing communities. The Data Center Coalition reports that in 2024, more than $200 billion in tax dollars were created by data centers. "We don't have financial issues," Casilio said. "But, I can see where, financially, a data center may make sense in some cities." For now, Clarence has no plans to even consider data centers, Casilio said. "It takes a special place to develop a data center and Clarence isn't that place," Casilio said. If a data center project was proposed for Clarence, it would be shot down

artigo.texto: Chinese battery manufacturer CATL has concluded a cooperation agreement with Battery Manufacturing in Egypt (BME) to support battery pack production in the country. BME will fund and develop the planned facility, source battery cells from CATL, and supply the assembled packs directly to local automakers. Under the deal, CATL will provide licensing for its battery pack technology alongside production equipment and technical instruction, while BME bears full responsibility for facility investment. The arrangement aims to build Egypt’s domestic battery manufacturing capability and supports the broader electrification of local commercial vehicle fleets. The facility is planned for initial annual production of 1 GW/h, with a focus on packs for heavy commercial vehicles. BME intends to expand capacity to 5 GW/h in the longer term, extending its product scope to cover passenger vehicle battery applications and stationary energy storage for solar and wind. BME was established by Egyptian commercial vehicle manufacturer MCV and automotive solutions provider Auto D. CATL’s contribution extends beyond cells to encompass technology licensing, production equipment, and engineering support. The Egypt partnership forms part of CATL’s broader approach of deploying its battery technology through licensing agreements across multiple markets. Source: CATL

artigo.texto: From flexible electrodes to biodegradable architectures, researchers are redesigning battery materials so that electrochemical reactions can do far more than supply power. Paper: Biointegrated Battery-Based Electroceuticals. AI-generated abstract conceptual image created using ChatGPT/OpenAI A recent review in the journal Advanced Materials examines how biointegrated batteries can function as therapeutic platforms. The review covers battery-based electroceuticals for tissue regeneration, cancer therapy, cardiac pacing and defibrillation, antimicrobial treatment, and precision drug delivery. These systems combine electrochemical energy storage with localized electrical stimulation, therapeutic ion and reactive oxygen species release, gas generation, and controlled drug administration. The Need for Biointegrated Electroceuticals Electroceuticals use electrical or electrochemical signals to regulate biological processes and produce therapeutic effects. Conventional implantable systems use batteries to power separate therapeutic components such as stimulators, sensors, or drug-delivery devices. This separation increases device complexity and limits miniaturization. It also creates additional interfaces between the energy source and therapeutic component. The biointegrated batteries highlighted in the review offer a different approach. Their electrochemical reactions can generate therapeutic outputs directly at the treatment site. During discharge, these systems can produce electric fields, reactive oxygen species, gases, and metal ions that influence biological processes. The battery acts as both an energy source and an active therapeutic component. Successful biointegration requires careful control of battery materials and architecture. Electrodes, electrolytes, and supporting structures must provide sufficient electrochemical performance while maintaining biocompatibility, mechanical flexibility, and, where required, controlled biodegradation. Metals and their alloys, conductive polymers, carbon-based materials, hydrogels, and physiological fluids provide different options for constructing these systems. Evaluating Battery-Based Therapeutic Applications The review examines three major therapeutic functions of biointegrated batteries: electrical stimulation, electrochemical regulation of the tissue microenvironment, and controlled drug delivery. Researchers have developed flexible, miniaturized, and biodegradable battery architectures using materials such as Zn, Mg, Ag, Cu, and MnO2, together with conductive polymers and hydrogel-based electrolytes. Zn–Ag and Zn–Cu batteries can generate electric fields that reproduce aspects of the endogenous electrical environment around damaged skin. Flexible Zn–MnO2 batteries and hydrogel-based systems provide additional strategies for sustained stimulation. The rechargeable Zn–MnO2 design discussed in the review requires external charging and metal-wire stimulation electrodes, which limits portability and autonomous operation. Researchers have also developed tubular battery structures for nerve regeneration, which can maintain close contact with damaged nerves and deliver electrical signals locally. Cardiac applications require precise control over electrical output. For pacing, biointegrated batteries can supply low-voltage current that integrated electronics shape into controlled pulses, while some designs use the battery electrodes directly for stimulation. For defibrillation, a higher-current battery output can charge high-voltage capacitors, which then deliver the therapeutic discharge. These examples demonstrate how researchers can adapt battery architecture, output, and geometry to the requirements of different tissues and therapeutic targets. These systems can also use their electrochemical reactions to alter the local biological environment. Electrode reactions can generate reactive oxygen species, gases, and metal ions with therapeutic effects. Controlled generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) can contribute to cancer treatment and antibacterial activity, while hydrogen and nitric oxide can influence oxidative stress, cellular signaling, and tissue regeneration. Depending on the electrode chemistry, batteries can release Zn²+, Mg²+, Mn²+, Cu²+, and Li+ for applications including antimicrobial therapy, tissue repair, neuromodulation, and cancer treatment. Materials and Mechanisms Shape Therapeutic Performance Electrical stimulation is a key mechanism in battery-based electroceuticals. Skin injury can disrupt endogenous transepithelial potentials, producing electric fields that guide cell migration and proliferation. Battery-generated fields can mimic these signals and influence membrane transport, calcium signaling, mitochondrial activity, metabolism, and gene expression. Electrical stimulation can support wound healing, nerve regeneration, and bone repair. It can guide cell migration, promote Schwann-cell activity and axonal growth, and promote osteogenic differentiation. These effects show how battery-generated signals can regulate cellular behavior. ROS-generating batteries can create localized oxidative conditions to target cancer cells and bacteria. Gas-generating systems can produce hydrogen or nitric oxide at the treatment site. Metal-ion-generating batteries can release controlled concentrations of biologically active ions. Treatment outcomes depend on electrode chemistry, reaction kinetics, product concentration, release rate, and tissue interactions. These devices can also enable controlled drug delivery. Conductive polymers can act as both electrochemical materials and drug reservoirs. Redox reactions can regulate drug release. Battery-generated electric fields can drive therapeutic molecules through tissues using iontophoresis. Other systems can open drug reservoirs through electrochemical reactions. artigo.texto: Schaeffler and CATL deepen collaboration on Battery Management Systems and Integrated PowerBox Solutions - Schaeffler is shaping the rail freight transport of the future - The autonomous axlebox generator, modular power system and electromechanical actuators are accelerating the automation of rail freight wagons - First projects are undergoing field tests At InnoTrans 2026 in Berlin, Schaeffler is showcasing the axlebox generator, modular power system ITRS (Innovative Technology for Railway Systems) and electromechanical linear actuators – innovative system components that are already readying freight wagons for automated and interconnected rail logistics. Frank Steinmetz, who heads rail freight transport activities within the rail sector at Schaeffler, says: Our innovations form the basis for automated processes in rail freight transport, whether for digital automated couplers or automated opening and closing systems. ”They enable loading and unloading processes to be accelerated while substantially reducing downtimes. A reliable and operationally safe power supply is a key prerequisite for the ongoing development of such solutions – and that’s precisely what we are facilitating in collaboration with our partners in the rail industry.” As a key component of the ITRS system architecture, axlebox generators offer an autonomous power supply for rail freight wagons and provide the technical basis for digitalization, connectivity and automation in rail freight transport. Electromechanical linear actuators replace pneumatic or hydraulic systems and offer significant advantages in operation: they support the digital monitoring of positions and speeds, are robust and durable – even under harsh operating conditions – and work according to the “power-on-demand” principle, where energy is only consumed if the actuators are actively engaged. Axlebox generator for autonomous electricity production Thanks to their autonomous energy supply, Schaeffler axlebox generators are enabling key functions in the next generation of rail freight cars. They generate energy within the power system as the basis for automation solutions, to reduce or completely replace manual activities. These include the automatic triggering of actuators for the automatic opening and closing of tarpaulins, doors and hatches on bulk cargo wagons. Axlebox generators represent a permanent and reliable energy source for other electronic components used for communication, for sensors to capture load status, for GPS trackers, or for automated brake testing. Schaeffler axlebox generators are designed for standardized European bogie configurations and axles in rail freight transport (Y25 and UIC standard) and can therefore be used in new vehicles or retrofitted to existing freight wagons. First automation projects undergoing field tests Schaeffler is working with its Slovenian partner Realtronik on solutions for automating rail freight wagons based on the modular, integrated system ITRS. ITRS is a power system consisting of a Schaeffler axlebox generator and coordinated battery management system from Realtronik, which provides a high-performance onboard power supply for the corresponding applications. The first successful pilot projects in the market using the power system are receiving positive feedback from customers and highlight the need to push technologies for the automation of freight wagons to be able to increase the share of rail freight in the overall market. Linear actuators for electrified freight cars With its EWELLIX electromechanical linear actuator series CAHB-2xE and CAHB-2xS (smart variants with integrated controller) and the powerful EMA series of high-performance linear actuators (EMA50 to EMA100, 10kN to 50kN), Schaeffler is replacing pneumatic or hydraulic systems with a highly efficient alternative. In harsh railway operations, the electromechanical linear actuators offer significant advantages: they support the digital monitoring of positions and speeds and are largely unaffected by temperature fluctuations over a large range. In addition, they work according to the “power-on-demand” principle, using energy only if directly activated. In the event of an unforeseen power failure, they are self-locking, which keeps the flaps in a secure position. To overcome the pressing challenges in rail freight transport, the associated logistics have to be digitalized, interconnected, and automated. By presenting the axlebox generator, ITRS power system, and electromechanical linear actuators at InnoTrans, Schaeffler is showing how automation solutions for rail freight transport can already be technically supported and implemented. The bottom-up approach with incremental extensibility, depending on requirements and degree of automation, enables fast and cost-efficient solutions for automation and digitalization. Electromechanical linear actuators replace pneumatic or hydraulic systems and offer significant advantages in operation: they support the digital monitoring of positions and speeds, are robust and durable – even under harsh operating conditions – and work according to the “power-on-demand” principle, where energy is only consumed if the actuators are actively engaged. Axlebox generator for autonomous electricity production Thanks to their autonomous energy supply, Schaeffler axlebox generators are enabling key functions in the next generation of rail freight cars. They generate energy within the power system as the basis for automation solutions, to reduce or completely replace manual activities. These include the automatic triggering of actuators for the automatic opening and closing of tarpaulins, doors and hatches on bulk cargo wagons. Axlebox generators represent a permanent and reliable energy source for other electronic components used for communication, for sensors to capture load status, for GPS trackers, or for automated brake testing. Schaeffler axlebox generators are designed for standardized European bogie configurations and axles in rail freight transport (Y25 and UIC standard) and can therefore be used in new vehicles or retrofitted to existing freight wagons. First automation projects undergoing field tests Schaeffler is working with its Slovenian partner Realtronik on solutions for automating rail freight wagons based on the modular, integrated system ITRS. ITRS is a power system consisting of a Schaeffler axlebox generator and coordinated battery management system from Realtronik, which provides a high-performance onboard power supply for the corresponding applications. The first successful pilot projects in the market using the power system are receiving positive feedback from customers and highlight the need to push technologies for the automation of freight wagons to be able to increase the share of rail freight in the overall market. Linear actuators for electrified freight cars With its EWELLIX electromechanical linear actuator series CAHB-2xE and CAHB-2xS (smart variants with integrated controller) and the powerful EMA series of high-performance linear actuators (EMA50 to EMA100, 10kN to 50kN), Schaeffler is replacing pneumatic or hydraulic systems with a highly efficient alternative. In harsh railway operations, the electromechanical linear actuators offer significant advantages: they support the digital monitoring of positions and speeds and are largely unaffected by temperature fluctuations over a large range. In addition, they work according to the “power-on-demand” principle, using energy only if directly activated. In the event of an unforeseen power failure, they are self-locking, which keeps the flaps in a secure position. To overcome the pressing challenges in rail freight transport, the associated logistics have to be digitalized, interconnected, and automated. By presenting the axlebox generator, ITRS power system, and electromechanical linear actuators at InnoTrans, Schaeffler is showing how automation solutions for rail freight transport can already be technically supported and implemented. The bottom-up approach with incremental extensibility, depending on requirements and degree of automation, enables fast and cost-efficient solutions for automation and digitalization. artigo.texto: US Department of Energy Selects Coreshell Technologies for $50 Million Award to Scale Domestic Battery Manufacturing with Metallurgical Silicon (MGS) Anodes Award will fund expansion of production capacity, creating more than 100 operational jobs and strengthening U.S. supply chain independence for American mobility and defense applications SAN LEANDRO, Calif., Aug. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Coreshell Technologies announced that it has been selected by the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Manufacturing Deployment Office (MDO) for a $50 million award under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act. The award will fund the expansion of Coreshell’s manufacturing facilities, establishing the first U.S. gigafactory dedicated to producing lithium-ion batteries with anodes made entirely from metallurgical silicon (MGS) that supplants graphite, the most challenging Chinese critical mineral to remove from battery supply chains. Coreshell’s patented technology leverages abundant MGS to completely replace graphite, a critical mineral that is heavily concentrated in China (>93% of global supply). Coreshell pairs this innovation with dry-coating cathode technology developed with subrecipient AM Batteries. Together, the two companies will build out approximately 2 gigawatt-hours of electrode manufacturing capacity and 1.5 gigawatt-hours of cell assembly capacity. The project is expected to create more than 100 domestic jobs across production, technical, and administrative roles, with hiring phased alongside construction and equipment ramp-up. These batteries will not only comply with the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), but they will be the first scalable cells in the US to fully eliminate supply chain vulnerabilities from China. Jonathan Tan, CEO and co-founder of Coreshell, said: This award is about more than building a factory. It’s about liberating the batteries that power America from a supply chain we don’t control, “Today, the anode material in nearly every lithium-ion battery traces back to Chinese graphite processing. By proving that domestically sourced metallurgical silicon can replace that graphite at scale, we’re giving the U.S. automotive and defense industries a path to energy storage that isn’t hostage to a foreign supply chain. This DOE award lets us build that capability right here in the US.” Domestic mineral producers, including Coreshell’s supply partner Ferroglobe, already produce more than 100,000 tons of MGS per year, giving Coreshell’s approach a secure, scalable U.S. feedstock in a segment of the battery supply chain that is almost entirely foreign-controlled today. By anchoring both anode active material and cell production onshore, the project is designed to reduce U.S. reliance on foreign batteries for the electric vehicle industry while also supporting specialized applications for the U.S. military, where secure, domestically sourced battery supply chains are a growing national security priority. AM Batteries will contribute its Powder-to-Electrode™ dry coating process for cathode manufacturing as a subrecipient, eliminating solvent-based wet coating and the associated solvent-recovery and management infrastructure. AM Batteries’ dry electrode manufacturing reduces capital costs, operating costs, and safety risk while enabling higher performance cells. Hieu Duong, CTO of AM Batteries, said: This project is about proving that a 100% domestically produced high-performance battery cell can be cost-competitive with mass-market cells from Asia. “The U.S. will not win by simply replicating existing technologies or the status quo; we must create fundamental advantages in manufacturing and materials. By combining AMB’s platform with Coreshell’s MGS anode technology, we can lower cost, improve performance, and help build a globally competitive battery industry in the West.” READ the latest Batteries News shaping the battery market US Department of Energy Selects Coreshell Technologies for $50 Million Award to Scale Domestic Battery Manufacturing with Metallurgical Silicon (MGS) Anodes, source

21 de setembro de 2026
Por Rayllanna Cardoso, especial para a Broadcast, e Elizabeth Lopes
Brasília, 21/09/2026 – A avaliação negativa do governo do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) oscilou de 44% para 45%, enquanto a positiva passou de 37% para 35%, segundo pesquisa BTG/Nexus divulgada nesta segunda-feira, 21. As variações ocorreram dentro da margem de erro de dois pontos porcentuais.
Entre os entrevistados, 38% consideram o governo péssimo, e 7%, ruim. Outros 20% avaliam a gestão como boa, e 15%, ótima. A parcela que classifica o governo como regular permanece em 18%, enquanto 1% não soube ou não respondeu.
A avaliação positiva chega a 50% entre os eleitores com 60 anos ou mais, 49% entre aqueles que estudaram até o ensino fundamental e 46% no Nordeste. Entre as mulheres, 43% consideram o governo ótimo ou bom, e 36%, ruim ou péssimo.
A avaliação negativa alcança 60% no Sul, 56% entre os evangélicos, 55% entre os homens e os trabalhadores formais e 52% entre os eleitores com ensino superior. Entre os jovens de 16 a 24 anos, 57% classificam o governo como ruim ou péssimo.
Aprovação pessoal
Ao serem questionados sobre o desempenho pessoal de Lula, 50% afirmaram que desaprovam o trabalho do presidente, enquanto 46% disseram que aprovam. Outros 4% não souberam ou não responderam. Na rodada anterior, a desaprovação era de 49%, e a aprovação, de 47%.
A aprovação de Lula chega a 60% entre os eleitores com 60 anos ou mais, 59% entre aqueles com ensino fundamental, 58% no Nordeste e 54% entre as mulheres. A desaprovação alcança 64% entre os evangélicos, 63% no Sul e 61% entre os homens, trabalhadores formais e eleitores com renda familiar superior a cinco salários mínimos.
Entre os entrevistados que aprovam o desempenho do presidente, 85% declaram voto em Lula no primeiro turno, 4% em Ronaldo Caiado (PSD), 3% em Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ) e 3% em Augusto Cury (Avante). Entre os que desaprovam, 68% votam em Flávio, 9% em Cury, 7% em Caiado e 6% em Renan Santos (Missão). Lula registra 1% nesse grupo.
A Nexus entrevistou 2.006 eleitores com 16 anos ou mais, por telefone, entre os dias 18 e 20 de setembro. A margem de erro é de dois pontos porcentuais, para mais ou para menos, com nível de confiança de 95%. A pesquisa está registrada no Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) sob o protocolo BR-00485/2026.

artigo.texto: BYD India has said the Seal U SUV is the first model it is considering for its Indian plug-in-hybrid entry, with a launch targeted within 2026. The company has not announced an exact launch date. This is a PHEV, so it combines a rechargeable battery with a petrol engine. BYD describes DM-i as an electric-first system: the battery and electric motor handle most normal driving, while the petrol engine supports efficiency and extends range when required. How often the engine starts will depend on battery charge, speed, temperature and driving demand. BYD says DM-i vehicles can exceed 1,200 km using a full battery and a full fuel tank. The company also said it would publish the Seal U’s exact range when the model is announced. Until then, the figure should not be presented as an ARAI-tested India range or a guaranteed real-world result. A plug-in hybrid delivers its biggest daily-fuel benefit when the owner charges it regularly. BYD’s India executive said a person driving about 50 km a day with home or workplace charging could remain mostly in EV mode. Without regular charging, the petrol engine has to do more work. Overseas Seal U and Sealion 6 versions use different engines, batteries, drivetrains and equipment. Claims such as a 26.6kWh battery, 140 km EV-only range, 336hp output or a 15.6-inch screen describe particular global variants. BYD has not confirmed that complete package for India. BYD India confirmed that the Seal U would be imported, while declining to discuss future localisation. An imported launch can affect pricing, but no India price, variant list, battery warranty or homologated efficiency figure has been released. Buyers should wait for the official India specification sheet.

artigo.texto: On Aug. 18, the Amherst County Board of Supervisors voted to end by-right approval of data centers. The same day, a developer filed an application. That is where Virginia is in the fall of 2026: every county south of the Occoquan has a proposal on the table, every board is writing rules at the speed of a public comment period, and the share of Virginians who would welcome a data center next door has fallen from 69 percent to 35 percent in three years. The money is real. Loudoun County took in $1.2 billion in data-center property taxes this fiscal year, 39 percent of its budget, and cut its real-estate rate ten years running. That is why the applications keep coming to Amherst, Botetourt, Pittsylvania and Halifax, and why every board that says no eventually gets asked again. What is also real is that Loudoun got the money and almost nothing else. Two hundred buildings, and not one of them warms a school, dries a crop or grows a tomato. Every one of them throws its heat into the sky through a cooling tower, at the owner’s expense, because nobody ever asked for anything different. Virginia has now asked. This spring the General Assembly passed HB 323, the first law in the United States directing a state to put data-center waste heat to use. It cleared the Senate 39 to 0. It orders Virginia Energy to find the opportunities, connect the data centers to the heat users, study what the Nordics and the Dutch already do, and hand the legislature a strategic plan. That report was due Sept. 1. The 2027 session is where it becomes law or becomes a shelf. Here is what Southside and the Valley should ask for that Loudoun never did. Every data center is a furnace. Nearly all the electricity that goes in comes out as heat, and the newest liquid-cooled halls put it out as warm water, exactly the temperature a greenhouse wants in a Virginia January. A two-and-a-half-acre greenhouse on that water can grow on the order of 695,000 pounds of fresh produce a year with no boiler and nothing burned. Write a covenant into the rezoning that at least 15 percent of it goes to the host community, and one building’s waste feeds about 400 of your neighbors, year-round, from the fence line. Add the fish house that runs on the same loop, the farm store, and the homes on radiant floors at the end of it, and the campus that was going to take the farmland has instead built the farm, and the jobs that come with it are agricultural, not just electrical. None of this requires a subsidy. It requires a question. Loudoun never asked, “Where does the heat go?” because in 2010 nobody knew it was worth asking. Every county in the commonwealth knows now. So three things, in order: To Virginia Energy and the HB 323 work group: Name a demonstration site. A plan that says waste heat is promising and should be studied further is the same plan every state has. A plan that says here is the county, here is the campus, here is the greenhouse, and here is the date the first harvest comes off the line is the one other states copy. Southside has the land, the power corridors, the research institutes and the appetite. Put the pilot where the applications are landing. To the 2027 General Assembly: Make heat reuse a condition of the site assessment, not a line in a study. The state already requires an applicant over 100 megawatts to assess impacts on farmland, water, parks and sound. Add one column: what beneficial use will be made of the heat, and what share of it goes to the host community. Developers will price it in, because they price in everything a county asks for, and the ones who plan for it will win the rezonings the ones who don’t are losing. To every board of supervisors with an application in front of it this fall: You do not have to choose between Loudoun’s money and Amherst’s no. Ask the applicant where the heat goes. If the answer is “the cooling tower,” you have learned what kind of neighbor they intend to be. If the answer is “the farm,” you have a site plan worth voting for. Virginia wrote the law. Nobody in the country has done that yet. The only question left is whether we are the first state to use it or the first state to file it. Andrew Potter is the founder and CEO of Intelligent Harvest, a Lynchburg company that develops greenhouses and community farms powered by data-center waste heat.

It orders Virginia Energy to find the opportunities, connect the data centers to the heat users, study what the Nordics and the Dutch already do, and hand the legislature a strategic plan. That report was due Sept. 1. The 2027 session is where it becomes law or becomes a shelf. Here is what Southside and the Valley should ask for that Loudoun never did. Every data center is a furnace. Nearly all the electricity that goes in comes out as heat, and the newest liquid-cooled halls put it out as warm water, exactly the temperature a greenhouse wants in a Virginia January. A two-and-a-half-acre greenhouse on that water can grow on the order of 695,000 pounds of fresh produce a year with no boiler and nothing burned. Write a covenant into the rezoning that at least 15 percent of it goes to the host community, and one building’s waste feeds about 400 of your neighbors, year-round, from the fence line. Add the fish house that runs on the same loop, the farm store, and the homes on radiant floors at the end of it, and the campus that was going to take the farmland has instead built the farm, and the jobs that come with it are agricultural, not just electrical. None of this requires a subsidy. It requires a question. Loudoun never asked, “Where does the heat go?” because in 2010 nobody knew it was worth asking. Every county in the commonwealth knows now. So three things, in order: To Virginia Energy and the HB 323 work group: Name a demonstration site. A plan that says waste heat is promising and should be studied further is the same plan every state has. A plan that says here is the county, here is the campus, here is the greenhouse, and here is the date the first harvest comes off the line is the one other states copy. Southside has the land, the power corridors, the research institutes and the appetite. Put the pilot where the applications are landing. To the 2027 General Assembly: Make heat reuse a condition of the site assessment, not a line in a study. The state already requires an applicant over 100 megawatts to assess impacts on farmland, water, parks and sound. Add one column: what beneficial use will be made of the heat, and what share of it goes to the host community. Developers will price it in, because they price in everything a county asks for, and the ones who plan for it will win the rezonings the ones who don’t are losing. To every board of supervisors with an application in front of it this fall: You do not have to choose between Loudoun’s money and Amherst’s no. Ask the applicant where the heat goes. If the answer is “the cooling tower,” you have learned what kind of neighbor they intend to be. If the answer is “the farm,” you have a site plan worth voting for. Virginia wrote the law. Nobody in the country has done that yet. The only question left is whether we are the first state to use it or the first state to file it. Andrew Potter is the founder and CEO of Intelligent Harvest, a Lynchburg company that develops greenhouses and community farms powered by data-center waste heat.

artigo.texto: Democrats are now running against data centers. This is smart politics, given how unpopular the internet warehouses have become. Whether this is smart policy, well, that’s a different matter entirely, one we’ll have to deal with another day. However, no policy gets made if candidates don’t get elected, so let’s look at what Democrats are saying — specifically congressional candidates Tom Perriello in the 5th District and Beth Macy in the 6th District, who have both now made data centers part of their campaigns. In both cases they have made specific charges about their Republican opponents — incumbents John McGuire and Ben Cline — that can be fact-checked. The charge: Perriello says ‘McGuire voted for a $362 billion corporate tax break for data centers.’ The facts: McGuire voted for a more general corporate tax break that data centers are using. This is one of those charges that is true but selective. Perriello is referring to tax breaks in HR 1, aka the “One Big Beautiful Bill.” These aren’t specific to data centers, they apply to any manufacturer — although Politico recently reported that tech companies have been the main beneficiaries of them. “The law made it possible for companies to frontload the deduction of the full cost of new equipment from their taxes, a huge benefit for technology companies known as ‘hyperscalers’ that are driving the data center boom across Virginia and the country,” a statement from Perriello’s campaign said. Here’s how Politico reports what’s going on: “The tech world is pouring oceans of money into chips, data centers, power supplies and other components of the artificial intelligence infrastructure. And that’s eligible for generous tax breaks on investments Republicans included in their 2025 tax cuts. The tax incentives weren’t designed with AI in mind specifically — they’re available for all kinds of business investments. But it’s the tech industry that’s making the most of them, putting a major dent in corporate tax receipts.” The Democratic criticism is that tech companies don’t need this tax break, that they’d be investing in AI-related technology anyway, so this tax provision amounts to a giveaway that is costing the national treasury and driving up the national debt. The National Association of Manufacturers backed HR 1, partly because of that provision, which it said would “supercharge manufacturing.” So far, that hasn’t happened, though. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics shows that the number of manufacturing jobs in the U.S. is almost exactly the same as it was before the bill was passed. In Virginia, the number of manufacturing jobs has declined, from 239,100 in June 2025 (the bill became law the next month) to 229,300 in July 2026, the most recent statistics available. Data at the local level is harder to find, but the Federal Reserve says that manufacturing jobs have declined over the past year in the two biggest metro areas in the 5th District, Charlottesville and Lynchburg. This seems to be a case where the intent of the provision and its actual application are two different things. Its intent was to boost manufacturing; instead, it’s boosted tech companies — some of which are manufacturing companies, just not in ways we usually think of. We’ll come back to this point later, but it’s not as if there was a specific bill to give tax breaks for data centers that McGuire voted for. Instead, he voted for HR 1, which included a provision aimed at manufacturers that data center companies have used. The charge: Macy says Cline has “voted three times to let data centers pay no sales tax, sticking us with the bill.” The facts: That’s true. Those votes were also 10-18 years ago when the context was different. These three votes are all when Cline was in the General Assembly, not Congress. Now we’re getting back to the origin of the data center boom in Virginia. HB 1388 in 2008 was the first tax data center tax bill in Virginia. It was introduced by Del. Tommy Wright, R-Lunenburg County, when Virginia was in contention for an Apple data center that was looking at Mecklenburg County. Wright’s bill created a sales tax exemption for data centers that located “in a Virginia locality having an unemployment rate above 4.9 percent for the calendar quarter ending November 2007” and created “at least 100 new jobs paying at least twice the prevailing average wage in that locality.” The bill — framed as a way to lure a tech industry to an economically distressed part of rural Virginia — was so noncontroversial that it passed the House of Delegates 97-2 and the state Senate 40-0. Yes, even state Sen. Louise Lucas, D-Portsmouth, who has become the most vocal opponent of data centers, voted for it. Gov. Tim Kaine, a Democrat, signed the bill into law. Apple eventually passed over Mecklenburg in favor of North Carolina but the county did later land Microsoft. Virginia’s loss of Apple in 2009 spooked state leadership. There was a strong feeling that Virginia was falling behind North Carolina economically. The economy then was weak — this was the era of the Great Recession — and Republican Bob McDonnell won the 2009 governor’s race on the slogan “Bob’s for Jobs.” Come the 2010 General Assembly session, Del. John O’Bannon, R-Henrico County, introduced a bill — HB 302 — to expand the tax break for data centers statewide. This bill was also so noncontroversial that it passed the House 97-0 and the Senate 40-0 (again, with Lucas as one of those 40). McDonnell signed it into law. The intent was to make Virginia competitive in creating a technology economy and it worked — maybe too well, some might see it now. The state’s data center boom owes its origin to this measure. artigo.texto: 60 Minutes Transcript: The data center uproar America, and the world, are in the midst of one of the most profound technological revolutions in human history, with artificial intelligence poised to transform nearly every aspect of how we live and work. Behind this seemingly invisible revolution is something very physical: data centers. They are the factories of the AI age, vast industrial warehouses, packed with powerful computer chips consuming enormous amounts of electricity. With more than 3,000 of them across the country, and another 1,500 proposed, data centers are now one of the top issues in the midterm elections. So we went to Texas, where everything is bigger, including the development of data centers, to understand the backlash happening nationwide. Norah O'Donnell: All this agricultural land will look like what? Jazmin Villegas: It'll be nothing but data center buildings, concrete. Norah O'Donnell: This is just part of it? Jazmin Villegas: Yes. This is just one little bit, as far as you can see. Jazmin Villegas lives on this quiet farm just outside Dallas, Texas. When she learned that a data center campus almost three times the size of this one a few miles away would be built next door, this mother of five and Marine veteran felt called back to duty. Norah O'Donnell: How did you become the go-to person at the center of this fight against the data centers? Jazmin Villegas: Ma'am, just because I'm not in uniform doesn't mean that my service to this country has ended. I stand strongly behind my oath that I took when I enlisted to, you know, protect and defend this Constitution against all enemies, foreign and domestic. Norah O'Donnell: And you believe the data centers are an enemy? Jazmin Villegas: We're not sure. That's the thing. It might not be an enemy, per se. But how do I know that these chemicals or this pollution, water, air, noise, isn't going to affect my community, isn't going to affect me? In town halls and on social media, data centers have become vessels for other worries and fears: of rising prices, the power of the tech elite, congestion and crowding, and a dawning AI era that threatens livelihoods and futures. Resident at VA town hall: We are struggling to pay our bills. In Loudoun County, Virginia, which has the world's highest concentration of data centers, electricity bills have surged in the last year, at least in part because of growing power demand. Resident at Arizona town hall: We live in the desert. We can't waste water. They will waste water. In Chandler, Arizona, residents worry about water being used to cool data centers when the state already has a shrinking supply. And in Red Oak, Texas, where Villegas lives, construction workers' cars clog the roads for miles before dawn. There, they are concerned about all of these things. And they accuse the city council of operating in secrecy. Resident at Red Oak town hall: And now you've been caught, you've been caught making decisions without transparency. Jazmin Villegas: Not one single person in that room was for the data center. And the city council just went ahead and approved it. Norah O'Donnell: How did that make you feel? Jazmin Villegas: Angry. But instead of feeling defeated, it's, like, "Oh. Challenge accepted." Michael Webber: The pressure is real, the people are concerned. And I think they have a right to be concerned because they don't know what's going to happen. Michael Webber is a professor at the University of Texas whose specialty is the relationship between water and energy. When tech companies want to build in Texas, they call Weber for advice. Michael Webber: I tell them, "You need to pay your taxes, and hire people, and be power-flexible, water-positive, and carbon-negative." Norah O'Donnell: You have kind of a less technical, more direct message for some of these tech companies. Michael Webber: Don't be a jerk. Don't-- don't take the water. Don't break the grid. Don't ruin the land. Webber says data centers have been around for decades, but the speed of the construction and the size of those built for AI are unprecedented. Michael Webber: The primary difference is they're larger. In the old days, and by old days I mean, like, two years ago, a large data center might have been five megawatts. A new data center for AI might be 1,000 megawatts. It's, like, 200 times larger. So the scale is much different. Norah O'Donnell: You look at the numbers. They're mind-boggling. Meta, Amazon, Google, Microsoft expected to spend 1.5 trillion building data centers through next year. Why do we need so many? Michael Webber: I talk to a lot of smart people, and some say this will satiate. But then there are other smart people who say the demand for intelligence will never be sated. So we will always want more data centers. We will always want more intelligence. That intelligence developing inside these hulking warehouses, supporters believe, will generate what's called "AGI" or artificial general intelligence, that can match or surpass human capabilities. That means in addition to autonomous cars, and robotic factories, this additional computing power could pave the way for groundbreaking discoveries like curing cancer. And data centers aren't universally loathed – building trade unions want more because of how much skilled labor is needed to build them. On the issue of water, they often aren't as draining as many believe. A CBS news analysis found golf courses nationwide use more than twice as much water as data centers. Michael Webber: There's a race to power, a speed to power right now, where all the AI companies are in a race to train up their models to win the AI arms race, they call it. Norah O'Donnell: You're saying this is like a new arms race? Michael Webber: There's national security implications on the line, as well as great economic gains on the line. We in America want to have it first before a bad actor, say, China or someone like that. In Texas, attracting big tech was the goal of Republic

artigo.texto: Data center developer tried to "razzle dazzle" while sharing few specifics, Texas county commissioner says A data center project came to the table in a Texas county a year ago, promising a big win, but providing few specifics, according to a local county commissioner. While most existing data centers are in urban areas, according to the Pew Research Center, 67% of planned data centers are for rural areas, like Hood County, Texas, where attorney Dave Eagle is one of five elected officials on the commissioners' court, which votes on data center proposals. Eagle's impression is that the companies think they're dealing with "country bumpkins" when they make their pitches. "They just basically approached us in a way that they're going to bring a lot of jobs in here. They're going to be good neighbors. They're going to really upgrade the community. But they wouldn't tell us exactly what they wanted to do," Eagle said. "They basically came in here to razzle dazzle me." The company behind the proposal, which turned out to be Amazon Web Services, asked the county for up to 90% in property tax rebates for 30 years, according to a pitch obtained by 60 Minutes. Eagle voted against the project in Hood, but it's moving forward in the next county over, where AWS got the tax rebate it wanted. In a statement, an Amazon spokesperson told 60 Minutes, "Amazon evaluates many potential options to develop sites, and Hood County was one of those options. We ultimately decided to not build in Hood County." It continued, "Where we do invest, we work with local leaders to create jobs and generate revenue for public services." What's behind the data center boom Eagle isn't alone in questioning the boom in data centers across the country. There are already more than 3,000 data centers in the U.S., according to Pew Research Center, with another 1,500 proposed. Data centers have been around for decades, but as AI booms, the need has grown. AI data centers are packed with powerful computer chips consuming enormous amounts of electricity. New data centers are larger than old ones, according to Michael Webber, a professor at the University of Texas who holds chairs in the departments of engineering and public policy and has written books on the relationship between water and energy. Tech companies call Webber for advice when they want to build in Texas. "In the old days, and by old days I mean, like, two years ago, a large data center might have been five megawatts," Webber said. "A new data center for AI might be 1,000 megawatts. It's, like, 200 times larger. So the scale is much different." Hyperscalers including Meta, Amazon, Google and Microsoft are expected to spend $1.5 trillion building data centers through next year, according to Wall Street estimates compiled by FactSet. Webber said some believe the U.S. will reach a point of data center satiation, with construction leveling off, while others question whether that day will ever come. "There are other smart people who say the demand for intelligence will never be sated," he said. "So we will always want more data centers. We will always want more intelligence." The hope is that the data centers will provide the computing power needed to train models to reach artificial general intelligence that can one day match or surpass human capabilities. While AI has already enabled autonomous cars and robotic factories, supporters hope artificial general intelligence could also lead to groundbreaking medical discoveries. "There's a race to power, a speed to power right now, where all the AI companies are in a race to train up their models to win the AI arms race, they call it," Webber said, noting that there are national security and economic implications. "We in America want to have it first before a bad actor, say, China or someone like that." Rising fears over data centers Despite the positives, many on both sides of the political aisle are pushing back against the rapid spread of data centers. Texas mother of five and Marine veteran Jazmin Villegas felt called to duty when she heard about a planned data center campus next to her family home, where she keeps goats, horses, chickens, turkeys and honeybees. "Just because I'm not in uniform doesn't mean that my service to this country has ended," she said. "I stand strongly behind my oath that I took when I enlisted to, you know, protect and defend this Constitution against all enemies, foreign and domestic." Villegas admits she's not sure yet that data centers are an "enemy," but said she wants to know more about how they'll impact her community in the future, particularly in terms of health risks driven by water, air and noise pollution. While a CBS News analysis found that golf courses nationwide use more than twice as much water as data centers, residents in Chandler, Arizona — already worried about water supply — also raised concerns about the water used to cool data centers when the city council considered a proposal last year. And in Loudoun County, Virginia, home to the world's highest concentration of data centers, electricity bills have surged in the last year, at least in part because of growing power demand. "The pressure is real, the people are concerned," Webber said. "And I think they have a right to be concerned because they don't know what's going to happen." Emerging political flashpoint Texas Gov. Greg Abbott was a big proponent of investment from the tech industry in Texas. Last year while welcoming a $40 billion investment from Google, he said the state would be the "centerpiece for AI data centers for Google in the entire world." The Democrat running against him in November, Gina Hinojosa, has made data centers a key issue in her campaign and is calling for a temporary moratorium. Abbott has also changed his tune from last year. Last month, he paused approval of new data centers that would draw from the state's power grid until they complete an audit. "Texans come first," an Abbott spokesperson said. "

Por que a China está menos preocupada com alertas sobre IA? Entenda
Pesquisa da Morgan Stanley mostra que 80% dos chineses usam IA semanalmente, contra 54% nos EUA, refletindo visões opostas sobre a tecnologia
Ao contrário do que ocorre nos Estados Unidos, ninguém na China parece estar abertamente preocupado com a perspectiva de a humanidade ser destruída pela inteligência artificial em breve.
Lá, os cidadãos acessam serviços do governo local por meio de funcionários digitais movidos por IA; estudantes recebem feedback instantâneo sobre tarefas escritas ao enviar uma foto; e hóspedes de hotéis retiram encomendas entregues à sua porta por robôs.
A ampla adoção da IA na China atual ressalta o quanto o país abraçou a nova tecnologia. Uma pesquisa da Morgan Stanley divulgada na segunda-feira revelou que 80% dos entrevistados chineses usavam IA pelo menos semanalmente, superando em muito os 54% registrados nos EUA.
Mesmo enquanto executivos de tecnologia e pesquisadores americanos pedem uma desaceleração no desenvolvimento da IA citando sua ameaça existencial à humanidade, o público chinês permaneceu comparativamente impassível.
"Esta tecnologia foi criada para servir à humanidade", disse Xu Jingyuan, 22 anos, estudante de administração de Pequim. "Não devemos vê-la como algo a temer, mas como algo que traz mais comodidades às nossas vidas."
Ele disse que o governo é "absolutamente capaz" de gerenciar seus riscos.
Os comentários de Xu ecoaram os de várias pessoas com quem a CNN conversou nesta semana, refletindo uma divisão nas atitudes em relação à IA na sociedade chinesa e americana, bem como diferentes níveis de confiança na capacidade dos respectivos governos de lidar com as ameaças potenciais representadas pela tecnologia.
"Nos EUA, há uma percepção geral do público de que, sem denúncias, grandes corporações poderiam escapar da responsabilização ou do escrutínio devido à fraca supervisão governamental", disse Lian Jye Su, analista-chefe da empresa de pesquisa tecnológica Omdia.
"Já na China, acredito que existe uma confiança muito forte por parte do público de que, se qualquer m*erda acontecer, o governo vai intervir."
Analistas também apontam diferenças na exposição à IA, no discurso público em torno da tecnologia e no contexto cultural e histórico mais amplo como possíveis explicações para essa divisão.
Em uma pesquisa da empresa de pesquisa de marketing Ipsos realizada no início deste ano, 83% dos entrevistados chineses consideraram produtos ou serviços baseados em IA empolgantes, enquanto apenas 33% dos entrevistados nos EUA sentiram o mesmo.
Enquanto isso, outra pesquisa da consultoria de marketing Edelman mostrou que 86% dos entrevistados na China afirmaram confiar em seu próprio governo para fazer o que é certo, em comparação com apenas 39% nos EUA.
Uma diferença marcante entre as duas nações é o sistema político.
Enquanto denúncias de irregularidades são rotineiras nos EUA e os debates políticos frequentemente se tornam confusos, especial
