artigo.texto: Data centers: Brasil precisa resolver o gargalo da infraestrutura elétrica Em artigo à CNN Infra, João Carlos de Oliveira Mello alerta que, se conexão à rede demorar, investimentos podem procurar outros destinos A inteligência artificial colocou os data centers no centro de uma disputa global por investimentos. Países capazes de oferecer energia competitiva, segurança de suprimento, conectividade e regras previsíveis terão vantagem na economia digital. O Brasil reúne atributos importantes nessa corrida, em especial uma matriz elétrica predominantemente renovável. Porém, hoje há um descompasso entre a velocidade dos investimentos digitais e a expansão da infraestrutura necessária para atendê-los. Um data center pode entrar em operação em cerca de dois anos. Os reforços na estrutura do sistema de transmissão podem exigir de cinco a sete anos. Para projetos que disputam capital em escala global, essa diferença é decisiva. Se a conexão à rede demora, o investimento procura outro destino. O problema não está na falta de energia. O Brasil dispõe de grande potencial de geração renovável, mas enfrenta restrições na rede, tanto para escoar a produção quanto para conectar novas cargas. A chegada de empreendimentos que demandam centenas de megawatts e alta confiabilidade exige que o planejamento elétrico incorpore uma realidade que muda rapidamente. O país passou a adotar regras mais rigorosas para o acesso ao sistema de transmissão. O objetivo é legítimo: impedir que agentes sem projetos consistentes reservem uma capacidade escassa para fins especulativos. A questão é encontrar o equilíbrio. Garantias financeiras elevadas, exigidas quando ainda existem definições importantes sobre o empreendimento, podem afastar também investidores com projetos sólidos. A regulação precisa ser capaz de distinguir essas complexidades e diferenças. Critérios como maturidade do projeto, capacidade financeira, experiência de investidores e consistência técnica podem contribuir para a seleção de empreendimentos com condições reais de implantação sem impor a todos o mesmo nível de exigência. A tributação é outra questão que pode se tornar outro obstáculo. Equipamentos representam parcela relevante do investimento em um data center, e a diferença de custos em relação a outros mercados reduz a competitividade brasileira. Medidas tributárias capazes de corrigir essa desvantagem são importantes, mas precisam fazer parte de uma estratégia mais ampla e holística. A agenda digital deve estar alinhada ao planejamento do setor elétrico, à política tributária e às regras para infraestrutura tecnológica e tratamento de dados. O país não pode tratar cada uma dessas questões de forma isolada. A conexão entre elas é crucial. Também é necessário aproximar os horizontes de planejamento. O setor elétrico trabalha com obras de longa maturação por razões técnicas, ambientais e regulatórias. A economia digital opera em ciclos muito mais curtos. Essa diferença não desaparecerá, entretanto, a adoção de processos mais eficientes, planejamento antecipado e soluções de transição podem reduzir seus efeitos. Data centers são parte da infraestrutura que sustentará computação em nuvem, serviços digitais e aplicações de inteligência artificial. Os países que atraírem esses investimentos ampliarão sua capacidade de processamento e sua inserção nas cadeias tecnológicas globais. O Brasil ainda pode ocupar uma posição relevante nesse mercado. Para isso, precisa oferecer um caminho previsível entre a decisão de investir e a conexão à rede. Regras devem afastar a especulação sem transformar a falta de infraestrutura em uma barreira adicional. A corrida global por capacidade computacional já começou. Se a rede elétrica brasileira não acompanhar a velocidade dessa transformação, o investimento encontrará outro destino. * João Carlos de Oliveira Mello é CEO e fundador da Thymos Energia

artigo.texto: Anitta é coroada rainha de bateria da Grande Rio; veja Artista ocupa o posto antes ocupado pela influenciadora Virginia Fonseca; a cantora também assina um dos samba-enredos que competem na grande final deste domingo (20) A cantora Anitta, 33, foi coroada Rainha da Bateria da escola de samba Acadêmicos do Grande Rio no início da noite deste domingo (20). A coroação acontece durante a grande final de samba-enredo da agremiação em Duque de Caxias, na Baixada Fluminense. A artista recebeu a coroa diretamente de Eloína dos Leopardos, travesti pioneira e considerada a primeira rainha de bateria da história do Carnaval brasileiro. Veja galeria de fotos acima. Com a coroação, Anitta assume o posto antes ocupado pela influenciadora Virginia Fonseca, 28. Anunciada como a nova rainha em setembro, Anitta afirma que o enredo da escola se conecta com o momento atual de sua carreira musical. Neste ano, Anitta lançou o álbum "Equilibrium", que retrata sua conexão com a ancestralidade e espiritualidade por meio de sua religião, o candomblé. Em 2027, a escola vai levar para a Marquês de Sapucaí o enredo "Sankofa Tabon - Os Retornados da Costa do Ouro e a Estrela Negra da Liberdade", para contar a trajetória de africanos escravizados que, após a liberdade, retornaram ao continente africano. A cantora, inclusive, assina uma composição de samba-enredo ao lado de Arlindinho, Igor Leal, Fred Camacho, Fabian Juarez e Diego Nicolau. Veja o momento da coroação a seguir: HISTÓRICO! Anitta sendo coroada por Eloína dos Leopardos, travesti pioneira e considerada a primeira rainha de bateria da história do carnaval brasileiro. pic.twitter.com/0xI3YRB6V2 — Anitta Press (@AnittaPress) September 20, 2026 🚨 ANITTA SAMBANDO pic.twitter.com/BBKm10Hlh8 — Anitta Press (@AnittaPress) September 20, 2026 Chegada de Anitta na Grande Rio Após uma série de especulações, Anitta foi oficialmente anunciada como rainha de bateria no dia 6 de setembro. Em uma publicação nas redes sociais, a artista disse que o enredo escolhido pela Grande Rio para falar sobre fé e ancestralidade teve uma conexão imediata com o seu momento de vida e carreira. "Sabendo a importância do carnaval na vida de tantas milhares de pessoas, e para a história de um povo lutador que há décadas faz dos desfiles um ato político e revolucionário. E por isso nada na minha presença pode ser maior do que a escola, o desfile, a comunidade e os profissionais que trabalham nesse espetáculo", afirmou ela. Substituindo o reinado da influenciadora Virginia Fonseca, 27, a cantora garantiu ainda que, como tudo o que faz, se esforçará para dar o seu melhor, mesmo com a agenda cheia e a rotina agitada. *Com informações de Carolina Ferreira, da CNN Brasil

artigo.texto: The threat of a data center being built in Beacon Falls has proven so unpopular with residents that they’re objecting even before any formal proposal comes forward. Homeowners are organizing lawn sign displays and a social media campaign, while three separate online petitions got under way this summer urging town leaders to kill the idea immediately. “We should say ‘no’ to this. We have a beautiful, peaceful town. We want to keep it like that,” longtime resident Brian Hourigan said Wednesday. “What would it do the water supply? What about the environmental impact — and the noise? They run 24/7.” The response is a dramatic turnaround from four years ago, when the town appeared eager to get a smaller data center on the same property. It was never built. Now, following the lead set by data center opponents in West Haven, Groton, Morris and other communities, a group of Beacon Falls residents is calling on their town to pass a moratorium. Officials of the 6,000-population town in the Naugatuck Valley convened a public information meeting in August to emphasize that there’s no formal application pending. But residents countered that recent commercial real estate ads are promoting the property with the phrase “Largest data center in Connecticut.” The listings speak of a “100MW green-powered data center” and a 294,000-square-foot building, and include computer renderings of a massive structure marked “Beacon Falls Technology Center.” An online listing by The Agency, a California-based real estate brokerage, states “Beacon Falls presents a rare, clean slate opportunity to develop a purpose built digital infrastructure campus across 49 acres with up to 100MW of utility power in place – one of the most compelling and supply constrained sites available in the Northeast. “For equity partners and co-developers, the asset offers significant long term appreciation potential in a sector where institutional appetite continues to substantially outpace available product.” The listing also states the project would ultimately have 33 fuel cells on site. Torrington-based O&G Industries, among New England’s most powerful construction and paving companies, is listed as the developer of the project. O&G owns 49 acres of woods and former gravel pits off Lopus Road. “We are presently marketing 1 Lopus Road as a data center,” company President David Oneglia wrote in an email Thursday. The controversy illustrates just how deeply public opinion has switched against data centers. Across the country, many communities were trying to lure data center projects, drawn largely by the prospect of major new revenue from taxes and fees. In Beacon Falls, for instance, residents at a town meeting in 2022 unanimously authorized selectmen to sign a contract for a 32MW data center on the same parcel off Lopus Road. The agreement would have given the town $6 million over the first three years, and more than $2.5 million a year after that. But that project never went forward. The mood was vastly different when selectmen met Monday night: Several residents spoke against allowing any data center in town, and at least two asked about imposing a moratorium against them. Nobody spoke to support a data center or raised the issue of revenue. When the Economic Development Commission hosted a public meeting Aug. 24, the message was about the same: Nearly a dozen people spoke opposing data centers in town, while none endorsed the idea. Selectmen have repeatedly said that nobody has applied to build a data center in town, and that they have to avoid premature decisions. In a July 31 social media post, Selectman Peter Betkoski urged the public to be patient and rejected complaints that town leaders have been secretive. “What I find most concerning are the accusations that there have been ‘backroom deals’ or that elected officials have somehow hidden information from the public. Those are serious allegations. They don’t just question opinions — they accuse public officials of improper or even illegal conduct,” he wrote. On Thursday, Betkoski told The Courant that it’s too early to offer opinions. “It’s simple: there is no application. When there’s an application we can talk about the pros and cons and make a fair decision. I can’t now because the decision would become prejudiced,” Betkoski said. “So there’s really no comment.” First Selectman Gerard Smith was away this week; a message referred callers to Selectman Michael Krenesky. Krenesky did not return two calls this week. Online petitions signed by more than 3,000 people are pushing for more transparency about what’s happening — and a hard line against data centers. “In our tranquil community of Beacon Falls, a storm is brewing. Plans for a colossal data center — slated to become the largest in our state — threaten to overshadow our town’s serene landscape and delicate ecosystem,” reads one. “Our elected officials owe us transparency and action,” says another petition on the topic. “As residents, it’s our duty to stand up for the environment we cherish and the financial well-being of our community. We must demand comprehensive evaluations and clear communication before any irreversible steps are taken.”

artigo.texto: The Evolution of Data Center Design: Meeting the Demands of AI AI acceleration is redefining first principles AI training and inference have raised the stakes for how fast we can build and how reliably we can operate. The result is a step‑change in expectations for thermal performance, electrical architectures, deployment velocity, and resiliency. Our industry’s response will shape the next wave of capacity and the sustainability and community impact of facilities located near where people live and work. At ebm‑papst, we see three themes converging: hybrid cooling as the operating norm, HVDC readiness in new builds, and resilient, local‑for‑local supply chains that keep projects on schedule despite global volatility. No matter the theme, the mandate is the same: upfront design for efficiency, acoustics, interoperability, and redundancy. Hybrid cooling is here to stay Rack-level liquid cooling is becoming unavoidable for modern chip thermal loads; air alone cannot remove that heat density. Yet liquid does not eliminate the need for air movement in the data center. Airflow management around enclosures, corridors, and supporting systems remains critical to equipment reliability and serviceability. Facilities maintain cool temperatures inside the data center by rejecting heat outdoors, commonly through air cooled chillers, cooling towers, or dry coolers. What that means for design teams: - Plan for coexistence: Expect rack-level liquid cooling and air throughout the room, coordinated by controls that understand both domains. - Engineer for acoustics: As campuses move closer to communities, noise abatement for outdoor equipment will become a siting and permitting issue. - Target every watt: Efficiency is capacity. Watts saved in cooling translate into watts available for computing, especially in power‑constrained markets. Power density keeps rising without bigger footprints Computing density continues to rise, while real estate and retrofit constraints remain tight. Operators are asking for more airflow and higher static pressure in the same mechanical footprint. That challenges the entire system, from fan and motor selection to controls and mechanical integration. The winning designs will deliver higher power density without sacrificing efficiency or acoustics. Practical implications: - Specify equipment that can scale output within fixed geometry while maintaining high wire‑to‑air efficiency. - Use model‑based design and digital twins to simulate thermal interactions across the room and on the roof line before steel is cut. - Treat controls as a first‑order lever: smarter modulation beats brute force. Aligning electrical and thermal strategies for HVDC While retrofits to high‑voltage DC (HVDC) are often impractical for existing sites, new builds increasingly evaluate HVDC‑ready architectures (frequently discussed around ~800 VDC). Higher voltage means lower current for the same power, which can reduce copper in bus bars and conductors and lower the cost. HVDC distribution can also simplify power quality, reducing harmonic mitigation hardware on sensitive circuits. For thermal systems, this shift is more than an electrical detail. It affects drive selection, controls, and EMI/EMC considerations across fans, pumps, and outdoor equipment. Designing cooling assets to be compatible with HVDC ecosystems helps future‑proof facilities as the powertrain evolves. Interoperability first: BMS and protocol pluralism No two owners standardize their operational technology stacks in the same way. To stay deployable, cooling equipment should be BMS‑agnostic, supporting a wide set of protocols, including Modbus, BACnet, PROFINET, and others. This “interoperability-by-default” mindset reduces integration friction and shortens commissioning timelines, especially on fast‑tracked AI builds. Couple that with on‑premises digital twins that mirror plant behavior, and operators can test control strategies in software, apply AI‑guided optimization, and roll successful tactics into production with confidence. We’ve consistently seen strong alignment between simulated and realized efficiency gains when these models are calibrated and maintained. Supply‑chain resilience is a design decision Localization is more than a procurement strategy; it’s a project‑schedule strategy. A local‑for‑local manufacturing model (Americas, Europe, Asia) lowers tariff exposure, reduces transit time, and provides redundant regional capacity when disruptions strike. In a market where schedules are measured in weeks, not quarters, the difference between six weeks of ocean freight and a domestic lead time can define a project’s critical path. The most effective operators share multi‑year demand signals. Two‑to‑three‑year forecast corridors, supplemented by longer‑range directional views, enable upstream suppliers to secure critical components and expand capacity ahead of demand. That collaboration is how the industry turns macro uncertainty into dependable delivery. The grid constraint is a catalyst for better designs Many U.S. metros face power availability constraints that will shape site selection, phasing, and even micro‑siting. Some operators are assessing on‑site generation (including low‑ or zero‑carbon options) while advocating for utility‑led capacity expansions. Regardless of which path wins in each market, the mechanical plant must be ultra‑efficient, acoustically responsible, and ready to ramp in step with staged electrical availability. What we’re working toward as an industry - Hybrid cooling that’s quiet, efficient, and serviceable at scale. - HVDC‑ready cooling assets that integrate cleanly into evolving powertrains. - Interoperable controls that plug into any owner’s BMS ecosystem. - Digital‑twin‑driven operations that turn models into measurable savings. - Local‑for‑local resiliency with redundant regional manufacturing and long‑range planning. - Community‑minded design that respects neighbors while unlocking compute growth.

Enterprises Adopt Colocation for AI and Hybrid Cloud Initiatives Enterprises are strategically choosing colocation data centers to host AI applications, deploy a hybrid cloud model, add incremental capacity, improve connectivity, and reduce costs. Enterprises are increasingly choosing colocation data centers to host AI inference computing, which performs best using higher cabinet densities than are supported in most legacy corporate data centers. Modern colocation facilities support 35 kW cabinets with air cooling and 70-150 kW cabinets using optional liquid-cooling solutions. Because liquid cooling can be added once higher-density cabinets are needed, enterprise users with uncertain densification timelines can avoid stranding capital expenditures on infrastructure, making this “pay-as-you-go” model attractive. AI inference computing is highly iterative, requiring rapid, continuous interaction with large volumes of corporate financial, operational, and research data. Enterprises optimize AI inference computing performance by placing it near their other data centers to enjoy ultra-low round-trip telecom latencies. Enterprises can also install AI applications in edge colocation data centers near specialized data sources and use cases, such as factories, financial market feeds, and research labs. Colocation is available near almost every major city, but most public cloud regions operate from only a few major data center markets in each country. Colocation also offers cybersecurity advantages for AI applications. Because AI inference computing accesses valuable, confidential corporate data, many enterprises in highly regulated industries like financial services and healthcare prefer to perform inference internally in private colocation suites with dedicated network circuits and self-operated firewalls rather than sending that data off-site to third-party AI startups. Hybrid Cloud Adoption and Rebalancing Public cloud adoption remains strong: 74% of enterprises accelerated cloud migrations last year, according to Foundry’s 2026 Cloud Computing Study, seeking the flexibility, agility, and low capital investment offered by the cloud. However, prompted by rapidly escalating cloud costs and several highly publicized cloud outages, many enterprises are rethinking “cloud only” strategies by shifting to a hybrid cloud plus colocation or on-premises model. VMware’s Private Cloud Outlook 2026 indicates that 83% of enterprises have completed or are planning to repatriate workloads back from the public cloud, driven by security, cost, compliance, and performance concerns. In the push toward hybrid cloud, many enterprises now tailor workload placement to whichever delivery path works best for each specific application and data set. Enterprises often choose public cloud for dynamic capacity and cloud-native applications, but colocation and on-premises for predictable workloads and those that underperform technically or are cost-prohibitive in public cloud. Colocation also effectively hosts private clouds seeking the advantages of public cloud in a more controlled computing and security environment. Capacity Expansion Without Long Build Cycles Enterprises seek scalable data center capacity for both AI and traditional corporate computing (research, accounting, finance, sales, and legal), which is vital to all businesses. AFCOM’s 2026 State of the Data Center Report indicates that 75% of enterprises expect AI workloads to increase overall capacity requirements. Colocation offers incremental capacity expansion, allowing enterprises to increase or decrease capacity as needs change. Enterprises often prefer colocation to expanding on-premises capacity because on-premises data center construction can be expensive, time-consuming, and, in some cases, impossible due to the age of legacy facilities or physical limitations. Cost Predictability and Governance Colocation typically offers lower occupancy costs than public cloud for stable, predictable workloads. Most new colocation campuses are massive – often 50+ MW – delivering economies of scale in both upfront construction costs and operating expenses unavailable at smaller on-premises data centers. An enterprise seeking 2 MW of new capacity can occupy it at much lower cost in colocation than in a new on-premises data center. Colocation also avoids unpredictable, unbudgeted cost overages in public cloud deployments, often driven by unforeseen variable usage, opaque fees, and weak monitoring tools or practices. Enterprise users in Flexera’s 2026 State of the Cloud Report estimate that 29% of their cloud spending is wasted. Application Performance and Networking Enhancement Colocation supports legacy applications not written to be cloud-native, which often perform poorly in public cloud environments, while other corporate applications require lower telecom latency than is available from public cloud placements when corporate data centers aren’t located near cloud campuses. Some enterprises enhance connectivity for their computing portfolio using dedicated networking cabinets in interconnection-focused colocation facilities near their primary data centers. In this topology, enterprises secure competitively priced metro-area circuits from 20+ telecom carriers and cloud direct-connect circuits available in urban carrier hotels. International Operations and Data Sovereignty Many US-based multinational corporations operate their domestic data centers in-house but turn to international colocation suites for worldwide operations where data sovereignty, low-latency access to foreign operations and customers, or audit and compliance requirements necessitate local computing. International colocation providers also usually offer à la carte managed services that are valuable to enterprises without local IT staff. artigo.texto: Grid Constraints Steer Dutch Data Centers Beyond Amsterdam Amsterdam remains a top European data center hub, but power constraints are shifting new capacity to Rotterdam and other regional Dutch markets with available grid connections. Amsterdam’s data center market continues to grow, but the very infrastructure that made it a European hub increasingly determines where new capacity can be built. As of Q1 2026, the city was Europe’s fourth-largest data center market, with inventory up 11% year over year, or 64.3 MW, according to CBRE’s 2026 market review. Its vacancy rate tightened to 9.4%, evidence that customers continue to absorb capacity even as power constraints and planning restrictions limit development. JLL’s latest EMEA report shows that in H1 2026, Amsterdam delivered 16.3 MW, while Paris added 72.5 MW over the same period. Amsterdam still offers the connectivity, customers, and operators of a top-tier hub, but faster growth is shifting toward locations that can provide large power blocks on reliable schedules. The Dutch market is therefore set to become more geographically dispersed. Amsterdam remains the commercial and network center, while Rotterdam, Groningen, Eindhoven, and other regional markets compete for projects the capital cannot accommodate. Amsterdam’s Network Advantage Holds Amsterdam’s status within the FLAP-D group – Frankfurt, London, Amsterdam, Paris, and Dublin – rests on an interconnection ecosystem built over decades. In 2025, the Amsterdam Internet Exchange (AMS-IX) handled 35.66 exabytes of traffic, four times its 2015 volume, and ended 2025 with 902 connected parties. That density keeps carriers, cloud providers, content companies, and enterprises close to the networks they need, conferring an advantage on established colocation operators that newer markets cannot quickly replicate. “Amsterdam is characterized by the availability of skilled labor and an established infrastructure by large colocation service providers such as Equinix and Digital Realty,” said Luis Fernandes, senior research manager for cloud, data centers, and enterprise infrastructure at IDC, in an interview with Data Center Knowledge. He also noted the large number of subsea cables landing in the Netherlands from multiple regions. Geography reinforces this position. Amsterdam offers low-latency access to major European business centers, a mature enterprise customer base, and an energy market where operators can pursue renewable power purchase agreements (PPAs). “Add to this a favorable energy mix with a large component of offshore wind farms, as well as a prime market for sustainable PPAs,” Alex Mariage, head of regional operations at global data center consultancy BCS, told Data Center Knowledge. “This continues to make Amsterdam a very attractive and traditional opportunity for global investments.” These advantages support demand, but they do not guarantee a grid connection. The challenge is to preserve Amsterdam’s network ecosystem while placing workloads where power is actually available. The Equinix AM3 data center tower in Amsterdam. (Image: Getty Images) Deliverable Power Dictates the Next Build Deliverable power now outweighs land prices, incentives, and even fiber in site selection. Developers need to know when a connection will arrive, how much capacity it will provide, and whether equipment can be procured in time to use it. “Site selection in 2026 is driven primarily by deliverable power,” Assad Noori, executive director and EMEA head of data centers at JLL, told Data Center Knowledge. “If developers cannot secure megawatts on a predictable timeline, incentives, land costs, and fiber connectivity become secondary.” “If developers cannot secure megawatts on a predictable timeline, incentives, land costs, and fiber connectivity become secondary.” – Assad Noori, executive director and EMEA head of data centers at JLL AI has amplified the volume of requests reaching utilities and developers. Noori noted that single-site requirements, once in the 30-60 MW range, can now reach 300 MW, while transformer lead times can extend up to three years. Power commitments and long-lead equipment orders must therefore precede construction by years. “Cost and delivery timeline are now co-equal with availability in site decisions,” he said. Behind-the-meter generation can help when grid queues become too long. Noori advises developers to establish their queue position, connection cohort, offtake and export rights, backup service terms, exit rights, and penalties before committing to a site. Amsterdam’s limited land has encouraged taller data centers, enabling more intensive site use but complicating planning and permitting. Flood risk is addressed through national and regional defenses, with some facilities adding perimeter floodgates. Mariage said the Dutch engineering response to land and water constraints is mature, but the electricity bottleneck is now slowing projects. “Grid congestion is the key challenge here,” he said. “Every investor will confirm that this aspect is the top constraint slowing down projects and investments at the moment.” Capacity Shifts to Rotterdam and Regional Hubs Amsterdam’s constraints do not suppress demand; they widen the search radius. National policy generally restricts hyperscale facilities to designated zones in Hollands Kroon (including Middenmeer) and Het Hogeland (home to Eemshaven). Meanwhile, colocation and other developments are testing a broader field of Dutch locations. Rotterdam stands out for certain workloads, combining port infrastructure, proximity to Amsterdam, an established business base, and experience in reclaiming former harbor land. The AMS-IX added a Rotterdam point of presence in April 2026, strengthening the city’s role on the national connectivity map. artigo.texto: Insight and analysis on the data center space from industry thought leaders. Same Roof, 10 Different Gases: What a Data Center Is Quietly Holding Data centers’ reliability equipment – UPS batteries, refrigerants, and generators – creates hidden gas hazards that cause both safety incidents and costly outages. A year ago this month, during maintenance at South Korea’s National Information Resource Services (NIRS) in Daejeon, a UPS battery failure triggered a fire. The fire destroyed 384 lithium-ion batteries and took 647 government systems offline. Recovery was projected to take four weeks. Nothing about a facility like that would have told you it was dangerous: filtered air, locked doors, no flare stack – nothing that looks remotely like a process plant. Yet the very equipment that makes a data center dependable also makes it hazardous. UPS strings, chillers, standby generators, switchgear, suppression, and the water treatment skid are all essential; together, they introduce something close to 10 gas and chemical hazards hidden behind doors that mostly stay shut. Batteries, Then Everything Else Nine times out of 10, when an operator asks me about “gas,” they are asking about the batteries. Lead-acid on float can evolve hydrogen, and flammable concentrations begin at just 4% by volume. Hydrogen is invisible and odorless, and it migrates through gaps you did not know existed. Lithium-ion removes the hydrogen risk, but it introduces another: thermal runaway can vent flammable and toxic gases within minutes, often adjacent to live DC equipment. Refrigerant is typically the largest chemical volume on site, sitting behind more joints than anyone has counted. Because most refrigerants are heavier than air, leaks settle into plant rooms and pits, and when they do, they can take your cooling with them. Generator exhaust goes where the wind and the building let it. With short stacks, nearby intakes, and still air, exhaust can re-enter “fresh air” systems. Every test or run of a standby generator puts carbon monoxide and nitrogen dioxide somewhere. Sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) is an asphyxiant; under arcing, it decomposes into hazardous byproducts that accumulate in low, poorly ventilated areas. Clean-agent and inert-gas suppression systems require concentrations for occupied spaces, which limits tactics when people may be present. In Daejeon, responders used gas-based suppressants such as carbon dioxide rather than water to protect critical state infrastructure. Even so, the fire’s intensity meant it took firefighters 22 hours to extinguish it completely. Water treatment adds its own risks. Chlorine is a familiar one, and at an Apple data center in Maiden, North Carolina, in 2015, a spilled cooling-system cleaning chemical put five people in the hospital. Underneath many of these scenarios is the same mechanism: oxygen depletion. Why There’s More Than There Used to Be Data center capacity is on course to go from 103 GW to 200 GW this decade, according to JLL’s 2026 Data Center Outlook report. The gases have not changed. There is simply more of everything now, and it arrives faster than it used to. Lower-GWP blends, some of which are mildly flammable, are being retrofitted into plants designed for something else. Liquid cooling, unusual five years ago, is now assumed, which means a great many more joints right beside servers. The building itself can work against you. Data centers are sealed, secure, and pressure-managed for the equipment’s benefit, and this containment slows leaks rather than letting them dissipate. In a room nobody visits, a leak can sit for a week. The person who opens that door may be the first to encounter the hazard. The Uptime Argument Uptime Institute lists power and cooling as the leading causes of significant outages, with cooling alone responsible for 19% of outages; more than half of serious incidents cost over $100,000. Daejeon was both a safety incident and an availability incident. No one separates the two afterward because, in practice, they are one and the same. What I’d Check First Nobody has a single list of what is in the building. The battery data lives with the UPS vendor. Refrigerant quantities are stamped on the chiller. Suppression information is in a fire file somewhere. Dosing chemicals are handled by a contractor who turns up once a month. Consolidating that information is a dull afternoon’s work, and it can go out of date the moment a contract changes. Mounting height is the first thing I would look at. Too often, detectors end up at head height because installers can reach that easily. Hydrogen does not stop at head height. These incidents above occurred during planned work, not because of equipment “breakdowns.” The Daejeon event happened during a job to make the site safer. The Maiden case was scheduled maintenance. It pays to know who is on the schedule next month and what substances and procedures they bring. And buy detectors you can actually access for routine maintenance. If a sensor requires a permit, an escort, and a scheduled access time, calibration will slip. Eight years later, it can read several percent off, with the paperwork still in order. Notably, the Daejeon batteries reportedly passed an inspection in June of that year. Finally, treat rooms for what they are, not for the roof they share. A switch room and a chiller hall pose different questions, require different detection strategies, and entail different failure consequences. They just happen to be in the same building.

artigo.texto: Designing Layered Drone Defenses for Data Centers Drone threats to data centers are rising and real. Operators should adopt layered defenses – physical hardening, detection systems, redundancy, and regulatory coordination – to build resilience. Drone activity around critical infrastructure is rising, and data centers are not immune. Until recently, few operators considered drones a serious risk. That’s changing fast. The threat is no longer theoretical. In spring 2026, drone strikes disrupted operations at AWS facilities in the Persian Gulf. While that incident occurred months ago, it continues to underscore an evolving risk landscape for operators. How should the industry respond? The most effective response favors resilience, lawful defensive measures, and operational readiness over attempts at interdiction. Why Drone Risks Are Increasing for Data Centers Consumer-grade drones are inexpensive, widely available, and increasingly capable. Their accessibility means more devices in the sky near more facilities on the ground, elevating both intentional and accidental risks. Even small drones can damage exposed mechanical systems or interfere with critical cooling and power infrastructure. While military-grade platforms pose the highest risk in conflict zones, non-state actors and lone individuals could still cause localized disruption. Layered Physical and Detection Controls A layered defense blends practical hardening with multi-sensor detection and clear operational workflows. 1. Physical Drone Defenses Physical hardening should prioritize airflow-safe protection and impact mitigation: - Install protective cages or netting on roofs or around critical components to create a physical buffer against drones. - Deploy radar or other detection systems that trigger physical protection measures. - Where feasible, relocate vulnerable components, such as cooling towers, from prominent rooftops to ground-level areas behind barriers and fencing. - Apply materials for thermal and infrared signature management to help reduce long-range target identification. Any such treatments must remain compliant with building codes and equipment performance requirements. 2. Redundancy and Resilience Planning Even the best defenses can’t guarantee prevention. Treat drones like any other external disruption and design to limit the blast radius. - Intra-site redundancy. Within a site, build multiple cooling and power subsystems so the facility can continue running if one is damaged. - Inter-site failover. Across sites, maintain tested failover runbooks to quickly and safely shift workloads or traffic to other data centers. - Recovery procedures. Include maintaining and regularly rehearsing incident response and disaster recovery plans that specifically account for drone-related disruptions. 3. Location Strategy and Regulatory Environment Site selection should now explicitly consider drone risks alongside traditional criteria. - Conflict-prone regions. Areas vulnerable to military activity carry elevated risks of military-grade threats and may warrant additional protective measures. - Local sentiment and governance. Jurisdictions with strong support for critical infrastructure protections and effective law enforcement coordination can reduce non-military threats. - Regulatory maturity. Regulatory maturity is increasingly important: consider the availability of U-space/UTM services, prevalence of Remote ID compliance, and responsiveness of aviation and public safety agencies. - Terrain and concealment. Hilly, vegetated sites can limit sightlines and complicate the low-altitude approach path, while still preserving necessary detection coverage. Reduce nearby public vantage points and easy launch locations that have clear sightlines to exposed plant, and ensure property boundaries discourage unauthorized drone operations. Airspace Restrictions and Community Coordination Only national aviation authorities can establish enforceable airspace restrictions. Rather than seeking informal “no-fly zones,” operators should collaborate with authorities to raise awareness of critical infrastructure and improve response coordination. Publish site advisories, update perimeter signage, and engage with drone service providers and UTM platforms to increase geofencing awareness around sensitive areas. Build local relationships so that law enforcement and emergency management teams understand the facility’s risk profile. Conclusion Drones introduce low-cost, high-disruption risks that data center operators must plan for as part of business-as-usual resilience. The strongest posture is layered: harden exposed infrastructure, deploy multi-sensor detection, formalize detection-to-response operations, and design for redundancy and failover. Combine these measures with location awareness and regulatory coordination. The industry has clear evidence that drone disruptions are not hypothetical. By focusing on resilience, operators can reduce both the likelihood and impact of drone-related incidents.

artigo.texto: COMMERCE CITY, Colo. — Commerce City leaders are deciding Monday night if the city should hit pause on data center development. At their regularly scheduled meeting, city council will consider a six-month moratorium on approving data center development plans or zoning applications. See the full story from Alex Dowd in the video below Council communications say the city’s land development code doesn’t address some of the “unique characteristics of data center facilities.” The draft ordinance says data centers can have significant impacts on city infrastructure like power and water supply, neighborhood character and surrounding land use. With growing interest in building these large scale computer system warehouses, city council officials are deciding if they should take a step back and “establish a reasonable period of time during which permit applications, site development plans and amendments, and zoning applications for new or expanded data centers will not be processed or approved.” The ordinance says that during the six-month pause, officials and city staff will take the time to research and potentially develop amendments to existing regulations that specifically address data centers. A survey from Magellan Strategies shows that Colorado residents are overwhelmingly opposed to data centers in their neighborhoods with 86% of surveyed voters opposing a data center near their neighborhood. This isn’t the first time a Colorado city has considered this type of pause. In early August, Aurora City Council voted down a similar six-month moratorium. Instead, Aurora officials opted to create regulations to address community concerns heard during that meeting. Weeks later, the council voted unanimously to ban evaporative cooling systems for new developments. That’s an option for Commerce City officials. While the staff recommendation is to pass the six month ban as written, councilmembers have the option to accept, amend, revisit or reject this ordinance. If accepted, the city won’t be able to approve any data center development plans or applications until March 2027. That timeline can be extended with another council vote. artigo.texto: Democrats try to ride data center backlash to election victory in rural US Midwest Mounting public anxiety about AI, cloud-computing infrastructure has transformed data center construction into a contentious midterm elections issue No company has announced plans for a data center in Defiance, a city of 17,000 people surrounded by soybean fields in northwestern Ohio. But people in the aptly named community are not taking any chances. After learning the county’s economic development group had fielded inquiries from tech companies, residents spent months gathering signatures for a November 3 ballot measure to ban all but the smallest data centers. City officials announced a six-month moratorium on new project approvals. The fight in Defiance is part of a broader political backlash throughout Ohio — and across the nation — where mounting public anxiety about AI and cloud-computing infrastructure has transformed data center construction from an economic success story into a contentious midterm elections issue. Many in Defiance were already concerned about the impacts of AI development on farmland, electricity demand and water consumption. Their misgivings deepened this summer after the release of state tax records showing Ohio had foregone more than $2 billion in sales-tax revenue through data-center incentives in 2024 and 2025, benefiting companies such as Amazon and Meta. Some 71% of Ohioans would now support a temporary ban on new data center construction, according to an August 31 poll from Bowling Green State University. "Most people feel preyed upon by big business," said Becca Rupp, founder of Citizens for Responsible Development - efiance. The groundswell building against data centers during election season has given Democratic candidates a new opening in the rural US Midwest, where they have struggled to compete during Donald Trump's presidency. Ohio is one of a handful of states with competitive races expected to decide control of Congress. Ohio's Republican Governor Mike DeWine has suspended new applications for data center tax exemptions pending legislative reforms, but state lawmakers did not act before summer recess, leaving the future of AI development in Ohio uncertain — and ripe for political attack. Clash over tax incentives Democratic US Representative Marcy Kaptur faces one of the toughest reelection races of her four-decade congressional career, in a newly redrawn district that includes Defiance and other conservative rural areas. She has leaned heavily into data-center messaging, running television ads accusing her Republican opponent Derek Merrin of supporting the unpopular tax incentives. In a statement, Kaptur linked data centers to rising utility costs and wider concerns about corporate influence. "Politicians are letting these companies pass the costs of their enormous energy and utility demands onto Ohio ratepayers, then handing them billions in tax breaks to sweeten the deal," she said. Residential electricity bills in Defiance rose 10% to 15% in June from a year earlier, according to utility FirstEnergy. Merrin did not respond to requests for comment. In a Facebook post last week, he said Kaptur was “blaming me for a tax break for data centers that was enacted BEFORE I was even elected to the Ohio legislature.” The issue has also featured prominently in the state's closely watched US Senate race, pitting Republican incumbent Jon Husted against former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown, who lost his old seat in 2024. With recent polls showing Brown leading, Republican groups have poured $14 million into advertising in Ohio in the past week alone, hoping to boost Husted's chances. Brown has repeatedly criticized his opponent for promoting AI infrastructure development and tax incentives, describing him as "data centers' best friend." “Ohioans, not Jon Husted and his billionaire friends, should get to decide if data centers are built in their community,” Brown’s campaign said in a statement. Husted's campaign rejected the criticism, noting he has sponsored legislation that would require data-center operators to cover the cost of building more electricity generation and transmission. “Sherrod Brown had three decades in Congress to lead on this issue,” campaign spokesperson Amy Natoce said in a statement. “Instead, he did nothing and is suddenly pretending to care in the middle of an election year.” Tax subsidy disclosure galvanizes activists Lyn Cox, a leader of the local advocacy organization Conserve Ohio, said disclosure about the scale of tax subsidies transformed what had been a series of scattered zoning disputes into a statewide political issue. "I think it was a huge turning point," said Cox, who lives in rural Waterville Township, about 40 miles (64 km) from Defiance. She said candidates from both parties have been forced to engage with activists and develop formal policies on data-center development. Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who previously voiced support for attracting tech investment, released an "Ohioans First" data-center proposal that would eliminate local property-tax abatements for data centers, direct revenue toward homeowner rebates and require projects to cover incremental residential electricity costs. His opponent, Democrat Amy Acton, has proposed restricting tax incentives, requiring developers to pay for their own power infrastructure and mandating union labor standards. Both candidates have also called for limiting construction on productive farmland. Cox remains skeptical of campaign promises from both parties. "They're just words," she said. "They both came up with a policy because they're starting to understand this is a sleeper issue." Conserve Ohio is pursuing a state constitutional amendment in 2027 that would ban the construction of data centers using more than 25 megawatts of power, while supporting similar local ballot initiatives across the state. artigo.texto: A new design direction has been presented to improve the performance of all-solid-state batteries, which have a lower risk of fire. The principle by which the rotation and arrangement of anions inside solid electrolytes facilitate the movement of lithium ions has been identified, and is expected to be used to develop solid electrolytes with high ionic conductivity. The Korea Basic Science Institute (KBSI) announced on the 21st that a research team led by Senior Researcher Youngju Lee of the Intelligent Secondary Battery Strategy Research Group has elucidated how anion rotation in next-generation solid electrolyte materials enhances battery performance. The research findings were published on June 26 in the international journal Small. An all-solid-state battery is a type of battery that uses a solid electrolyte instead of a flammable liquid electrolyte. While the risk of fire is lower, lithium ions find it more difficult to move freely within the solid electrolyte. To improve battery performance, it is crucial to increase the speed of ion transport. The research team focused on the anion "borohydride" contained in argyrodite-type solid electrolytes. Argyrodite-type materials are considered promising candidates for next-generation all-solid-state batteries due to their high ionic conductivity and good processability. Borohydride is an anion consisting of four hydrogen atoms bonded to a central boron atom. Within the crystal structure of the solid electrolyte, it can change orientation while rotating in place. Previous studies had shown that incorporating borohydride can increase the ionic conductivity of solid electrolytes, but the precise role of borohydride rotation in lithium-ion transport had not been clearly understood. Using solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy and molecular dynamics simulations, the team found that borohydride rotation and lithium-ion movement repeatedly interlock with each other. When the rotation of borohydride was restricted in the simulations, lithium-ion diffusivity dropped to nearly half. This confirmed that borohydride rotation assists the long-range migration of lithium ions. The position of borohydride also turned out to be important. When borohydride simultaneously occupies two distinct crystallographic sites inside the solid electrolyte, the space through which lithium ions move forms uniformly. As a result, the energy difference required for lithium ions to move between adjacent sites decreases, allowing them to travel smoothly over long distances. This study presents a new direction for all-solid-state battery design, suggesting that not only the composition of the solid electrolyte but also the arrangement and dynamics of internal species must be considered. The results are expected to help efficiently develop high-performance solid electrolytes in which lithium ions move rapidly, reduce trial and error in research, and accelerate the commercialization of all-solid-state batteries with superior safety and performance. Senior Researcher Youngju Lee said, "We have clarified how the rotation of surrounding anions within solid electrolytes facilitates lithium-ion transport," adding, "These findings can serve as a new design criterion for enhancing ionic conductivity in solid electrolytes for all-solid-state batteries." doi.org/10.1002/smll.73722

artigo.texto: From Backup Power to Grid Infrastructure: Why BESS Needs a New Identity India’s need for energy storage stems from the changing demands of its power system. As renewable capacity and electrification rise, the grid must manage power across different hours and locations while ensuring reliability. September 21, 2026. By News Bureau India’s conversation around Battery Energy Storage Systems has remained tied to a familiar image: a battery waiting in the background until the grid fails. That is too limited for the electricity system India is building. The scale of renewable addition makes clear why. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy reported that India added 44.5 GW of renewable capacity in 2025, nearly twice the capacity added in the comparable period a year earlier. Solar and wind are changing the shape of supply; demand does not follow the same pattern. A grid with more variable generation needs assets that can respond, rebalance and dispatch when the system requires them. That is why BESS needs a new identity. Its value lies in the services it delivers to the power system, not simply in the electricity it holds. Backup is One Application, Not the Definition Traditional backup is event-driven. It is called upon after a disruption. Grid-scale storage should be engaged before stress reaches the consumer: absorbing renewable surplus during high-generation hours, releasing power into evening peaks, regulating frequency, supporting voltage where needed and reducing renewable curtailment. Storage can make intermittent generation more schedulable, reduce reliance on costly peaking power and, in constrained areas, defer a portion of network reinforcement. The central point is straightforward: it makes the grid and connected renewable capacity more useful. The Economics Must be Measured Across the System A narrow upfront-cost comparison has kept storage stuck in the backup category. The right comparison is no longer a battery versus a diesel generator alone. It is a battery versus the system costs it can avoid or optimise over its life: curtailed clean generation, peak procurement, diesel use, poor power quality and capacity built for only a few high-demand hours. Storage must be valued as a bundle of services. A project created for arbitrage is different from one designed for ancillary services or congestion relief. The contract must be clear about cycles, dispatch duration, availability, response time and degradation, rather than leave them as an afterthought. Deployment is now real. In a March 2026 Press Release, the Ministry of Power reported 798 MWh of installed BESS capacity in projects above 1 MWh and 35.8 GWh under construction. That gap shows the move from pilots to system-scale assets has begun; delivery must now meet a higher performance standard. Engineering Must Match Infrastructure Responsibility Once a BESS is asked to perform critical grid functions, it cannot be treated as a commoditised container. Indian conditions make that clear. High ambient temperatures, diverse duty cycles, changing load profiles and grid-quality variations test a battery in ways a standard datasheet cannot capture. Cell selection, thermal architecture, protection systems, BMS, EMS, fire safety, site integration and remote diagnostics work as a single system. Long-term performance depends on how it is designed, commissioned and operated. Procurement should look past a low headline tariff and ask for availability guarantees, safety architecture, augmentation planning, service response and data visibility through the life of the asset. Storage projects will earn trust by delivering predictably during peaks, grid events and high-renewable periods. That is an operations standard, not merely a hardware standard. The Grid has to Buy Outcomes, Not Boxes Policy has recognised energy storage as an integral part of the power system, and the market is beginning to follow. The next step is practical. Utilities, distribution companies and renewable developers need procurement structures that identify the service required at a particular location: evening-ramp support, peak shaving, renewable firming, frequency response or resilience. Payments should reflect the availability and quality of that service. This gives technology providers a use case to design around, rather than a generic tender that risks oversizing or underutilising the asset. It can also make projects more bankable, strengthen operational accountability and give financiers a clearer view of performance risk. India’s need for energy storage stems from the changing demands of its power system. As renewable capacity and electrification rise, the grid must manage power across different hours and locations while ensuring reliability. BESS should therefore be treated as flexible, dispatchable infrastructure that strengthens system balance and responsiveness. The question for the sector is no longer, “How many hours of backup can this battery provide?” It is, “Which grid service can it reliably deliver, at which point in the system, and under what operating conditions?” That identity shift will make BESS central to India’s power transition. - Hiren Pravin Shah, Managing Director & CEO, REPLUS Engitech The scale of renewable addition makes clear why. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy reported that India added 44.5 GW of renewable capacity in 2025, nearly twice the capacity added in the comparable period a year earlier. Solar and wind are changing the shape of supply; demand does not follow the same pattern. A grid with more variable generation needs assets that can respond, rebalance and dispatch when the system requires them. That is why BESS needs a new identity. Its value lies in the services it delivers to the power system, not simply in the electricity it holds. Backup is One Application, Not the Definition Traditional backup is event-driven. It is called upon after a disruption. Grid-scale storage should be engaged before stress reaches the con

artigo.texto: Vena Energy’s Tailem Bend BESS 3 in South Australia and EnergyAustralia and Banpu Energy Australia’s Wooreen BESS in Victoria have both entered the Australian Energy Market Operator’s (AEMO) Market Management System (MMS). This is according to Geoff Eldridge of GPE NEMLog, who tracks project data across Australia’s National Electricity Market (NEM). Both units, known in AEMO’s system as TB3B1 and WOORB1 respectively, entered the MMS on 15 September 2026. Eldridge noted that MMS registration is not the same as full commercial operation but marks a step that allows a unit to move into testing and commissioning ahead of normal market operation. Tailem Bend BESS 3 is registered with an operating maximum of 204MW, a registered capacity of 263MW, and 408MWh of storage, giving it a two-hour storage duration and a ramp rate of 82MW per minute. In July 2025, EnergyAustralia sold a 50% share in the project to Thailand-based Banpu Public Company, trading in Australia as Banpu Energy Australia, in a deal worth in the region of AU$700 million (US$490 million). artigo.texto: Existing assets can provide crucial benchmarks for the vital task of correctly sizing a battery storage system and other crucial design decisions, writes Ashutosh Vats, head of BESS business development at 3E. Battery storage projects can start losing revenue as soon as they begin operating. The challenge is to learn from what happens in real-world operations and to use that information to improve the assumptions behind the next project. This article looks at why battery sizing assumptions can have a bigger impact on project economics than many developers realise, and how using real operational data alongside financial models can lead to more realistic and reliable investment cases and ultimately change what it means for a battery project to be ‘bankable.’ Battery storage is now the fastest-growing power technology in the world. The International Energy Agency (IEA) reports 108GW of new capacity deployed in 2025, representing a 40% jump from 2024 and 11 times the installed base just four years earlier. Here comes the uncomfortable part for developers and IPP working on their first BESS projects: that financial model was built on assumptions and every one of them begins to drift the day the asset goes live. Consider how a typical battery sizing study works. To identify the best configuration, the model simulates how the battery would operate over several years, using detailed forecasts of electricity prices and renewable generation. It effectively assumes that the future is known perfectly. This is not a weakness of the approach. The aim is to establish a theoretical benchmark: the maximum revenue a battery could generate if it had perfect information and could always make the right decision. A financial model that assumes, say, 2% annual capacity fade but meets 4% in the field will overstate revenue every single year, compounding across the debt term. The gap can be the difference between a project that services its debt and one that does not. Yet most models still rely on manufacturer curves, and most operational platforms simply pass through the state of health (SoH) reported by the on-site battery management system (BMS), which is often supplied by the same OEM that issued the warranty in the first place. Therefore, the assumptions that determine whether a BESS project is financeable are often the ones that are hardest to assess from a datasheet. The most reliable evidence comes from batteries that are already operating in the market. This is where the feedback loop becomes important. It needs to be based on independent, physics-based measurements rather than on information provided by equipment suppliers. An independent digital twin can track how connected batteries actually perform over time. Instead of relying only on specifications, it can show how a battery is really behaving in the market: how its state of health changes, how different degradation mechanisms affect performance, how much revenue it captures, and how available it is during the periods when electricity prices are highest. This is the principle behind SynaptiQ, 3E’s asset performance platform: independently measure how batteries actually perform across an operating fleet and use that evidence to improve the models used for future projects. The same operational data can then feed back into 3E’s BESS sizing tool. This means that degradation assumptions are no longer based solely on manufacturer specifications. They can be informed by how batteries using the same chemistry have actually aged under comparable operating conditions, duty cycles and climates. Every new BESS project can ‘learn’ from what came before it At the development stage, investors can use the sizing tool to test different battery sizes and market strategies and assess how they would perform under different scenarios. The built-in optimisation process can then identify configurations that offer the best balance between technical performance and financial returns. In Spain, for example, where co-location development of PV plants and/or wind farms with battery storage is thriving, understanding how the different technologies will generate electricity in order to optimise revenue stacking through the right BESS size requires an optimisation tool capable of integrating numerous variables, go-to-market strategies and real simulation of how the different assets will operate through time. Over the last 2 years, simulations have increasingly shown a need for 4-hour batteries instead of 2-hour batteries to obtain optimal profitability and NPV. For investors and lenders, this changes the way we should think about bankability. A project will always depend on assumptions about future prices, degradation, availability and revenues. But those assumptions become more robust when they are continuously tested against the performance of real operating assets. The value of closing this loop is simple: every new BESS project can learn from the batteries that came before it. Operational data improves the models, better models lead to better sizing decisions, and those decisions provide investors and lenders with a more realistic view of the project’s potential performance. The BESS market is expanding rapidly, and large amounts of capital are being committed to new projects. artigo.texto: Flow Power has broken ground on its 100MW/223MWh Bennetts Creek battery energy storage system (BESS) in Victoria, marking construction start on the renewable energy generator and retailer’s first large-scale standalone battery project. Bennetts Creek is located near Hazelwood North in Victoria’s Latrobe Valley, a region historically associated with coal mining and coal-fired power generation in the state. Flow Power reached financial close on the project in December 2025, with financing provided by banks Westpac and SMBC Australia. The company did not disclose the terms of that financing, but said its majority shareholder, Canadian pension trust OPSEU Pension Plan Trust Fund (OPTrust), supported the transaction. The project is expected to be completed in 2028. Flow Power has also engaged Zenviron, a joint venture between engineering group Monadelphous and renewable energy developer ZEM Energy, as balance-of-plant contractor for Bennetts Creek. Anza Power, backed by global infrastructure investor I Squared Capital, signed a tolling agreement with Amazon Australia for the 50MW/200MWh Bairnsdale BESS in East Gippsland. That was described as Amazon’s first standalone battery storage tolling deal in the Asia-Pacific region and the first agreement of its kind in Australia for a non-energy business contracting a standalone battery storage system directly. Bennetts Creek differs from both models. Flow Power is financing and developing the project independently through bank debt and shareholder support, rather than through a state equity stake or via a corporate offtake agreement, adding a third financing pathway to the cluster of battery storage projects concentrated around the Latrobe Valley as the region’s coal-fired generation continues to retire. The firms have committed to 16GWh of capacity in 2027, with 190GWh reserved for 2028-2031, Eve Energy announced in a filing on the Shenzen stock exchange last week (18 September). China-based Eve Energy said it could not yet estimate the boost to its finances that the deal would bring, but its share price saw a sharp 6-7% jump when it made the announcement. Eve added that framework agreement was subject to change, including from industry policies or market conditions which could prevent the co-operation proceeding as expected. artigo.texto: A US battery storage pilot sponsored by tech giant Google has demonstrated how batteries can capture surplus renewable energy and deliver it during hours with greater fossil generation. Announced 17 September, the demonstration created what the project partners describe as the first environmental revenue stream for battery energy storage system (BESS) assets. The three-month pilot, conducted by Quintrace, part of global sustainable energy infrastructure investor Quinbrook Infrastructure Partners, developer esVolta and renewable energy procurement advisor LevelTen Energy, used hourly, time-stamped Granular Certificates (GCs) to allocate solar energy to grid-connected BESS and shift it to hours when Google’s energy consumption exceeded its renewable supply. esVolta contributed its 240MW/480MWh Anole project and 100MW/200MWh Burksol project to the pilot. Quintrace provided the software platform used to implement verification, whilst LevelTen managed the registry accounts to prevent double-counting and provided the transaction framework for the storage-shift agreements. However, the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi), a corporate climate action organisation, is beginning to require hourly reporting for large energy users, and the GHG (greenhouse gases) Protocol is currently evaluating how to address this issue. The pilot was designed to demonstrate both a commercial pathway that gives BESS operators a carbon-based revenue stream and a tracking pathway that accurately accounts for and retires the hourly certificates behind it. Google contracted for defined daily charging and discharging windows based on forecasted gaps in carbon-free energy generation, and the operators dispatched their batteries in line with those guidelines. Contract structure maintains operator control The agreements had a distinctive structure: Google contracted with the battery operators to time-shift environmental attributes it already owned, without tolling the batteries or assuming any merchant or dispatch risk. This structure left the operator in full control of their assets, including pre-defined flexibility to pursue energy price signals and to respond to grid emergencies. Over the pilot period, the batteries charged with renewable energy during the defined mid-day charging window and discharged during the defined evening window, with each hour verified by Quintrace against the EnergyTag standard. Across the three-month pilot, the batteries charged and discharged a total of 9.2GWh during the respective windows. Quintrace’s software follows renewable energy from the moment it charges a battery to the moment it is sent back to the grid. The company claimed its dynamic loss calculations ensure the clean energy claimed is only the clean energy actually delivered. The software can also apply different accounting approaches to fit each agreement structure between battery operator and buyer. Earlier this month, Google announced with renewables developer-operator MN8 Energy, zinc hybrid cathode battery and storage system maker Eos Energy Enterprises, that the companies would be backing the Mammoth Solar project in Kanawha County, West Virginia. The project combines 86MW of solar, 10MW/100MWh of Eos’ Z3 zinc-based long-duration energy storage (LDES) solution, and a 70MW/280MWh lithium-ion (Li-ion) BESS. The latest announcement adds to a growing number of Google-backed pilots and investments into BESS and LDES. If you put it behind the meter and you are using it solely for a specific customer, you’re losing some of the functionality of the asset.” NeoVolta secures $53 million capacity reservation for Ontario AI data centre projects In other news, San Diego-based home battery storage company NeoVolta has announced that its majority-owned subsidiary, NeoVolta Power, has entered into a binding capacity reservation agreement with Infinite Grid Capital (IGC) to provide BESS equipment for Northern Ontario Edge artificial intelligence data centre projects for calendar year 2027. Announced 17 September, the approximately US$53 million binding commitment represents the first major commercial commitment under NeoVolta Power’s previously announced utility-scale framework with IGC, which contemplates approximately 1.1GWh of potential BESS deployments and approximately US$200 million of potential supply across multiple markets. The capacity reservation agreement is intended to support the Northern Ontario Edge AI data centre project and represents an initial commercial step within NeoVolta’s broader relationship with IGC. NeoVolta hosted a grand-opening ceremony for its NeoVolta Power facility in Pendergrass, Georgia, on 17 September. The 210,600-square-foot facility is a purpose-built domestic BESS manufacturing platform designed to assemble commercial, industrial and utility-scale energy storage products. The company’s initial Pendergrass production line is advancing through commissioning and site acceptance testing, with the production ramp remaining on track for Q4 of 2026. artigo.texto: Vishal Mittal, founder and CEO of Delectrik makes the case for flow batteries to meet India’s long-duration needs in an exclusive ESN Premium interview. Vishal Mittal founded Delectrik in 2016, drawing on a background in chemical engineering and 25 years of experience in fuel cells and flow batteries to pursue the goal of creating an effective vanadium redox flow battery (VRFB) for renewable energy storage. The startup found it hard to do business in the price-conscious Indian market. So, the flow battery manufacturer went further afield and instead made its first customer deployments overseas, in Australia. Delectrik—the name is a portmanteau of “decentralised electric network”—began with kilowatt-hour scale batteries. Repeat customer orders saw the systems scale up to 20-foot, then 40-foot and into the megawatt-hours. Yet the company, completely self-funded, was still bootstrapped: “surviving based on margins on the products we were selling,” Mittal says. The answer was, again, about scale: this time, to pursue opportunities that brought the company’s focus back to India. Having built a low-cost battery technology, the next logical step was to close a first utility-scale contract. “That’s when we started focusing on the Indian market, because as an Indian company, directly going from small megawatt-hour to utility-scale contracts overseas is very difficult,” Mittal says. India also has an energy sector in which state-owned or partially state-owned companies supply about half of the grid’s electricity. It was a subsidiary of one of these, NTPC, that awarded Delectrik an initial 600kW/3,000kWh flow battery pilot in June 2024. NTPC had always sought alternative technologies to lithium-ion (Li-ion) batteries and was “quite excited” to see Delectrik as an Indian company exporting advanced energy storage technology overseas, Mittal claims. The 3MWh, 5-hour duration system has now been in successful operation for close to a year at NTPC’s R&D centre, NTPC Energy Technology Research Alliance (NETRA) in Uttar Pradesh. “NTPC were quite excited in terms of what we were doing as an Indian company with all these exports,” leading to that initial contract, Mittal says. NTPC’s 100MWh project This paved the way for the later award of a milestone project for India’s non-lithium energy storage sector. In February 2026, NTPC subsidiary NTPC Renewable Energy invited bids to deploy a 100MWh VRFB long-duration energy storage (LDES) system at Khavda renewable energy park in Gujarat. Delectrik was selected to provide the system in July, after making a joint bid with infrastructure solutions provider Bondada Engineering. The project must be designed as a 16.7MW VRFB with 100MWh capacity (~5.9-hour duration) and will be built at the 30GW Khavda complex, which features a mix of renewable energy and storage technologies. Due to the size of the projects up for tender, Delectrik did not satisfy some of the commercial requirements for bidders, such as minimum company turnover in the tens of millions of dollars. So, the company paired with EPC Bondada, which carried out the bidding, but the project will effectively then be handed back to Delectrik as the OEM-plus-EPC. The flow battery player is now bidding on several projects overseas, and Mittal hints at interest in tenders in Australia, Japan, South Africa and the ASEAN region. The CEO won’t share details about the flow battery’s costs but argues that the NTPC tender win is evidence that Delectrik has developed a competitive technology. “You could argue ‘these are the benefits of the technology,’ but at the end of the day, when you actually talk to utilities, they can pay some premium, but they’ll not pay a very significant premium over where lithium is today, so I think that’s where our advantage comes in, in terms of where we are with respect to our cost points,” the CEO says. “India is a fairly price-sensitive market, and if we have been able to close such large projects with actual utilities—these are not Amazon or Google’s data centres—these are power utilities, which look at every cent and penny.” This is why, Mittal says, Delectrik is “very bullish” that the company could “get to a gigawatt-hour-scale order book in the next 12 months.” Why would the market choose flow batteries? Nonetheless, utilities are not trialling flow batteries for purely economic reasons. The drivers are manifold: decoupling from China-dominated lithium battery supply chains, the thermal safety advantage and perhaps most of all, the potential for low-cost, long-duration energy storage (LDES) at scale are among them. “The market is now demanding longer duration storage. Even in India, where it started with 2-hour, 4-hour, now that the penetration of renewable energy is increasing, the market really needs these 6-hours+ of storage,” Mittal says, and the utilities and power generators are typically the ones willing to take the forward bet on technology. India is pursuing goals of 500GW new non-fossil fuel energy generation by 2030 and net zero emissions by 2070. The Central Electricity Authority (CEA) has modelled a need for ~74GW/411GWh of energy storage in India by 2031-2032. Crucially, this includes two technology types: 47GW/236GWh of battery storage and 27GW/175GWh of pumped hydro energy storage (PHES). artigo.texto: The US energy storage industry is targeting 225GW/1TWh of storage deployments by the end of 2032, according to an analysis published by the Energy Storage Coalition (ESC). Released this month (September), the report, titled The Terawatt-Hour Opportunity, said that battery energy storage systems (BESS) offer the speed to power, reliability and flexibility to address America’s energy demand challenge whilst fortifying energy security, provided policy and regulatory frameworks enable the industry to scale at the pace the US power system demands. The US energy storage industry has undergone one of the fastest expansions of any part of the American power sector. In just a few years, energy storage has moved from an emerging technology to what the ESC describes as a foundational backbone of the American power grid. Energy storage capacity has grown from 1.5GW at the end of 2020 to 52GW by mid-2026, with the industry now targeting 225GW by the end of 2032.
