artigo.texto: This story was reported and written by our media partner the Virginia Mercury. Gov. Abigail Spanberger on Friday unveiled a package of legislative proposals to rein in the data center industry in Virginia, with goals to tighten environmental regulations, increase cost allocation for the industry, and make the proposal process more transparent by barring non-disclosure agreements between localities and data center developers. The plan does not include a moratorium on data center development while the details of the plan are refined, a step several environmental and advocacy groups and citizens have demanded in recent weeks. Dubbed the “Data Center Accountability Framework,” Spanberger’s plan outlines five pillars as key priorities: transparency, environmental protections, lowering energy costs, promoting clean energy, and focusing on local workers. “The Framework is a thorough plan to end data center secrecy, protect our environment, lower energy costs for families, bolster our clean energy economy, and make sure Virginia workers have the protections and assurances they deserve,” Spanberger said in a press conference to announce the plan at the Virginia State Capitol. Spanberger also signed Executive Order 22, which will kick-start her plans for clamping down on the industry ahead of the next legislative session that will begin in January 2027. Transparency Perhaps the most concrete of the directives is a measure to ban nondisclosure agreements between data centers and executive branch agencies, departments, state boards and commissions. It also bars these agencies from requiring such agreements for data center projects. The order does not impact the use of nondisclosure agreements by localities, but the governor said she plans to work with the General Assembly to pass a law banning the agreements at the local level. In the framework package, the governor also proposes eliminating by-right local approvals of data centers that use more than 25 megawatts of power. Many counties statewide have taken steps towards requiring conditional use permits,which require public hearings and a vote of approval from local leaders. Additionally, the governor wants to remove data centers from Virginia’s fast-track permittingprocess that allows permit approvals for the projects to speed up when they are proposed in “business ready” locations. The fast-track process is a remnant of Gov. GlennYoungkin’s administration, which encouraged and supported the rapid build out of the state’s data center industry as a means to boost Virginia’s business reputation. Environmental protections The framework directs lawmakers to develop policies to create standards for energy efficiency, water use and land impacts. Budget language that passed the General Assembly in June directed the Department of Environmental Quality to identify “water scarcity areas,” data centers’ water use for cooling could put drinking water availability at risk. Data centers located in those areas, mainly east of Interstate-95, will have to reduce their water use. The framework also outlines a plan to expedite noise regulations that were also in the budget language, but does not state when those regulations will be put into place. Currently, DEQ has until 2029 to research the lowest possible sound levels data centers could operate on and make that the standard across the board. Lower energy costs Spanberger’s new data center plan requires utilities to allocate more of the energy infrastructure costs largely spurred by data centers onto the industry. Dominion Energy has already taken action on this front, after the utility created a new rate class, GS5, which mostly includes data centers and large manufacturers. The State Corporation Commission approved the new rate class last November. Like the recommendations in the framework from the governor, the G5 rate classincludes 14-year contracts, as well as specific cost allocations for energy generation, distribution, and transmission costs. The SCC also recently directed Dominion to create a new tariff to directly assign the cost of high-voltage transmission lines that are only necessary due to data centers to those customers. Spanberger supported the tariff, which is reflected in her framework. Tech giant Microsoft has already put the State Supreme Court on notice that it could appeal that order. Microsoft representatives said in an email last week that the company hopes “any rates ultimately put in place are transparent, fair, and reflect the costs each customer creates.” But filing notice of appeal, they continued, “Microsoft preserves its ability to challenge any implementation that does not meet these expectations.” Elevating clean energy, hiring Virginia workers Another component of Spanberger’s plan looks to limit the amount of power data centers can produce on-site through natural gas generators and other “behind the meter” methods that don’t draw from the electric grid. The plan also proposes making it easier for data centers to bring clean energy options on-site by reforming utility charges for clean energy investments. PJM, the regional grid operator for 13 states including Virginia, recently proposed a new rule to direct data centers to pay for their power generation or cover their energy needs by backstop power purchases. This would help bring more power on the grid when it’s strained on very hot and cold days. Several recent proposals by data centers in the commonwealth show the industry’s growing interest in building its own gas turbines to power data facilities. That method skirts around the Virginia Clean Economy Act, which requires the retirement of carbon emitting power sources by utility companies by 2050. The framework prioritizes hiring local workers to build data centers and using local businesses for procurement and contractors. artigo.texto: Data centers dos EUA garantem à Mitsubishi pedidos firmes de turbina a gás até 2030 Atualizado A Mitsubishi Heavy Industries prevê que a demanda global por turbinas a gás permanecerá forte no próximo ano, com um aumento nos negócios nos Estados Unidos abastecendo a carteira de pedidos da empresa, segundo o chefe das operações norte-americanas em declaração ao “Nikkei Asia”. "Observando o ritmo de pedidos para o período de janeiro a junho de 2026, espera-se que a demanda fique no mesmo nível do ano passado ou até mais alta, ultrapassando novamente a marca de 100 gigawatts este ano", disse na segunda-feira Takao Tsukui, presidente do conselho e executivo-chefe (CEO) da Mitsubishi Heavy Industries America. Os Estados Unidos estão impulsionando grande parte dessa demanda devido à expansão de data centers voltados para a inteligência artificial (IA). A necessidade de geradores de energia de carga de base, capazes de operar de forma estável 24 horas por dia, está aumentando. A demanda global por turbinas a gás em 2025 atingiu o nível mais alto desde 2000, segundo a Mitsubishi Heavy. A empresa japonesa é uma das três maiores fabricantes mundiais de turbinas a gás para geração de energia, ao lado de suas concorrentes GE Vernova e Siemens Energy. O principal produto da Mitsubishi Heavy é a turbina de grande porte e alta eficiência da série J, utilizada em usinas de ciclo combinado a gás (GTCC). Esperava-se, anteriormente, que as usinas termelétricas se tornassem um negócio em declínio devido à transição global para a redução das emissões de carbono. No entanto, a disseminação da IA impulsionou uma maior demanda por eletricidade. Os pedidos de turbinas a gás estão se acumulando na Mitsubishi Heavy. "A carteira de pedidos atual é excepcionalmente grande e está em um nível recorde", disse Tsukui. "Em particular, o cronograma para produtos com entrega prevista para o período de 2029-2030 está bastante apertado." Os preços contratuais das turbinas a gás da Mitsubishi Heavy também subiram 20% em relação ao mesmo período do ano anterior. "Mudanças nos custos de mão de obra e nos preços das matérias-primas forçaram elevações de preços, e o impacto das cadeias de suprimentos também é significativo", afirmou Tsukui. A alta nas taxas de juros também foi citada como um fator relevante. Principais concorrentes também relatam um cenário de forte demanda por turbinas a gás. Os pedidos de turbinas de pequeno e médio porte "já cobrem um horizonte de cerca de cinco anos", disse recentemente Yoshinori Kanehana, presidente do conselho da Kawasaki Heavy Industries, ao “Nikkei Asia”, no estado norte-americano de Indiana. A forte demanda gerada por data centers e pela energia a hidrogênio aumentou as consultas de novos clientes, fazendo com que a Kawasaki Heavy tenha dificuldades em acompanhar o ritmo dos pedidos, disse Kanehana. As fabricantes estão acelerando investimentos de capital para atender à demanda. A Mitsubishi Heavy Industries planeja dobrar sua capacidade de produção de grandes turbinas a gás até o ano fiscal de 2030, em comparação com o ano fiscal de 2024. A empresa investirá mais de 100 bilhões de ienes (US$ 635 milhões) em polos de produção no Japão e nos Estados Unidos. Espera-se que a demanda de energia dos data centers dos Estados Unidos mais do que dobre, chegando a 66 GW no próximo ano — um aumento em relação aos 31 GW previstos para 2025 —, segundo estimativas do Goldman Sachs. No entanto, a oposição à construção de data centers está ganhando força em alguns estados, e essas instalações tornaram-se um tema relevante nas eleições de meio de mandato dos Estados Unidos. Revisões e atrasos nos cronogramas de construção também estão se tornando frequentes. "É necessária a aceitação da sociedade para que as pessoas compreendam o impacto positivo que a IA terá em suas vidas", disse Tsukui. Algumas empresas de desenvolvimento de IA estão defendendo regulamentações e medidas de segurança mais rigorosas. "Todas as empresas estão plenamente cientes de que a IA deve ser um produto seguro", afirmou Tsukui, acrescentando que "o setor está em crescimento e não há preocupações quanto a investimentos em um futuro próximo". 22/09/2026 23:50:22

artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no Data centers trocam água por químicos permanentes para resfriar I.A Publicado 21/09/2026 • 06:00 | Atualizado há 6 horas KEY POINTS Foto: pexels A expansão da inteligência artificial aumenta a demanda por data centers e, com ela, a necessidade de sistemas para controlar o calor gerado pelos equipamentos. Nesse processo, os PFAS, conhecidos como “químicos eternos”, ganham espaço em tecnologias de refrigeração. Um relatório da organização ChemSec aponta que grandes produtores mundiais de PFAS estão ampliando a capacidade de produção diante da demanda relacionada à infraestrutura de inteligência artificial. Além disso, entre as empresas citadas estão a japonesa Daikin, a francesa Arkema e a americana Chemours. Leia também: Anthropic alerta para sistemas de inteligência artificial capazes de desenvolver novos modelos IA Segundo a Fortune, a demanda está concentrada principalmente em três áreas: refrigeração de data centers, fabricação de semicondutores e produção de materiais para baterias de íon-lítio. Os equipamentos utilizados para processamento de I.A geram grandes quantidades de calor. Dessa forma, para controlar a temperatura, sistemas mais recentes podem utilizar substâncias químicas fluoradas que incluem PFAS, em vez de água. A alternativa aparece enquanto o consumo de água se tornou uma das preocupações relacionadas à expansão dos data centers. Porém, os PFAS também geram questionamentos por sua resistência à degradação. As fortes ligações químicas dessas substâncias dificultam sua decomposição no ambiente. Essa característica favorece aplicações industriais, incluindo sistemas de refrigeração, fabricação de semicondutores e equipamentos industriais. Dados da Pesquisa Nacional de Saúde e Nutrição dos Estados Unidos, citados pela Fortune, encontraram PFAS no sangue de 97% dos americanos. O avanço da I.A também impulsiona a construção de data centers. Um estudo de 2026 da BOMA apontou que essas instalações representaram quase 46% da construção privada nos Estados Unidos em 2025. Uma década antes, a participação era inferior a 5%. Segundo dados da Statista citados pela Fortune, os gastos com construção de data centers passaram de US$ 1,8 bilhão (cerca de R$ 9,25 bilhões) em 2014 para US$ 41,1 bilhões (R$ 211,34 bilhões) em 2025. A ChemSec afirma que a Chemours produz ou utiliza mais substâncias PFAS do que qualquer outra empresa analisada pela organização. A companhia também desenvolve produtos para refrigeração de data centers e amplia a produção de refrigerantes à base de PFAS. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC Leia também: Startup lança coleira com I.A que promete traduzir latidos e miados A organização estima que entre metade e dois terços da receita de US$ 5,8 bilhões (R$ 29,82 bilhões) da Chemours venham da produção de PFAS. A Daikin, segundo o relatório, pretende triplicar sua capacidade de produção em resposta à demanda do setor de semicondutores. A Arkema também iniciou uma expansão na América do Norte e na Ásia. Em julho, 17 organizações ambientais enviaram uma carta à Agência de Proteção Ambiental dos Estados Unidos (EPA) contra o pedido da Chemours para acelerar a aprovação do Opteon 2P50, composto PFAS destinado a sistemas de refrigeração de data centers. Os grupos afirmaram que a empresa teria subestimado possíveis riscos à saúde e ao clima e questionaram as evidências toxicológicas disponíveis. Segundo a carta, data centers de hiperescala podem armazenar dezenas de milhares de litros de fluido dielétrico em centenas de tanques. A Chemours contestou as preocupações. Segundo a empresa, o sistema funciona em circuito fechado e libera pouca quantidade de gás durante a operação. A companhia também lançou novos refrigerantes em agosto. Leia também: Teck Check: IA já virou obrigação, mas diferencial está nos dados e na estratégia, diz CEO da HSM Em janeiro, 192 cidadãos franceses e quatro organizações ambientais entraram com uma ação contra Arkema e Daikin por alegações de poluição relacionada a PFAS. A Arkema afirmou que se defenderá das acusações, enquanto a Daikin declarou que acelerou investimentos desde 2022 para controlar melhor suas emissões. Segundo uma análise da ChemSec de 2023, os maiores fabricantes de PFAS tiveram cerca de US$ 4 bilhões (R$ 20,57 bilhões) em lucros em 2022, enquanto os custos sociais associados às substâncias foram estimados em US$ 17,5 trilhões (R$ 89,98 trilhões) por ano. Assim, a expansão da I.A cria uma demanda adicional por sistemas de refrigeração capazes de lidar com o calor dos equipamentos. artigo.texto: Os data centers ganharam espaço nos planos de governo dos principais candidatos à Presidência. Lula, Flávio Bolsonaro, Ronaldo Caiado, Romeu Zema e Renan Santos defendem, com diferentes propostas, a expansão da infraestrutura necessária para desenvolver e operar sistemas de inteligência artificial. A ideia é ampliar a capacidade computacional do país. Mas há diferenças sobre o papel do Estado, os incentivos fiscais, a presença de empresas estrangeiras e as exigências ambientais. Especialistas ouvidos pela BBC ressaltam que mais servidores não significam, automaticamente, soberania digital. O que está nos planos Lula relaciona os data centers à soberania digital. Seu programa prevê infraestrutura computacional nacional, serviços de nuvem e supercomputadores desenvolvidos ou operados por instituições brasileiras. Também estabelece exigências relacionadas à eficiência energética, fontes renováveis, impactos sobre os sistemas elétrico e hídrico e conteúdo local. Caiado propõe incentivos tributários condicionados a exigências ambientais, tecnológicas e sociais. Flávio Bolsonaro e Zema apostam na atração de investimentos privados, com ênfase em energia barata e confiável e em regras capazes de estimular a instalação dessas estruturas. Renan Santos defende incentivos e zonas econômicas especiais para inteligência artificial. Augusto Cury trata a IA como infraestrutura estratégica de Estado, mas não apresenta uma proposta específica para data centers. Entre as propostas aparecem: - incentivos tributários para atrair empresas; - exigências de energia renovável e eficiência; - transferência de tecnologia; - zonas especiais para inteligência artificial; - contrapartidas sociais e ambientais. Mais servidores não garantem soberania Para Luca Belli, professor da Fundação Getulio Vargas, a instalação dessas estruturas não garante, por si só, autonomia tecnológica. “Você pode ser um quintal para data centers de outros, que simplesmente vão absorver os seus recursos naturais e energéticos”, afirma. Na avaliação do especialista, os projetos deveriam envolver universidades, laboratórios, startups e governos locais. A intenção seria formar profissionais e estimular o desenvolvimento de tecnologia brasileira. Belli também chama atenção para a dependência de fornecedores estrangeiros. Segundo ele, a computação em nuvem é dominada por um pequeno grupo de empresas americanas, enquanto a produção de chips avançados também está concentrada em poucos fabricantes. O custo de energia, água e infraestrutura Os servidores operam continuamente e consomem muita energia. A refrigeração das máquinas pode exigir água, e grandes instalações podem demandar novas estruturas de transmissão e distribuição elétrica. Leia mais: - Redata: Lula sanciona incentivo para criar mega data centers no Brasil - Xixi pode ajudar a resfriar data centers? A resposta é mais curiosa do que parece - Data center de IA ameaça desregular clima na Amazônia O Idec defende regras para determinar onde esses empreendimentos podem ser instalados, quais impactos precisam ser estudados e quem deve pagar pelos custos adicionais. No complexo da Scala no Rio Grande do Sul, organizações questionam aspectos do licenciamento ambiental e do fornecimento de energia. Incentivo fiscal já está em discussão A expansão dos data centers não depende apenas das promessas dos candidatos. Uma política para atrair esses empreendimentos já avançou no Congresso. No início de setembro, o Senado aprovou o Redata, projeto que cria um regime especial de tributação para empresas do setor. A proposta prevê a suspensão de impostos sobre importação, PIS/Cofins e IPI. Em contrapartida, as empresas precisam cumprir requisitos relacionados ao uso de energia renovável ou de baixa emissão, sustentabilidade e eficiência hídrica. O governo estima uma isenção de R$ 5,2 bilhões em 2026. O incentivo coloca em prática parte da discussão presente nos planos de governo, mas também evidencia uma questão central da reportagem: quais benefícios o Brasil terá em troca de abrir mão de receitas e oferecer sua infraestrutura para grandes operações de computação? Essa preocupação se conecta à própria disputa internacional em torno da inteligência artificial. Em entrevista à Folha de S.Paulo, a ministra da Ciência, Tecnologia e Inovação, Luciana Santos, afirmou: “Os Estados Unidos ameaçam cessar o fornecimento a quem fizer negócios nessas áreas mais críticas com a China.” O Brasil tenta manter relações com diferentes parceiros tecnológicos, enquanto busca ampliar sua capacidade computacional. Nesse cenário, a discussão sobre data centers vai além da quantidade de estruturas que o país conseguirá atrair. Envolve também a tecnologia que poderá ser desenvolvida aqui, os benefícios econômicos gerados pelos projetos e os custos de energia, água e infraestrutura que ficarão no país. Valdir Antonelli é jornalista com especialização em marketing digital e consumo. Bruno Capozzi é jornalista, mestre em Ciências Sociais e editor executivo do OD.

artigo.texto: Lockton, the world's largest privately held independent insurance brokerage, today announced the availability of its Builders Risk & Property Program, an insurer partner program designed to help data center owners, developers, operators and investors navigate the transition from construction to operations with speed and certainty. Developed by Lockton's Data Centers & Digital Infrastructure Practice (opens a new window), the Builders Risk & Property Program is one component of Lockton's broader advisory approach to data center risk. The industry-leading solution is designed specifically for the complexities of modern data center development, with a curated coverage structure that addresses the sequencing and operational challenges inherent in large, multiphase projects while providing greater coverage certainty from construction through operations. Lockton’s new program is supported by more than $6 billion in builders risk capacity and $7.5 billion in operational property capacity, enabling Lockton to more quickly and efficiently support some of the industry's largest hyperscale, colocation, enterprise, and digital infrastructure projects. Unlike traditional construction projects, data centers often become operational in stages while portions of the facility remain under construction. This creates the potential for coverage gaps and administrative complexity during project transitions. "Lockton's Builders Risk & Property Program is another tool that helps us create tailored solutions at the right tempo for our clients," said James Nelson, U.S. Practice Leader for Data Centers and Digital Infrastructure at Lockton. "Every data center project is different, and our role is to guide clients through evolving risks across the asset lifecycle with strategies informed by their development plans, operational goals, and long-term growth objectives." Supported by Lockton's Data Centers & Digital Infrastructure (DCDI) Practice, the program can serve as one element of a broader risk strategy. The client’s Lockton serve represent 36GW+ of the current DCDI market. Through early engagement, Lockton advisors work alongside clients to evaluate project-specific risks, optimize risk transfer, align coverage with lender requirements, and support a seamless handoff from construction to operations. The result is a ready-to-deploy, fully customizable solution built for the full data center lifecycle. Connect (opens a new window) with a member of Lockton’s Data Centers & Digital Infrastructure Practice to learn more.

artigo.texto: Regional Arts and Culture: Roswell Symphony Orchestra Opens Season With America 250, Featuring Gershwin’s “Porgy and Bess” ROSWELL, NM — The Roswell Symphony Orchestra is back from summer break and preparing a tribute to the country’s 250th anniversary to launch its latest musical season. On Sept. 26, the RSO will present America 250, a concert program honoring the signing of the Declaration of Independence with patriotic pieces from various eras. Audiences can look forward to hearing compositions by Aaron Copland, George Gershwin, Leroy Anderson and John Philip Sousa, plus a medley of U.S. military branch songs and an invitation to sing along with the symphony to an arrangement of “America, the Beautiful.” The Gershwin portion of the program features selections from “Porgy and Bess,” which the composer called a “folk opera” when it premiered in 1935. The work blended classical composition with jazz, blues and spirituals in a way that was new at the time, and many of its melodies became standards in their own right, including “Summertime,” “I Got Plenty o’ Nuttin’,” “It Ain’t Necessarily So” and “Bess, You Is My Woman Now.” Set in Charleston, South Carolina’s fictional Catfish Row, the opera follows love, hardship and hope in a tight-knit community, with a score that ranges from tender lullabies to joyful, soaring moments. RSO Music Director Dr. John Farrer described the anniversary as a once-in-a-lifetime milestone, calling the concert “our chance to celebrate this very special occasion.” He said the program is made up of enjoyable, beautiful, well-composed and accessible music, and that he and the orchestra will be having a good time as well. The concert begins at 7 p.m., a new start time for the orchestra. It will be held at Pearson Auditorium, 101 W. College Blvd., on the New Mexico Military Institute campus. Tickets are available at roswellsymphony.org, by calling 575-623-5882 or at the door, and range from $20 to $35. Students attend all symphony concerts free of charge. The rest of the season After the season opener, the RSO has three more concerts on the calendar: • Christmas Classics — Sunday, Dec. 13, 2026, at 2:30 p.m., a holiday matinee.• Classical and Romantic — Saturday, March 6, 2027, at 7 p.m., with guest violin soloist Nathan Meltzer featured on the Mozart Violin Concerto.• Rhapsody in Blue — Saturday, April 24, 2027, at 7 p.m., featuring Gershwin’s “Rhapsody in Blue” with returning guest piano soloist Evren Ozel. “I think the rest of the season will be absolutely terrific,” Farrer says. About the RSO The orchestra traces its roots to the basement of the First Methodist Church, where it first gathered on July 28, 1959. That original group was made up of lawyers, accountants, teachers, florists, housewives and geologists — amateurs determined to give the region a professional-sounding orchestra. Farrer took the podium for the 1972 season, following William Kirschke, Thomas Lewis and founding director Glenn Cunningham. He is a recipient of the Governor’s Award for Excellence and Achievement. Today the orchestra’s professional musicians travel from cities within a 200-mile radius of Roswell, including Lubbock, Amarillo, Santa Fe, Albuquerque, Las Cruces, El Paso, Portales and Alamogordo. Its mission is to bring the best of orchestral literature to Roswell and Southeast New Mexico through an annual concert season and music education programs for children and young adults. artigo.texto: CSI's 2.3 MWh Mobile BESS Earns TÜV Certification to Applicable UL 9540 Requirements LIVERMORE, Calif., Sept. 22, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Coulomb Solutions Inc. (CSI), a leading provider of commercial electrification and mobile energy storage solutions, today announced that TUV has certified CSI's 2.3 MWh Mobile BESS base model eBESS2.3-1.0-01 is compliant with applicable UL 9540:2023 requirements, marking an important milestone in the continued commercialization and deployment of CSI's high-capacity mobile energy storage systems. TÜV Rheinland conducted a field evaluation, inspection, testing, and applicable technical assessment of CSI's 2.3 MWh base model and confirmed compliance with the applicable requirements of UL 9540:2023, the Standard for Energy Storage Systems and Equipment. UL 9540 is the recognized system-level safety standard for Energy Storage Systems (ESS), evaluating the system as an integrated unit; including batteries, power conversion equipment, controls, enclosures, protection systems and other critical components. UL 9540:2023 certification addresses the safety of the complete energy storage system, including: - System-Level Safety: Evaluation of the batteries, power-conversion equipment, enclosure, controls, protection systems, and associated equipment as one integrated operating system. This includes pack, cell, and unit fire testing per the stringent UL9540A procedure. - Component Safety Standards: Evaluation of applicable component-level safety requirements, including standards such as UL 1973 for battery systems and UL 1741 for inverters, converters, and associated power-conversion equipment. - Electrical and Mechanical Protection: Evaluation of electrical, mechanical, thermal, and other potential system hazards. - Controls and Communications: Assessment of system protection, charging and discharging controls, communications between system components, fault response, and other critical operating functions. - Environmental and Enclosure Safety: Evaluation of system materials, enclosures, environmental protection, and other features intended to support safe operation of the equipment. "Achieving UL 9540 certification for our 2.3 MWh Mobile BESS base unit represents another major milestone for CSI and, more importantly, for our customers," said David Mazaika, CEO of Coulomb Solutions Inc. "Customers deploying large mobile energy storage systems need confidence not only in performance and reliability, but also that the complete system has been evaluated against rigorous safety standards. UL 9540 certification provides that additional level of assurance." CSI's 2.3 MWh Mobile BESS is designed specifically for applications where additional electrical capacity is required but sufficient permanent grid infrastructure is unavailable, delayed or uneconomical. The system combines approximately 2.3 MWh of energy storage with an integrated 1 MW power conversion system providing 480VAC power. This allows customers to rapidly deploy substantial electrical capacity for applications including commercial fleet and heavy-duty EV charging, data centers and high-load facilities, construction and remote work sites, utility and grid-support applications, peak shaving and demand-charge management, entertainment or sporting events and other temporary-power applications. Unlike conventional stationary BESS installations, CSI's Mobile BESS systems are engineered for frequent transport and deployment, using commercial vehicle-grade LFP battery technology, integrated thermal management and a rugged system architecture. CSI also recently announced an optional bidirectional Megawatt Charging System (MCS) configuration for its next generation model eBESS2.3-1.0-02 MWh Mobile BESS. This enables the system to provide up to one megawatt of high-power charging to compatible commercial electric vehicles and equipment. This configuration will also go through the full suite of UL testing as well. "Grid capacity is one of the biggest barriers to electrification," Mazaika added. "Our goal is to help commercial EV fleets, construction firms, sports and entertainment venues, data centers and other customers access to safe, certified power where they need it—without waiting years for permanent infrastructure upgrades. Achieving UL 9540 certification is an important step toward enabling those deployments at scale." About Coulomb Solutions Inc. (CSI) Coulomb Solutions Inc. (CSI) provides transportable Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS), advanced battery systems for commercial electric vehicles, low-voltage batteries and electrification components for the North American commercial vehicle market. CSI's Mobile BESS solutions deliver scalable, rapidly deployable power for fleet charging, commercial and industrial operations, grid support, temporary power and other applications requiring flexible electrical capacity. CSI's mission is to accelerate commercial electrification while providing innovative energy storage solutions that help customers overcome electrical infrastructure constraints. artigo.texto: Na Austrália, estado decide proibir data centers em áreas residenciais Governo de Victoria determina ainda que esse tipo de construção precisará ter sua própria fonte de energia renovável Um dos maiores estados da Austrália decidiu proibir a construção de data centers em áreas residenciais, além de determinar que essas unidades terão de “trazer sua própria fonte de energia renovável”. A medida faz parte de uma série de regras voltadas para apazigar protestos de cidadãos, em meio à explosão na demanda por data centers para sistemas de inteligência artificial (IA). O estado de Victoria, onde fica Melbourne, a segunda maior cidade do país, anunciou nesta terça-feira que, apesar de os data centers serem vitais à economia, essas medidas são necessárias para assegurar que as fontes locais de água e eletricidade não sofram impacto significativo. O premier estadual, Ben Carroll, vai exigir que os data centers compensem a demanda adicional de energia com geração própria, além de pagar por melhorias na rede elétrica. Também terão de usar apenas água de reúso ou imprópria para consumo humano para refrigerar seus sistemas. Além disso, fica proibido construir data centers em áreas residenciais. Terá de haver pelo menos 150 metros entre a unidade e qualquer casa. O primeiro-ministro australiano, Anthony Albanese, tem pressionado por padrões nacionais para data centers, na tentativa de equilibrar os ganhos com a explosão da demanda e as preocupações dos cidadãos. O Westpac Banking Corp. estima que o gasto com a construção de data centers pode atingir 225 bilhões de dólares australianos (US$ 160 bilhões), sendo a maior parte nos próximos três anos.

artigo.texto: Rethinking Data Center Cooling: Modern Solutions for a Growing Challenge Key Highlights - Data centers are experiencing unprecedented growth, necessitating advanced cooling solutions to prevent overheating and equipment failure. - Traditional cooling methods are often insufficient for high-density racks, leading to hot spots and increased energy costs. - Innovative technologies like liquid cooling, in-row systems, and AI-driven controls improve thermal management and reduce energy consumption. - Thermal de-stratification helps achieve uniform temperature distribution, enhancing cooling efficiency and equipment longevity. - Investing in modern cooling technologies supports sustainability goals and enables data centers to scale efficiently for future demands. From metropolitan hubs to rural outposts, data centers are the beating heart of our connected world, housing the servers and networking equipment that power everything, from streaming platforms and cloud computing to e-commerce, banking, and medical systems. And as the digital age accelerates, data centers are sprouting up at an unprecedented rate—based on recent market research, the global data center market is expected to grow to over $400 billion by 2027. Substantial growth has placed significant demands on today’s digital infrastructure—especially among hyperscale data centers, massive facilities that often span hundreds of thousands of square feet and require state-of-the-art engineering to accommodate the cooling needs of a delicate and sensitive environment. With this, data center operators must take a step back, consider their current approach to cooling, and identify crucial areas for improvement to stave off a potential heating emergency. Why Cooling Matters More Than Ever The surge in data centers calls for a reassessment of the facility cooling landscape, bringing to light sophisticated cooling technologies with great potential. The servers, switches, and storage arrays within data centers generate enormous amounts of heat, sometimes enough to raise the temperature by several degrees within minutes. If not correctly managed, this heat may degrade performance, damage equipment, and even cause costly downtime. The stakes are high: downtime or component failure can result in millions of dollars in losses, not to mention disruption to critical services. Unfortunately, as rack power densities steadily climb and data center equipment becomes more archaic approaches are simply unable to keep pace, leading to hot spots, uneven airflow, and increased energy consumption. Risks of Outdated Cooling Systems “Sensitive” is an understatement when it comes to data center equipment—even slight temperature fluctuations can shorten hardware lifespan and result in operational failures and compromised data integrity. Many operators are unaware that according to industry standards, the recommended temperature for the best server performance is between 18 and 27 degrees C. (64 to 80 degrees F.). It’s also important that humidity is strictly controlled. Straying from these parameters can cause servers to reduce performance or even shut down. Traditional cooling methods, including raised-floor air distribution and basic HVAC, struggle to keep up with the concentrated heat loads of densely packed racks. As rack densities rise to 15 kW, 30 kW, or even higher, conventional cooling can’t deliver the targeted, efficient thermal management required. What many data center operators don’t know is that the energy used for cooling can account for up to 40% of a data center’s total electricity consumption, making efficiency improvements critical for both business and environmental protection. Modern Cooling Tech is the Smart Investment To confront these challenges, the industry is turning to cutting-edge cooling solutions created for efficiency, scalability, and sustainability. One leading approach is thermal de-stratification, which eliminates layers of warm and cool air within the data center. The method is simple. Thermal de-stratification mixes the air in a room so that temperature and humidity are the same from floor to ceiling, breaking up thermal layers that promote uniform temperature distribution, prevent hot spots, and improve the effectiveness of cooling systems. The burden on HVAC is then notably reduced, resulting in energy savings and making it a critical component in the pursuit of more efficient and reliable cooling in modern data centers. In addition to reducing risk, cutting-edge cooling also enables higher server density, supports future expansion, and helps organizations meet increasingly strict sustainability mandates. Some of the most promising technologies include: - Liquid Cooling: Technologies such as direct-to-chip cooling and immersion cooling are changing thermal management. Direct-to-chip cooling circulates coolant directly over the hottest server components, such as CPUs and GPUs, enabling highly efficient heat transfer. Immersion cooling, on the other hand, submerges entire server boards in non-conductive dielectric fluids, resulting in outstanding heat removal and the ability to support much higher rack densities than traditional air-cooled approaches. These methods considerably reduce the need for air conditioning and can lower total data center energy use by up to 20% or more. - In-Row and Rear-Door Cooling: These systems bring cooling right to the heat source, which limits energy waste and improves temperature control. In-row cooling units are placed between server racks, removing hot air before it mixes with the room's cooler air. Rear-door heat exchangers, installed on the back of server cabinets, use chilled water or refrigerants to absorb heat as it exits the equipment. These approaches permit exact environmental control, reduce the risk of hot spots, and make it possible to scale cooling capacity as data center needs evolve. - AI-Driven Climate Control: The combination of AI and machine learning is bringing about new l

artigo.texto: India is preparing to introduce a new incentive scheme to encourage domestic processing of lithium and nickel, two critical minerals that are increasingly important for electric vehicles, battery manufacturing, energy storage and advanced industries. The proposed scheme, which is expected to be launched after the necessary approvals, is aimed at developing a stronger domestic processing ecosystem and reducing the country’s dependence on imported processed critical minerals. Building a Stronger Critical Mineral Supply Chain Lithium and nickel have become strategically important as India expands its electric mobility, renewable energy and energy-storage sectors. Lithium is a key raw material for lithium-ion batteries, while nickel is used in stainless steel and several high-energy-density battery technologies. Greater domestic processing capacity could help connect mineral resources with downstream manufacturing, creating opportunities across refining, battery materials, components and other industrial applications. Four States to Develop Processing Hubs The government has cleared plans for critical mineral processing parks in Gujarat, Maharashtra, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh. These parks are being planned as integrated ecosystems where mineral resources, processing facilities and downstream industries can develop together. Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh are expected to play a role in rare-earth processing, while Odisha and Maharashtra are being positioned for activities linked to nickel and lithium. The state-level approach is expected to encourage investment in processing infrastructure while creating stronger links between mining, mineral processing and manufacturing. Boost for EV and Battery Manufacturing The proposed incentives could provide additional momentum to India’s growing electric vehicle and battery manufacturing ecosystem. A stronger domestic supply of processed lithium and nickel could give battery and energy-storage companies greater access to critical inputs while opening opportunities for new investments in mineral processing, battery materials and related technologies. For manufacturers, developing these capabilities within India could also strengthen supply-chain resilience and reduce exposure to disruptions in international markets. Investment and Employment Opportunities The development of critical mineral processing parks could create opportunities for investment across mining, chemical processing, engineering, logistics and advanced manufacturing. As processing capacity expands, associated industries could also benefit from new demand for infrastructure, equipment, transportation and specialised services. This could create employment opportunities in both mineral-rich regions and emerging industrial centres. The initiative therefore has implications beyond the mining sector, with potential benefits extending across India’s wider manufacturing and clean-energy economy. Government Push for Faster Mine Development Alongside the new processing incentives, the government is also focusing on faster operationalisation of mining blocks that have already been auctioned and received the required clearances and leases. Delays in bringing such blocks into production can slow the availability of domestic mineral resources. Faster development could provide a more reliable raw-material base for processing facilities and downstream industries. Towards an Integrated Critical Mineral Ecosystem The proposed lithium and nickel scheme forms part of a wider effort to establish an end-to-end critical mineral value chain in India. By combining mining, domestic processing, dedicated industrial parks and downstream manufacturing, the government is seeking to strengthen the country’s position in sectors such as electric mobility, batteries, renewable energy and advanced materials. The success of the initiative will depend on how quickly processing capacity is established, investments are mobilised and mining assets are brought into production. If implemented effectively, the measures could support greater domestic value addition and create new business opportunities across India’s emerging critical-minerals economy.

artigo.texto: - China is becoming the global leader in sodium-ion battery production, outpacing the rest of the world. - Chinese companies like CATL and BYD are bringing sodium-ion batteries into electric vehicles and energy storage systems. - China holds over 400 GWh of current and planned sodium-ion battery capacity compared to only 11 GWh in the rest of the world. - Sodium-ion batteries use more abundant materials than lithium, offering supply chain opportunities for Africa, especially given the availability of agricultural and industrial feedstocks. The shift is being driven by the rapid expansion of Chinese production, with companies including CATL and BYD moving sodium-ion batteries from laboratories into electric vehicles and energy-storage systems. The US and Europe are also developing competing technologies, with American companies such as Natron Energy and French battery developer Tiamat investing in sodium-ion technology, although their production capacity remains far behind China’s. According to the Financial Times, China has more than 400 GWh of operating and planned sodium-ion battery capacity, compared with just 11 GWh across the rest of the world. Chinese carmaker Changan is also expected to launch the world’s first mass-produced sodium-ion-powered electric vehicle this month, using batteries supplied by CATL. “The West has missed the boat” on being first to sodium-ion, Max Reid, head of battery costs at CRU Group, told the FT. He said scaling the supply chain would require “$100mn worth of investment per plant plus” and that little of that investment was currently taking place outside China. Why Africa could have a role Sodium-ion batteries do not require lithium and can use more abundant materials, potentially creating a different supply chain from the one that has made China dominant in conventional lithium-ion batteries. The technology could be particularly relevant to Africa’s growing demand for electric mobility and energy storage. The FT notes that sodium-ion batteries have lower energy density than lithium-ion cells, but offer advantages in safety, charging and performance in extreme temperatures. Those characteristics could make them suitable for smaller electric vehicles, including three-wheelers, as well as stationary storage and data centres. DON'T MISS THIS: Months after U.S. listed Nigeria as emerging lithium source, Chinese-backed firm targets country’s projects with 240,000-tonne trial mine The potential African opportunity extends beyond battery assembly. Sodium-ion batteries use hard carbon as an anode material, and the FT identifies trees, coconut shells and oil and gas byproducts as potential sources for producing it. This could create openings for African producers with access to agricultural and industrial feedstocks, although significant investment and technical development would still be required. The International Energy Agency says sodium-ion batteries are entering the scale-up phase, but their supply chain remains heavily concentrated in China. Nearly all existing global manufacturing capacity is located there, while more than 95% of capacity expected in 2030 is also projected to be in China..

artigo.texto: U.S. Energy Storage Market Reaches Record 18.9 GWh in Q2 2026 The U.S. energy storage market installed a record 18.9 GWh of battery energy storage systems in the second quarter of 2026, according to the latest U.S. Energy Storage Monitor report released by the American Clean Power Association (ACP) and Wood Mackenzie. Energy storage installations increased 17% year-over-year (y-o-y), while installed power capacity declined 7% y-o-y. The national average duration of installed battery energy storage systems increased from 2.8 hours to 3.5 hours, driven by resource adequacy needs. Utility-Scale Storage Installations Decline in Q2 Utility-scale deployments totaled 4.7 GW/17.6 GWh in Q2, an 8% y-o-y decline in MW terms as key markets become increasingly saturated. However, installations during the first half of 2026 were up 5% y-o-y, with the report indicating that full-year 2026 installations are expected to remain on par with 2025. Average project duration continued to increase in Q2 2026. The report attributes some of this increase to a long-duration project in California designed to meet state targets and utility-contracted storage assets deployed in Texas. “Battery storage is one of the most important tools we have to meet growing electricity demand,” said John Hensley, Senior Vice President of Markets and Policy Analysis at American Clean Power. “Storage can be deployed quickly, strengthens reliability, and helps the grid make better use of both existing and new generation. With a strong pipeline and continued technology improvements, the outlook for storage remains exceptionally strong.” CCI Storage Returns to Historical Deployment Levels The Community, Commercial and Industrial (CCI) sector installed 48 MW in Q2, returning to historical deployment levels following California's record first quarter, which was driven by the state's Net Energy Metering 2.0 grandfathering deadline. Overall, the CCI market declined 2% y-o-y. Growth in Hawaii, New Mexico and Texas offset some of the decline. The residential sector recorded its fourth-largest quarter on record in Q2 2026, installing 676 MW. This represented a 15% quarter-over-quarter (q-o-q) decline and a 3% y-o-y increase. The national residential storage market is expected to contract 4% in 2026 amid tax credit elimination, consumer hesitancy and a transition in third-party ownership. California, Texas, Puerto Rico, Arizona and Illinois accounted for 88% of residential storage capacity installed in Q2, although all five markets declined q-o-q. Puerto Rico experienced the largest decline in absolute terms, with installations falling from 129 MW in Q1 to 73 MW in Q2. Storage Market Expected to Expand Through 2031 The report projects that utility-scale storage will grow at an average annual rate of 8% over the next five years as data center demand increases. The CCI sector is projected to grow 27% between 2026 and 2031 as deployment expands beyond California into emerging markets such as Maryland and Texas. The residential market is expected to rebound between 2027 and 2031, growing at an average annual rate of 9%. Overall, the U.S. energy storage market is projected to reach 207 GW and 715 GWh of cumulative installed capacity by 2031. "Data center buildout strengthens the U.S. storage outlook across all sectors. Storage can provide needed capacity faster, cheaper and more reliably than gas alone," said Allison Feeney, research analyst at Wood Mackenzie. "As hyperscalers increasingly face grid-connection bottlenecks, utility-scale storage will enable speed to power for data centers." The report also notes that the role of distributed storage is expanding beyond customer-focused applications. Virtual power plants (VPPs) are increasingly being positioned as a way to support load growth while creating participation opportunities for CCI and residential storage. Supply Chain Conditions Could Affect Near-Term Growth Supply chain dynamics, including potential trade restrictions, could contribute to near-term bottlenecks in the storage market. The utility-scale segment may experience some stagnation in 2026 and 2027 as the industry adjusts to these conditions. Growth is projected to resume in 2028, with the utility-scale market expected to expand at an average annual rate of 11% through 2031 as domestic cell manufacturing increases. "The slowdown in EV demand has become an unexpected tailwind for storage. Manufacturers are repurposing idle EV cell capacity, accelerating the domestic supply base just as trade policy makes it most valuable," said Allison Weis, Global Head of Energy Storage at Wood Mackenzie.

artigo.texto: How Communities Can Plan for AI Data Centers Before the Projects Arrive Key Highlights - Communities should integrate digital infrastructure into long-range land-use plans to better manage data center development and reduce conflicts. - Early engagement with residents and stakeholders is crucial for developers to build trust and align projects with community priorities. - AI infrastructure development is outpacing municipal planning cycles, necessitating proactive, forward-looking strategies. - Frameworks like the Open Infrastructure Exchange's Digital Infrastructure Framework help municipalities ask the right questions early in the planning process. - Not all data centers are suitable for every location; responsible development involves assessing land use, community needs, and infrastructure capacity before approval. The collision between AI infrastructure development and community opposition has become one of the defining data center stories of 2026. Developers are pursuing larger campuses, more power and compressed delivery schedules as AI accelerates demand for computing capacity. Meanwhile, local planning boards, elected officials and residents are increasingly being asked to make decisions about facilities whose scale, energy requirements and technological purpose may be unlike anything previously contemplated in their comprehensive plans. That gap is where Ilissa Miller believes much of the conflict begins. Miller, founder and CEO of iMiller Public Relations and a board member of the Open Infrastructure Exchange (OIX), joined the Data Center Frontier Show to discuss the OIX Digital Infrastructure Framework, an effort designed to give municipalities a more systematic way to think about data centers and other digital infrastructure before an individual development application lands in front of them. The idea is straightforward: communities routinely create long-range plans defining where homes, commercial development, industry and other land uses should go. Digital infrastructure should be part of that process as well. "Our vision for the framework was to help solve the problem by empowering communities to think about digital infrastructure," Miller said, so municipalities can incorporate it into their comprehensive master plans and maintain control over how land is ultimately used. That distinction is key. The framework is not intended to convince communities to approve data centers. Nor does it prescribe what a town or county should decide. Instead, Miller said, it is meant to help public officials ask the right questions early enough to make those decisions deliberately. The Data Center May Not Be in the Plan One of the industry's recurring problems is deceptively basic: many municipalities never anticipated data centers when writing their zoning codes and comprehensive plans. A parcel might already be designated for industrial development and still lack data centers as an explicitly permitted use. Miller offered the example of a former paper mill site. A community's existing rules may clearly allow certain industrial operations there — potentially even uses considerably less benign than a modern data center — while remaining silent on digital infrastructure. That can force developers through a conditional-use process before detailed project review has even begun. "You first have to be able to develop what you're proposing," Miller said. "And then you have to go through the planning and the review process from there." To industry participants accustomed to development timelines, those steps may appear obvious. To residents encountering a proposed data center for the first time, they may not be. Miller argues that this procedural gap contributes substantially to distrust. An early zoning or conditional-use hearing can be interpreted as approval of a finished project when it may instead be one stage in a longer process involving design review, utility questions, engineering changes and additional public oversight. The OIX framework is intended in part to make that decision-making environment more legible. It also encourages local officials to distinguish between the questions directly within their jurisdiction and those requiring engagement with utilities, counties or other entities. Land use may be a municipal responsibility. Power allocation or water supply may involve a separate authority. Local leaders, Miller said, should nevertheless be able to obtain that information and use it to inform their decisions. The goal is not fewer questions. It is better-directed ones. When Opposition to AI Becomes Opposition to Data Centers That distinction becomes especially important as AI enters the debate. Miller said community resistance increasingly extends beyond concerns traditionally associated with data center development — land, water, electrical demand, noise, construction and taxes — into broader anxiety over artificial intelligence itself. "Most opposition is about more than the data center itself," she said. In many public debates, the two have effectively become synonymous: data center means AI, and opposition to aspects of AI becomes opposition to the physical infrastructure enabling it. Miller does not dismiss those concerns. She acknowledged significant unresolved questions surrounding AI and the guardrails governing its deployment. But she argues that debates over AI governance and debates over local land use should not be treated as the same thing. AI policy may ultimately be shaped substantially at the state and federal levels. A planning board considering whether an industrial parcel is suitable for a data center is confronting a different question. The confusion is understandable. AI companies themselves have sent conflicting messages about automation, employment and the technology's broader societal effects. artigo.texto: Despite stock stress, CATL likely to retain EV battery dominance in China, analysts say CATL’s tech edge and brand safeguard its EV battery lead, though carmakers are seeking alternative suppliers Contemporary Amperex Technology Limited’s (CATL) dominance in the Chinese electric vehicle (EV) market is unlikely to slump over the coming year given its brand recognition and edge in technology, analysts said, though its shares have already tumbled amid the battle with profit-squeezed EV makers. Chinese carmakers have been doubling down on efforts in recent weeks to reduce their reliance on CATL – in September, Xiaomi and Li Auto highlighted their partnership with tier-two battery manufacturers, including CALB Group, while Xpeng planned to make in-house battery packs this year. Amid concerns about a potential loss of market share, CATL’s Shenzhen-listed shares have lost 25.7 per cent since mid-August and 36.5 per cent from their all-time high seen in early May. On Monday, the equities of the Fujian-based firm fell by a further 1.6 per cent in Shenzhen and 0.59 per cent in Hong Kong.

artigo.texto: Data Centre West 2026: Alberta Moves From Data Center Ambition to Execution Key Highlights - Alberta has moved beyond potential discussions, focusing now on rapid project delivery amid AI-driven demand growth. - Certainty in power supply, permitting, and community acceptance is critical for Alberta to scale its data center industry. - AI inference workloads are reshaping infrastructure needs, emphasizing flexibility in cooling, power, and connectivity. - Hybrid power solutions—grid, onsite generation, and storage—are likely to define Alberta’s data center architecture. - Regulatory clarity and infrastructure readiness are essential; Alberta’s success depends on swift, coordinated execution. The most revealing thing about Data Centre West 2026 may have been how little time anyone spent making the basic case for Alberta. That case has largely been made. For several years, Western Canada’s data center conversation revolved around potential: abundant energy resources, available land, a cool climate, growing cloud demand, favorable economics and the possibility that Alberta could develop into a meaningful alternative to North America’s increasingly constrained data center hubs. In Calgary this September, the conversation had moved on. “Why Alberta?” has increasingly been replaced by a much more consequential question: How quickly can you actually deliver? Across the opening keynote and a succession of panels covering hyperscale development, colocation, AI inference and power, Data Centre West returned repeatedly to the same dividing line. Announced megawatts are plentiful. AI demand is real. Capital is available. What is scarce is certainty. Certainty that a first block of power will arrive when promised. Certainty that the transmission, generation and fuel behind it are real. Certainty that cooling infrastructure can support rapidly changing rack densities. Certainty that a project can make it through permitting and community review. And certainty that a data center built for the current AI cycle will remain useful when the next generation of compute arrives. That is a different stage of market development. Alberta is moving from proving that it belongs in the data center conversation to confronting the much harder work of becoming a data center market at scale. From Potential to Proof Western Canada Data Centre Alliance founder and president Vlad Oujegov opened the conference by pointing to a room of roughly 500 attendees and an Alberta market that, only a few years ago, would have been difficult to imagine at that scale. Oujegov said he had recently counted more than 30 open full-time data center positions on Alberta job boards, even as the province remained near the beginning of its development curve. More significant was his contention that the scale of projects now entering Alberta is capable of transforming the local industry almost overnight. Oujegov said the Meta project announced this summer could increase Alberta’s existing data center industry tenfold over several years. The message was not simply that large projects are coming. It was that Alberta is beginning to acquire the characteristics of an infrastructure cluster: cloud deployments, colocation capacity, power development, construction expertise, suppliers and specialized labor beginning to reinforce one another. That point was picked up by Bill Kleyman, CEO of Apolo, in his opening keynote. Kleyman placed Alberta inside a much larger global contradiction. AI demand is producing extraordinary development pipelines, but only a fraction of what is proposed is actually making its way into construction. Citing data presented in his AFCOM State of the Data Center 2026 research, Kleyman pointed to a global development pipeline of approximately 264 GW, with only about 6.9% under construction. The implication was straightforward: the industry has to become much better at separating actual demand from option value. A 1-GW data center campus on a presentation slide does not carry the same value as the first 50 or 100 MW that can actually be energized. “Not all megawatts are created equal” became one of the morning’s recurring ideas. And increasingly, power is not simply one input in the data center development process. It is the scheduler. Hyperscalers Are Buying a Date That shift was especially clear during the morning’s Hyperscale Outlook panel. Angela Adam of eStruxure said customers no longer ask why Alberta. They understand the market proposition. What they increasingly want to know is whether an operator can deliver capacity on a specific date. Customers, Adam said, are no longer simply buying megawatts. They are buying a credible date around which they can construct their own business plans. That distinction changes how data centers have to be developed. Waiting for a completely signed customer contract before beginning work may protect against speculative development, but it can also make competitive delivery dates impossible. Building everything to a highly customized specification before the customer is committed creates the opposite problem. The emerging strategy sits somewhere between the two. How so? Advance the things that take the longest and can serve the widest range of customers: land, power, permitting, operating pathways and community acceptance. Preserve enough flexibility to configure the final facility around the customer once the contract is signed. Dermot Callaghan of Beacon Data Centers, who previously spent a decade developing infrastructure at Google, reduced hyperscale deliverability to three elements: energy, development pathway and scalability. Hyperscalers, he said, can see through headline gigawatt numbers quickly. They want to know where the electrons are coming from, whether equipment and permits are real, how quickly the first data hall can be placed in service, and whether the supply chain and labor force can continue delivering after that first tranche. artigo.texto: As the world pivots toward cleaner power solutions, choosing between fuel cells and long-duration storage is a challenge for many. Bloom Energy Corp (BE +1.33%) and Eos Energy Enterprises Inc (EOSE -0.25%) represent two distinct paths. EOSE & BE: Performance Comparison Key Financial Metrics Bloom Energy focuses on solid-oxide fuel cells that generate electricity onsite, while Eos develops zinc-based batteries designed for utility-scale storage. Both companies target the growing demand for grid reliability but operate with vastly different financial profiles and technological risks. The case for Bloom Energy In its latest annual report, filed for the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, Bloom Energy notes that it serves customers across nearly 1,000 sites. The company provides solid-oxide systems used for both electricity and hydrogen production. A major agreement with American Electric Power Co (AEP +0.20%) involves up to 1 gigawatt (GW) of fuel cells, and the company also has a prospective $5 billion financing framework with Brookfield Corp(BN -0.34%) for AI infrastructure projects. In FY 2025, revenue reached about $2 billion, which represents growth of approximately 37% compared to the previous year. Despite this growth, the company reported a net loss of more than $88 million for the period, equating to a net margin of negative 4%. This follows a trend of narrowing losses since the company reported a net loss of $302.1 million in FY 2023. As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio was roughly 6x. This liquidity measure suggests the company can cover its short-term obligations with its current assets. The debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 3.9x, meaning total debt is nearly four times the value of shareholder equity. Free cash flow was around $57 million, which represents the cash remaining after paying for capital expenditures. The case for Eos Energy Enterprises Eos Energy Enterprises manufactures zinc-based battery storage systems for utilities and industrial stocks. According to its latest annual report, filed for the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, Eos primarily sells products within the United States. Customer concentration is a significant factor here, as two customers accounted for roughly 51% and 19% of revenue. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business. In FY 2025, revenue reached approximately $114.2 million, a massive increase of 630% over the prior year. However, the company recorded a significant net loss of more than $1.7 billion. This loss was much wider than the $964 million loss reported in FY 2024, highlighting the high costs of scaling a newer energy technology. Based on the December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio was nearly 4.9x. This indicates a healthy ability to meet short-term liabilities with liquid assets. The debt-to-equity ratio was negative 1.0x, indicating that total liabilities exceed the total value of shareholder equity. Free cash flow was negative $265 million, which is the cash used for operations and capital projects during the year. Risk profile comparison Bloom Energy faces risks from the emerging nature of the hydrogen market and long sales cycles that can delay revenue recognition. Dependence on sole-source suppliers for critical raw materials and exposure to trade tariffs also impact its net margin. Additionally, the company is currently managing a securities fraud class action lawsuit that could result in unexpected legal costs or settlements. Eos Energy Enterprises deals with a history of losses and a constant need for outside capital to fund its expansion. Scaling its manufacturing capacity in Pennsylvania carries execution risks, especially while competing with companies like Tesla Inc (TSLA +0.96%) or Fluence Energy Inc (FLNC -1.62%). Volatility in the lithium market can also affect the relative cost-competitiveness of its zinc-based storage solutions compared to traditional alternatives. Valuation comparison Eos Energy Enterprises appears cheaper based on its Forward P/E calculated from future earnings estimates, while Bloom Energy carries a much higher P/S ratio. Valuation metrics sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers. Which stock would I buy in 2026? The current fiscal year, 2026, looks to be a major step-ahead year for Eos Energy Enterprises. The business has already sold more product through the first half of the year than it did in all 2025, shipping $126 million of gear to clients. Longer term should be much greater. Management says it has nearly $25 billion of business pipeline, meaning proposed energy storage devgelopments Eos could bid on, and an $807 million backlog, which are firm orders for the company's products. 2026 revenue is seen more than doubling. Just recently, Eos scored a high-profile deal to support the PJM grid after joining with Alphabet Inc (GOOG -0.99%) and MN8 Energy on a solar energy storage project in West Virginia. Bloom Energy's core product is its Energy Server, a stand-alone power source for commercial and industrial customers. The Energy Server is based on solid oxide fuel cell technology and runs on natural gas, biogas, or hydrogen. The business aims to reduce its production costs by about 10% per year to attract more customers (its main markets are the U.S. and Korea). The AI datacenter boom is a tailwind for Bloom, which should see revenue leap 85% to $4.1 billion in fiscal 2026. That has Wall Street expecting a swing to net income of about $658 million. That picture for both companies tells us two things: Eos is exciting and has a developing business, while Bloom has a developed business with lots of room to grow. Bloom's ability to meet immediate data center demand is a tremendous advantage. However, its ratios are too rich for our liking. Eos, with its attractive P/S ratio compared to Bloom, along with its recent business advances, provides it the nod here.

artigo.texto: As Chinese carmakers diversify beyond CATL batteries, Beijing warns of market overreaction MIIT-linked commentary dismisses “de-CATLisation” concerns as normal supplier diversification and warns cutthroat price competition poses a far bigger threat A publication under China’s industry ministry has pushed back against market chatter of “de-CATLisation” as a growing number of the battery giant’s automotive partners diversify their suppliers, with the company’s shares falling recently. The publication followed several Chinese carmakers, including Xiaomi, Li Auto and Xpeng, expanding partnerships with battery suppliers other than CATL or announcing plans to develop batteries in-house. The moves this month have fuelled talk of a shift away from the industry giant and speculation about its market position. By Wednesday, CATL’s Shenzhen-listed shares had fallen about 25 per cent from their mid-August level and nearly 35 per cent from a record high reached in early May. The shares were down 1.19 per cent on the day.

artigo.texto: O rateio dos custos da contratação de baterias, a participação de projetos de armazenamento localizados junto a usinas existentes e medidas para evitar pressões sobre atrasos e aumento de custos devido às exigências de conteúdo local estão entre as principais discussões levantadas por agentes do setor elétrico na consulta pública da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) sobre os leilões de baterias (BESS) previstos para dezembro. A consulta sobre a minuta do edital ficou aberta de 30 de julho a 14 de setembro e recebeu 88 contribuições, que foram divulgadas na segunda-feira (21/9). Confira as contribuições na íntegra. Abaixo, a agência eixos traz um resumo das principais discussões levantadas: Rateio de custos Com mais de 6 mil projetos cadastrados nos leilões, um dos temas que divide os agentes é a possibilidade de os custos da contratação das baterias serem rateados com os consumidores, e não apenas entre os geradores, conforme prevê a legislação atual. O deputado federal Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania/SP) apresentou um projeto para revogar o dispositivo da lei vigente e redistribuir os custos, o PL 3.716/2026. A discussão já levanta a hipótese no setor de adiamento dos certames. Nas contribuições à Aneel, associações de geradores e desenvolvedores propõem que o edital adote uma redação neutra para acomodar eventuais revisões legislativas que visem compartilhar os custos com os consumidores finais. A proposta foi citada pela Abeeólica, Absolar, Abiape, Apine, Eneva, Engie, EDP e Serena. Segundo esses agentes, os benefícios do armazenamento são de natureza sistêmica para todo o Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN), portanto os custos devem ser divididos entre todo o setor. Já entidades e conselhos de consumidores argumentam que é necessário se ater à legislação atual, que prevê o rateio entre os geradores. Abrace, Concen e Abradee afirmam que a expansão de renováveis intermitentes gerou a necessidade de capacidade firme, por isso, o custo do armazenamento deve ficar com o segmento de geração, sem onerar as tarifas da população. Colocalização Outro tema que divide os agentes é a instalação do sistema de baterias junto à infraestrutura de usinas existentes, em projetos colocalizados. A minuta do edital proposta pela Aneel restringe o leilão aos projetos de armazenamento autônomos, devido à possibilidade de incertezas no despacho centralizado operado pelo ONS. A Axia Energia (ex-Eletrobras) e conselhos de consumidores de energia defendem o modelo proposto pela Aneel, e argumentam que a participação de projetos colocalizados pode gerar riscos na liquidação da CCEE e não agregar potência incremental real à rede. Por outro lado, associações de fontes renováveis e geradores defendem que a colocalização permitiria aproveitar a infraestrutura existente, otimizando o uso da rede e reduzindo custos operacionais. Além disso, afirmam que esses projetos poderiam absorver a energia cortada pelo curtailment, o que permite lances mais competitivos no leilão. Para isso funcionar, no entanto, é necessário que o ONS mantenha prioridade de despacho sobre as baterias. Entre os agentes a favor desse modelo estão a Absolar, Abeeólica e a Abiogás, assim como geradores renováveis como a Atlas Renewable Energy, Engie, Neoenergia, EDP, Statkraft, Scatec, Serena, Renova Energia, Elera, Rio Alto, Baterias Moura e a Bolognesi. A Petrobras, que já indicou que pretende participar dos certames, também defende a possibilidade de colocalização com projetos existentes, com a cessão total ou parcial do montante de uso do sistema de transmissão previamente contratado por uma usina geradora para o BESS no mesmo ponto de conexão. Conteúdo local Gera preocupações no setor o primeiro leilão exclusivo para projetos com o mínimo de conteúdo local estabelecido pelo Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES). Diversos agentes alertaram a Aneel para o fato de que a cadeia fornecedora no Brasil ainda é incipiente e limitada e defendem regras de flexibilização e transição, além de mecanismos de cura, como a possibilidade de troca de um fornecedor por outro equivalente cadastrado no BNDES, em caso de falhas nas entregas. Afirmam que há restrição de fornecedores, riscos de atraso, prêmios de risco no lance e possibilidade de aumento de custos. Estimativas apresentadas por conselhos de consumidores de energia alertam para um sobrecusto de 20% a 40% nos projetos devido às exigências de contratação nacional. Tempo curto Outra preocupação é a curta janela prevista entre a emissão das outorgas dos projetos vencedores dos leilões, prevista para maio de 2027, e o início do suprimento, em agosto de 2028. As empresas alertam que o prazo efetivo para o desenvolvimento dos projetos será de apenas 15 meses. A Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae) pede maior coordenação entre o cronograma dos certames e os procedimentos de acesso ao sistema elétrico. A entidade propõe tratamento prioritário para os empreendimentos contratados, com procedimento específico e simplificado nas etapas de acesso. “O primeiro LRCAP-Baterias será uma referência para os próximos ciclos de contratação de armazenamento no país. Por isso, é importante que a Aneel tenha, nesta etapa, uma leitura técnica muito próxima da realidade dos projetos”, disse o diretor-executivo da associação, Fabio Lima, em nota. A Absae defende ainda mudanças no mecanismo de recebimento da receita fixa e uma melhor calibração das exigências econômico-financeiras, com o fim da diferenciação nos critérios aplicados a empresas individuais e consórcios e a harmonização das bases de cálculo.

artigo.texto: City council adopts resolution regarding large-scale data centers in Lubbock, starting process for potential moratorium LUBBOCK, Texas (KCBD) - An effort to halt data centers in Lubbock, spurred by citizen petition, has culminated in compromise. As part of the ‘Save Lubbock’ group, Stephen Sanders says he’s been working with city council the last several months to see what can be done about large-scale data centers. While his 18-month moratorium ordinance proposal was not feasible under Texas law, he says a 90-day proposal by the council is a meaningful step “It gives our city time to establish guardrails, protect out resources, consider the long-term effects on our neighborhoods, and develop a clear plan, rather than rushing forward without adequate preparation,” Sanders said. The resolution to start the moratorium process was approved 5-2. While the ordinance is drafted, city planning staff is tasked with developing new guidelines on water use, power reliability, zoning, noise and lighting for any large scale center. A work session will also be scheduled within 90 days so experts can brief the council on potential data center impacts. District 6 councilman Tim Collins voted against this resolution. He says with the regular Texas legislative session set to end in May 2027, he believes now’s not the time to institute this. “We are going to receive a great deal of information,” Collins said. “A great deal of information about power requirements, a great deal about water needs, a great deal of information about what the state is going to require data centers to do. We only have one tool, and that’s this moratorium. If we exercise that tool today, come June, we’re out. We’re out of the game.” District 4 councilman Tim Green also voted not to adopt the resolution, saying he feels technology around data centers has changed and its potential for Lubbock’s economy could be significant. “If it threatens Lubbock’s water supply, we shouldn’t approve it, and we won’t approve it,” Green said. “If a company can demonstrate it can operate responsibly, then let’s look at it.” District 5 councilwoman Jennifer Wilson says she wants business to come to Lubbock, but not at any cost to our resources. “I want it to be the right project, in the right location, and in the right circumstances that it benefits us here in west Texas,” Wilson said. Mayor Mark McBrayer added that given what’s going on right now in the state, this will give the city plenty of time to assess the situation. “Given ERCOT’s situation, no one’s coming to Lubbock in the next year anyway with a data center,” McBrayer said. “We are staking a position that we want to wait for our legislators at the state level to give some direction, to give some further guidance in areas where only they can give guidance.” If the optional 90-day moratorium extension were to be approved by council, a potential large-scale data center would not be considered until June of 2027.
