A sanção do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata) reduziu a diferença estimada de custos para a instalação de data centers no Brasil em relação aos Estados Unidos e ampliou os incentivos para novos investimentos no setor. Segundo estudo da FGV Projetos divulgado pelo Movimento Brasil Competitivo (MBC), implantar um data center no país custava 26,7% mais do que nos Estados Unidos antes do novo regime. Com os incentivos federais, essa diferença é estimada em 17,7%. O Redata, sancionado em 15 de setembro, estabelece benefícios tributários para a instalação, modernização e ampliação de centros de processamento de dados, em meio à expansão da demanda por infraestrutura para inteligência artificial. O levantamento estima ainda que um data center de 100 megawatts (MW) voltado à IA pode mobilizar cerca de R$ 25 bilhões em investimentos e gerar até 37,2 mil empregos diretos, indiretos e induzidos. Os números representam uma estimativa para um empreendimento desse porte e não investimentos já contratados após a criação do regime. Leia também: Data centers podem consumir 30% da energia do país, diz diretor-geral do ONS O novo regime reduz a carga tributária incidente sobre equipamentos utilizados na implantação e expansão dos data centers, um dos fatores apontados pelo setor como desvantagem do Brasil na disputa por esses investimentos. A tributação estadual, no entanto, permanece fora do Redata. O ICMS não integra o regime federal e segue em discussão no Conselho Nacional de Política Fazendária (Confaz). Para o MBC, mudanças nesse ponto podem complementar os incentivos federais e reduzir ainda mais a diferença de custos em relação a outros mercados. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC O avanço dos projetos de data centers também aumenta a demanda por infraestrutura elétrica. Segundo o levantamento divulgado pelo MBC, projetos do setor que aguardam etapas relacionadas à conexão de energia somam 26,2 GW, indicando a escala da demanda potencial associada à expansão dos centros de dados no país. A efetivação desses projetos, porém, depende de fatores como disponibilidade da rede, capacidade de transmissão e avanço dos processos de conexão. A matriz elétrica brasileira, com elevada participação de fontes renováveis, é apontada como uma vantagem na atração desses empreendimentos, principalmente diante do crescimento da demanda por capacidade computacional ligada à inteligência artificial. Para ter acesso aos benefícios do Redata, as empresas precisam cumprir contrapartidas previstas no regime, incluindo investimentos em pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação e requisitos ligados ao consumo de energia e água. O regime também estabelece uma parcela mínima da capacidade de processamento destinada ao mercado brasileiro. Para Tatiana Ribeiro, diretora-executiva do MBC, as novas regras melhoram as condições para atrair investimentos em infraestrutura digital. “Temos energia limpa e um enorme potencial de mercado. O que precisamos agora é de segurança jurídica para transformar essa janela de oportunidade em investimentos bilionários”, afirmou. artigo.texto: Operadores de data centers voltados ao mercado australiano captaram ao menos US$ 35 bilhões no ano, segundo nota técnica do Reserve Bank of Australia obtida pela ABC. O montante supera em 46% os US$ 24 bilhões levantados durante todo o ano de 2025 e equivale a mais de sete vezes a média anual registrada entre 2020 e 2024. A análise considera empréstimos sindicalizados, títulos, capital público e privado e algumas transações privadas. Foram examinadas operações de AirTrunk, CDC, Firmus, Goodman, Macquarie Technology e subsidiárias de Stack Infrastructure e Equinix. O banco central considera a captação um indicador antecipado do volume potencial de novas construções, enquanto autoridades monetárias acompanham globalmente o risco de uma bolha de investimentos em inteligência artificial. Principais fatos e números - Operadores australianos captaram ao menos US$ 35 bilhões no ano. - O volume é 46% superior aos US$ 24 bilhões levantados em 2025. - A captação supera em mais de sete vezes a média anual de 2020 a 2024. - O levantamento inclui crédito, títulos e aportes de capital público e privado. - A análise abrange sete grupos operadores ou suas subsidiárias. - Há dezenas de projetos aprovados de data centers de IA ainda não construídos. Por que isso importa para empresários e investidores A escalada do financiamento sinaliza uma possível expansão da construção de data centers na Austrália, abrindo oportunidades para fornecedores de energia, equipamentos, engenharia, conectividade e serviços financeiros. Para investidores e operadores, porém, o ritmo elevado amplia a exposição a riscos de excesso de capacidade, pressão sobre água e eletricidade e eventual revisão das condições de crédito. O alerta sobre uma possível bolha global de investimentos em IA reforça a necessidade de testar demanda, contratos e retorno dos projetos. A captação indica intenção de investimento, mas não garante que todo o capital resulte em obras.

artigo.texto: Envision Energy Powers Morocco's First Large-Scale Battery Storage System at OCP's Benguerir Mining Site BENGUERIR, Morocco, Sept. 21, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Envision Energy, a global leader in green technology, today announced the successful energisation of Morocco's first large-scale lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery energy storage system at OCP Green Energy's Benguerir mining site. The 25 MW / 125 MWh system was supplied and commissioned by Envision Energy under a contract signed in late 2025, and is now undergoing testing before entering commercial operation. Envision Energy provided the full storage system and led the commissioning work, integrating the BESS with the site's solar generation, grid conditions and industrial load profile. The system is designed to shift surplus solar power from daytime generation to peak consumption hours, reducing the site's peak-hour electricity bill by approximately 25%. With five hours of storage capacity, the BESS functions as an industrial energy management tool rather than a short-duration grid asset. It is supported by USD 20 million from the Clean Technology Fund, managed through the African Development Bank Group, and is designed for a 25-year lifetime with daily charge-discharge cycles. For OCP, the value lies not in battery capacity, but in the system's ability to reduce peak-hour costs over a 25-year operating life. "The successful energisation of Morocco's first large-scale battery storage project demonstrates the reliability, flexibility and cost-effectiveness of integrated renewable-plus-storage solutions in industrial applications," said John Lee, General Manager of Envision Energy for the Middle East and Africa. "Envision is proud to be part of this landmark project and to contribute green technology to Morocco's energy transition." As highlighted in OCP Group's official press release announcing the milestone, Omar Kadir, CEO of OCP Green Energy, said: Storage is the natural extension of our energy strategy. It allows us to reconcile the variable output of renewable energy with the continuous needs of our industrial platforms, while strengthening the reliability of our energy supply. Beyond OCP Group's own needs, this technology paves the way for a more harmonious integration of renewable energy into the national power system. By bringing greater flexibility and resilience to the grid, it will help accelerate the deployment of renewable capacity." The project marks a significant milestone for battery storage and industrial decarbonisation in Morocco. It supports the country's target of achieving 52% of installed electricity capacity from renewable sources by 2030 and serves as a benchmark for industrial decarbonisation across Africa.

artigo.texto: LOS ANGELES — New large-scale AI data centers are now off-limits in unincorporated Los Angeles County. Planning Director Amy Bodek issued an immediate prohibition Thursday, directing county staff to halt development of the facilities while officials move to add a permanent ban to the zoning code. The county’s current rules do not specifically regulate data centers used for AI-related storage, processing, and generation. The move follows months of pressure from residents as cities across Los Angeles County confront their own data-center fights. “I introduced it in response to concerns raised by San Gabriel Valley residents who were understandably concerned about the effects of data centers in their communities, concerns that have since been reflected nationwide,” Board of Supervisors Chair Hilda Solis said. The Board of Supervisors unanimously approved the motion, directing county departments to study potential health, environmental, and safety effects on nearby communities, including impacts on electrical and water resources. The motion also directed county departments to study zoning changes, environmental review, and protections for residents living near the facilities. “As a necessary next step to address these concerns, the county's report back on that motion identified zoning changes that would prohibit these facilities. The need for such a ban has only been further underscored by alarming developments from the AI sector on catastrophic impacts the technology may have on humanity,” Solis added. Solis said she plans to bring further recommendations from the Departments of Regional Planning and Public Health to the board. She thanked county departments, residents and other stakeholders who raised concerns about data centers, saying she remains committed to ensuring technological growth does not come at the expense of public health, environmental protections or residents’ quality of life. Bodek’s directive will block the facilities in unincorporated areas while that work moves forward. The county order does not apply to incorporated cities, where local governments control zoning. In El Segundo, a proposal to convert the Hyatt Place hotel into a five-story AI data center was withdrawn after residents packed a Planning Commission meeting and submitted hundreds of pages of public comment. The proposal would have required 49.5 megawatts of electricity, 5,423 gallons of water a day, and 16 diesel backup generators. More than 100 people crowded into the meeting, with attendees spilling into the hallway and more than 700 pages of public comment submitted before the developer withdrew the application, as Westside Current reported. The San Gabriel Valley has seen similar fights. In January, Monterey Park residents attended a community meeting hosted by San Gabriel Valley Progressive Action, which describes itself as a “grassroots, community-driven organization focused on environmental justice, transparency, and equitable development in the San Gabriel Valley.” The organization says it is not affiliated with a political party. Residents and the group criticized SDCF Monterey Park, LLC’s plan to demolish vacant commercial buildings at 1977 Saturn St. and build a 218,400-square-foot, single-story data center on 15.8 acres. LA Public Press previously reported on the project, which was introduced in 2024. Residents raised concerns about potential air, land, and water pollution. The Monterey Park City Council imposed a 45-day moratorium, then extended it while staff developed planning and zoning rules. Voters approved Measure NDC in June, prohibiting all data centers unless a future vote repeals the restriction. The measure was the first of its kind in California. The City Council of neighboring Industry unanimously approved a zoning change in February allowing construction of a battery-storage site. The action sparked criticism from city residents and people living nearby in La Puente, Rowland Heights, Avocado Heights, Hacienda Heights and South San Jose Hills. Opponents feared it could clear a path for a data center at the mostly vacant Puente Hills Mall. The No Data Centers SGV coalition opposed the project. Its members include San Gabriel Valley Progressive Action, Avocado Heights Vaquer@s, Puente Hills Community Preservation Society, SGVoices, Party for Socialism and Liberation, and No Data Center Monterey Park. El Monte and Baldwin Park later voted to establish yearlong bans on proposed data centers within their city limits. Data centers are not new, but their construction has increased in recent years. The Data Center Coalition, which describes itself as “the trade association for the data center industry with members that own data centers operate and maintain data center infrastructure both nationally and globally,” reported that data centers supported more than 665,000 California jobs in 2024 and generated $14.1 billion in state and local taxes. California has at least 287 data centers. Amazon and Alphabet are expected to spend a combined $700 billion on data centers globally by the end of the year, according to The New York Times. Editor’s Note: This story includes reporting from City News Service, a content partner of Westside Current.

artigo.texto: Massachusetts Invests $40 Million in On-Site Battery Storage to Enhance Grid Resiliency By the microgrid Massachusetts seeks grid resiliency, but mainly through battery storage. The state’s Department of Energy Resources last week awarded more than $40 million to 36 distributed energy projects supporting community and safety priorities. The grants are part of DER’s Advancing Massachusetts Power Energy Storage Grant Program. “This is about lowering energy costs and keeping the lights on when communities need it most,” Gov. Maura Healey said in a statement. “These investments will help schools, affordable housing, community centers and other critical facilities stay powered during outages while strengthening our grid for the future. We’re also making sure first responders and local officials have the training and tools they need as more energy storage comes online across Massachusetts.” Growing Need for Battery Storage Across Midwest Microgrid Knowledge Quickchat Video with ELM The statewide program will focus on using battery storage to be ready in the event of outages. For example, Acushnet Ford Middle School will have a 250-kW/1,728-kWh (1.73-MWh) battery system installed, while Springfield Water and Sewer will host a 2.5-MW/10-MWh battery storage system. Other locations include apartment complexes, community centers, schools, public works and even a jail facility. All told, more than 13 MW of batteries will be installed. Massachusetts Energy and Environmental Affairs Secretary Rebecca Tepper noted that batteries supplied more electricity to the grid so far this year than in all of 2025—indicating the energy resource’s growth pattern both in New England and around the U.S. Utility-scale battery storage capacity has grown by an average rate of 70% annually in the U.S. over recent years, according to the federal Energy Information Administration. Battery storage capacity is gaining new appreciation for its ability to handle voltage ride-through and transient load from AI computing as well as providing grid smoothing, balance and resiliency services. “Communities need reliable power and the confidence that new energy technologies are being deployed safely,” Massachusetts Lt. Gov Kim Driscoll said in the government statement. “These grants will help cities and towns strengthen critical infrastructure, prepare first responders and local officials, and take advantage of storage technology that can save money and improve resilience.” Total U.S. battery storage capacity surpassed 52 GW this summer and could reach 70 GW by early 2027, according to reports. Many of these installations are made in tandem with renewable energy and even gas-fired power generation both as part of microgrids and behind-the-meter for digital infrastructure. Click here to see a list of all the Massachusetts sites granted under the Advancing Massachusetts Power Energy Storage Program About the Author Rod Walton, Microgrid Knowledge Managing Editor Managing Editor For Microgrid Knowledge editorial inquiries, please contact Managing Editor Rod Walton at [email protected]. I’ve spent the last 18 years covering the energy industry as a newspaper and trade journalist. I was an energy writer and business editor at the Tulsa World before moving to business-to-business media at PennWell Publishing, which later became Clarion Events, where I covered the electric power industry. I joined Endeavor Business Media in November 2021 to help launch EnergyTech, one of the company’s newest media brands. I joined Microgrid Knowledge in July 2023. I earned my Bachelors degree in journalism from the University of Oklahoma. My career stops include the Moore American, Bartlesville Examiner-Enterprise, Wagoner Tribune and Tulsa World, all in Oklahoma . I have been married to Laura for the past 36-plus years and we have four children and one adorable granddaughter. We want the energy transition to make their lives better in the future. Microgrid Knowledge and EnergyTech are focused on the mission critical and large-scale energy users and their sustainability and resiliency goals. These include the commercial and industrial sectors, as well as the military, universities, data centers and microgrids. The C&I sectors together account for close to 30 percent of greenhouse gas emissions in the U.S. Many large-scale energy users such as Fortune 500 companies, and mission-critical users such as military bases, universities, healthcare facilities, public safety and data centers, shifting their energy priorities to reach net-zero carbon goals within the coming decades. These include plans for renewable energy power purchase agreements, but also on-site resiliency projects such as microgrids, combined heat and power, rooftop solar, energy storage, digitalization and building efficiency upgrades.

artigo.texto: NORTH PORT — City commissioners OK'd an 18-month moratorium on data centers late Tuesday — with some stipulations for an application that was already submitted. The first hearing for a moratorium on North Port data centers packed commission chambers earlier this month. A total of 409 people left comments: 287 in person, 75 e-comments and 47 voicemails. The second hearing Tuesday saw a fraction of the attendees, but dozens still filled the meeting room seats — far more than for a usual meeting. There was about three hours of public comments related to the controversial topic. The overwhelming majority were opposed. The motion that passed through second reading temporarily halts the building of data centers in North Port. But it also allows the process for acceptance, processing and review — but not approval — of an application for a data center that North Port received. The application was previously under a non-disclosure agreement, but is now publicly available. Vice Mayor Barbara Langdon made the motion to pass the moratorium through second reading and Commissioner Phil Stokes seconded. The vote passed 3-2 with Commissioners Demetrius Petrow and David Duval dissenting. Petrow was the lone no vote on the first reading. He said people do not feel represented in the city. He wanted the moratorium to apply for all data centers, including the existing application. “People do not want this,” he said. Duval voted with the majority, then, but changed his mind for the second hearing, saying it was apparent people did not want a data center in their city. He was also worried about a potential lawsuit. But changing his mind Duval said, “if they want to sue us, I say let them sue us." Stokes said the motion was the "most responsible" way for the city to go, and that’s why he supported it. City Attorney Michael Fuino told commissioners at the previous meeting and on Tuesday that the developer who submitted the application would doubtlessly sue North Port if their project was halted. And they would have grounds to do so based on state laws, he said. Citing things like the data center potentially using too much water, therefore not being allowed, Stokes said he would rather see the project "die from its own weight," or when the city is in a better position to defend itself. Langdon said it was just "too risky" to include the current application in the moratorium. Mayor Pete Emrich said if the door was shut to the developer and the lawsuit was filed, taxpayers would have to foot the bill. Then, he said, if the developer wins the lawsuit, they would get to build the data center anyway and taxpayers would have lost money for nothing. “Thats a loss-loss in my opinion,” Emrich said. Prior to the decision, dozens of commenters shared their concerns about data centers. Things like environmental concerns, noise, water and more were brought up by each commenter. Jeff Walsh, who lives in the Atwater area in the eastern part of the city, a few miles away from where the data center would be built, said that living in the city has become a nightmare. He said the economic benefit, or "fairytales" of what data centers can bring are peddled by those in favor of them. “Please listen to us. The facts are out there,” he said. Charlotte County resident Tim Ritchie left a number of public comments on the subject. During one, he said he was there on behalf of the residents of Charlotte County as the data center would impact the neighboring community as well. He said the 18-month moratorium is a "hoax," and leaders "dropped the ball." He also said the water is simply not available that will be required. Krystal Ortiz said not all development is good development. She said the applicant claims they will use 15,000 to 23,000 gallons of water per day, but she thinks it will be more. The electric load numbers are not yet public which concerns her too, she said. A number of young public commenters told commissioners they were voting on their futures. The applicant pursuing a data center is North Port 300 LLC, which owns land in the largely undeveloped Yorkshire area of eastern North Port. The project called Deep Park includes 896,000 square feet of buildings, including about 123,200 square feet dedicated to office space. The project would include seven data center buildings. Also included in the project are 62 acres of commercial development located closest to Interstate 75, such as restaurants and bars, hotels and some “light industrial” facilities along with 107 acres of apartments and homes, and 112 acres of retail like banks, offices, storage and the data center.

artigo.texto: Ground-breaking ceremony: STRABAG to build infrastructure for a large-scale battery storage facility in Waltrop 22 September 2026 - Forward-looking energy infrastructure supports security of supply and strengthens the energy transition in Germany - Start of development work: A large-scale battery storage park with a capacity of around 900 MW and a storage capacity of approximately 1,800 MWh is being built in Waltrop STRABAG AG is to undertake the construction of the infrastructure for the development and operation of the Waltrop Battery Park, one of Germany’s largest battery storage projects. The plant, developed by Trianel Batteriepark Waltrop GmbH & Co. KG (TBW) is set to make a significant contribution to grid stabilisation, congestion management and increasing the flexibility of the electricity market, with a planned capacity of around 900 MW and a storage capacity of approximately 1,800 MWh. The project is scheduled to come on stream in the second half of 2028. The ground-breaking ceremony on 21 September 2026 marked the first milestone in the construction process. STRABAG is responsible for developing the entire site, thereby laying the groundwork for the construction and operation of the battery storage park. The scope of work also includes the turnkey construction of the associated buildings for the 380 kV substation, as well as the provision of the necessary infrastructure for its construction and operation. Complex construction logistics The project’s location in the port area gives rise to specific requirements. During construction, access to a pipeline crossing the site will be ensured. Equally, ongoing port operations, the use of infrastructure for heavy-goods transport and the need to keep mast sites for existing extra-high-voltage power lines clear are taken into account. Existing groundwater monitoring points are also integrated into the construction processes.

artigo.texto: vHive expande sua plataforma líder do setor de digitalização para o mercado de data centers AGÊNCIA DE COMUNICAÇÃO Conteúdo de responsabilidade da empresa 23 de setembro de 2026 A tecnologia de digitalização da vHive, comprovada em campo, permite que operadores de data centers eliminem a lacuna entre a infraestrutura física e o gerenciamento digital, impulsionando a automação, a otimização do espaço e a precisão. NOVA YORK, 23 de setembro de 2026 /PRNewswire/ — A vHive, líder global em software de digitalização de ativos de ponta a ponta, anunciou hoje a expansão de seu mecanismo WorldTwin AI(TM) para o setor de data centers. Esse movimento estratégico leva a expertise da vHive em Gêmeos Digitais, testada em campo, dos setores de telecomunicações e energia renovável, nos quais a empresa digitalizou com sucesso infraestruturas físicas críticas e complexas para operadoras e empresas de torres em diversos mercados, para atender às necessidades críticas e em rápida evolução do mercado de data centers. Com a aceleração da demanda impulsionada pela IA, os data centers vêm se expandindo a um ritmo sem precedentes, criando ambientes de infraestrutura complexos e em constante transformação. As atuais soluções de gerenciamento de infraestrutura de data center (DCIM) geralmente se concentram nas camadas de rede e lógica, deixando frequentemente uma desconexão com a realidade física da instalação. A vHive preenche essa lacuna ao conectar o físico e o digital e fornecer uma única fonte de verdade que abrange andares, racks e até mesmo equipamentos específicos, beneficiando tanto os operadores da instalação quanto seus clientes de colocation. “Os data centers são a espinha dorsal da economia moderna de IA, mas muitos operadores enfrentam uma ‘lacuna de visibilidade do inventário’ porque seus sistemas digitais estão desconectados dos ativos físicos instalados no local”, disse Yariv Geller, CEO e cofundador da vHive. “Ao aplicarmos os mesmos princípios de IA Física que aperfeiçoamos nos setores de telecomunicações e energia renovável, estamos permitindo que os operadores de data centers deixem para trás as planilhas estáticas e manuais e passem a ter uma compreensão dinâmica, sempre atualizada e estruturada de suas instalações. Estamos criando uma ponte onde o ativo físico, o modelo digital e o software de gestão funcionam como um único sistema.” A solução da vHive automatiza a captura de dados de campo ou de instalações, utilizando tecnologias autônomas para criar Gêmeos Digitais inteligentes e precisos. Isso permite que os operadores cataloguem e mapeiem equipamentos, visualizem a densidade dos racks, identifiquem o espaço disponível no piso e nos racks e acompanhem as mudanças ao longo do tempo, no mesmo ritmo em que a configuração de sua infraestrutura evolui. “O mecanismo extensível WorldTwin AI(TM) da vHive usa nosso modelo proprietário World Model, que permite uma compreensão completa da instalação, possibilitando que os operadores simulem mudanças, identifiquem espaços disponíveis para acelerar a integração de novos clientes e verifiquem o status da construção em relação ao planejamento”, disse Tomer Daniel, CTO e cofundador da vHive. “A expansão das telecomunicações e da energia renovável para os data centers é uma evolução natural para nós. Na verdade, alguns de nossos clientes oferecem ambos os serviços. Seja uma torre de rádio ou um rack de servidores, o principal desafio permanece o mesmo: a necessidade de uma compreensão precisa da infraestrutura por meio de um fluxo de trabalho automatizado e repetível que garanta que os bancos de dados digitais correspondam aos locais físicos.” Os principais benefícios da plataforma de digitalização de data centers da vHive incluem: - Captura de dados simples e automatizada: utilizando câmeras comerciais para inspecionar um centro de dados. - Fonte digital unificada da verdade: concilia registros físicos díspares com o estado real da instalação, desde o layout do andar até os equipamentos individuais montados em racks. - Otimização de espaço e capacidade: identifica instantaneamente unidades de rack não alocadas e espaço livre disponível para maximizar o uso da capacidade e acelerar o retorno do investimento. - Gestão de locatários simplificada: capacita as operações de data centers e os locatários de colocation com visualizações digitais 3D interativas de seus ativos físicos dedicados, aumentando a transparência sem a necessidade de visitas físicas ao local. - Eficiência operacional: automatiza a verificação de estoque, reduzindo o tempo e o trabalho necessários para auditorias e documentação manuais. - Análises avançadas: fornece informações sobre a topologia espacial e a densidade dos racks, permitindo que os operadores otimizem o gerenciamento de energia e refrigeração em ambientes de alta densidade. - Compreensão física: utiliza a IA do World Model da vHive para fornecer recursos de compreensão física que permitem diagnósticos preditivos e fluxos de trabalho de manutenção automatizados. - Conectividade com soluções de monitoramento em tempo real: sobrepõe dados de sensores de monitoramento de energia e temperatura em tempo real a uma representação espacial 3D da instalação. - Alinhamento interdepartamental: elimina os atritos tradicionais entre o planejamento, a construção, as operações e a manutenção por meio de uma fonte única de informações, alinhando a realidade física ao planejamento lógico para uma integração mais rápida dos locatários. Com um histórico comprovado na digitalização de mais de 120 mil ativos de infraestrutura crítica ao redor do mundo, a vHive está em uma posição única para ajudar os operadores de centros de dados a superar os desafios do crescimento em hiperescala e da escassez de talentos. Com a automação do processo de digitalização, a vHive permite que as equipes se concentrem no desempenho e no tempo de atividade, em vez de perderem tempo com a entrada manual de dados e a verificação do local. artigo.texto: The Rise of Battery Storage, Constraints in Supply Chain and a Holistic Path Forward: Jacobs Perspective Dallas-based engineering and solutions provider Jacobs is working on utility-scale, distributed energy and digital infrastructure projects worldwide. The greatest benefit of that diverse workload is seeing generational technology evolution up close on many fronts. And that evolution is diversifying as demand rises and solutions multiply, growing from the singularity of past coal-fired power generation to a diverse set of options with natural gas, solar, wind, hydrogen and large-scale batteries. Energy and infrastructure-sector companies aiming at long-term success must multiply their work in a so-called Industrial Compute Age involving exponential data computing, automation and re-industrialization growth. The commercial and industrial energy transition is scaling up at a pace perhaps not in action since the manufacturing glory days of the 1950s. The only thing slowing down this acceleration might be the supply chain to feed it. “It’s no surprise to see some supply chain constraints,” said Fiachra Ó’Cléirigh, executive vice president and general manager for Energy and Power at Jacobs, in an exclusive interview with EnergyTech.com. “OECD (Organization for Economic Co-Operation and Development) countries are competing for the same supply chain. High demand can cause scarcity.” Time to power: Double-edged sword must swung with care This pressure on the global supply chain is across the board. It might be grid constraint in one sector and lack of resource adequacy in another. The documented shortfall in utility-scale generation is helping drive a movement toward “behind-the-meter” and off-grid power solutions for cloud-based and AI-enabled data facilities which do not want to be chained to delayed utility interconnections for energy. And yet those developers need reasoned counsel on how to do these power connections with safety, resiliency, sustainability and affordability in mind. Time to power is a double-edged sword which must be swung carefully. Some of it might be hype or a bubble, but the overall challenge is critically real and immediate. “One of the challenges for utilities is understanding the load and scaling up to meet what the connected load will be,” Ó’Cléirigh of Jacobs noted. “At the fringes you will see some speculation . . . but . . . utilities are smart people who recognize what the hyperscalers and credible developers look like.” No universal answers, not even behind the meter Next-gen digital infrastructure surely requires vast amounts of energy capacity to empower what AI does, but those companies also are bound by the rules of accounting and affordability like any other business. Projects must meet the cost-benefit threshold as well as the cost curve. So behind-the-meter might not always provide the universal answer, but energy storage certainly plays a part, Ó’Cléirigh told EnergyTech. “You’ve got a very special time in the market, recognizing the value in the market for batteries,” he said. “They can be solutions to problems they couldn’t solve a number of years ago, simply on cost.” Battery storage emerges as a versatile energy jack of all trades Battery storage has long provided balancing services in intermittent renewables such as solar and wind, helping to smooth the so-called “duck curve” as it is known in California, describing when electricity demand is highest and solar capacity is lowest, or vice versa. Installation is never cheap, but lithium-ion battery and storage costs have fallen nearly 90% in the past two decades, according to Bloomberg NEF and other research. These days, battery storage plays in grid services markets, direct-current applications and can respond to transient load fluctuations in AI factories within milliseconds. It matches that versatility with a very competitive price point these days below $80 per MWh, compared to $1,000/MWh in the early 2010s. “The real catalyst” in the growth of battery storage applications “is the cost curve,” Ó’Cléirigh pointed out. “As batteries are more cost-effective, they can provide more solutions. If you go back two decades, the financial cases didn’t stack up because where they were in the cost curve.” Lithium-ion is predominant but only one of the battery technology options available as demand drives innovation and innovation drives new methods. Energy storage project developer BaroMar has contracted Jacobs to develop the preliminary design for a first-ever underwater, long-duration energy storage pilot project off the coast of Cyprus. The 4-MWh pilot utilizes marine technologies and compressed air storage to take excess electricity off the nearby grid and store it below the sea surface at a relatively low levelized cost of energy. Equally exciting on the energy storage versatility front are projects involving Jacobs in Europe and Australia. The former is the 700-kilometer SuedLink high voltage transmission line which is designed to move wind-generated electricity in the North Sea to northern German and its southern states. That’s not all—SuedLink also is designed to move solar power generated in southern Germany up north to other markets. Jacobs also is working on an Australian project which moves hydropower one direction and solar the other. The macro grid still matters Ó’Cléirigh, who is based in Ireland, sees that kind of capability as universal for battery storage in the future. He does see the currently hyped “behind-the-meter” movement as viable within critical limits, but not a universal solution in itself. “Grid-tied and on-site solutions can co-exist,” he said, a viewpoint shared by at least one hyperscaler in Amazon Web Services. AWS is maintaining its utility relationships as it builds out the next generation in its cloud-based networks. The grid is indispensable for what’s coming, even if it is playing catch-up. “It’s a grid buildout, and that’s the bread and butter of what we’ve got to do,

artigo.texto: Gamma Technologies Partners with Illinois-based Energy Solutions Powerhouse Gotion Illinois to Accelerate Next-Generation Battery Design WESTMONT, Ill.–(BUSINESS WIRE)–Gamma Technologies (GT), the leading provider of multi-physics systems simulation software, today announced a strategic partnership with Gotion Illinois, a market-leading energy storage solutions innovator that is also based in Illinois. Gotion Illinois is focused on innovating and delivering the next generation of battery technology, and its Illinois facility reflects that ambition at scale — from raw material intake to EV, data center-ready battery solutions to turnkey energy arbitrage and renewable-supported systems on an industrial scale. The collaboration pairs Gotion Illinois’ global project experience, rapid US growth and technology-forward roadmap with GT’s simulation and productivity platform, enabling faster, more accurate, and more collaborative battery design across the full development lifecycle. Gotion Illinois’ U.S. manufacturing footprint represents one of the most ambitious battery buildouts in the country, spanning raw material processing through finished, deployment-ready battery systems for electric vehicle, data center, and countless commercial and industrial applications. As Gotion Illinois scales this Gigafactory, the company is standardizing on GT-AutoLion to give its manufacturing, design, R&D, chemistry, thermal, controls, and battery engineering teams a single, trusted source of truth — improving speed, efficiency, and cross-team alignment at every stage of cell, module, and pack development. Dr. Nitesh Gupta, Battery Research and Simulation Engineer at Gotion Illinois, said: Working with Gamma Technologies gives our teams a shared, accurate platform we can rely on from raw material selection all the way through pack-level validation, “The ability to de-risk our global supply chain, optimize and size our systems early, and verify performance well before physical testing has fundamentally changed how quickly and confidently, we can move from concept to production.” Across Gotion Illinois’ engineering organization, GT-AutoLion is being used for a range of critical design and validation workflows: - Battery Pack Safety Analysis: GT-AutoLion can capture the decomposition of different species during thermal runaway. Gotion Illinois’s cell team will be scaling this model into different thermal management topologies to evaluate propagation risks. - Design of experiments and model calibration: Gotion Illinois will leverage GT’s productivity tools, including streamlined case setup and DOE capabilities, to evaluate how cell design parameters (such as electrode loading) impact key performance indicators like power density — while also simplifying model calibration. - Pack thermal management and integration: Gotion Illinois’s pack design and integration team is using AutoLion to evaluate different thermal management topologies and incorporate components — including compression pads, busbars, and interconnects — as models scale from cell to module to pack. - Mechanical-electrochemical coupling: Gotion Illinois will explore how different mechanical boundary conditions can impact cell, module, and pack performance. - Next-generation chemistries: Gotion Illinois will be utilizing GT-AutoLion’s material database to evaluate emerging chemistries like sodium-ion and solid-state batteries. - Tool consolidation: Among the most significant benefits Gotion Illinois has identified is the ability to consolidate multiple point tools into a single, unified simulation platform — reducing complexity and improving consistency across teams. Dimple Shah, CEO of Gamma Technologies, said: Gotion Illinois’ scale is remarkable — the sheer volume of raw material coming in, and the EV and data center-ready battery solutions going out, is unlike anything being built from the ground up in the U.S. today, “What makes this partnership so meaningful is how Gotion Illinois is using our platform: as a shared language across manufacturing, design, R&D, chemistry, thermal, controls, and battery engineering teams. From material selection and global supply de-risking to early verification and holistic validation, GT was built to give teams exactly this kind of speed, accuracy, and trust — and we’re proud to support Gotion Illinois as they scale.” GT-AutoLion enables Gotion Illinois to evaluate design trade-offs earlier in the development process, reduce reliance on costly physical prototyping, and give distributed engineering teams a consistent, validated foundation for decision-making — from raw material and cell design through module, pack, and system-level performance. artigo.texto: Advertisement|Remove ads. Shares of Solidion Technology Inc. (STI) surged for a second session on Friday following an explosive triple-digit percentage rally, as the battery technology company shared additional details about the use cases for three new types of lithium batteries it developed. At the time of writing, STI stock was up nearly 100% premarket and was the top percentage gainer on Stocktwits. The company said it has secured patents for its lithium-sulfur, lithium-air, and anodeless lithium metal batteries, which are now ready for commercial use. The lithium-air battery has the potential for the highest energy density capacity and is targeted mainly toward space economy applications. The lithium-sulfur battery, with its mid-range energy density, is suitable for data centers, long-range electric vehicles, aviation, and marine applications. The anodeless lithium metal battery is designed for smaller applications like commercial drones, light electric vehicles, and electronic gadgets. The breakthrough in battery technology comes amid soaring demand for energy, which is at an all-time high this year, largely driven by the aggressive buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure and extreme weather conditions. Moreover, the excitement around space exploration and NASA’s plans to establish a Moon Base has opened up an opportunity for alternative energy providers to provide their offerings that can be deployed outside Earth. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment about the STI stock remained in ‘extremely bullish’ territory amid ‘extremely high’ message volume over the last 24 hours. One user on the platform called the rally “a massive multi-day run.” Another user wrote: “battery sector finally getting its momentum.” STI stock has more than tripled in value so far this year and has surged sixfold over the last 12 months, outperforming the S&P 500. artigo.texto: LA VERNE, Calif. (KABC) -- A fire erupted at a battery storage unit at a Metropolitan Water District facility in La Verne on Tuesday, prompting nearby schools to evacuate. The lithium battery fire was reported around 11:40 a.m. near a solar panel field on the northeast side of the facility in the 3200 block of Wheeler Avenue. Crews from the La Verne Fire Department and Los Angeles County Fire Department responded. One employee suffered minor injuries and was taken to a local hospital, according to La Verne Fire Department Battalion Chief Mark Savage. Shortly after 3 p.m., the L.A. County Fire Department said the fire had been knocked down. AIR7 video shows firefighters dousing the flames with water. La Verne fire crews were still monitoring the scene and mopping up, noting that there was still a risk, with more lithium batteries at the site. By Tuesday evening, no flare-ups had been reported, and crews were using a drone to monitor the batteries. Firefighters estimate there are fewer than 20 lithium batteries in the storage facility. "These things do not like any kind of additional heat, and the understanding is, there is something going on with that bank now that it is reacting to the previous heat that it was exposed to," said Batt. Chief Mark Savage. "So we are monitoring closely. We have reinitiated cooling measures for that battery bank now. But it's one of those things that, once it gets started, it's extremely difficult to stop, if not impossible to stop." The fire prompted evacuation orders and warnings near Bonita Avenue and Wheeler Avenue and a shelter-in-place for the surrounding residential neighborhood. Click here to see if you are in an impacted area. Some evacuation orders were later downgraded to warnings. By early Tuesday evening, firefighters said the orders were only impacting the approximately 185 properties closest to the facility. La Verne police said shopping centers along Wheeler Avenue north of Foothill Boulevard were evacuated as a precaution. Grace Miller Elementary School, located just east of the facility, was under a shelter-in-place order, and Holly Oak Street south of the campus was closed to traffic. Savage said students appeared to be released from the school while firefighters battled the blaze. Parents told Eyewitness News that Ramona Middle School and Bonita High School were also affected. Holy Name of Mary School, Damien High School and the University of La Verne were evacuated. The university said all classes were canceled until further notice. Eyewitness News spoke to Ramona Middle School parents who arrived to pick up their kids. By the time most parents arrived, it was already the school's normal pick-up time. "They're blocking off Wheeler, so it makes it a little hectic but scary at the same time, so we're just here getting the kids out of safety," said parent Irene Flores. "We got it on our phones, the emergency message to evacuate our facility. So might as well come get the kids, make sure they're safe," said parent Jason Wagner. "In La Verne, we've never seen these kind of things." The Metropolitan Water District said its water supply was not affected by the fire. The cause of the fire is still under investigation. Savage said nothing like this has happened there before, but it's raising concerns for neighbors who had no clue that the water treatment plant housed massive battery banks with the potential to catch fire. If you're wondering if you live near a facility that houses potentially dangerous or hazardous items, you can find out. Back in May, 7 On Your Side did an investigation and we shared the Environmental Protection Agency's interactive map, where you can learn about the enforcement and compliance history of facilities near you. City News Service contributed to this report.

artigo.texto: Brazil has expanded a sustainable farming support programme, applying it to four carbon removal technologies and boosting the potential for removals by 500 million tonnes in this decade, an official said on Monday. The Brazilian Low-Carbon Agriculture (ABC) Plan provides subsidies for farmers to use sustainable farming practices and carbon removal (CDR) methods, such as below-market interest rates. With the eight technologies it has so far covered, the government aims to capture 1.1 billion tonnes of CO2e between 2020-30. But last Wednesday, the government approved the addition of four CDR technologies: biochar, enhanced rock weathering (ERW), bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS), and soil organic carbon (SOCs), according to Eduardo Bastos, president of the Agrocarbon Chamber under Brazil’s Ministry of Agriculture, and chair of the Brazilian Agribusiness Association. “It’s really, really recent, not even published in the papers, but we just got the approval to include four more technologies,” he told the Puro.earth CDR Summit during Climate Week NYC. “That, combined, can capture more than 500 mln tonnes.” The ABC Plan initially supported six technologies in its first decade, from 2010-20, including recovery of degraded pastures, no-till farming, planted forests, and animal waste management. It had already added two more for the second 10-year run, from 2020-30 – bio-inputs, which maximise the use of natural materials instead of agrochemicals, and sustainable irrigation systems – before approving the CDR methods last week. That potential for carbon removals sounds huge, but it fits with Brazil’s wider plans to tackle agriculture emissions by recovering about 40 mln hectares or more of degraded land, said Bastos. That’s about the size of the Netherlands and Germany. “Brazil is at 850 mln ha, but we are talking about including 40 mln more of degraded lands into productive lands. So we will need all the carbon technologies we can deliver on the ground to help farmers to produce more food, feed, and fuel,” he said. “It’s fully interlinked.” Selling carbon credits from the removals will further help to lower interest rates for farmers, Bastos added. Agriculture is a significant contributor to Brazilian greenhouse gas emissions, he noted. Deforestation is the biggest, accounting for around 1.2 bln tonnes out of 2.1 bln in total. That’s followed by agriculture, with around 643 mln tonnes, of which around 500 mln is methane from livestock. Also, the agricultural sector has been excluded from Brazil’s emissions trading system (Portuguese: SBCE), slated to come online around 2031. Senate lawmakers in 2023 exempted it, recasting agriculture as a sometime generator of carbon credits for the voluntary market and the SBCE – not a participant in cap-and-trade. Government programmes like the ABC Plan help to provide security for carbon removal developers, said Chloe Bigio, chief commercial officer of InPlanet, an ERW developer in Brazil. “We have that scale [of farmland] and that opportunity in Brazil. We have the feedstock. We have the right weather conditions. We have the right expertise from an agronomic perspective,” she said. “But then there is a sense of security that a company gets from the policies, the law.” Bolivia, similarly, is moving to build a climate investment framework that provides investor certainty for developers, including carbon removals, Jorge Avila, Bolivia’s vice minister of environment, biodiversity, climate change, and forest management and development, told the Puro event. The Framework Law for Climate and Biodiversity Finance is in the final stages of legislative approval, expected to be wrapped up in the coming weeks, a Bolivian source said on the sidelines. In what Avila called a turning point for the country, the law will create: a national agency responsible for registering projects, ensuring compliance, and providing technical support; a national carbon registry; and a high-level governance body to ensure transparency, equal participation, and strategic oversight. China imposed a 2% levy on lithium-ion batteries, used in electric vehicles and energy storage systems, from Sept 1, which rises to 4% on the same date in 2027. Beijing announced in July that it would end a decade-long exemption for solar and lithium-ion batteries from consumption taxes, as part of efforts to rein in intense competition in industries central to the clean-energy transition. After the July announcement, some customers began taking delivery of batteries ahead of schedule in anticipation of the tax, according to Lin. Unlike the EV battery business, energy-storage projects often have fixed budgets and financing approvals, “making it difficult to pass on additional costs,” he said in Ningde, where CATL is headquartered. Lin said the company’s energy storage output was in line with expectations for the year so far, with production-line utilisation above 90%. He attributed this to an investment boom in domestic standalone energy storage projects and early deliveries of overseas orders due to export tax rebate changes, which are keeping capacity high for the fourth quarter. China’s energy-storage sector has developed rapidly over the past few years, boosted by surging demand both at home and abroad. While global demand is expected to maintain strong growth next year, Lin said domestic demand will be harder to predict. “We’re seeing that returns on energy storage projects in many provinces are now declining, and investment in many projects is being paused or postponed. So there may be some fluctuations next year,” he added. Uploaded by Liza Shireen Koshy

artigo.texto: What are consumers who fixate on battery performance when shopping for cars afraid of? If we take 2021 as the inflection point for the accelerated sales growth of new energy vehicles in China, this round of popularization has gone through five years by this year. As the driving range and service time continue to accumulate, some problems that were not obvious in the early stage have gradually emerged, among which the power battery has attracted the most attention. Last year, a Chinese self-owned brand filed a lawsuit against a second-tier power battery supplier over cell quality and related losses; earlier this year, a luxury brand launched a global recall for some vehicles due to the risk of overheating in partial battery modules that may cause fires; a few months later, the "banana battery" incident once again sparked huge public controversy. Apart from safety incidents, battery issues are also increasingly frequently included in daily vehicle complaint cases. The Q2 2026 report released by CarQuality.cn shows that "power battery failure" entered the TOP 20 new energy vehicle complaint problems for the first time, ranking 6th, with the number of fault complaints doubling month-on-month; in the same period, the complaint volume of pure electric vehicles increased by 70.2% month-on-month. Regulatory standards are also tightening accordingly. The mandatory national standard GB 38031—2025 *Safety Requirements for Traction Batteries Used in Electric Vehicles* issued by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology has been implemented since July 1, 2026, further strengthening safety requirements such as "no fire, no explosion". Authorities including the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology have previously required vehicle manufacturers and power battery enterprises to jointly investigate abnormalities in temperature, voltage, current, insulation and other indicators, and form a closed loop of risk warning, fault handling and after-sales service. Most consumers are unable to study every parameter and test item of batteries one by one; after an accident, it is also difficult for them to identify which link the responsibility lies in on their own. For ordinary people, one of the most intuitive solutions is to find a trustworthy battery brand, and then include models equipped with that brand's batteries in their selection range. A large number of consumers have chosen CATL to take on this role. According to NielsenIQ's 2026 Global New Energy Vehicle Consumer Research Report, 37.1% of Chinese respondents said they would consider giving up purchasing their desired model if it is not equipped with CATL batteries. The era has come when a single battery can determine whether a vehicle is purchased or not. 01 Why do consumers choose vehicles based on battery brands? In the era of fuel vehicles, few people would ask who supplies the fuel tank or a core component of the engine before buying a car. In the era of new energy vehicles, however, batteries can hardly stay hidden behind the vehicle brand, as they determine safety, driving range, energy replenishment efficiency, vehicle residual value and long-term maintenance cost at the same time. In the NielsenIQ survey, 80% of Chinese respondents believe that battery is the key factor determining the safety of new energy vehicles, and another 80% think that battery quality represents the overall quality of the vehicle. The gap between the actual driving range and the nominal driving range is the most prominent pain point in current battery experience; the charging speed presents a mismatch of "high importance, low satisfaction". For car owners, these problems will finally converge into a simple judgment: after several years, the battery determines whether the car can still complete daily travel safely and stably. The difficulty lies in that a power battery never works independently as a single cell. Cells, modules, Pack structure, thermal management system, software warning and vehicle layout together form the safety chain. Any deviation in any link may be manifested as a "battery problem". The recall of a new vehicle-making force brand is a direct example: the risk source points to the anti-corrosion performance of coolant, while the final disposal covers coolant, power battery and front motor controller. Commercial disputes can also reflect the complexity of responsibility boundaries. Last year, a Chinese self-owned brand filed a lawsuit against a second-tier power battery supplier over cell quality and related losses. It also takes a long process for carmakers and suppliers to clarify the responsibilities among cells, system integration, verification standards and actual use scenarios. Similar problems did not appear for the first time. In 2019, multiple fire accidents occurred after a model under the new energy brand of a traditional carmaker was launched. A senior executive of the carmaker's battery business summarized the responsibility attribution dilemma in the industry at that time very directly: vehicle manufacturers may look for causes from the battery, while battery enterprises will also check the vehicle system design; some accidents cannot be fully reproduced in the laboratory, and the legal proof and compensation boundaries are very complicated. When the responsibility division is inherently difficult, the subsequent handling can hardly fully meet the expectations of car owners. Therefore, brands begin to play the role of "risk compressor". The NielsenIQ survey shows that 79% of respondents believe there are obvious quality differences between different battery brands, 79% think that well-known and high-quality battery brands will increase their willingness to buy cars, and 76% are willing to pay extra fees for that. artigo.texto: The rapid expansion of data centers has become one of the most tangible expressions of the artificial intelligence revolution. But debate about their environmental, economic and social impact threatens their future development. And rightly so. Every cloud service and AI application depends on massive physical infrastructure that takes up land, consumes energy, uses water and requires ever-increasing investment. International experience suggests that as the data center industry scales up, tensions emerge. In Ireland, data centers accounted for 21 percent of the country’s electricity consumption in 2023 and could reach 32 percent this year. In the US, their share of demand is expected to triple from 4 percent in 2023 to a projected 12 percent by 2028. No surprise, then, that this is a source of growing political and public concern. A Gallup poll found that 71 percent of Americans oppose data center construction in their local community. Beyond concerns over energy and water consumption, evidence increasingly points to other unwelcome local effects. Researchers at Cambridge University have identified what they call a “data heat island effect,” whereby large facilities can raise temperatures in surrounding areas. Given these realities, the question isn’t whether data centers are needed — they are — but how they are developed. What type of data centers do we need? And who will govern their expansion? Economic experience teaches a simple lesson: that proactive regulation is more effective than reactive intervention. And it’s certainly much better than no intervention at all. Having clear rules from the start makes it possible to separate responsible projects from unsustainable ones, align private incentives with public interests and ensure that investment and growth go hand in hand with protecting critical resources and communities. International experience is, again, instructive. Ireland tightened its rules only after data centers became a major source of pressure on the electricity grid. In the US, the state of New York has adopted a temporary moratorium, and a growing number of projects have faced delays or cancellation as local resistance intensified. The lesson could not be plainer: Failing to plan and regulate up front ends up being costlier and less effective. Spain is still a long way from facing that kind of pressure. And yet, our healthy economy and renewable capacity has sparked huge investor interest in building data centers, meaning their energy needs are certain to outstrip expectations. Current estimates of electricity demand for computing power run as high as 4 gigawatts by 2030, but requests and permits granted for this type of facility exceed that target several times over. While many of these projects are unlikely to materialize, the rapid upward trend is obvious. We are approaching a tipping point, and we must act to stay ahead. In August, my government launched a public consultation on a new regulatory framework designed to do exactly that. The proposal starts from a straightforward principle: Access to the electricity grid is a scarce strategic asset and should not be held up by projects that lack credibility, viability or a meaningful contribution to the economy and society. Our proposal introduces energy- and water-efficiency standards. Data centers will have to disclose key performance indicators, letting us assess and compare their resource use and discourage waste. Any increase in electricity demand must also be accompanied by additional renewable capacity. The framework includes requirements to make sure that a significant portion of data center consumption is supported by newly built clean-energy projects. The logic is economic and environmental. Large new power consumers should not compete with existing demand or drive greater reliance on fossil fuels; they should help catalyze investment in the energy transition. The regulation recognizes, too, that data centers are a strategic asset. In a world where Europe still relies heavily on non-European digital capabilities, the framework combines safeguards on how data is controlled — and how the infrastructure is managed — with incentives designed to expand Europe’s technology sector and strengthen the continent’s sovereignty. Our objective must be to trade in bytes, not in watts. Spain wants to fully capture the opportunities created by data centers and AI. Yet the challenge is making sure the infrastructure expands in line with the capacity of the power system, that valuable energy resources are directed toward useful projects and that this all makes Europe less dependent technologically. The goal is not to slow down growth or constrain innovation. Quite the opposite: It is to ensure that they remain economically sustainable, and environmentally and socially fair. Countries that understand this will be the ones best positioned to lead the next phase of the digital economy. Pedro Sanchez Pedro Sanchez is the prime minister of Spain. He wrote this for Bloomberg Opinion. The views expressed here are the writer's own. — Ed. (Tribune Content Agency) khnews@heraldcorp.com

A demanda da empresa é para […] Fazenda avalia impacto do Redata no orçamento para enviar MP ao Congresso Rafael Bitencourt, da Agência iNFRA O assessor especial do Ministério da Fazenda Igor Marchesini disse nesta terça-feira (19) que o governo está finalizando estudos sobre o impacto da isenção de tributos para o setor de data centers, previsto no programa Redata, para enviar a MP (Medida Provisória) sobre o tema ao Congresso Nacional. “[A MP] […] ANEEL discute o quanto pode avançar sobre cortes para geração distribuída, diz diretora Marisa Wanzeller, da Agência iNFRA A diretora da ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) Agnes Costa disse nesta quarta-feira (23) que a reguladora está discutindo “o quanto pode ou não avançar” em cortes obrigatórios (chamados de curtailment) para MMGD (Micro e Minigeração Distribuída), “juridicamente e tecnicamente”. A diretora relata a CP (Consulta Pública) 45/2019, que […] Ação do BNDES para reindustrialização do Nordeste prevê aplicação de R$ 10 bi da Agência iNFRA O BNDES (Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social) destinará R$ 10 bilhões em projetos de inovação, reindustrialização e desenvolvimento sustentável. O anúncio foi feito na última quarta-feira (16), durante reunião estratégica entre o banco de fomento e a Fiec (Federação das Indústrias do Estado do Ceará). De acordo com o órgão, […]

artigo.texto: Supercapacitors are well positioned to see deployment in data centers, in order to solve the challenge of protecting data center equipment from rapid power demand surges and voltage drops caused by AI training and prompting. In total, the market for supercapacitors in data centers is expected to reach over US$950 million by 2037 according to IDTechEx's recent report "Supercapacitors for Data Centers 2027-2037: Technologies, Applications, Players and Forecasts." However, several questions remain for supercapacitor deployers and data center operators: where and how exactly should supercapacitors be effectively deployed? AI Data Usage Patterns - Voltage Sags, Peak Shaving and Critical Load Requirements Hyperscale data centers are seeing significant construction, driven primarily by deployment of AI across a number of industries and services. AI data centers have distinct power demand profiles compared to conventional data centers, due to large transient loads and short-term peaks in power demand. These spikes can be challenging for conventional power architecture to handle. Extreme power demand spikes lead to voltage sags, which in turn can lead to temporary shutting down of servers, equipment failures and grid-wide instability. Solving these issues can help to make AI data centers both more profitable and more palatable for neighboring authorities and locations that might otherwise oppose development. Power architecture and backup power systems must therefore be adapted to handle AI power profiles. This requires rapid charging/discharging times (as spikes can be at ms-scale), durability over many charge-discharge cycles, high power density (to reduce footprint for large critical loads) and easy integration into existing power architectures (especially for retrofitting of data centers). Supercapacitors are well positioned for this use-case, as is explored in IDTechEx's recent report. Data Center Architecture Data center designs vary depending on the data center type, location and power supply. However, several features of data center power architectures are consistent. Computations are performed by servers within a rack, which also contains switches, routers, storage and rack-level backup power, e.g. battery backup units (BBUs). Multiple racks are placed together to form an aisle, at the end of which is the power distribution unit (PDU), which routes power to the racks from the facility's centralized power room and includes buffering devices to protect equipment from power surges. The facility's centralized power room will contain both power architecture connecting the facility to the grid, or routing electricity from the grid connection point to the aisles, as well as uninterruptible power supply (UPS), in the form of battery storage units, which will be turned on automatically in the event of a blackout, to bridge the gap between grid outage and diesel generator activation. Supercapacitors may be deployed at rack-, aisle- and UPS room-level, offering different advantages and disadvantages depending on placement. Supercapacitor Placement: In-Rack, In-Aisle or In UPS Facility In-rack supercapacitor placements, e.g. within BBUs, are likely to be optimal for new-build AI data centers. This is because in-rack deployment allows for voltage stabilization of low-voltage equipment within the rack/server, which might not otherwise be sufficiently protected from power demand surges at the rack-level. In addition, by deploying at the rack-level, supercapacitor deployments can be made more specific, thereby potentially reducing the overall power demand. For example, in a data center in which not all racks will be utilized for AI, or in which training/prompting is split from standard computation, supercapacitor deployments at rack-level may be limited to appropriate racks. However, aisle-level and UPS room-level deployments are likely to be easier in terms of retrofitting, as well as allowing for higher compute density within the rack. IDTechEx predicts that this will lead to aisle-level and UPS room-level deployments being more popular in the short term, especially in co-location data centers. UPS room-level deployments offer an additional advantage compared to rack-level deployments, in that a rack-level deployment will not protect high-voltage equipment and power architecture at the facility level, for example cooling systems. As a result, IDTechEx predicts that by 2037, rack-level and UPS room-level deployments will be the most popular for supercapacitors in data centers. For a more detailed analysis of supercapacitor placement, as well as application and use-case analysis, see the recent report by IDTechEx: "Supercapacitors for Data Centers 2027-2037: Technologies, Applications, Players and Forecasts".

artigo.texto: Yasin Yehya Crowcon Detection Instruments Yasin Yehya is a Product Manager at Crowcon Detection Instruments with over 10 years of experience in gas detection, hazardous-area safety, and industrial flame and gas systems. His background spans product management, technical sales, and engineered safety solutions, giving him a practical perspective on both the technology and the challenges customers face in the field. He works across global product strategy, certification, portfolio development, and market applications, with a particular interest in functional safety, hazardous-area certification, and emerging industrial safety technologies. He is passionate about turning complex technical challenges and customer needs into practical safety solutions—because safety-critical technology doesn’t have to be complicated or boring.

artigo.texto: News Should Tesla move away from its battery technology? Should Tesla replace its current battery system when it works so well? The 18650 battery cells Tesla Motors has been using in its Model S, have proven to perform very well compared to other types of battery chemistries on the market. The cylindrical battery which measures 18 mm wide and 65 mm in height, hence its name 18/650, has been the main component of Tesla’s battery pack, but could there be a possibility that it would soon move away from this proven technology? Tesla isn’t married to 18650 Tesla Chief Technology Officer JB Straubel has recently said the company isn’t married to cylindrical cells and the company would move to flat cell manufacturing if and when there are greater advantages to replacing the 18650. This has started speculations in the world of investors, yet again. News Tesla Semi lands the biggest electric truck deal in U.S. history Tesla leads a record 2,500 truck order, but not every truck will be a Semi. Tesla has landed the largest electric truck order in U.S. history. ZET SCALE, a new alliance of shippers and carriers, named Tesla its primary manufacturer on Tuesday for an initial order of 2,500 electric Class 8 trucks. The deal alone would nearly double the number of electric heavy trucks operating in the country. According to the press release from Catalyst Mobility, the nonprofit formerly known as CALSTART, Kenworth, RIDE and Volvo were also selected as secondary manufacturers that carriers can pick if their operations call for it. No split between the four brands has been published, so the exact number of Semis in the order is not yet known. Tesla was selected as the primary OEM for the largest electric Class 8 order in the US by ZET SCALE, a new shippers’ alliance With 2,500 Semis on order, this will double the entire US electric Class 8 fleet We’re serious about scale, and ZET SCALE is too!… pic.twitter.com/IiTAdzgken — Tesla Semi (@tesla_semi) September 22, 2026 Tesla won the top slot through a competitive request for proposals. The alliance, which Catalyst Mobility runs with the Smart Freight Centre, scored bidders on price, range, charging capability and production capacity. Pooling freight demand from founding shippers, including Microsoft and PepsiCo, let every truck maker bid lower than it would for a single fleet. “The Tesla Semi is designed for lower cost per mile operations than diesel,” said Dan Priestley, director of the Tesla Semi program, as noted in the press release. The financing is built to pull in carriers who have avoided electric trucks. ZET Financial is issuing the purchase order for all 2,500 units and will place them with fleets through a fair market value lease. The trucks will be deployed over the next few years across 10 freight hubs in Los Angeles, Stockton, Bakersfield, Seattle and Tacoma, Houston, Dallas, San Antonio, Chicago, Atlanta, and the Newark and New York area. ZET SCALE says the first order is only the opening round, with a longer term goal of 10,000 trucks or more. Even if Tesla ends up with only a majority share, it would still be the biggest Semi deal to date. Einride’s 500 unit order in August was the previous record, and WattEV’s 370 truck order in May was the largest California deal at the time. Einride’s CEO has since said he expects all 500 trucks delivered by the end of 2027. The announcement lands two days before Tesla formally inaugurates its Semi factory in Nevada on September 24. The 1.7 million square foot plant sits next to Gigafactory Nevada’s 4680 cell lines and is designed for 50,000 trucks a year. artigo.texto: Ireland proposes deal to end spat over EU carbon market permits Ireland proposed a compromise plan to adjust the European Union’s carbon market supply controls, seeking to end a dispute between member states over surplus emission allowances. Ireland, which holds the EU rotating presidency until the end of this year, wants to introduce additional assurances a broader reform of the emission trading system should gradually tighten the limit on excessive carbon permits kept in a reserve for potential interventions Ireland's plan was on Monday shared with member states as part of talks on revising the Market Stability Reserve (MSR) regulation, according to people with knowledge of the issue. The design of the MSR, which absorbs surplus permits from the market and can release them in the case of price shocks, has divided EU member states as the bloc seeks to reconcile its ambitious climate policies with the need to protect its industry in the face of rising energy prices and tougher global competition. The revision of the reserve was originally put forward by the European Commission in April, after EU leaders called on the bloc’s executive to take steps to reduce energy costs that were already stubbornly high before the Iran war. The proposal was to make the MSR more flexible by scrapping invalidation of permits it absorbs from the market and keeping them usable for potential future interventions. The Irish presidency will seek agreement on the MSR on Wednesday, said a spokesperson for the presidency, adding the proposal was time-sensitive and European leaders had called for its urgent adoption. The goal was to reach a fast deal on the MSR adjustment to calm the market and then discuss potential further changes during a broader reform of the ETS, which the commission unveiled in July and member states discuss separately. The MSR became a key feature of the ETS in 2019, when it began absorbing surplus permits from the market once a certain threshold of allowances in circulation was reached. The legislation currently in force invalidates any allowances held in the reserve above a threshold of 400 million on January 1 each year. The commission sought to overturn that provision to build a bigger buffer of permits that could be used to stabilise the market. Earlier this month, Ireland proposed letting the excess allowances sit in the MSR until the end of 2030. From the start of 2031, the reserve could keep up to 800 million allowances, with the level to be potentially reduced during the post-2030 reform of the ETS. In a last-minute push to further tighten the regulation, Germany called for an annual 4% reduction of the threshold starting in 2028, in line with the declining emissions cap. The country also wants to maintain the rate at which the MSR absorbs allowances at 24%, and to reduce the level triggering the withdrawal of surplus permits from circulation. It should be set at 650 million compared with the current 833 million. The German proposal was opposed by a group of countries including Poland and the Czech Republic. In its new compromise, the Irish presidency is seeking to resolve the spat by embedding in the deal an additional commitment to include in the broader ETS reform an annual reduction of the limit on surplus permits in the reserve. The proposal will be discussed on Wednesday by ambassadors representing member states to the EU. If they reach a deal, it will become their stance for talks with the European Parliament on the final shape of the MSR regulation.

artigo.texto: Multiple residents sought answers and raised concerns over a proposed data center during a 2nd Ward meeting Tuesday night. A zoning analysis application has been submitted for 1265 Hartrey Ave. to determine whether a “computer processing center” would be a permitted use for the site. Ald. Krissie Harris (2nd), said during the ward meeting she had not seen a formal proposal for the data center, and would not make a decision on it until she had more information about the proposal and discussed it with the property owner. “I don’t have an opinion yet because I have not heard what it is, I know circumstantially about data systems and data centers, but I don’t know firsthand, and I always try to get my information before I make a decision,” she said. Harris clarified that while she had previously met with the building’s owner to discuss a separate proposal for an energy storage facility, she had not discussed the proposed data center with them yet. A 4th Ward resident said she had “extreme concerns” about the environmental, economic and sociological impacts of having a data center in Evanston, and she expected the city to be a “leader in the nation” in ensuring these centers would not impact the community. Meanwhile resident Michael Courier expressed concerns over data centers disproportionately using more energy and water than other technologies, as well as opposition to artificial intelligence since he saw it harming workers and people’s way of life. “Evanston should not be complicit in the technologies that destroy what we hold dear and everything we love about this city,” he said. Prior to the ward meeting, Courier was outside the Robert Crown Center distributing leaflets expressing opposition against data centers. Reed Beidler of Lark Management, told Evanston Now the proposed facility would be a “rowboat” compared to the massive data centers that have faced fierce opposition throughout the country. According to a memo provided by Beidler, the proposed data center, which would have between four to eight full-time employees, would be contained entirely within the existing building envelope, and the existing utility infrastructure would be able to support the new facility.
