artigo.texto: TEXAS — Mason McCallister said it was an act of God that sent him down a gravel road near his home in Bells, Texas, one Sunday last December. It wasn't the normal route he and his family take back from church, but he decided to detour so his daughters could shout hello to their grandmother as they drove by her home. What he saw that day catapulted him into a debate playing out around the country — and especially in Texas — over data centers. It's one that may now affect the outcome of key elections in the Lone Star State. As they rolled past, flashes of red caught McCallister's eye among the lush green of the area's gentle hills. "Driving down that road, I just see survey markers everywhere," McCallister, a real estate agent, told CNBC. "And I knew at that time what was happening. I could feel it" — a data center is coming, he said. McCallister's home is less than a mile from the survey markers, in a rural stretch between Dallas and the Oklahoma border. He and his wife, Heather, built the house on 26 acres, where they keep three horses and a donkey and host frequent family gatherings at a long farmhouse table on their spacious back patio. The outcry over data centers — warehouses that contain the hardware for powering artificial intelligence and other technology — was only a faint murmur when McCallister first saw the survey markers. In the months since, it's become a dull roar, as increasingly more projects are proposed and built, and general anxiety over AI and its potentially humanity-ending powers grows. Across Texas and the country, people have flooded local meetings to protest proposed projects, citing concerns about the use of water and other resources, noise and light pollution, rising utility costs and falling property values. Some towns and cities have moved to block their development, as anti-data center advocacy groups and social media pages proliferate. Polling shows the economy and cost of living are top of mind for voters in the runup to the 2026 midterm elections. But some political strategists say data centers are a potent enough issue that they could shift the balance of power in Texas, potentially paving the way for Democrats to win statewide for the first time since 1994. Democrats have their sights set on the governor's mansion, as well as an open U.S. Senate seat, and the outcome of the Senate race could determine control of Congress. Populists on both the left and the right — including Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Josh Hawley, R-Mo. — were quick to try to rein in data centers and protect consumers against associated utility cost increases. But Democrats have broadly staked out a clear position against data centers, as President Donald Trump cheers development of new facilities. That dynamic has left Republicans — including Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, who is running for reelection, and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is running for Senate — playing defense as public opinion turns against the facilities. "I don't think Republicans have a clear, standard message on data centers and AI at this moment," said Brendan Steinhauser, a GOP strategist and CEO of The Alliance for Secure AI Action, who has called data centers a "sleeper issue" of this election cycle. The survey markers set McCallister on a hunt for answers that included knocking on neighbors' doors, approaching surveyors in fields near his house, chasing down local officials and eventually cornering Rhett Bennett, the CEO of Black Mountain, a Fort Worth-based energy and natural resources development company he discerned had designs on the land. Black Mountain did not respond to multiple requests for comment from CNBC about the potential project. But McCallister said Bennett — whom he confronted at a public meeting, with a Texas Tribune reporter in tow — confirmed the company was exploring a data center near his house. McCallister fears that if it is completed, it could effectively envelop his property. McCallister said he and his wife never planned to sell their house, so any potential hit to their property value isn't particularly worrying. He says his primary concerns are water and power usage. Other data center opponents CNBC spoke with in Texas said they were concerned about noise and light pollution as well as the long-term economic and job displacement impacts of AI, which some of the facilities power. More than anything, the ordeal has made McCallister — who said he's a lifelong Republican and voted for Trump three times — question his political leanings. The GOP, he said, has been too slow to react. "I'm definitely frustrated with the Republican Party. I have gone literally out of my way to warn them, to tell them what's happening," he said. "Y'all should have picked up on this much earlier than y'all did." 'Let Data Reign' Trump's outright dismissal of data center concerns and his reluctance to regulate rapidly evolving AI have complicated the issue for Republican leaders such as Abbott and Paxton, who are fighting for their political lives in one of the most closely watched states in the 2026 election. "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign," Trump posted on Truth Social on Aug. 31. With Trump's unyielding stance on the issue, Abbott and Paxton face a dilemma: Either they defy Trump, the de facto head of the Republican Party, and their donors with tech and data center-industry connections. Or they anger a sizable bloc of data center opponents that has emerged within their base. Fifty-seven percent of Texas voters polled by the Texas Politics Project said they opposed a data center being built in their community, including 43% of Republicans, 54% of independents and 60% of rural voters. artigo.texto: Opposition to data centers continues to mount in the US. That’s according to research group Data Center Watch, which said some 45 data center projects worth $68 billion were blocked or delayed by local pushback between April and June this year. Communities across the country are now pushing through moratoriums on new construction, often before developers can apply for permissions. Some 30 statehouses introduced or adopted rules pertaining to issues such as data center siting, electricity and water, the group said in a report Sept. 21 provided to Bloomberg News. The research quantifies growing concern about the rapid pace of expansion of artificial intelligence, both in the construction of new computing clusters and its proliferation into daily life. There are now 843 opposition groups across 49 states, with Hawaii the exception. “New groups continue to emerge, opposition is appearing across a wide range of states and jurisdictions, and online petition signatures continue to grow,” lead analyst Miquel Vila said. Data Center Watch is a project from AI intelligence company 10a Labs. Home to the biggest investors in AI infrastructure, the US is experiencing a bipartisan backlash against facilities that critics say harm the environment and siphon away resources in order to fuel AI systems that many fear will imperil jobs and livelihoods. Tech giants like Amazon.com Inc., Meta Platforms Inc., Microsoft Corp. and Alphabet Inc. — the so-called hyperscalers — argue they need the facilities to win a race against China to develop potentially world-changing AI. President Donald Trump has dismissed opposition to data centers and concern about advances in AI as a “sick conspiracy,” saying “the only one that is happy about it is China.” The number and value of disrupted projects fluctuates by quarter, with the first three months of this year seeing 75 cases worth roughly $130 billion facing opposition in the US. The 45 projects affected during the second quarter represented more than half of all new large-scale developments Data Center Watch began tracking during the period. Opposition by public figures and the use of social media are amplifying concerns. One petition against a project in Tennessee garnered over 500,000 signatures on online activism platform Change.org, accounting for more than one third of those on the service during the quarter, Data Center Watch said. For the first time since it began its research two years ago, Data Center Watch also reported on protests against data centers outside the US, given increased international opposition. Much as in the US, local campaigns are targeting specific projects, governments’ planning authorizations and worries about resource usage, sometimes coordinating nationally. The group highlighted opposition across European nations, Australia, South Africa and beyond. “As with many other trends, the US has generally been at the forefront, but the phenomenon is increasingly becoming global,” said Vila. “We anticipate that this will just become more prominent as data center development expands across the globe.” Photo: A Microsoft Azure and Amazon Web Services data center in Aldie, Virginia. artigo.texto: La Verne lithium battery storage fire forces evacuations near water district facility LOS ANGELES - Evacuation orders were issued after a fire broke out at an outdoor lithium battery storage unit near a solar panel field at a Metropolitan Water District facility in La Verne Tuesday. What we know: The fire was reported around 11:40 a.m. at the facility in the 3200 block of Wheeler Avenue. According to the La Verne Fire Department, a small explosion occurred in the battery unit which stored lithium batteries. Hazmat crews were brought in, and fire crews were mainly spraying the area with water to prevent the flames from spreading. Metropolitan said the water supply was not affected. Nearby neighborhoods evacuated Due to the hazardous nature of lithium batteries, evacuation orders were issued in the areas around the facility. La Verne police said shopping centers along Wheeler north of Foothill Boulevard were evacuated as a precaution. Shelter-in-place orders were issued for Grace Elementary School and Bonita High School. An evacuation center was established at the La Verne Community Center on 3680 D St. By 2:30 p.m., the fire was mainly out. The fire department said one civilian was injured and taken to a hospital. No additional details were released. A short time after that, some evacuation orders were downgraded to warnings, while others were reduced to advisories. artigo.texto: CBTS acquires Recovery Point Systems, adding disaster recovery services and data center space The Cincinnati technology services company is adding managed disaster recovery, ransomware recovery, and a Tier III data center in Maryland through the deal, which follows a new chief technology officer and the launch of its Forge Agents AI platform earlier this month. CBTS has acquired Recovery Point Systems, a Maryland-based disaster recovery provider. The deal adds managed recovery services and company-owned data center space to the Cincinnati company's infrastructure, cloud and security business. CBTS announced the acquisition Sept. 10. Terms were not disclosed. Bank Street Group LLC was Recovery Point's exclusive financial adviser on the transaction. By the numbers - 1994: Year CBTS was founded in Cincinnati - 3,000+: Clients served by CBTS and its OnX Canada division - 30+: Years Recovery Point has provided data protection and colocation services - 115,000: Square feet at Recovery Point's Germantown, Maryland, data center - 6: Consecutive years Recovery Point has appeared in the Gartner Market Guide for Disaster Recovery as a Service What Recovery Point brings Recovery Point provides fully managed Disaster Recovery as a Service (DRaaS) and cyber resiliency services for enterprise IT environments. Its clients range from Fortune 500 companies to small and midsize businesses, along with federal, state and local governments. The company manages recovery across complex, multi-platform environments, including legacy and mainframe systems, and handles plan development, testing and governance. The deal also gives CBTS Tier III data centers that Recovery Point owns and operates. The announcement describes them as fiber-dense and ready for expansion. The same facilities run Recovery Point's colocation business, which lets clients use one provider for hosting, resilience and recovery. Recovery Point's flagship facility is in Germantown, Maryland, about 25 miles from Washington, D.C. The company has described the site as a 115,000-square-foot Tier III data center certified by the Uptime Institute, with direct connections to Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud. With the acquisition, CBTS now offers: - Fully managed DRaaS with orchestrated execution and measurable service-level agreements - Ransomware Recovery as a Service (RRaaS), with AI-powered backup validation - Cyber resiliency across hybrid, multi-cloud and legacy environments - Recovery testing and performance assurance as standard practice Why CBTS made the deal CBTS tied the acquisition to AI. As AI workloads drive up data volume and infrastructure demand, the company noted, enterprises need resilient, scalable environments they control, without the cost of building their own. The announcement also cited a Palo Alto Networks report finding that nearly 30% of security teams take more than a full day to resolve a single incident. "Resilience is now a board-level obligation, not an IT project. With Recovery Point, CBTS delivers what enterprises increasingly demand: a trusted partner who can modernize their infrastructure, secure it, and recover it end-to-end, under pressure, with measurable outcomes," CBTS CEO Kristin Russell said in the announcement. Recovery Point CEO Jack Dziak described the deal as a gain for both client bases. "With CBTS, our clients gain access to a full range of enterprise technology platforms, and CBTS gains a proven partner in cyber resilience," Dziak said. A busy stretch for CBTS The acquisition capped a run of announcements from CBTS. On Aug. 31, the company named Mark Giles chief technology officer. Giles is a 10-year CBTS veteran and former U.S. Marine Corps data systems chief who previously led the company's AI adoption as vice president of AI. The new role brings AI, product management and emerging technology under one strategy. The next day, CBTS launched Forge Agents, a platform that builds AI agents from a plain-language description of a task. It is aimed at midmarket and regulated organizations and draws on a library of 187 prebuilt components and 34 cross-industry blueprints. Forge Agents builds on Forge AI, the company's AI advisory and engineering offering launched in March. CBTS told trade outlet Channel Dive that the Recovery Point facilities strengthen its ability to host AI infrastructure in environments customers can control. About the company CBTS designs, builds and operates technology infrastructure for midmarket and enterprise organizations across North America, with expertise in AI, data, applications, platforms and security. The company has been named to the CRN Tech Elite 250 for seven consecutive years and ranks No. 49 on the CRN Solution Provider 500.

artigo.texto: ROANOKE COUNTY, Va. – A new data center could be coming to Roanoke County. After weeks of questions from neighbors, the Regional Industrial Authority confirmed that Clearview Dynamics is looking at Roanoke County’s Wood Haven Technology Park as a possible site for a data center. 10 News community journalist Bella Walser sat down with the president of the Roanoke Regional Partnership, John Hull, to ask whether another company is behind Clearview Dynamics LLC, which is a company that formed just this year. “Clearview Dynamics, more appropriately, is entering into a due diligence process,” Hull explained. “And these companies, they have obligations to their shareholders and their owners and so forth. The situation is simply this: It is early in the process. We’ve heard the community, right? There’s a desire for transparency. We simply can’t be more transparent than this.” There is a lot that still remains unknown, and many questions were met with a redirection to submit a formal Freedom of Information Act request. Stay with 10 News as this breaking news story continues to develop.

artigo.texto: Steady attention is crucial when keeping watch over hundreds of data centers worldwide, facilities essential to online banking, messaging and artificial intelligence (AI) services that society uses. Analysts are surrounded by digital maps and dashboards at the Singapore operations center of US firm Digital Realty Trust Inc, a global operator of the warehouse-like sites filled with whirring servers. The goal is not simply to react when something breaks, but to detect warning signs, such as a sudden rise in temperature, early enough to prevent disruption. Photo: AFP Daniel Naing, 37, and his colleagues at the center in Singapore handle thousands of system alerts flagging signs of trouble each week. The operations center and its two sister hubs, in Europe and the US, provide round-the-clock oversight of more than 300 data centers across six continents. Digital Realty rents its server space to about 6,000 companies, with power loss and equipment failure the most common issues. There are procedures for earthquakes and typhoons, and an approaching storm thousands of kilometers away is enough to put the team on standby. Demand for data centers is a political hot potato in many places, as tech companies race to develop AI tools that require massive amounts of computing power. Without them “nothing works” in our high-tech world, Digital Realty managing director and Asia Pacific head Serene Nah said. Data centers are essential infrastructure — a matter “almost like national security,” she said. “We need to be up running all the time.” However, Nah said that “our business is very misunderstood” and has little support from the public, who believe data centers emit “a lot of carbon or heat” or “use up a lot of water.” “Yet everyone’s scrolling their phones every day,” and for each swipe “the data needs to go somewhere.” The company is prioritizing renewable energy such as solar panels and closed-loop server cooling systems that continuously recycle water, Nah said. Data centers operate 24 hours a day, so the Singapore center takes the 7am to 7pm shift before hand-off to Europe. Engineers must respond to an alert within minutes. The teams liaise with on-site staff and call on a global network of experts to help, while keeping clients updated. The company’s operations center in Singapore is housed inside one of three data centers that the company runs in the city-state. Most areas of the data center, whose roof is lined with solar panels, are off-limits for security reasons. AFP was shown a room where rows of black server cabinets formed long, narrow corridors, with bundles of yellow cables running overhead and the computer servers’ high-velocity fans emitting a soft hum. AI is accelerating the growth and complexity of data centers, but for the operations center, humans remain indispensable, said Terence Tang, head of the Asia Pacific global command center. “We still need human intervention to really look at whether or not those are genuine outages, genuine alerts and alarms, because sometimes AI or automation can give you false positives,” Tang said. artigo.texto: CATL Plunges 25% in a Month as Chinese Automakers Accelerate Supply Chain Diversification Shares of CATL (Ningde Times), the world's largest EV battery maker, have taken a direct hit from supply chain diversification moves by Chinese automaker customers. On the Shenzhen Stock Exchange, CATL closed at CNY 297.10 (approximately $44) on September 21, down 1.61% from the previous session, barely holding above its 52-week low of CNY 295.55 (approximately $44). The stock has fallen 24.04% in September alone and is down 36.5% from its early May high this year. The decline was equally steep on the Hong Kong exchange. CATL's H-shares plunged 6.01% on September 15 to close at HK$516 (approximately $66), the lowest level since March this year. The following day, shares fell as low as HK$486.4 (approximately $62) intraday, marking a roughly 38% decline from the June peak of HK$792.87 (approximately $101). A-shares also tumbled 6.16% in a single day on September 15, erasing approximately CNY 91.4 billion (approximately $13.6 billion) in market capitalization, and on September 16 the CNY 300 (approximately $45) level was breached intraday. Compared with the year-to-date high of CNY 467.34 (approximately $70) recorded on May 7, more than CNY 700 billion (approximately $104.4 billion) in combined A-share and H-share market value has evaporated. The direct catalyst behind the stock plunge is a series of "de-CATL" moves by major automaker customers. Li Auto recently invested CNY 2.65 billion (approximately $395.2 million) to become Sunwoda's second-largest shareholder. The new L8 model launched in June this year is equipped with Sunwoda batteries across all trims, replacing CATL batteries. Li Auto's management has characterized the relationship with Sunwoda not as a simple supply contract but as a "long-term interest community," pledging to strengthen joint R&D and manufacturing cooperation. Xiaomi's moves have also heightened market wariness. On September 4, Xiaomi unveiled its in-house "Dragon Armor" battery brand, announcing that its new EV lineup would feature cells from CALB and Sunwoda. Given that CATL was the primary supplier for the previously launched SU7 and YU7 models, this represents a clear strategic pivot. Xpeng has also increased the supply share from EVE Energy, while Huawei's smart car brand Aito has moved away from a CATL-exclusive supply arrangement by adding CALB and Gotion High-Tech. According to industry estimates, Li Auto and Xiaomi account for approximately 13.6% of CATL's installed capacity in China. While this figure alone is not immediately fatal, what concerns the market is not the number but the direction. China Retreats, Japan Expands While Chinese automakers are diversifying their supply chains, CATL's customer base is also shifting in other directions. The breakdown by customer is as follows: The moves by four Japanese automakers are particularly notable. Toyota, which formed a comprehensive partnership with CATL in 2019, announced in April 2026 that its Indonesian production subsidiary TMMIN would enter an EV business alliance with CATL. This marks the first time Toyota has sourced CATL batteries outside China. The CATL plant being built in West Java is targeted to begin operations in late 2026, with Toyota establishing a dedicated line inside the facility to receive batteries for locally produced hybrid vehicles. The batteries are expected to be nickel-based ternary lithium-ion cells. Honda acquired approximately 1% of CATL in 2020 and subsequently signed a 123 GWh long-term procurement agreement covering 2024–2030, while Nissan agreed in May 2025 to supply batteries for Dongfeng Nissan passenger vehicles. Daihatsu plans to launch a kei EV co-developed with CATL in Japan as early as 2026. The fact that overseas customers, led by Japan, are filling the gap left by shrinking Chinese demand demonstrates that the "diversified customer base" cited as a counterargument is more than rhetoric. The quality of overseas revenue is also higher than domestic. Overseas sales accounted for 31.48% of CATL's first-half 2026 revenue, but overseas gross margin was 29.97%, significantly exceeding the 21.16% achieved in China's domestic market. Profitability Gap Drives Supply Chain Restructuring The reason automakers are willing to absorb the costs and risks of supply chain transition to reduce CATL dependency stems from profitability pressure. CATL posted net profit of CNY 43.284 billion (approximately $6.5 billion) in the first half of this year—more than double the combined net profit of 15 major listed Chinese automakers (CNY 21.048 billion) over the same period. CATL's first-half consolidated gross margin reached 23.93%, while Li Auto's second-quarter automotive segment gross margin was 9.4%, down 10 percentage points year-over-year. Batteries, which account for 30–40% of EV costs, are the single most expensive component. Amid weak domestic demand in China and ongoing price wars, total profits across the Chinese auto industry fell 20% in the first seven months of this year. Meanwhile, CATL has maintained pricing power leverage backed by its mid-40% share of China's power battery market. A battle over product definition rights is also at play. Li Auto's new L8 is a prime example. The performance specifications, system design, software, and pack integration are led by Li Auto, with Sunwoda handling only cell manufacturing. This represents a new supply chain model in which control over battery solutions shifts from suppliers to automakers. The attitude of second-tier battery makers has also encouraged this transition. Unlike CATL, companies like CALB and Sunwoda are desperate for each individual customer and can respond far more flexibly on pricing and development timelines. Li Auto's acquisition of a Sunwoda stake is likewise interpreted not as a purely financial investment but as a strategic move to strengthen supply chain control. artigo.texto: Novelis Inc., headquartered in Atlanta, has expanded its advanced coated aluminum solutions portfolio for battery and energy storage applications. Novelis says it combines high-performance automotive-grade aluminum sheet with surface technologies to help manufacturers improve production efficiency, enhance component durability and tailor material properties to the requirements of electric mobility and stationary energy storage systems. Battery enclosures, casings, electrical connectors and other battery components benefit from Novelis’ automotive aluminum solutions, which combine lightweight performance, enhanced formability, corrosion protection and application-specific electrical insulation capabilities, the company says. By pairing automotive-grade aluminum with advanced coating technologies, Novelis says manufacturers in the electric mobility and energy storage space can improve production reliability, reduce manufacturing complexity by eliminating external lubrication and additional e-coating processes and tailor material performance to the requirements of specific battery applications. The use of high-recycled-content, low-carbon aluminum helps support sustainability objectives and circular business models. “Leveraging decades of automotive expertise, we have developed aluminum solutions that combine advanced surface technologies with high-performance sheet products for demanding battery applications,” says Milan Felberbaum, director of research and development for Novelis Europe in Zurich. “By integrating these capabilities, we help customers improve manufacturing efficiency while supporting battery performance and durability.” Novelis says its water-based coating technology, which is in use on the company’s advanced coating line in Germany, has been a differentiator. The coating, which is applied to aluminum coils before forming, remains effective after stamping, improving corrosion protection and formability while reducing battery manufacturing complexity and cost. The system also can be engineered to provide electrical insulation properties where required, which allows manufacturers to tailor material performance to the needs of specific battery applications. Novelis says its advanced aluminum solutions support both battery performance and circular business models through increased recycled content and closed-loop recycling.

artigo.texto: CATL Debrecen began trial production at its newly built battery cell factory on 22 September 2026 after completing the regulatory and technical requirements needed to launch operations. The trial phase will be used to set up, optimise and validate production equipment and manufacturing processes before series production begins. The Chinese battery manufacturer announced plans for its second European production site in Debrecen in August 2022, aiming to strengthen its presence in the European automotive and e-mobility supply chain and serve major carmakers operating across the continent. Construction of the first battery cell building started in summer 2023. By spring 2026, the facility had been equipped with production technology, while an occupancy permit was granted in August. Trial production begins on two battery cell lines Following the approval of the necessary permits and completion of the conditions required under its integrated pollution prevention and control permit, CATL Debrecen launched trial operations on the first two production lines of its cell manufacturing facility on 22 September. According to the company, the main purpose of the trial phase is to configure, optimise and validate both the equipment and the manufacturing processes ahead of full-scale series production. The trial period will also allow engineers to monitor production performance and make adjustments before commercial output begins. Earlier regulatory concerns addressed before launch Before issuing the occupancy permit, the Hajdú-Bihar County Government Office carried out a series of on-site inspections at CATL’s facilities. The checks followed earlier deficiencies and issues that had raised concerns among some local residents during the permitting and construction process. According to CATL, representatives of the authority confirmed that the company had remedied all deficiencies identified earlier in the procedure before trial production was allowed to begin. The company said it would continue cooperating closely with the Hungarian government and competent authorities, particularly on environmental protection as well as employee health and workplace safety. CATL added that environmental, occupational health and safety indicators would also be closely monitored throughout the trial phase, with the results proactively submitted to the authorities. If you missed it: Exclusive interview – Chinese Ambassador: Hungary-China ties on a ‘steady track’ as Budapest emerges as a potential robotics hub CATL Debrecen targets 100 GWh production capacity Once all parts of the project are completed, the Debrecen plant is expected to become CATL’s largest manufacturing base outside China. The planned annual production capacity is 100 GWh, making the investment one of the largest battery manufacturing projects in Hungary and a major component of the country’s rapidly expanding electric vehicle supply chain. CATL says its Debrecen facility will supply leading European car manufacturers, several of which have already developed significant electric vehicle production capacity in Hungary and the wider region. The plant has been designed with flexible production lines intended to adapt to the requirements of different automotive customers. More than half a million battery modules already produced Battery cell production is not CATL’s first manufacturing activity in Debrecen. The company has been producing battery modules at the site since autumn 2024 and says it has manufactured approximately 537,000 modules since production began. The start of trial cell production therefore marks another major step towards the full operation of the Debrecen complex. Environmental and workplace safety remain under scrutiny CATL said it would continue working with authorities during the trial period and reiterated its commitment to environmental protection, employee health and workplace safety. The company also said it supports regulatory transparency and remains open to inspections by the relevant authorities. The Debrecen investment is significant not only for the city and the surrounding region, but also for Hungary’s industrial strategy and Europe’s electric mobility supply chain. Once series production begins and the entire facility reaches its planned capacity, the factory is expected to become one of CATL’s most important production centres outside China. artigo.texto: O povo indígena Anacé, que luta em defesa de seu território não demarcado na Região Metropolitana de Fortaleza (CE), deflagrou uma série de mobilizações contra a operação de um mega data center de 10 bilhões de dólares ligado ao social-imperialismo chinês, como a ocupação do canteiro de obras e bloqueios de rodovias em Caucaia, que Ministério Público Federal (MPF) e a Defensoria Pública da União (DPU) a ajuizarem uma ação civil pública (ACP) contra a infraestrutura. O mega data center é associado à ByteDance, controladora do TikTok, em parceria com a Omnia e a Casa dos Ventos no Complexo Industrial e Portuário do Pecém (CIPP), e avançou sem o Consentimento Livre, Prévio e Informado (CLPI) e sob licenciamento ambiental irregular, ameaçando a Lagoa do Cauípe e poços de 1.500 famílias Anacé em 28 aldeias. A ação civil pública ajuizada pelo MPF e pela DPU visa impedir a operação do empreendimento até que o Estudo e Relatório de Impacto Ambiental (EIA/Rima) sejam elaborados e a consulta prévia seja realizada. A comunidade soube do projeto em maio de 2025 via investigação jornalística publicada pelo The Intercept. Ao Conselho Indigenista Missionário (Cimi), o cacique Roberto Anacé ressaltou a recusa em aceitar abordagens corporativas sem o devido protocolo oficial: “Não autorizamos isso. Primeiro eles nos violam. E agora pedem a gente em casamento? Oferecem mundos e fundos. Os povos indígenas vivem isso no Brasil inteiro, não somos mais bestas.” O avanço judicial sustenta-se em laudo técnico expedido pelo Centro Nacional de Perícia do MPF, o qual classificou como tecnicamente inadequado e inadmissível o licenciamento conduzido por meio de Relatório Ambiental Simplificado (RAS). Os peritos comprovaram que a obra exige uma potência energética de até 300 megawatts e envolve edificações pesadas para servidores, geradores a diesel, subestação elétrica, linha de transmissão e estação de tratamento de esgoto. O relatório atestou a ausência de comprovação de viabilidade hídrica, a omissão sobre os impactos cumulativos com outras estruturas e o fracionamento indevido do processo, exigindo a realização de EIA/Rima e audiências públicas com participação social. Inconformados com o desrespeito aos seus direitos, os indígenas intensificaram as ações em Caucaia. Em abril de 2026, os Anacé paralisaram o tráfego com bloqueios nas rodovias CE-085 e BR-222. Em junho de 2026, a comunidade ocupou o canteiro de obras do data center e notificou o MPF, o governo estadual e a prefeitura sobre o fechamento do local. A mobilização dá continuidade ao ato de agosto de 2025, quando marcharam até Fortaleza e ocuparam as sedes da Superintendência Estadual do Meio Ambiente (Semace) e da Fundação Nacional dos Povos Indígenas (Funai) para exigir o cancelamento das licenças concedidas sem a escuta formal das lideranças. Enquanto as corporações TikTok e Omnia contestam a perícia alegando legalidade no uso hídrico e a Casa dos Ventos defende que opera com “abastecimento de energia 100% renovável”, os Anacé condenam o roubo das águas e reiteram que a instalação fere o território tradicional. Pilhagem hídrica e a cumplicidade da burocracia estatal A apreensão central dos moradores incide sobre o consumo industrial de água em uma região historicamente castigada pela severa estiagem. O município de Caucaia registrou situação oficial de emergência por seca em 16 dos últimos 21 anos, fato que torna dramática a chegada de um empreendimento de hiperescala. O mega data center será erguido a cerca de dois quilômetros da Lagoa do Cauípe, área de inestimável importância comunitária para a população originária. O cacique Roberto Ytaysaba Anacé e os moradores denunciam que a sucção desenfreada de água para o resfriamento contínuo dos sistemas de servidores ameaça exaurir os lençóis freáticos e provocar o esgotamento definitivo dos poços artesianos que abastecem 1.500 famílias Anacé distribuídas ao longo de 28 aldeias no território tradicional não demarcado. A pressão hídrica e ambiental sobre a zona praiana tende a se agravar com o plano de expansão aprovado pela burocracia estatal. Em agosto de 2026, o Conselho Nacional das Zonas de Processamento de Exportação (CZPE) autorizou a implantação de outro data center da empresa Voltalia em Caucaia, projetado para a ZPE Ceará, com investimentos estimados em R$ 181,7 bilhões. O incentivo à proliferação de parques tecnológicos é patrocinado pelo governo federal. No dia 16 de setembro de 2026, o presidente Luiz Inácio sancionou a Lei 15.504/26, que cria o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata), concedendo benesses fiscais para a compra de equipamentos com a promessa de atrair entre 500 bilhões e 1 trilhão de reais. Paralelamente, o Ministério do Meio Ambiente (MMA) foi limado das articulações interministeriais que formulam a política nacional do setor, priorizando exclusivamente as exigências do capital privado. O modelo adotado pelas secretarias ambientais baseia-se na flexibilização das regras de controle. Empreendimentos industriais de alto impacto hídrico e energético têm sido indevidamente enquadrados na categoria de “construção civil”, classificação de baixo a médio impacto similar à usada para kartódromos e parques de vaquejada. Esse estratagema burocrático suprime a exigência do EIA/Rima e cancela a realização de audiências públicas. Monopólios imperialistas avançam por todo o País O assédio corporativo perpetrado no Brasil por grandes monopólios tecnológicos imperialistas repete-se na Região Sul. Em Eldorado do Sul, no Rio Grande do Sul, o projeto Scala AI City é promovido pelo fundo de investimentos DigitalBridge do país Estados Unidos (EUA). Com aporte inicial de R$ 3 bilhões, a “cidade data center” avança no entorno da aldeia Guarani Tekoa Guajayvi e do assentamento camponês Belo Monte, atropelando o direito à consulta prévia e gerando insegurança na produção dos camponeses. artigo.texto: What we know about Delaware County’s potential data center plan, ‘Project Trainer’ Link Logistics is testing the waters for a data center that would sit around 100 feet from homes in Trainer, Pennsylvania. This story is part of the WHYY News Climate Desk, bringing you news and solutions for our changing region. From the Poconos to the Jersey Shore to the mouth of the Delaware Bay, what do you want to know about climate change? What would you like us to cover? Get in touch. Delaware County residents are organizing in response to a potential data center proposal. Trainer Borough, with a population of less than 2,000, is located about 10 miles south of Philadelphia International Airport along the Delaware River and is also home to the Monroe Energy oil refinery. Borough officials gave preliminary zoning approval last month for a data center to be built in an industrial and residential area along Ridge Road at the borough’s border with Lower Chichester Township. But the property owner’s lawyer says no formal proposal has been made. Here’s what we know. Is a data center coming to Trainer, Pa.? It’s too soon to say. There is currently “no formal application” for a data center in Trainer Borough, according to a statement posted on the borough’s website. Link Logistics is currently advertising the roughly 24-acre site as a build-to-suit warehouse called the Juniper Pointe Logistics Center. But in August, Link Logistics’ lawyer requested a preliminary zoning determination from the borough for a “proposed data center” at the site. WHYY News obtained a copy of the correspondence through a public records request. What do we know about the possible data center proposal? Link Logistics’ request, signed by lawyer Leonard B. Altieri III, included a “preliminary test fit” drawing showing a two-story data center labeled “Project Trainer.” The data center would use 120 megawatts of electricity and would likely include a 3-acre electrical substation to connect the data center to the electric utility’s infrastructure and backup gas or diesel-powered generators, according to Altieri’s letter. The development would also likely include a security building. Cooling of the data center equipment would be done using a closed-loop system, Altieri said in an interview. It would not require a supply of process water, according to his letter. Altieri said that none of these details are final because his client has not yet decided whether to pursue the data center project. “No application has been submitted and no plans have been designed,” he said in an interview. “We’re purely at the due diligence phase of this.” Asked whether PECO had received any request for service at the site, a spokesperson said the company cannot discuss potential customers or prospective customer projects for privacy and confidentiality reasons. Where would the data center be located? The site where Link Logistics is considering building a data center is located at 4001 Ridge Road, mostly in Trainer. A small portion on the southwest edge of the site is located in Lower Chichester Township. The site sits between Congoleum, a vinyl floor manufacturing facility, a small self-storage facility and a construction equipment supplier. Rows of homes sit roughly 100 feet away from the site across Ridge Road to the northwest and about 200 feet away across a set of train tracks to the southeast of the site. What happens next? Trainer Borough’s zoning officer, Charles Remaley, confirmed to Altieri in August that the property’s industrial zoning allows for development of a data center “by-right.” “The proposed development is therefore permitted with respect to use,” Remaley wrote. “Any Required site plan, subdivision, building, engineering, environmental, or other Governmental approvals shall be obtained separately as applicable.” If Link Logistics chooses to pursue the data center project, it will need to submit a site plan for approval by the Trainer Borough Planning Commission and Borough Council. The project would also likely need environmental permits from the state of Pennsylvania, including stormwater and erosion control permits and air pollution permits for backup generators. Gov. Josh Shapiro recently signed an executive order reserving a more efficient process of environmental permit review for data center proposals that commit to meeting the Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development, or GRID, standards and have already received local approval. Link Logistics also sought preliminary zoning approval from Lower Chichester Township, for the portion of the site that lies within that municipality. In a letter dated July 22, Frank E. Hendron, Lower Chichester Township zoning officer, said a data center is not a permitted use under the site’s current zoning. The preliminary test fit drawing included in Altieri’s August letter to Trainer Borough shows the data center building located only within the portion of the site located in Trainer. A Link Logistics spokesperson said in a written statement provided by Altieri on Monday that the company is “pleased to have received a favorable Preliminary Opinion from Trainer Borough.” “This is not a building permit; any project, should we decide to pursue, will require an application and Borough approvals,” the spokesperson wrote. The environmental advocacy group Chester Residents Concerned for Quality Living is hosting a community meeting about the possible proposal Sept. 23 in Boothwyn. artigo.texto: O Movimento Brasil Competitivo (MBC) emitiu nota destacando que o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata) precisa estar associado a uma discussão sobre o Imposto sobre Circulação de Mercadorias e Serviços (ICMS) no Conselho Nacional de Política Fazendária (Confaz). A entidade apontou que mesmo com o regime, implantar um data center no Brasil é mais oneroso do que nos Estados Unidos – cerca de 17% a mais –, conforme dados da Faculdade Getulio Vargas (FGV). Para o movimento, o avanço da pauta será um complemento ao Redata. Somente com o regime, a FGV estima que cada data center de 100 MW voltado à IA deve atrair cerca de R$ 25 bilhões em investimento e gerar mais de 37 mil empregos diretos. Visão da Moody’s sobre o Redata Para a Moody’s, agência internacional de análise de risco, o Redata proporciona maior previsibilidade financeira ao Brasil. Segundo ela, isso “é mais importante do que o tamanho da economia tributária em um setor no qual elevados investimentos iniciais precedem a geração de receita por vários anos”. A Moody’s acredita que o regime tende a melhorar o rating dos desenvolvedores da tecnologia. No entanto, esse processo deverá ser gradual e conforme o cumprimento de requisitos previstos no regime, que envolvem sustentabilidade, desenvolvimento local e risco de penalidade. O regime estabelece que os data centers deverão usar eletricidade proveniente de fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão de carbono e consumo máximo de 0,05 litro de água por kWh nos seus sistemas de resfriamento. Além disso, 2% do valor dos equipamentos deverão ser destinados para a pesquisa nacional, desse valor, ao menos 40% deverão ser direcionados para as regiões Norte, Nordeste e Centro-Oeste. As empresas também deverão dedicar 10% de sua capacidade para o mercado interno e instituições públicas. Em caso de descumprimento, o regime prevê o pagamento dos impostos antes isentos, com juros.

artigo.texto: Galesburg wants to get ahead of data center development before it starts. The City Council takes up a first-reading ordinance tonight establishing a 180-day moratorium on new data center permits, giving the city time to set its own rules before any project arrives. The moratorium, running through April 3, 2027, is one of several items on a council agenda tonight that also includes the retirement of a longtime police K9, a $3.2 million transit fleet grant, and two transportation grant applications worth a combined $3.373 million. Eric Hanson, Galesburg city manager, joined Galesburg’s Morning News on Monday, Sept. 21. Listen to the full interview below. Data center moratorium The city says it has no active data center proposals on file, but has been contacted by interested parties. City Manager Eric Hanson said the pause is meant to give Galesburg time to watch for potential state legislation on data centers, expected either during this fall’s veto session or next spring’s general session, before setting its own rules. “We want to be able to control what the future looks like and make sure that any development that comes here related to technology is something that is in the best interest of our residents,” Hanson said. He said the biggest concerns are the electricity and water demands data centers place on local infrastructure, and the potential for higher utility costs for residents. K9 Dax’s retirement Also on tonight’s agenda: the retirement of Galesburg Police K9 Dax, a five-year veteran of narcotics detection and evidence recovery. Dax was purchased by the department in 2021 at a year and a half old and is now 7 â old enough, city officials say, that retraining him with a new handler isn’t practical. He’ll retire to live with his longtime handler, Officer Jacob Thompson, as a family pet, with Thompson covering all future expenses. “It’s great to have these exceptionally trained animals available,” Hanson said. “And then obviously to the officers who take the time and commitment that it takes to be a K-9 officer is significant.” Transit fleet and grant applications Council will weigh a $3.2 million grant application to replace and expand the city’s public transportation fleet â 22 vehicles in all, including one minivan, 14 medium-duty paratransit vehicles and seven super-medium-duty vehicles. No local match is required. Hanson credited Transit Manager Kraig Boynton for identifying the funding opportunity, saying the upgrade supports the city’s push to take transit countywide and would replace aging vehicles, including several Gillig buses he described as “well past their prime.” Council will also consider two Illinois Transportation Enhancement Program grant applications. One would put $920,000 toward a $2 million project completing sidewalk, lighting and crosswalk improvements on Simmons Street between Cherry and Prairie streets and between Kellogg and Seminary streets â filling gaps on either side of a middle section the city finished previously. If awarded, Hanson said preliminary engineering could begin next year, with construction in 2028. The second application seeks $350,400 toward Phase II engineering for a shared-use path and sidewalk project on East Main Street, from Grand Avenue to east of Walnut Street. The city has also applied for a competing Highway Safety Improvement Program grant covering the same engineering costs; only one of the two would be awarded. Hanson said grant decisions typically take four to six months, with an answer likely by spring. Treat Street and bicycle disposal Also on tonight’s consent agenda: a resolution closing Main Street from Chambers Street to the public square for Treat Street on Halloween. The road will close from 10 a.m. to 1:30 p.m., with the event running 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. This year’s citywide trick-or-treat hours are 5 to 8 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 31. Council will also consider a first-reading ordinance changing how the city disposes of abandoned bicycles held by the police department. Because bicycle listings on Purple Wave Auctions no longer draw enough bidders to be cost-effective, functional bikes will now be donated to charitable organizations, with inoperable bikes scrapped. City officials say the change has no budget impact. The Galesburg City Council meets tonight at 6 p.m. at Galesburg City Hall. artigo.texto: Shares of Alibaba jumped around 3% in Hong Kong on Tuesday after the Chinese technology giant unveiled a new artificial intelligence chip and plans to sharply expand its data center footprint, stepping up its bet on the infrastructure powering the AI boom. At its cloud unit's annual flagship Apsara Conference in Hangzhou, Alibaba introduced the Zhenwu V900, its next-generation AI chip that it said delivers three times the performance of its predecessor, the Zhenwu M890 released in May. The company also announced plans to expand Alibaba Cloud's global data center capacity to more than 20 gigawatts by 2032 as part of a broader roadmap spanning chips, cloud infrastructure and AI models. The announcements underscore Alibaba's growing push into the machinery behind the AI boom, amid a flurry of AI infrastructure investments by its Western tech peers as the race for computing power intensifies. Earlier this month, Nvidia outlined plans to work with Australian partners to support up to 2 gigawatts of AI infrastructure in the country by 2027, while Meta in July unveiled plans for its first data center in Canada, a 1-gigawatt facility in Alberta expected to cost about $9 billion and take up to three years to complete. Alibaba's new Zhenwu AI chip is scheduled for mass production and commercial release in the first quarter of 2027. Its existing Zhenwu chips are already used by more than 650 customers across industries including automotive, finance, energy and manufacturing. The company also said its next-generation Qwen 4 model is currently in training and outlined plans for future Qwen 4.5 and Qwen 5 model series. Eddie Wu, CEO of Alibaba Group, said machine thinking still had an "enormous growth runway," comparing today's AI development with the early stages of electrification, adding "AI coding is simply the light bulb of the machine intelligence era." Alibaba's domestic peer Huawei also unveiled new AI infrastructure last week that it said can scale to as many as one million processors.

artigo.texto: A new company has a plan to make the dirty gas turbines powering data centers more efficient: liquid carbon dioxide. American Supercritical came out of stealth Wednesday, announcing $8 million in funding. It wants to retrofit inefficient gas turbines that many data centers rely on for power with units that can generate more power, without adding more emissions (though the gas-fired turbines will continue to emit carbon pollution). The technology can also theoretically be used on a wide variety of energy sources at a time when power demand is skyrocketing. “We want to start with gas turbines but eventually expand beyond that,” says cofounder Simon Shuham. Most large gas-fired power plants in the United States use an array of heat engines in what’s known as a combined-cycle process: First, turbines generate electricity from burning compressed air and natural gas, then a separate engine uses the hot exhaust to make steam and create additional energy. But for a variety of reasons, data centers across the US have opted to power their operations with what are known as simple-cycle turbines, and exclude the steam component. These turbines are much less efficient than combined-cycle plants. Usually, only about 35 percent of the energy from simple-cycle turbines is converted to electricity, while the rest escapes as exhaust. (In combined-cycle plants, that figure hovers closer to 60 to 65 percent.) That exhaust includes greenhouse gases, making plants that run on simple-cycle turbines a much worse choice for the environment than combined-cycle plants. The size of some of these plants combined with their inefficiency is a recipe for climate disaster. A massive data-center power plant in Texas that Amazon is building with just simple-cycle turbines, for instance, is permitted to emit more than 33 million tons of greenhouse gases per year—more than the annual total of some small countries. But all these small, inefficient turbines could be a great match for supercritical CO2 technology, American Supercritical’s founders say. Carbon dioxide becomes supercritical when it’s pressurized and held at a certain temperature. In this state, it gets the density of liquid but still behaves like a gas, meaning it can move energy more efficiently through much smaller amounts of equipment. American Supercritical wants to attach its units to small gas turbines and help generate more energy. While the turbines themselves would still use gas, the supercritical CO2 unit can use the hot exhaust generated from those turbines to create additional electricity. Instead of using that heat to boil water and create steam, the heat is transferred directly by the pressurized CO2 to generate additional energy with no additional emissions. “We’re essentially building miniature combined-cycle plants,” says Shuham. Using supercritical CO2 also can eliminate or greatly reduce water use in the power generation process—something that’s drawn intense scrutiny when it comes to data centers. Importantly, the CO2 involved operates in a closed-loop system, meaning that it doesn’t have to be refilled. Cofounder Matthew Carlson, who researched supercritical CO2 for more than a decade, likens it to refrigeration systems that circulate CO2 to facilitate cooling. The company plans to initially sell a 10-megawatt unit—relatively small by gas plant standards. By American Supercritical’s math, adding supercritical CO2 units could increase turbines’ efficiency by up to 50 percent without adding any more greenhouse gas emissions or water use. But retrofitting all of the country’s inefficient gas turbines powering data centers with supercritical CO2 units won’t reduce emissions to zero. Natural gas production and use, even with efficient turbines, warms the planet. Data centers also represent a massive new source of pollution—right at a time when the world needs to be scaling back on its use. Using supercritical CO2 for power has been studied for more than 50 years in US national labs. Over the past two decades, research has moved away from theory toward trying out practical applications, assisted by technological breakthroughs that help with the pressurization process. Doug Hofer, an adviser to American Supercritical who spent two decades at GE as a turbine engineer, says that one important innovation has been the development of more compact and more affordable heat exchangers—devices that help both heat and cool the CO2. American Supercritical isn’t the only company trying to bring this technology to market, says Subith Vasu, a professor of engineering at the University of Central Florida, who runs a lab at the school’s Center for Advanced Turbomachinery and Energy Research. The companies still have hurdles to overcome to achieve commercial success. “Whenever you are venturing into new technologies, you need to have all the associated components, the supply chain,” in place, he says. Technical challenges also abound, he adds, “and cost has been a huge issue.” Hofer says that part of the delay has also simply been because larger companies are satisfied with the performance of traditional power plants and unwilling to invest in different technologies—and turbine makers are not interested in funding potential competitors. “It’s the innovator’s dilemma, right?” he says. “Getting this [technology] out there needs to have an outside influence.” The $7 trillion set to be invested in data centers globally by 2030 has helped open up a whole new potential market, especially for an industry racing to get as much power on the grid as it possibly can to come out ahead in the AI race. “There’s this incredible willingness to pay [for power], but they’re bottlenecked,” says Shuham. “The goal is to come in here, retrofit their existing systems, and give them the ability to build additional data centers—or get rid of some of the gas turbines.” Earlier this year, China announced that operations started at the world’s first geothermal plant using supercritical CO2. artigo.texto: Capacidade de remoção da unidade em Nebraska supera 800 mil toneladas anuais. A ADM está pronta para entrar no mercado voluntário de carbono com a geração de créditos a partir da captura e armazenamento de dióxido de carbono em sua unidade de etanol em Columbus, Nebraska. A instalação possui uma capacidade de remoção superior a 800 mil toneladas de CO₂ anualmente. De acordo com a empresa, os créditos estão atualmente em processo de certificação e emissão pela plataforma Puro.earth, especializada em infraestrutura para remoção de carbono. A ADM espera concluir a primeira emissão de créditos até o final deste ano, dependendo da aprovação da auditoria. ✨ Caso o processo receba aprovação, a ADM iniciará um ciclo de geração de créditos que durará 15 anos. A operação de captura de carbono em Columbus teve início em 2025 e se realiza em colaboração com a Tallgrass, uma empresa de infraestrutura energética. Considerada a maior instalação de captura de carbono em uma planta de bioetanol no mundo, o CO₂ gerado durante a fermentação do etanol a partir do milho é capturado, purificado e comprimido. Posteriormente, o gás é transportado para Wyoming, onde é armazenado permanentemente no subsolo em poços de CCS aprovados pelas autoridades ambientais estaduais. artigo.texto: The data center backlash is reshaping American politics — one community at a time With striking speed, the widespread debate around data centers has become a fault line in American communities, cutting across political parties, splitting constituencies and forging unexpected alliances. In city halls and county commission chambers, east to west and north to south, people are squaring off against their local representatives. It starts with distrust Data centers have "upended politics as we know it," says Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution. It's more than a not-in-my-backyard issue, he says — it also reflects existential fears that artificial intelligence will take jobs or eliminate humanity entirely. "People just feel like they no longer have control over the technology, [and] that worries them," West says. "This is a real grassroots movement. It's ordinary people all across the country, both Republicans and Democrats." For this story, NPR traveled to data center hot spots and spoke to dozens of activists, politicians, developers and everyday Americans. The picture that emerges is complicated. Data centers have been an economic boon for some communities, helping to lower land taxes and providing jobs. At the same time, the proliferation of secretive deals that often involve elected officials signing nondisclosure agreements has exacerbated suspicions. A recent poll by The Economist and YouGov of nearly 1,600 adults found that about two-thirds of Americans oppose new data center construction in their communities. A rare cocktail of concerns has fueled the opposition, according to Chris Borick, a political science professor at Lehigh University. "It's aligning interests in ways that aren't traditional," he says. "If you're in power right now and you are dealing with this issue, you have a target on your back." Elected officials have had to scramble to recalibrate. "It's a recognition that the ground shifted under their feet and they were not ready for that to happen," Borick says. Parties are divided In Loudoun County, Va., data centers are driving a wedge between fellow Democrats. On one side is Juli Briskman, a member of Loudoun County's Board of Supervisors, who has led efforts to slow further data center development. On the other is Phyllis Randall, also a Democrat and the board's chair, who has argued in favor of data centers for the tax revenue they bring into the county, even while acknowledging they are "a double-edged sword" for nearby residents. Briskman is running to unseat Randall in next year's primary. She says her opposition to data centers dates back to 2020, when the board was seeing land-use cases seeking to convert residential and flex-industrial properties into the centers. "I feel like I have been singing this song for a while, and now all of a sudden everyone's grabbing my music and singing along with me," Briskman says. Randall did not respond to NPR's request for comment. Briskman is tapping into a sentiment in her area. Kasey Hatch lives near Loudoun County's Vantage VA2 data center, which is powered by eight natural-gas-fired turbines. Residents say the turbines produce a constant low-pitched rumble along with a high-frequency whine that has become a major source of noise complaints in the surrounding neighborhoods. Hatch, an IT infrastructure engineer for a bank who uses AI in her job, says she and her staunchly Republican cousin "never saw eye to eye on politics." But to her surprise, the last time they met, they were "on the same page about everything" when it came to data centers. At the grassroots level, that translates into Democrats and Republicans working together on an issue of mutual interest. Nusheen Farahani also lives near VA2 and is part of a group of women organized against the facility who regularly show up at public hearings. "I'm a liberal and I'm a Democrat, and the people that are in our little team … not all of them are liberals or Democrats," Farahani says. A similar story is playing out in Minnesota, Pennsylvania and Indiana, to name just a few, where locally organized groups are uniting against data centers — and elected officials. According to the Data Center Opposition Report, which tracks grassroots nonprofits on the issue, some 640,000 people are active in the anti-data center movement and 220 new groups sprang up in just the three months from June through August. They are driven by a feeling that government is part of the problem, according to Ben Green, an assistant professor at the University of Michigan's School of Information. With that comes a real sense of abandonment, he says. "If the policymakers, if my city council or zoning board or township board and governor, if they're on the side of the companies, who's standing up for me?" The economic impact Data centers have been around for a lot longer than the recent AI hype, quietly humming along in the background of the modern internet, powering cloud computing and storing vast amounts of data. AOL set up in Loudoun County, for example, back in the 1990s, giving the tech industry an early beachhead in the county that has only grown due to demand from government agencies in nearby Washington, D.C. To be sure, these facilities have brought economic benefits to the counties where they are located by creating billions of dollars in private investment, construction jobs and a limited number of well-paying positions at the data centers themselves, all the while providing an infusion of tax dollars that have stabilized and even lowered the tax burden for ordinary property owners. And among the many people NPR spoke to for this story who oppose data centers, nearly all acknowledge using AI in their daily life. Farahani, for example, says she "begrudgingly" uses chatbots for certain tasks "to make things easier." artigo.texto: At Tuesday’s Second Ward meeting, residents took the opportunity to speak out against a data center’s potential move into West Evanston, though Councilmember Krissie Harris said it’s too early to make any decision on the matter. Tuesday’s meeting followed the RoundTable reporting that an unnamed applicant filed a zoning analysis application with the city for “determination of use for a computer processing center” on Sept. 16. The application appeared on the Sept. 18 city manager’s report and is for a property in the Second Ward at 1265 Hartrey Ave. While the report did not provide further details, Planning Manager Liz Williams confirmed Monday night that the application is for what’s better known as a data center. About five residents attended the meeting in person at the Robert Crown Community Center and 20 joined virtually, mostly to discuss the data center application. According to a memo from Reed Beidler, the property manager for the Hartrey space, the zoning analysis application “asks that the City confirm that the use of a portion of an existing industrial building located at 1265 Hartrey Ave (approximately 20,000 sq. ft.) as a computer processing center is a Permitted Use” of the property under the city’s zoning code. Lark Management, the Evanston property management company that owns the space, last updated a listing for the portion of the property in question in August 2024. Beidler, who property records show is the taxpayer for the space, is listed as a contact for the rental. During Tuesday’s meeting, Harris said she previously met with the property owner about a separate “energy storage plant” in the space but was not aware of the data center possibility and had not yet read the zoning analysis application. “There has been no discussion about the data center,” she said. “I have not seen the proposal yet, and the property owner does want to meet with me about that. I don’t have an opinion yet.” Outside of Robert Crown on Tuesday, resident Michael Courier, a labor union worker, was handing out papers that read “no data centers in Evanston,” and he encouraged residents to speak at the upcoming City Council meeting on Sept. 28. “Data centers disproportionately use more energy and water than other technologies. Data centers also can cause noise pollution and destroy the peacefulness of our neighborhood,” Courier said. “Once the data center is created, few workers are needed to maintain the infrastructure of the building. AI is harming workers, and it is hurting our way of life. Evanston should not be complicit in the technologies that destroy what we hold dear and everything we love about the city.” Although Beidler’s memo identifies the property as 20,000 square feet, the actual size is 19,650 square feet, which one resident pointed out would fall just outside the city’s Healthy Buildings Ordinance. “That feels really icky,” the resident said. “Is this going to get past that ordinance, which is designed to force organizations that are large enough to have an impact on sustainability, on environmental prosperity? It feels like this is a way to cheat that system.” Harris said she plans to follow up with Beidler for a meeting to get clarity on the application. The large property, a former industrial building, also has vacant space from the closures of the Rebuilding Exchange and the WasteShed at 1245 Hartrey Ave. It still houses several other businesses and entities, including the Evanston Township High School Day School at 1233 Hartrey Ave. and Saint Errant Brewing at 2000 Dempster St. Margo Milanowski contributed to reporting

artigo.texto: Raritan Township adopts ordinance banning data centers RARITAN TOWNSHIP, N.J. (Hunterdon county) — Data centers are now prohibited throughout Raritan Township after the Township Committee recently adopted an ordinance amending the municipality’s Land Development Code. The ordinance adds data centers to the township’s list of prohibited uses, banning them in all zoning districts. The amended code also specifies that warehouses, flex spaces and research facilities cannot include data centers. The ordinance establishes a distinction for businesses and other permitted uses that use computer servers as part of their regular operations. Accessory server rooms remain permitted when they are located within a principal building and used solely to support the principal use of the property. The server space cannot exceed 10% of the building’s gross floor area or 2,000 square feet, whichever is less. Mayor Brad Perry and the entire Township Committee supported the ordinance, according to the township. Township officials said the ordinance is part of Raritan Township’s broader approach to land-use planning and establishing regulations that reflect the community’s long-term planning objectives.

artigo.texto: What if energy storage could be built directly into the materials that make up everyday products? Our Engineering, Chemistry and Anthropology departments are part of a major new project exploring materials that can combine energy storage and structural performance. Rethinking energy storage The five-year project, called EleComp (Electric Composites), brings together expertise from Durham University, Imperial College London and the University of Bristol. It is backed by a £7m Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC) Programme Grant. EleComp aims to develop a new generation of multifunctional materials that challenge conventional ideas about batteries and structures. Researchers will focus on structural power composites, materials that combine mechanical strength with energy storage. Multifunctional materials Most products today use separate batteries that must be housed, protected and connected to the structures around them. Structural power composites offer a different approach. They could allow energy storage to become part of an object's structure rather than a separate component. In future, this could mean vehicle body panels, aircraft components or consumer products can perform both a structural role and store energy. Researchers believe this could lead to lighter, more resource-efficient designs. Tackling scientific challenges Developing materials that are both strong and effective at storing energy presents significant scientific challenges. The EleComp team will investigate how structural electrodes, electrolytes and material interfaces can be designed to balance mechanical performance with electrochemical function. The project will also develop new manufacturing, testing and modelling approaches to support future applications. Researchers will draw inspiration from natural systems and work across disciplines to better understand the performance and long-term potential of these materials. Development and optimisation Dr Natasha Shirshova from our Department of Engineering is coordinating Durham's work on EleComp. Our experts from Departments of Engineering and Chemistry will be leading the development of key materials at the heart of structural batteries, including advanced structural electrolytes and next-generation electrodes that combine strength with storage. Our researchers will also work to optimise how these materials interact and pioneer new testing methods to assess their mechanical and electrochemical performance simultaneously. Alongside this work, Durham is also central to shaping a sustainable roadmap to guide the responsible adoption of this technology across industry and beyond. Colleagues in our Anthropology department will lead an innovative approach to responsible innovation by coordinating collaborations between the different disciplines and stakeholders involved in the project. Potential benefits for society Structural energy storage materials have attracted increasing international attention. In 2025, the World Economic Forum identified structural energy storage materials as one of its leading emerging technologies. The technology could support advances in sectors including transport, aerospace, consumer electronics, healthcare and infrastructure. By combining multiple functions in a single material, researchers hope to reduce material use and improve overall efficiency. The project will also explore wider societal questions, examining how multifunctional materials could influence the design and use of future technologies.

artigo.texto: O potencial de transformar créditos de carbono em ativos financeiros. Além de servir a objetivos ambientais, os créditos de carbono estão sendo cada vez mais reconhecidos como um ativo capaz de se conectar com fluxos de capital internacionais. Báo Tin Tức•23/09/2026 Com o objetivo de estabelecer a Corporação Financeira Internacional do Vietnã (VIFC-DN) em Da Nang , a cidade está se esforçando para criar um ecossistema de financiamento de carbono, desde sistemas de medição, relatórios e avaliação (MRV) até ferramentas financeiras especializadas, abrindo assim mais oportunidades para mobilizar recursos para o crescimento verde. Do potencial de redução de emissões a ativos valiosos No processo de transição para um modelo de crescimento verde, o desafio não é apenas reduzir as emissões de gases de efeito estufa, mas também mensurar, verificar e traduzir os resultados dessa redução em valor econômico real. O Vietnã possui grande potencial para créditos de carbono provenientes da agricultura, silvicultura e energias renováveis; somente a região central pode explorar esse potencial em setores como o de café Robusta, pimenta, pellets de madeira e projetos de energia renovável. No entanto, potencial não se traduz em comercialização. Uma floresta que absorve carbono, uma área de produção agrícola que reduz emissões ou um projeto de energia renovável só podem gerar créditos valiosos se puderem demonstrar o quanto as emissões foram reduzidas e se esse resultado puder ser verificado de forma independente com dados. O Dr. Nguyen Phuong Nam, fundador e CEO da KLINOVA Company, acredita que a conclusão abrangente das regulamentações sobre inventário de gases de efeito estufa, critérios de classificação verde, financiamento verde, Plano de Transição Energética Justa (JETP), sistemas MRV, precificação de carbono e padrões ESG é crucial para conectar o mercado doméstico aos padrões globais. É também aqui que o mercado de carbono deixa de ser uma questão ambiental e passa a ser uma questão financeira. Quando as reduções de emissões são medidas, relatadas e validadas por meio de um sistema suficientemente confiável, esses resultados podem ser creditados, negociados e se tornar um ativo capaz de gerar valor. No plano de desenvolvimento do VIFC-DN, o mercado de carbono está agrupado com finanças verdes, gestão de fundos, serviços financeiros e fintech. Da Nang pretende construir infraestrutura de mercado, um sistema de MRV (Monitoramento, Relato e Verificação) de acordo com padrões internacionais e instrumentos financeiros especializados, conectando assim o valor criado pela redução de emissões com os fluxos de capital internacionais. Não espere a emissão do certificado para procurar um comprador. Se o MRV (Monitoramento, Relato e Verificação) é uma condição para comprovar o valor dos créditos, então a abordagem de mercado determina o potencial de comercialização. Um dos pontos notáveis na orientação de desenvolvimento do mercado de carbono no VIFC-DN é a mudança de mentalidade de "desenvolver o projeto e depois encontrar compradores" para "identificar compradores desde o início". Segundo o Professor Nguyen Xuan Thao, Diretor do Centro de Estudos de Direito Asiático da Faculdade de Direito da Universidade de Washington (EUA), os proprietários de projetos precisam coordenar-se com os compradores desde o início. Identificar as necessidades e os critérios dos compradores desde o princípio ajuda o projeto a selecionar padrões adequados, a desenvolver um sistema de dados e a construir um processo de MRV (Monitoramento, Relato e Verificação) que atenda aos requisitos do mercado internacional. Você também pode gostar Essa abordagem visa evitar situações em que um projeto gera créditos, mas depois tem dificuldades para encontrar um mercado para eles. Para projetos de grande escala, ter um comprador competente envolvido desde o início também ajuda a construir confiança e a criar uma base para a captação de recursos para a implementação. O Dr. Kyle Holland, fundador e CEO da EP Carbon LLC e da Impact Inside, cita o caso da Chestnut Carbon, sua empresa, como um exemplo da potencial conexão entre projetos de carbono e financiamento de capital privado em larga escala. O projeto atraiu a Microsoft como principal compradora e recebeu uma linha de crédito de US$ 210 milhões liderada pelo Morgan Stanley. Essa história ilustra que por trás de um crédito de carbono certificado não existe apenas um projeto de redução de emissões. Existe toda uma cadeia de valor que engloba dados, tecnologia, sistemas de monitoramento, relato e verificação (MRV), organizações de avaliação, investidores, compradores e instituições financeiras. De acordo com a orientação do VIFC-DN, o mercado de carbono não deve ser apenas um local para negociação de créditos, mas também se tornar uma ligação entre projetos verdes no Vietnã e o capital internacional, ao mesmo tempo que forma a infraestrutura para a negociação e a descoberta de preços de carbono. O professor Nguyen Xuan Thao também enfatizou a importância de adotar proativamente mecanismos de cooperação internacional para a troca transfronteiriça de créditos de carbono, conforme o Artigo 6 do Acordo de Paris. Isso proporciona uma base para que os projetos verdes do Vietnã se conectem com centros de financiamento de carbono desenvolvidos na região, aumentando assim o valor dos créditos de carbono e as receitas em moeda estrangeira. Diferentemente do mercado doméstico de conformidade com as normas de carbono, o VIFC-DN concentra-se no segmento internacional do mercado voluntário de carbono e em instrumentos financeiros relacionados baseados em crédito. Essa abordagem visa integrar os valores de redução de emissões da agricultura, silvicultura, energias renováveis, etc., em um sistema de negociação transparente, além de abrir canais adicionais para conexão com recursos financeiros internacionais.
