artigo.texto: Switzerland-based Energy Vault has acquired a portfolio of more than 2.3GW of US battery energy storage system (BESS) development projects from Colorado’s Goshe Energy Storage. The transaction covers 15 projects and expands the company’s Asset Vault platform, which centres on energy storage and AI infrastructure assets. Discover B2B Marketing That Performs Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms. As part of the acquisition, Energy Vault will add two ready-to-build projects with capacities of 150MW and 200MW. Both are projected to become operational in the first quarter of 2028 and together are expected to generate around $30m in annual run-rate earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) once operational. The company said the acquisition brings forward Asset Vault-specific annual recurring EBITDA timelines and it now expects to reach more than $200m (SFr164.51m) in exit run-rate EBITDA by 2028 under its long-term infrastructure ownership strategy. Asset Vault president Cory Magnuson said: “This portfolio fits squarely within Energy Vault’s strategy of acquiring late-stage, de-risked development projects that can be moved efficiently toward construction and operation. “The team has a track record of originating and advancing high-quality BESS projects, and we are glad to have them join us as we continue to scale our owned-asset portfolio across US markets.” To support the development, construction and operation of its newly acquired portfolio, Energy Vault has secured a credit facility commitment of up to $40m from S2G Investments. This commitment continues a strategic partnership between S2G and Goshe and will fund various stages of project progress. The Goshe team, including development professionals with more than 75 years of combined experience in renewable energy, BESS project management and financial services, will join Energy Vault. Goshe CEO Bailey McCallum said: “Joining Energy Vault allows our team to continue the work we started – developing and delivering the storage projects the grid needs – with the backing of a large, vertically integrated and global platform. “We are pleased that S2G will continue as a financing partner through this transition, and we look forward to seeing this portfolio through to construction and operation as part of Energy Vault’s platform.” Energy Vault’s global portfolio currently includes more than 1.75GW of owned energy and AI compute infrastructure assets that are either operating or under construction. The company’s business model spans the full infrastructure life cycle, from development and construction to ongoing service agreements, aiming to generate stable, recurring revenue. In April 2026, Energy Vault signed a binding agreement to acquire an 850MW portfolio of BESS projects from a domestic energy storage developer in Japan.

artigo.texto: What's The Difference Between Data Centers And Crypto Mining? Almost everybody has a personal computer, but it's the servers that keep their modern services running. You pay a subscription for a streaming app? Servers house all the shows and movies you watch. You play games like "Final Fantasy XIV" and "Fortnite"? All your progress and ability to communicate with other players relies on servers. However, not all servers are built the same, and the differences are best illustrated by comparing data centers and crypto mining operations. The differences start with the purposes. Crypto mines produce currency (depending on your definition) by solving complicated math problems. The more problems a mining program solves, the more "money" it generates. Meanwhile, data centers support AI models, from their computations to their learning. Furthermore, while multiple users can access data centers and the AI models they house, each crypto mining operation is reserved for one user. The differences branch out from there. All data centers and crypto mines rely on components operating in parallel, with countless operations carried out at the same time. The more components an installation uses, the more calculations it can handle. Crypto miners primarily rely on GPUs (what few there are after the crypto market sank). These rigs still need CPUs and RAM — only enough to maintain multitasking — but the graphics cards are the main draw. Data centers, meanwhile, use the same components, and while GPUs still do most of the heavy computational lifting, data centers need way more RAM than crypto miners to provide a near-constant stream of data and then send the results to users. The price of doing business At the end of the day, both data centers and crypto mining rigs perform innumerable computations in parallel, but the same could also be said of modern computers. What truly sets them apart is the requirements needed to maintain their performance. While both data centers and crypto mines are energy intensive, AI models require way more power than crypto. For example, two crypto facilities in Sandersville, Georgia consumed enough energy to power around 110,000 households, whereas two similar data center facilities in Atlanta gorged themselves on enough electricity to keep about 458,000 houses lit. And yet despite that electricity going to large corporations, the average citizen is still paying ever-increasing power bills. An exponential power drain isn't the only side effect of running data centers and crypto mining facilities. People complain about the harm these locations cause, from noise pollution to water contamination, but again, data centers cause more harm than crypto mines. AI servers require more effort to stay cool — mostly because they are more sensitive to temperature changes — and thus require more water and electricity to achieve that goal. Somewhat ironically, data centers generally use more sophisticated cooling solutions than crypto mining buildings, which can rely on cheap fans yet still function. But this design makes crypto miners generate more noise, which is saying something since data centers often produce noises up to 96 decibels — well beyond the threshold of sounds harmful to human hearing.

artigo.texto: A participação da SOFAR na The smarter E South America marcou uma nova etapa da atuação da fabricante no Brasil, com a apresentação de soluções para diferentes aplicações de armazenamento de energia e o reforço de sua estrutura local de atendimento, logística e pós-venda. Entre os destaques do estande estiveram o PowerMagic 2.0, voltado ao segmento comercial e industrial; o PowerEasy, direcionado a aplicações residenciais e comerciais; e o PowerIn, desenvolvido para projetos comerciais e industriais de menor porte. David Zhong, CEO da companhia esteve no Brasil durante a feira e se reuniu pessoalmente com clientes e parceiros da empresa. Segundo o executivo, a companhia pretende ampliar os investimentos no mercado brasileiro, especialmente nos segmentos de armazenamento de energia. “A SOFAR está neste mercado há cerca de dez anos e hoje nós já estabelecemos um forte serviço local. E este mercado apresenta um grande potencial em armazenamento ESS, C&I e BESS. Eu e a nossa empresa investiremos cada vez mais recursos aqui”, afirmou Zhong. Como parte dessa estratégia, a fabricante inaugurou neste ano um novo centro em Jundiaí (SP), com mais de 2 mil m². A estrutura reúne estoque local de equipamentos e recursos destinados ao atendimento de garantias, à operação da companhia e ao suporte pós-venda. “Recentemente, alugamos um grande armazém, com mais de 2 mil m², para fortalecer nossos serviços e facilitar nossa operação local”, acrescentou o CEO. PowerMagic 2.0 Uma das novidades apresentadas pela SOFAR foi o PowerMagic 2.0, sistema de armazenamento de energia lançado recentemente e incorporado ao portfólio da fabricante no Brasil. Voltada a aplicações comerciais e industriais, a solução possui 125 kW de potência e 261 kWh de capacidade de armazenamento, distribuídos em cinco packs de baterias. Segundo a fabricante, o PowerMagic 2.0 reúne, em um único gabinete, o banco de baterias, um PCS de 125 kW, sistema de refrigeração líquida e os componentes necessários para a conexão à instalação elétrica do cliente. Eduardo Fróes, diretor LATAM da SOFAR, explicou que o sistema pode ser utilizado em diferentes estratégias de gerenciamento de energia, como arbitragem tarifária, peak shaving, regulação de tensão e frequência, além de outras aplicações conectadas à rede. Para projetos que exigem backup ou operação off-grid, a empresa também apresentou um gabinete capaz de integrar diferentes fontes de energia. De acordo com Fróes, o equipamento possui entradas em corrente alternada que permitem conectar, além do sistema fotovoltaico, geradores a diesel, PCHs (Pequenas Centrais Hidrelétricas) e outras fontes de geração. A configuração permite ainda a conexão de até três unidades de BESS em paralelo, ampliando a potência e a capacidade de armazenamento de acordo com a demanda da instalação. Essa arquitetura pode atender diferentes perfis de consumidores, incluindo indústrias e empreendimentos do agronegócio, principalmente em projetos que combinam mais de uma fonte de geração e exigem maior flexibilidade no gerenciamento da energia. De acordo com a SOFAR, o PowerMagic 2.0 está disponível em estoque no Brasil, e as primeiras unidades têm previsão de entrar em operação em projetos no país ainda em setembro. PowerEasy Outro equipamento apresentado durante o evento foi o PowerEasy, solução que integra inversores híbridos e baterias de baixa tensão para aplicações residenciais e comerciais. O sistema é compatível com diferentes padrões de tensão utilizados no Brasil, incluindo 127/220 V, 120/240 V e 220/380 V, característica que amplia sua aplicação em diferentes configurações da rede elétrica. Segundo a SOFAR, o produto oferece capacidade de sobrecarga de até 100%, que pode ser utilizada durante o carregamento das baterias e o atendimento simultâneo de cargas em corrente alternada. A solução também possui corrente de entrada de 20 A, permitindo a conexão com módulos fotovoltaicos de maior potência. Para aplicações comerciais e industriais de menor porte, a fabricante apresentou o PowerIn, que combina geração fotovoltaica e armazenamento de energia em uma única plataforma. De acordo com a empresa, o equipamento suporta sobredimensionamento fotovoltaico de até 200% e capacidade de sobrecarga de 150%. A solução conta ainda com um EMS (Sistema de Gerenciamento de Energia) integrado, responsável pelo controle dos fluxos de energia e pelo gerenciamento das cargas da instalação. O PowerIn também permite a expansão do banco de baterias, possibilitando adequar a capacidade de armazenamento às necessidades de cada projeto. Entre os recursos de segurança estão o grau de proteção IP66 e o AFCI baseado em inteligência artificial, destinado à detecção de falhas por arco elétrico. O sistema também oferece suporte a cargas desequilibradas. Segundo a fabricante, a integração desses recursos busca simplificar a instalação e reduzir incompatibilidades entre equipamentos, principalmente em projetos comerciais e industriais com diferentes configurações elétricas. Monitoramento pela SOFAR Cloud As soluções da fabricante podem ser acompanhadas por meio da SOFAR Cloud, plataforma própria de monitoramento e gerenciamento de energia. O sistema permite acompanhar a geração, o consumo, o armazenamento e o funcionamento dos equipamentos, oferecendo informações para a gestão de instalações residenciais, comerciais e industriais. Segundo a fabricante, a iniciativa representa um diferencial importante, pois busca garantir que cada solução seja instalada e entregue de acordo com o projeto e as especificações técnicas definidas pela SOFAR com o objetivo de contribuir para a capacitação e educação do setor, promovendo maior

artigo.texto: Virginia Curbs State Support for Large Data Centers, Plans Tighter Rules Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger barred new large data center projects from specified state development and expedited-review programs, taking immediate action while laying out broader restrictions on the industry’s electricity costs, environmental impacts and local approvals. Executive Order 22, signed September 18, excludes new projects with anticipated peak electricity demand of at least 25 megawatts from assistance provided by the Virginia Economic Development Partnership through its Business Ready Sites Program and similar discretionary development or expedited-review programs. The order also restricts new nondisclosure agreements involving agencies under the governor’s supervision. The measures accompany a wider Data Center Accountability Framework that Spanberger plans to advance through agency action and the 2027 General Assembly session. Its proposals include requiring local approval for facilities using more than 25 megawatts, stronger upfront financial commitments from developers and allocating more electricity generation and transmission costs to large users. Those proposals are not all requirements already in force. The initiative addresses a central tension for Virginia: data centers bring construction spending and local tax revenue, but their growing electricity needs require costly infrastructure. A December 2024 study by the state’s Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission identified Northern Virginia as the world’s largest data center market. That study found utility rates at the time appropriately allocated costs to data centers and other customers. It nevertheless warned that expansion would raise system costs, estimating that generation and transmission expenses could add $14 to $37 to a typical Dominion Energy (NYSE: D) residential customer’s monthly bill by 2040, excluding inflation. The commission also estimated the industry contributed $9.1 billion annually to Virginia’s economy, with most benefits arising during construction. The order directs the chief energy officer to work with utilities, the State Corporation Commission and regional grid operator PJM Interconnection on assigning costs driven by large data center loads to those customers. It does not itself establish a new electricity rate. Its transparency provisions also have limits. Agencies must honor existing contracts and nondisclosure agreements. Future agreements that prevent disclosure of material information about proposed commercial data centers are prohibited, absent extraordinary circumstances such as national security. The immediate restriction applies to bodies and employees under the governor’s supervision. Environmental measures largely initiate reviews and accelerate rulemaking. Within 180 days, the Department of Environmental Quality must submit findings on the cumulative effects of data center backup generators, including localized air pollution and options for cleaner equipment. The agency must also provide accelerated work plans for noise regulations and rules governing areas where evaporative cooling could threaten water supplies. The order directs that the Eastern Virginia Groundwater Management Area be designated a cooling water scarcity area. These deadlines concern findings and regulatory plans, rather than requiring every facility to install new equipment within six months. The broader framework proposes limiting on-site natural gas generation and prioritizing grid access for facilities meeting stronger clean-energy and emissions conditions. Spanberger’s administration will seek legislation to put additional provisions into law in 2027. The order also creates an artificial intelligence task force to develop executive and legislative responses to risks including job displacement, privacy violations and cyberattacks. It must examine existing enforcement powers and coordinate with leading AI developers. Another initiative, called VA-LEAD, would evaluate facilities through a tiered system covering resource use, infrastructure impacts, employment and community benefits. Proposed criteria and an implementation plan are due by the end of 2027, leaving important details of the administration’s longer-term approach still to be developed.

artigo.texto: - The Hungarian plant will become CATL's largest production base outside China once all facilities are ready. - The first 2 cell production lines began trial runs to prepare for equipment commissioning and process validation ahead of mass production. CATL (HKEX: 3750) has started producing battery cells at its Hungarian plant, moving closer to supplying European automakers at scale from a local facility. The plant secured all permits required for trial operations and began trial cell production on September 22, the Chinese battery giant said in a statement on Tuesday. The new cell factory in Debrecen met all prerequisites for trial operations, with its first 2 production lines beginning trial runs. Trial production is intended to set up, optimize and validate production equipment and manufacturing processes ahead of mass production. The company did not disclose a specific timetable for mass production in the statement. The plant obtained an occupancy permit in August, followed by all remaining relevant permits, and fulfilled all prerequisites under its Integrated Pollution Prevention and Control (IPPC) permit before starting trial operations. Local authorities conducted repeated on-site inspections before issuing the occupancy permit to follow up on issues that had raised serious concerns among residents, CATL said. Regulatory representatives confirmed that all deficiencies previously identified during the permitting process had been resolved. The company said it would continue monitoring employee health, safety and environmental indicators during trial operations and proactively submit the results to regulators while maintaining close cooperation with the government and relevant authorities. Trial cell production marks a significant step in CATL's efforts to expand its local supply capacity in Europe. The company has manufactured battery modules in Debrecen since the fall of 2024, producing 537,000 to date. The Hungarian plant will become CATL's largest production base outside China once all facilities are ready, with a capacity of 100 gigawatt-hours (GWh), the company said. CATL announced the project in August 2022 as its second European battery plant after its German facility, aiming to deepen its integration into Europe's automotive and electric mobility supply chains. Construction of the first cell building began in summer 2023, and production equipment installation was completed by spring 2026. CATL said the site uses flexible production lines to meet customer needs. The start of trial cell production comes later than the company's earlier production target. Reuters reported in September 2025, citing CATL's European general manager Matt Shen, that the company was aiming to begin production in late 2025 or early 2026. CATL is the world's largest maker of EV batteries, with global battery installations reaching 289.6 GWh in January-July, up 26.6% from a year earlier, according to data released earlier this month by South Korean market researcher SNE Research. The company's global market share rose to 39.9% in January-July from 38.0% a year earlier, approaching 40%.

artigo.texto: Mombak anuncia novo fundo e passa a contar com Salesforce como compradora de créditos de carbono A startup brasileira Mombak lançou seu segundo fundo de reflorestamento com meta de US$ 150 milhões e crédito de R$ 200 milhões do BNDES para restaurar a Amazônia. Além disso, fechou um contrato de venda de créditos de carbono com a Salesforce, somando-se a clientes como Google e Microsoft. Com a expansão do mercado, impulsionada pelas emissões da infraestrutura de IA, a empresa e o BNDES preveem uma demanda ampliada para além das big techs, atraindo setores como mineração, petróleo e siderurgia. A startup brasileira de remoção de carbono Mombak anunciou nesta segunda-feira que concluiu o primeiro fechamento de seu segundo fundo de reflorestamento e assinou um novo contrato de compra antecipada de créditos de carbono com a Salesforce , ao mesmo tempo em que aposta que a demanda se expandirá para além das empresas de tecnologia que ajudaram a construir o mercado. A empresa informou que o "The Amazon Reforestation Fund II" tem como meta arrecadar US$150 milhões para financiar projetos de restauração na Amazônia brasileira e terá acesso a uma linha de crédito de R$200 milhões do Fundo Clima, operado pelo BNDES . Os investidores estão de olho nas tendências de demanda no mercado emergente de remoção de carbono, onde empresas como Google , Microsoft e Meta surgiram como grandes compradoras, à medida que buscam lidar com as emissões ligadas à rápida expansão da infraestrutura de IA. "A gente só está conseguindo fazer a captação desse segundo fundo porque a gente conseguiu provar ao longo desses últimos cinco anos que existe um business, existe uma indústria. Esse produto que a gente se propôs a criar, essa solução, tem um mercado para ela", disse o presidente-executivo da Mombak, Gabriel Silva, à Reuters. O primeiro fundo da Mombak arrecadou US$120 milhões de investidores, incluindo um fundo da AXA , a CPP Investments e a Bain Capital, financiando projetos de restauração em 15 fazendas na Amazônia, onde a empresa plantou quase 15 milhões de árvores nativas. A empresa também anunciou um contrato plurianual de compra de créditos de remoção de carbono com a Salesforce, adicionando a empresa de software a uma lista de compradores que já inclui Google, Microsoft e McLaren Racing. O acordo segue a primeira emissão de créditos de remoção de carbono por reflorestamento da Mombak, realizada no início deste ano. A empresa espera uma segunda emissão, maior, de aproximadamente 80 mil toneladas métricas até o final de 2026. SURGIMENTO DE NOVOS COMPRADORES Embora as grandes empresas de tecnologia tenham ajudado a estabelecer o mercado para remoções de carbono de alta qualidade, tanto a Mombak quanto o BNDES esperam que a demanda se expanda para novos setores. "Ao longo do tempo, eu acho que você pode até esperar que a gente volte com anúncios de empresas que não são essas big techs", disse Silva, acrescentando que ganhos de produtividade e técnicas aprimoradas de reflorestamento estão reduzindo os custos e tornando os créditos acessíveis a uma gama mais ampla de compradores. A diretora socioambiental do BNDES, Tereza Campello, disse que as empresas de tecnologia estão reavaliando suas metas climáticas à medida que os custos associados a data centers com alto consumo de energia ficam mais claros, enquanto o interesse de setores como petróleo, mineração e siderurgia se intensificou. "A gente tem sido procurado por outros setores que não estavam com tanto apetite para a área de crédito de carbono, que têm se mostrado muito interessados", disse ela. Os créditos de carbono permitem que as empresas compensem as emissões de gases de efeito estufa por meio do financiamento de atividades que reduzam ou removam emissões em outros locais.

artigo.texto: Plataformas Broadcast Soluções de Dados e Conteúdos Soluções de Tecnologia A DoGo Power realizou o evento "Formando o Futuro da Energia" - Estratégia e Lançamento de Novos Produtos, lançando globalmente sua estratégia "Orientada a Cenários + Formação de 22 de setembro de 2026 XANGAI, 22 de setembro de 2026 /PRNewswire/ — A DoGo Power realizou o evento “Formando o Futuro da Energia” – Estratégia e Lançamento de Novos Produtos, lançando globalmente sua estratégia “Orientada a Cenários + Formação de Redes + IA”, juntamente com soluções inteligentes de armazenamento de energia para formação de redes para cenários comerciais e industriais (C&I) de grande e médio porte e em escala de serviços públicos. Robin Zhu, fundador e CEO da DoGo Power, afirmou: “Após uma rápida expansão em escala, o setor de armazenamento de energia entrou em uma fase de desenvolvimento de alta qualidade.” A adaptação de cenários, a formação de redes e a IA tornaram-se elementos essenciais da competitividade. O armazenamento de energia precisa deixar de ser uma “unidade de custo” e se tornar uma “unidade criadora de valor”. A DoGo Power concentra-se no armazenamento de energia em escala de rede para formação de redes elétricas, com o objetivo de ser líder em tecnologia de ponta para o novo tipo de sistema de energia. Buscamos cooperar com parceiros globais para fomentar um novo crescimento industrial através da inovação tecnológica.” A DoGo Power estabeleceu três centros de P&D e dois centros de simulação e testes na China, reunindo 19 grupos de especialistas interdisciplinares liderados por doutores, com mais de 60% da equipe dedicada à P&D. Seus três centros de produção globais oferecem uma capacidade de produção de 10 GWh na primeira fase. Apoiada por uma rede de vendas e serviços que abrange mais de 30 países e regiões, a DoGo evoluiu da exportação de produtos para a operação localizada. Orientação estratégica: Da industrialização da energia renovável à transformação das indústrias tradicionais pelas energias renováveis. A DoGo Power identifica um caminho de evolução em quatro estágios para um novo tipo de sistema de energia: 1-Expansão de P&D, da indústria e das tecnologias, 2-Formação de Grade para Estabilização, 3-IA para Maior Receita e 4-Integração Inteligente Holística. O setor encontra-se atualmente na Fase 2. Com base nisso, a DoGo desenvolve uma solução para a Etapa 3 e implementa negócios globais rumo à Etapa 4 sob dois pilares principais: Integrando EMS, PMS, PCS e BMS, a plataforma 4S constrói estações de armazenamento de energia inteligentes capazes de análise, otimização, tomada de decisões e atualização iterativa. Com o respaldo dessa base técnica, a DoGo fornece soluções em escala de rede adequadas para diversos cenários, requisitos de múltiplas energias e múltiplas escalas temporais em todo o mundo. Soluções de Novos Produtos Baseadas em Cenários Duas soluções emblemáticas de sistemas de armazenamento de energia (ESS) para formação de redes inteligentes foram lançadas para cenários comerciais e industriais (C&I) e de grande escala para concessionárias de serviços públicos. 1.Solução C&I Smart GFM ESS Adotando um design compacto do tipo “1 ESS substitui 8 gabinetes”, esta unidade de 3 metros consolida as funções de seis gabinetes ESS de 260 kWh+, um gabinete combinador, um gabinete on/off-grid e um transformador de isolamento. Isso reduz o CAPEX inicial em 1,2 centavos de dólar por Wh, diminui a ocupação de terras em 35% e encurta a entrega do projeto em 5 a 7 dias. Com suporte para acesso a múltiplas fontes, como painéis fotovoltaicos, geradores a diesel, pontos de recarga, rede elétrica e sistemas de gerenciamento, o sistema permite a comutação perfeita entre conexão e desconexão da rede em ?20ms, atendendo de forma confiável cargas sensíveis e de alta potência e concretizando o conceito de “1 contêiner equivale a 1 microrrede”. A capacidade de dimensionamento flexível suporta a implantação mista de diferentes séries e a compatibilidade com inversores de terceiros para maximizar a utilização dos ativos existentes. 2.Solução de armazenamento de energia GFM inteligente em escala de utilidade pública Desenvolvido para projetos com terrenos complexos e restrições de transporte, o contêiner pesa menos de 22 toneladas, dobrando as rotas de transporte viáveis em comparação com os contêineres convencionais de 20 pés e reduzindo os custos de logística marítima e terrestre. Seu design sem cabos elimina a necessidade de escavações e montagem de cabos no local, com o pré-comissionamento completo do sistema realizado na fábrica. Aproveitando a arquitetura dinâmica de taxa C, os clientes podem começar com uma implementação de duração de 2 horas para controlar o CAPEX e expandir por meio de gabinetes de expansão de data center para ajustar suavemente as taxas C e as durações de backup para corresponder aos modelos de negócios em evolução. No que diz respeito à geração, permite uma relação de 4:1 entre energia solar e armazenamento, duplicando a instalação de painéis fotovoltaicos sem necessidade de atualizações no ponto de acoplamento comum (PCC). Do lado da rede elétrica, opera de forma estável em redes fracas (SCR > 1), atenua as flutuações terminais e melhora a confiabilidade do fornecimento de energia em 0,03%. Do lado da carga, realiza a comutação entre sistemas conectados à rede e isolados em menos de 20 ms e fortalece a interação bidirecional entre fonte e carga. artigo.texto: KEARNEYSVILLE - A national group opposed to the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure stopped in Berkeley County Friday as part of a cross-country bus tour aimed at raising concerns about data center development. The Data Center Revolt and Humans First tour brought organizers and supporters to the Eastern Panhandle, where they met with local residents and Delegate Chris Anders, who has opposed legislation intended to make West Virginia more attractive to data center development. The group said its visit was prompted in part by the proposed Bedington data center campus in Berkeley County, which has been described as covering about 548 acres and nearly 2 million square feet, with as much as 600 megawatts of IT capacity. Brooke McGowan, who spoke during the event on behalf of the Data Center Revolt, said the group has been traveling across the country to hear from communities dealing with proposed data center projects. “Do the people who live, who have to live with all these decisions, actually have a voice in making?” McGowan said. She said residents should be asking questions about who will use the facilities, where their electricity and water will come from, who will pay for infrastructure and who will bear the risks associated with the projects. Anders, who represents West Virginia’s 97th House District, said his opposition is not to data centers themselves but to what he described as a lack of protections for communities where they are built. “I am not opposed to the existence of data centers. I'm not opposed to technology, I'm not opposed to investment, and I'm not opposed to bringing economic opportunity to West Virginia,” Anders said. “But I am opposed and will always be opposed to giving any corporation a blank check at the expense of the people who already live here.” Anders was one of three Republican delegates who voted against House Bill 2014 in 2025. The legislation established a framework for high-impact data centers and limited certain local regulatory controls over qualifying facilities. During his remarks Friday, Anders outlined several changes he said should be made to state law, including restoring local input, establishing buffers between data centers and homes, schools and churches, protecting private property from eminent domain, limiting the use of groundwater for cooling and protecting ratepayers from infrastructure costs. He also said he and another delegate introduced amendments during the 2026 legislative session intended to establish those protections. “There’s a difference between stopping them and making them be good neighbors,” Anders said. Anders said he believes the state’s proximity to Northern Virginia, home to a large concentration of data centers, is one reason companies are increasingly looking toward West Virginia. “We’re right next door to Loudoun County, the data center capital of the world,” he said. “Loudoun County put guardrails on data centers, right? So where are they going to come next? They’re going to hop the river and be over here.” Organizers said concerns about local control and property rights have been common throughout the tour. The tour launched in Austin, Texas, the previous Saturday and is scheduled to continue through several states, organizers said. Representatives said they have heard similar concerns from residents dealing with projects ranging from several hundred acres to thousands of acres. Amy Kremer, chairwoman of Humans First, said the organization wants residents to have a greater role in decisions affecting their communities. “The only way it’s stopped is by courageous warriors like Chris and others across the country who are standing up and pushing back and saying, no, we don’t have to take this,” Kremer said. Anders said he believes the debate should focus less on whether people support or oppose data centers and more on what protections should accompany development. “I don’t want to close West Virginia to investment,” he said. “But I refuse to open West Virginia for development without first protecting West Virginians.” Organizers said the bus tour will continue across the country, including stops in Pennsylvania, Ohio and Kentucky before traveling west.

artigo.texto: Texas Gov. Greg Abbott on Monday ordered the state's environmental regulator to halt all data center-related permits until the Electric Reliability Council of Texas completes an audit of the existing waitlist for data centers looking to connect to the state's grid. The audits were originally ordered by the governor's office in August, when Abbott also imposed a moratorium on new data center grid approvals. This directive expands the moratorium to environmental approvals through the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality. Texas was on track to surpass Virginia as the state with the largest data center market in the world by the end of the decade, according to a February report from JLL, but Abbott's Monday directive may slow that progress. Last month, analysts at BloombergNEF found that "almost 20% of the U.S.'s 253-GW data center pipeline" would be at risk with Texas's pause, or nearly 50 gigawatts in proposed data center capacity. This could result in upwards of $8 billion in data center revenue losses by Q1 2027. A report from advocacy group Data Center Watch claimed $68 billion in new data center development was delayed or cancelled last quarter due to local pushback — a risk that is bleeding into financial markets. Anthropic's much-anticipated IPO is poised to include negative public opinion towards AI and data centers as a risk factor in its forthcoming prospectus. The data center buildout has been a breakout issue in the 2026 midterm election, with a recent NBC News poll finding 64% of Americans would be less likely to vote for a candidate who "supports building local data centers." Abbott, who is running a tight race for his fourth term against state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, has specifically been caught in the middle of the firestorm. Abbott has had to reverse course on his 2025 claim that Texas, due to its sales tax exemptions for qualifying data centers, as well as its high-profile projects like OpenAI's Stargate, would be the "epicenter of AI development." "Next session, Governor Abbott will work with the Legislature to eliminate any financial incentives for data centers," the press release for the moratorium said. The TCEQ is expected to provide an update to the governor's office on its compliance with this directive by Oct. 19.

artigo.texto: Polo de data centers no futuro da região O Grande ABC pode subir para a nuvem, ao menos na intenção. A ideia veio de Akira Auriani (PSB), prefeito de Rio Grande da Serra, que levou ao Consórcio Intermunicipal a proposta de transformar a região em um novo hub de data centers. O plano ganhou força ontem (22), em São Caetano, diante do ministro do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços, Márcio Elias Rosa. Na teoria, a conta fecha: água e energia são o combustível dessas operações, e Akira garante ter ambas. O desafio é fazer a nuvem descer ao chão. Há um caminho nada glamouroso pela frente: rever Planos Diretores, mapear terrenos e desenhar incentivos fiscais. O próprio prefeito admite que “não é tão simples”. A promessa de empregos e renda é valiosa, mas, até o primeiro servidor ligar, há muita burocracia para processar. Bastidores Compartilhando Que o vereador de São Bernardo José Aurélio Bacelar de Pa ula, presidente do diretório municipal do Podemos, é aliado de primeira hora da presidente nacional da legenda, deputada federal Renata Abreu, que busca a reeleição, não é novidade. O diferencial de Aurélio, porém, parece ir além da lealdade partidária, tanto que o podemista deve acompanhar Renata em agendas de campanha pelo Estado. Na segunda-feira (21), por exemplo, na Associação dos Funcionários Públicos, o fiel escudeiro ficou até o fim do evento ao lado da deputada, enquanto alguns saíram à surdina e deixaram a presidente nacional à procura dos correligionários. A corrida eleitoral do ex-prefeito de São Bernardo Frank Aguiar (Podemos) por vaga no Congresso ganhou reforço estético. Em meio à rotina de campanha, o candidato a deputado federal abriu espaço na agenda para renovar a harmonização facial. Pelo visto, o “Cãozinho dos Teclados” quer garantir o retorno a Brasília com cara de recém-chegado à política. Afinal, para suportar a maratona até a urna sem demonstrar o cansaço na pele, um retoque no visual cai bem. De cá ou de lá? O vereador de São Caetano Bruno Vassari (PSB) tem marcado presença nas agendas de reeleição da deputada estadual Carla Morando (PSD) e da candidatura de Orlando Morando (MDB) à Câmara Federal. No entanto, em evento no município, o parlamentar endossou apoio aos correligionários Caio França (a estadual) e Tabata Amaral (a federal). A movimentação com os aliados de sigla, contudo, foi discreta: não houve sequer um registro fotográfico publicado em seu perfil oficial. Atenção! Os comentários do site são via Facebook. Lembre-se de que o comentário é de inteira responsabilidade do autor e não expressa a opinião do jornal. Comentários que violem a lei, a moral e os bons costumes ou violem direitos de terceiros poderão ser denunciados pelos usuários e sua conta poderá ser banida.

artigo.texto: XIAMEN, China, Sept. 22, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- At its “Powered Day in, Day out” launch event, HiTHIUM unveiled the ∞Power N4.0MWh, a 4 MWh sodium-ion battery energy storage system equipped with its new ∞Cell N785Ah cell. Designed for a 30-year service life, the solution is scheduled to enter full-scale production and delivery in 2027. HiTHIUM said the ∞Cell N785Ah was developed through integrated innovation in materials and manufacturing processes. It uses a polyanionic chemistry based on an NFPP cathode, hard-carbon anode and customized electrolyte, together with ultra-thick electrodes and long-life structural components. Wide-format stacking makes the cell compatible with HiTHIUM’s existing kAh-class lithium-ion manufacturing platform, supporting production scale-up. The cell is designed for 20,000 cycles at 70% state of health and supports storage durations from two to eight hours. At system level, a stacked-cell architecture reduces station footprint by 30%, while PCS rated-power utilization is more than 20% higher than in HiTHIUM’s previous-generation sodium-ion system. HiTHIUM also reports 24-hour comprehensive efficiency above 88%, with operating and standby auxiliary power consumption reduced by 30% and 50%, respectively. The system is designed to align its operating life with a 30-year power-station cycle. “30 years means 10,950 days of validation—a long-term commitment to our customers,” said Dr. Aileen Wang, Director of HiTHIUM’s Battery Research Institute. The product advances support HiTHIUM’s goal of accelerating sodium-ion industrialization. Dr. Nazar Yi, Chief Technology Officer of HiTHIUM, identified affordability and long-term resource availability as the two main requirements for large-scale deployment. HiTHIUM positions the new solution as part of an effort to treat electrochemical storage as long-life energy infrastructure and move levelized storage costs toward RMB 0.1 per kWh. The company views sodium-ion as complementary to lithium-ion rather than a replacement. It will initially target utility-scale storage before expanding into commercial and industrial, residential and broader energy-access applications. HiTHIUM also launched the ∞Edge Pioneer Program to test cells and systems in extreme environments and disclose progress over the next three years. About HiTHIUM Founded in 2019, HiTHIUM specializes in integrated energy storage solutions centered on battery and system technologies. Its capabilities span R&D, manufacturing, delivery, operation and maintenance, with operations across more than 40 countries and regions. HiTHIUM focuses on utility-scale, long-duration and grid-side energy storage. Its strategy combines purpose-built products for different storage durations with expanding global manufacturing, sales and service networks to strengthen localized delivery and lifecycle support. artigo.texto: Following seven fact-finding meetings over nine months, Gov. Tina Kotek’s Data Center Advisory Committee is asking the public to weigh in on a report detailing its findings. The 20-page “preliminary learnings and questions” report that the seven-member, governor-appointed group posted Friday includes more considerations than conclusions, and is a departure from the cost-benefit analysis of data centers in the state it was tasked with providing by mid-September. That charge changed recently when Kotek instead directed the group to synthesize its findings for the public before providing her with final recommendations by the end of the year — and after the November election. The public has until Oct. 24 at 5 p.m. to submit comments based on the report. Although the report does not include distinct policy recommendations, the group seems to have found consensus around a need for more responsible oversight of the data center industry and a more centralized information repository about Oregon data centers’ type, their water and energy use and the tax breaks they receive each year through state incentive programs. The committee’s findings land as the growth of the data center industry in the state has become a lightning rod in the Oregon governor’s race amid growing public backlash. Kotek and her Republican challenger, state Sen. Christine Drazan of Canby, have tried in recent months to paint themselves as the lone force to stop the industry’s proliferation in the state. Last week, Kotek shared her support for a statewide data center moratorium at a rally at the Oregon Capitol and unveiled a roughly one-year pause on approvals for any requests to develop data centers on state land or in state buildings. She also insisted that the state lacks the authority to mandate an all-out moratorium. Findings The committee has fielded more than 700 written comments, along with nine hours of verbal comments, since it first met in February. Roughly 90% of commenters expressed opposition to data centers. Utility affordability was the single most frequently listed concern. Most comments came from the Portland metro area, with relatively few from eastern Oregon counties, with substantial ongoing and proposed data center development, according to the report. “Our state has hosted data centers since the earliest generation of internet infrastructure, and these facilities have contributed to the prosperity of urban and rural communities alike across the state,” members wrote. “At the same time, the current unprecedented scale and speed of data center development has raised serious concerns for many Oregonians.” Oregon is among the top ten markets for data centers in the U.S., according to Pew Research, and has for more than 20 years attracted massive server facilities due to a lack of sales tax, moderate climate, relatively cheap electricity and generous property tax incentives for industrial development. But the widespread use of non-disclosure agreements and corporate secrecy around tech companies’ data centers means there is a considerable lack of information about their operations. An ECOnorthwest analysis found the state now hosts between 123 and 144 facilities, a massive increase from the eight data storage facilities in Oregon 25 years ago. The consulting firm found that almost 1 in every 100 jobs in Oregon is related to data centers. The committee wrote that the number of data centers is slated to grow significantly in the years ahead, with approximately 9,000 acres proposed for data center development. Much of that land is in rural areas or on the outskirts of cities. Most data centers in Oregon are small, “non-AI-oriented facilities” used for data storage, payment processing, cloud computing, content streaming, telecommunications and social media, according to the report. But of the 31 data centers in the process of getting sited in Oregon today, eight are hyperscale data centers meant for companies that do large-scale data storage and AI processing, the group wrote. Water, energy, tax breaks Beyond the difficulty of gathering information about the data centers, committee members enumerated what they’d learned about data centers’ growing energy, water and land demands. Committee members consider water quantity for data centers as a bigger issue than water quality, despite concerns from environmental and community groups that the facilities are pumping out water laced with forever chemicals, among others. The committee members found that seasonal water demands for irrigation in some parts of the state mean data centers are becoming unwelcome competition for resources that are already overallocated. When it comes to energy use, the members said the central questions are not only how much electricity Oregon data centers are consuming but how the industry can be leveraged to stimulate more investment in clean energy, grid modernization and other energy development in the state. The state’s lack of accounting for the property, income and other tax breaks data centers are receiving through industrial enterprise zone programs continues to be an issue, according to the report. Local and statewide tax experts and watchdogs who presented to the committee indicated that Oregon is being overly generous to data centers and the tax breaks are not necessary to keeping the facilities in the state. For instance, Morrow County’s assessor told the committee that the $7.2 billion estimated value of tax-exempt property owned by data centers in the county in 2025 was $3 billion more than the combined value of the Morrow County property subject to property taxes. The advisory group did not share any thoughts on whether Oregon’s tax programs should be scaled back for data centers. Instead, it posed a question that has come up repeatedly in meetings during the past nine months: “What should Oregon provide to attract data center investment,” the members wrote, “and what should Oregon and its communities receive in return?” Resour

artigo.texto: AUSTRALIA will support the Philippines’ renewable energy development, carbon market, and offshore wind industry through a P2-billion economic development grant over five years. “This is a program that has been developed jointly by the Australian government and the Philippine government to deliver better economic outcomes to boost infrastructure and to improve living standards in communities throughout the Philippines,” Australian Assistant Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade Matt Thistlethwaite told reporters in a briefing on Tuesday. Thistlethwaite said that renewable energy, the establishment of a carbon market, and the development of the offshore wind industry were among the priority areas discussed with Philippine government officials under the Promoting Growth, Resilience, Economic Stability and Sustainability in the Philippines (Progress) program. “We haven’t allocated funding to specific projects yet. We’re very much in the scoping phase,” he said. Thistlethwaite said the Australian government has already allocated the AU$45 million or P2 billion for the program, but individual projects will still have to be identified and approved through a partnership between the two countries. “That will rely on the requests from the Philippine government. This project is very much about providing support for the Philippines government to deliver on their priorities,” he said. Australia has appointed Boston Consulting Group as a partner that will work with Philippine government departments to develop the details of the projects and funding commitments over the five-year period. Thistlethwaite clarified that the grant should not be viewed as a single disbursement for already identified projects. “The individual projects will be determined by the Australian government in partnership with the Filipino government and the government departments,” he said. As projects are approved, Australia and the Philippines will announce them jointly. “At the moment, the funding has been allocated from the Australian Government. It’s now up to us to work together on providing that funding to individual projects,” Thistlethwaite said.

artigo.texto: Alibaba lançou o Zhenwu V900, descrito pela empresa como o chip de IA mais poderoso da China, enquanto prepara forte expansão de sua infraestrutura. O Alibaba Group (NYSE:BABA) apresentou na terça-feira um novo processador de inteligência artificial, descrevendo-o como o chip de IA mais poderoso da China, e delineou planos para expandir a capacidade de seus data centers para mais de 20 gigawatts até 2032. O CEO Eddie Wu apresentou o acelerador Zhenwu V900 na Conferência Apsara anual da Alibaba em Hangzhou, destacando o investimento da empresa em infraestrutura de IA e computação avançada. As ações da Alibaba listadas em Hong Kong fecharam em alta de 2% na terça-feira, enquanto as ações listadas nos EUA subiram mais de 3% nas negociações pré-mercado. O Zhenwu V900 oferece três vezes o desempenho do seu antecessor Segundo a Alibaba, o Zhenwu V900 oferece desempenho três vezes superior ao do processador Zhenwu M890 da geração anterior. Durante seu discurso de abertura, Wu afirmou: “O Zhenwu V900 é o chip de IA mais poderoso da China atualmente, oferecendo três vezes o desempenho de seu antecessor, o Zhenwu M890.” A alegação de desempenho foi feita pela Alibaba e não foi verificada de forma independente no relatório fornecido. Segundo Wu, o novo acelerador pode ser implantado em clusters com até 500.000 unidades para treinar modelos avançados de IA. O processador desempenhará um papel central nos planos da Alibaba de expandir a capacidade de seus data centers para mais de 20 gigawatts até 2032. Alibaba mira em modelos de IA maiores e infraestrutura de computação Wu também descreveu a ambição da Alibaba de treinar um modelo de IA contendo até 10 trilhões de parâmetros. Ele afirmou que a equipe de desenvolvimento do Qwen, da empresa, estava explorando o aprimoramento recursivo, uma abordagem que envolve sistemas de IA contribuindo para melhorias em suas próprias capacidades. A Alibaba investiu dezenas de bilhões de dólares no desenvolvimento de seus modelos Qwen e na construção da infraestrutura computacional necessária para suportá-los. A empresa também destinou recursos substanciais ao desenvolvimento de processadores de IA proprietários, visto que a China busca aumentar a produção nacional de semicondutores e reduzir a dependência de tecnologia estrangeira. Wu descreveu a demanda do cliente impulsionada por IA como “excepcionalmente robusta”, acrescentando que ela estava contribuindo para o crescimento da receita da Alibaba Cloud. Citi prevê potencial para US$ 160 bilhões em receita com nuvem até o ano fiscal de 2033 Analistas do Citi afirmaram que a expansão de infraestrutura proposta pela Alibaba pode impulsionar significativamente o aumento da receita com computação em nuvem nos próximos anos. Em uma nota de pesquisa, eles afirmaram: “Nossa visão preliminar é que a mensagem do CEO da Alibaba, Sr. Wu, de 20 GW de infraestrutura de IA até 2032, ou nossa projeção para o ano fiscal de 2033, poderia se traduzir em US$ 160 bilhões em receitas externas de nuvem até o ano fiscal de 2033, o que poderia representar um aumento de US$ 60 bilhões em relação à nossa estimativa atual de US$ 100 bilhões no ano fiscal de 2031.” Os analistas acrescentaram: “Isso também sugere uma taxa de crescimento anual composta (CAGR) de receita de aproximadamente 40% do ano fiscal de 2026 ao ano fiscal de 2033, o que implica que o ritmo de crescimento acelerado será mantido.” As projeções do Citi indicam que a receita externa com serviços em nuvem poderá atingir US$ 160 bilhões no ano fiscal de 2033, em comparação com a estimativa anterior de US$ 100 bilhões para o ano fiscal de 2031. Esses números representam as estimativas do banco, e não as projeções formais de receita da Alibaba. Os gastos de capital continuam sendo uma consideração fundamental O Alibaba não revisou sua previsão de despesas de capital de 380 bilhões de yuans. No entanto, o Citi afirmou que os comentários anteriores de Wu durante a teleconferência de resultados da empresa sugeriam que o investimento em infraestrutura de IA poderia permanecer elevado nos próximos anos. Os analistas também esperam que a Alibaba financie parte de sua capacidade computacional planejada por meio de parcerias com outros participantes do setor, o que pode envolver despesas operacionais em vez de investimento de capital direto. Os gastos da Alibaba com IA já afetaram a lucratividade. A empresa reportou uma queda de 75% no lucro líquido em seus resultados trimestrais mais recentes, com a compressão das margens ligada ao seu programa de investimentos. No entanto, a receita proveniente de serviços de computação e nuvem com IA aumentou acentuadamente durante o trimestre de junho, refletindo a crescente contribuição desses negócios para as operações do Alibaba. O Alibaba Group também é negociado na B3 por meio da BDR (BOV:BABA34). artigo.texto: Mais de 740.000 hectares de floresta, com potencial para desenvolvimento de créditos de carbono. O Parque Nacional Song Thanh é uma das maiores áreas florestais de uso especial na cidade de Da Nang . Com aproximadamente 76.000 hectares de floresta primária, esta área tem capacidade para absorver e armazenar uma grande quantidade de carbono. De acordo com cálculos preliminares, esta área florestal pode absorver centenas de milhares de toneladas de CO2 anualmente. Se convertermos 1 tonelada de CO2 em um crédito de carbono, a quantidade de carbono absorvida poderia gerar centenas de milhares de créditos de carbono. Segundo os proprietários de florestas de uso especial e proteção, no contexto dos atuais desastres naturais, se a cidade de Da Nang pudesse vender créditos de carbono, isso geraria receita adicional para a restauração florestal, a recuperação da biodiversidade e uma maior adaptação às mudanças climáticas. O Sr. Dinh Van Hong, Diretor do Conselho de Administração do Parque Nacional Song Thanh, em Da Nang, acredita que a venda de créditos de carbono é uma política viável e que essa receita pode contribuir para a melhoria da qualidade de vida das pessoas na zona de amortecimento, além de fortalecer a capacidade de proteção florestal. Da Nang está gradualmente desenvolvendo projetos de carbono florestal. Após a fusão com a província de Quang Nam, a cidade de Da Nang agora possui mais de 740.000 hectares de floresta, incluindo mais de 500.000 hectares de floresta primária. De acordo com os cálculos apresentados na proposta do projeto, a área florestal da cidade tem capacidade para absorver e armazenar carbono. Anteriormente, desde 2021, a província de Quang Nam foi autorizada pelo Primeiro-Ministro a desenvolver um projeto piloto para a venda de créditos de carbono florestal. Até o momento, a cidade de Da Nang aprovou o Projeto para o Desenvolvimento e Gestão de Créditos de Carbono Florestal para o período de 2026 a 2030, com uma visão para 2035. A cidade pretende ter de 1 a 3 projetos de carbono florestal aprovados até 2030, colaborar com pelo menos 2 parceiros nacionais e internacionais, concluir de 1 a 2 dossiês de registro de projetos e assinar pelo menos um contrato de compra de créditos de carbono. A cidade também almeja que pelo menos 70% dos proprietários de florestas, incluindo organizações, famílias e comunidades elegíveis, participem desta iniciativa. A floresta primária no Parque Nacional de Song Thanh tem potencial para gerar créditos de carbono florestal. De acordo com o plano, o Centro Financeiro Internacional de Da Nang colaborará com agências, unidades e organizações internacionais para estudar a viabilidade do desenvolvimento de projetos de carbono florestal vinculados a atividades de gestão, proteção e desenvolvimento florestal em diversas áreas potenciais. O Sr. Duong Duy Khanh, Gerente de Projetos de Restauração Florestal e Desenvolvimento de Meios de Subsistência na cidade de Da Nang, do WWF Vietnam, afirmou que o WWF está apoiando as localidades na finalização de planos de venda de créditos de carbono, visando a participação do Vietnã no mercado global de carbono. Da Nang almeja um mercado de créditos de carbono. Para gerar créditos de carbono negociáveis, os projetos precisam passar por diversas etapas, desde a identificação do potencial e o desenvolvimento do projeto, até a conclusão da documentação e, finalmente, a medição, avaliação e verificação dos resultados da redução de emissões ou do sequestro de carbono. Segundo os líderes do Comitê Popular da cidade de Da Nang, a cidade está implementando créditos de carbono e pretende integrá-los ao mercado global. Os benefícios dessa atividade são identificados como estando ligados aos interesses da nação e das comunidades da zona de amortecimento. Até 2030, Da Nang pretende ter projetos de carbono florestal aprovados, conectando simultaneamente o fornecimento de créditos de carbono florestal da cidade aos mercados de carbono nacionais e internacionais. A cidade identificou o desenvolvimento de créditos de carbono florestal como essencial para o manejo, a proteção e o desenvolvimento florestal, criando recursos adicionais para a restauração florestal, a conservação e a recuperação da biodiversidade e o apoio aos meios de subsistência das comunidades da zona de amortecimento. Com um plano estratégico elaborado até 2030, Da Nang está implementando gradualmente as condições necessárias para estabelecer projetos de carbono florestal e participar do mercado de créditos de carbono. artigo.texto: CATL Starts Trial Production of Battery Cells in Hungary CATL began trial production of battery cells on September 22, 2026, at its Debrecen plant in Hungary, after obtaining all the environmental authorizations required to launch the phase. Chinese battery maker CATL (Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited) began trial production on September 22, 2026, at its newly built battery cell factory in Debrecen, Hungary. The company states it fulfilled all preconditions required to launch this phase, which aims to set up, optimize and validate production equipment and manufacturing processes ahead of the start of series production. CATL says it continues cooperating with the Hungarian government and local authorities to maintain high standards on environmental issues as well as employee health and safety. A site announced in 2022 CATL announced the construction of this second European production site in Debrecen in August 2022, with the stated aim of integrating into the continent's automotive and e-mobility supply chain. This type of investment is part of a broader push to expand energy storage capacity in Europe, illustrated by the emerging market seen in North Macedonia or by the hybrid solar-storage contract signed between Salzgitter Flachstahl and Zelestra in Germany. Construction of the first cell building began in summer 2023, and the site had been equipped, by spring 2026, with the latest production technologies, according to the company. After obtaining the occupancy permit in August 2026, CATL says it gathered all authorizations required under its IPPC permit (Integrated Pollution Prevention and Control, an integrated pollution prevention and reduction permit) before launching, on September 22, trial production on the first two manufacturing lines at the site. Repeated inspections by local authorities Before issuing the occupancy permit, the HajdÃº-Bihar County Government Office carried out regular on-site inspections at CATL's facilities to follow up on issues that had raised concerns among local residents. According to CATL, authority representatives confirmed that the company had resolved all deficiencies identified earlier in the permitting process. The Debrecen site is set to supply European automakers, several of which have already built electric vehicle production capacity in Hungary in recent years. CATL has been manufacturing battery modules there since autumn 2024 and says it has produced 537,000 modules since then. Once all facilities are operational, the Hungarian plant would, according to the company, become its largest manufacturing base outside China, with an announced capacity of 100 GWh. Environmental and health monitoring CATL says it remains committed to working with the government and authorities to protect the health and safety of its employees. Environmental factors, along with employee health and safety, will be monitored throughout the trial production period, with results to be submitted proactively to authorities, according to the company. The group describes the investment as significant not only for Debrecen and its region but also for the Hungarian economy and Europe's e-mobility supply chain. CATL also states it is committed to transparency and says it welcomes authorities to visit its site at any time.

artigo.texto: Uso de PFAS para resfriar data centers gera questionamentos Substâncias fluoradas ganham espaço com a expansão da inteligência artificial; grupos ambientais questionam os riscos de seu uso. A expansão da inteligência artificial aumenta a demanda por data centers e por sistemas capazes de controlar o calor gerado pelos equipamentos. Entre as soluções em uso estão substâncias fluoradas que incluem PFAS, conhecidos como “químicos eternos”. Em alguns sistemas, elas são usadas em vez de água. A organização ChemSec afirma que fabricantes de PFAS ampliam a produção diante da demanda ligada à infraestrutura de inteligência artificial. O relatório cita Chemours, Daikin e Arkema. Segundo a organização, a Chemours desenvolve produtos para refrigeração de data centers e expande a produção de refrigerantes à base de PFAS. O uso dessas substâncias é questionado por sua resistência à degradação. Em julho, 17 organizações ambientais enviaram uma carta à Agência de Proteção Ambiental dos Estados Unidos contra o pedido da Chemours para acelerar a aprovação do Opteon 2P50, composto destinado à refrigeração de data centers. Os grupos questionaram os dados sobre possíveis riscos à saúde e ao clima. A Chemours contestou as preocupações. Segundo a empresa, o sistema opera em circuito fechado e libera pouca quantidade de gás durante o funcionamento. – Resumen (español) La expansión de la inteligencia artificial aumenta la demanda de refrigeración en los centros de datos. Algunos sistemas utilizan sustancias fluoradas que incluyen PFAS en lugar de agua. La organización ChemSec señala un aumento de la producción de estos compuestos, mientras grupos ambientales cuestionan sus posibles riesgos para la salud y el clima. Summary (English) The expansion of artificial intelligence is increasing demand for data center cooling. Some systems use fluorinated substances, including PFAS, instead of water. ChemSec reports growing production of these compounds, while environmental groups question their potential health and climate risks.

artigo.texto: Oakland is moving closer to hitting pause on new data centers, after a City Council committee approved a proposed 45-day moratorium following testimony from residents on both sides of the issue. While the temporary ban isn't in effect yet, it cleared a key hurdle when the council committee voted in favor of the measure, meaning the city wouldn't accept any new proposals during that period. Watch NBC Bay Area News free wherever you are Environmental concerns drove much of the opposition at the hearing. Among them is a planned project at a 20,000-square-foot downtown building intended to provide computing power for artificial intelligence and robotics. While the developer calls it an "innovation center," members of the public repeatedly referred to it as a "data center." "With the proliferation of Artificial Intelligence there have been a proliferation of data centers that are more resource intensive than the past… consuming significant amounts of electrical power and water," said Oakland City Councilmember Carroll Fife. Councilmember Rowena Brown echoed the need for oversight. "The moratorium is really important because we need to work and identify key regulations we need in our city… so really just to halt and put a pause." Public commenters voiced deep frustration over the wave of development. Local "It doesn’t matter the size of the data center, it's about whether or not we will allow our city to be the playground for the ultra rich," one public commenter said. Another added, "Communities are being asked to sacrifice… this isn’t fair and it’s something we shouldn’t be doing." However, not everyone opposed the projects. A small group of speakers argued that data centers could bring much-needed jobs and new revenue to the city. "What Oakland needs is not more taxes… we need manufacturing… what works… AI," a public commenter argued. The debate mirrors similar conflicts across the Bay Area. Cities like Gilroy and Richmond recently approved their own 45-day moratoriums amid neighbor concerns. The local pushes coincide with state action; Governor Gavin Newsom recently signed seven new data center laws addressing electricity and water use by operators. Brown, who voted in favor of the Oakland committee measure, emphasized that community involvement remains vital. "I would encourage the community to continue to show up and let their voices be heard," she said. The proposed moratorium now heads to the full Oakland City Council, with a final vote scheduled for Oct. 6.

artigo.texto: An Intertek lab in the UK found just 3.4 ppm of lithium in a sample of Donut Lab’s “solid-state” battery, and the Finnish startup is now using that result to argue its cell is neither lithium-ion nor sodium-ion. But the report measured just two elements, on a cell Donut Lab took apart itself. And nine months after CES, there’s still no production vehicle running on the battery. A two-element test The Finnish startup says the goal was to end the debate over what’s inside its cell. “We wanted to put this speculation to rest with an independent test demonstrating that it is neither a lithium-ion nor a sodium battery,” CEO Marko Lehtimäki said in the announcement. That speculation didn’t come out of nowhere. In June, battery researcher Ziroth and more than 20 experts concluded that the cell Donut Lab sent to VTT behaved like a high-nickel lithium-ion cell with a graphite anode, based on its voltage curve and swelling data. Intertek’s report, from its lab in Wilton, UK, is short. Analysts cut about 0.5 g of material from anode, cathode, and current collector pieces, digested it in nitric acid, diluted it to 50 ml, and ran it through an ICP-OES instrument. Results: 3.4 ppm lithium and 632 ppm sodium by weight. A lithium-ion cell carries lithium in the percent range. So if that sample is what Donut Lab says it is, there’s essentially no lithium in it. The lab work itself is fine. The problems start with everything around it. What the report doesn’t show Start with the scope. The job Donut Lab ordered was literally “Quantification of Li and Na by ICP-OES.” Nothing else was measured. The report tells you two things the cell isn’t and zero things about what it is. Potassium, magnesium, zinc, and aluminum were never tested, and Donut Lab still won’t name its chemistry beyond “widely available, affordable and geopolitically secure materials.” Then there’s the sample. According to Intertek, “the samples were delivered in a tear down condition by Donut Lab.” Intertek didn’t open a cell. It matched the pieces to another Intertek report (2608094STO-003) that hasn’t been made public, and the analyzed sample is labeled simply “Pouchcell – Cell 1.” The words “Donut Battery” appear nowhere in the report, and nothing ties this sample to the V1.5 cell that VTT tested for energy density. The press release also says the samples included “the electrolyte situated between” the anode and cathode. Intertek’s report says otherwise, three separate times: only anode, cathode, and current collector parts were analyzed. In a solid-state battery, the electrolyte layer is a pretty important place to look for lithium. And the report went through three versions in five days. The first was issued September 17. A September 21 revision updated the “sample description and origin of samples,” and a September 22 revision made a “wording change requested in experimental.” That’s a lot of editing for a report with a single two-column results table. Finally, Intertek notes that “opinions and interpretations contained herein are outside the scope of UKAS accreditation.” The line that “it is not even possible to build a functional battery with such small amounts of active materials” comes from Donut CTO Ville Piippo, not the lab. It makes the 409 Wh/kg claim harder to believe Near-zero lithium and sodium fits one theory that has followed Donut Lab since CES: a supercapacitor or hybrid capacitor, with carbon electrodes and an electrolyte that doesn’t rely on either element. That would line up with the fast-charging and cycle-life claims. It wouldn’t line up with energy density. Earlier this month, VTT measured 409.3 Wh/kg on a Donut “V1.5” cell, cycled between 2.3 V and 4.25 V. That’s a textbook lithium-ion voltage window, and 409 Wh/kg is a number advanced silicon-anode lithium-ion cells already hit. No rechargeable chemistry without lithium or sodium has come anywhere close to that in a real cell. So either Donut Lab has quietly invented a chemistry that beats every battery lab on the planet, or the cell VTT tested and the pieces Intertek analyzed aren’t the same thing. This report doesn’t tell us which. Electrek’s Take We don’t care much anymore whether Donut Lab’s battery is solid-state and these vague and limited tests that may or may not prove otherwise do very little to Donut Lab’s credibility. Solid-state cells exist. QuantumScape, Factorial, Samsung SDI, and Toyota all have them running in labs and prototype vehicles, and all of them are still working toward mass production. A startup with a promising solid-state prototype is not news in 2026. The only thing that made Donut Lab interesting was the production claim. At CES in January, it said it had the “world’s first solid state battery that is ready for use in OEM vehicle manufacturing,” with Verge motorcycles delivering to customers in Q1 2026. Lehtimäki said it was “already in production.” We’re now at the end of September. There’s no production vehicle on the road with this battery, the Q1 “production” bikes were pre-production units, and Lehtimäki himself admitted that the 409 Wh/kg cell “is not even the cell that’s going to be shipped to customers.” So the claim that set Donut apart turned out to be wrong, and every new report since has been built to answer a different question than the one that matters. artigo.texto: Perhaps even more controversial than artificial intelligence itself is the backbone that powers the technology: Data centers can be loud and polluting, while requiring tremendous amounts of electricity and water resources. These data centers are also a key to future economic growth. AI, like it or not, is here to stay. The question in Massachusetts has become: What approach should the Commonwealth take? Massachusetts is a knowledge economy that already leans heavily on AI. Turning our backs on data centers feels hypocritical. That doesn’t mean, however, that we should roll out the welcome mat with tax credits and let data center builders dictate the shots. Governor Maura Healey has offered up a solid framework to guide any future data center buildout. Her “bring your own clean energy” approach strikes the right note. It says to developers: Yes, you can build here but not on the backs of energy ratepayers. And you can’t burn planet-warming fossil fuels or pass along the costs of connecting your enterprise to the power grid. The governor wants data centers to either build their own clean energy supplies or pay into a ratepayer protection fund. The governor’s stated approach is to try to balance economic growth alongside protections for Massachusetts residents. Healey also signed an executive order this month requiring community approval before state permits are issued to new data centers. Jennifer Granholm, a former secretary of energy under former president Joe Biden, called the governor’s plans a “good blueprint for the rest of the country.” Granholm said Healey “isn’t reflexively saying ‘no’ to data centers, and she isn’t writing them a blank check either. She’s saying: if you want to build here, bring something to the table.” A framework from a governor can offer guidance to state agencies, but it doesn’t carry the weight of law. The Massachusetts Legislature is working on solutions, tucked into two behemoth energy bills making their way through the House and Senate. The House is proposing that data centers “procure” renewable energy to power at least 80 percent of a data center’s needs. The Senate has proposed putting a pause on growth to buy time to study the best path forward. The chamber is also discussing putting limits on tax breaks for data centers. (The governor halted applications for data center tax incentives in June.) As with any new and quickly evolving industry, many questions will need to be sorted out. A key sticking point: What could renewable energy procurement look like? Should data centers be required to physically build solar panels with battery storage, for example? Or, if data centers are relying on renewable power from the grid, how do we ensure this isn’t pushing another customer off of clean energy and onto fossil fuels? Should nuclear energy count as a clean source? Lawmakers and energy regulators should quibble over the details. But Beacon Hill also needs to prioritize getting some set of rules to the governor’s desk before this legislative session adjourns in January. There’s simply too much hand wringing, fear, and confusion in our communities not to establish a legally binding road map. If new guidelines are too onerous, data center developers may say no thank you and move onto the next state. That wouldn’t be the worst thing in the world. “It’s not a big loss,” Erin Baker, a University of Massachusetts Amherst professor who researches mathematical modeling of energy decisions, told the editorial board. “It’s not super clear to me what value we get from data centers in our community. They don’t have a lot of jobs.” In the other scenario, if rules for building data centers are too loose or not established, it would be much harder to go in reverse, warns Democratic state Senator Michael Moore of Millbury, who worries the state could someday be left with gigantic white elephant eyesores. It’s a fair point. The fact is, all technologies become more efficient with time. There’s no reason to expect otherwise with data centers, which should become more efficient and less polluting, and may no longer need vast facilities. If Massachusetts can establish rigorous standards, not outright bans on data centers, other states will undoubtedly follow suit, as Granholm suggested, and a national or regional standard could be set. That sounds much better than the current race to the bottom between states chasing short-term construction jobs. If done right, data centers could even become a way to lower our electricity bills. For example, if data centers were required to pay higher costs for the upkeep of transmission lines, that would help the rest of us. Or imagine a data center powered by solar panels with battery storage sending excess electricity back to the grid. Baker says all this will be tricky to operationalize. But making data centers work for us is worth trying. Editorials represent the views of the Boston Globe Editorial Board. Follow us @GlobeOpinion.

artigo.texto: La Verne lithium battery storage fire forces evacuations near water district facility The Brief - A small explosion and fire broke out in an outdoor lithium battery storage unit at a Metropolitan Water District facility in La Verne. - Hazmat and fire crews responded, prompting mandatory evacuations for nearby shopping centers, neighborhoods, and shelter-in-place orders for two schools. - The fire was largely extinguished by 2:30 p.m. The cause is unknown. LOS ANGELES - Evacuation orders were issued after a fire broke out at an outdoor lithium battery storage unit near a solar panel field at a Metropolitan Water District facility in La Verne Tuesday. What we know The fire was reported around 11:40 a.m. at the facility in the 3200 block of Wheeler Avenue. According to the La Verne Fire Department, a small explosion occurred in the battery unit which stored lithium batteries. Hazmat crews were brought in, and fire crews were mainly spraying the area with water to prevent the flames from spreading. Metropolitan said the water supply was not affected. Nearby neighborhoods evacuated Due to the hazardous nature of lithium batteries, evacuation orders were issued in the areas around the facility. La Verne police said shopping centers along Wheeler north of Foothill Boulevard were evacuated as a precaution. Shelter-in-place orders were issued for Grace Elementary School and Bonita High School. An evacuation center was established at the La Verne Community Center on 3680 D St. By 2:30 p.m., the fire was mainly out. The fire department said one civilian was injured and taken to a hospital. No additional details were released. A short time after that, some evacuation orders were downgraded to warnings, while others were reduced to advisories. An evacuation order remained in place in the immediate vicinity of the facility. The Source Information for this story came from the La Verne Fire Department. A statement was given by the Metropolitan Water District.

artigo.texto: What is repetitive re-trading (RTT) by BESS in the UK, and what is electricity markets operator NESO looking to do about it? What is repetitive re-trading (RTT) A key application of grid-scale battery energy storage system (BESS) is selling energy to the grid. This is typically done when prices are high, after batteries are charged by renewables or from the grid when the price is low. This approach allows companies to gain money from the grid for selling this energy, but there is a specific situation in parts of the UK grid currently where companies ‘sell’ their energy, but that energy doesn’t end up being distributed (for reasons explained further down). The companies can then sell this energy again making money multiple times before it is actually distributed. This scenario is called repetitive re-trading (RTT) and in theory can arise because companies know that there is already too much energy being distributed in a constrained area of the transmission network, but they can still bid to release that energy from their assets. Therefore, companies know that their energy won’t be needed but the bid needs to be paid if accepted, and it has created scenarios where companies are being paid by the government to not sell their energy because of network constraints.
