While the bidding and energy release process was designed to balance and stabilise the grid, it has turned into what some call a ‘cash cow for private investors’ at the expense of other energy consumers—a point that is argued by the Prospect trade Union. For many years RTT was mainly an issue with long duration assets, such as pumped storage, that could take advantage of high prices and export for long time periods, but the number of batteries now attached to the grid has meant that BESS are causing RTT issues as well. So, why does RTT actually happen? RTT happens when energy storage assets are located behind a constrained area of the transmission system. A discharge energy constraint is a part of the transmission system that caps how fast stored energy can be released from assets into the grid. The most common constraint is a thermal transmission constraint, which manifests when the amount of energy trying to flow through a power line exceeds the physical capacity of the line without causing thermal issues, such as overheating. Asset owners will notify the grid operators that they intend to discharge their assets (due to excess supply or high wholesale prices), which is accompanied by a bid—a price for that energy. This bid is then accepted, and the storage asset can theoretically be discharged. However, when there is a thermal constraint in the network, the National Energy System Operator (NESO) for Great Britain will reduce the output of attached storage assets by turning down the previously accepted bid and accepting a bid in the Balancing Mechanism. This then increases the output of an asset (or assets) elsewhere in the system that are not behind a constraint to replace the lost power. This leads to a curtailment in energy of the assets trying to sell from behind the constraint because the bids to sell the power at the high price are rejected and the energy is supplied from elsewhere that is not behind a constraint. In this scenario, the asset owner has still gained money from their bid, but they still have their stored energy. The money gained is the difference between the bid price and the wholesale market price. Under Transmission Constraint Licence Condition (TCLC) rules, the profit can’t be excessive and be roughly what would have been made if the constraint wasn’t there, plus any additional costs associated with the bid being turned down—but one could argue that it is effectively free money, and it is currently a legitimate way of bidding for energy dispatch. Bids are made in intervals (often half-hourly), but if the constraint still exists, asset owners can continue to bid and get paid without discharging their asset, creating a cycle that enables asset owners to continue to make money of the same stored energy—as NESO has to continue to accept bids and then turn them down when the constraint is still ongoing, a process known as ‘bidding the unit down’. Only when the constraint ends does the RTT cycle finish and the asset finally releases its stored power to the grid as it is no longer prevented from exporting. RTT is a consequence of the existing market design because asset owners are expected to optimise their own storage and discharge schedules based on the national wholesale prices, and when they potential gains are high, owners will schedule to release the energy. Aside from higher balancing costs, RTT can also cause inefficient discharge patterns. RTT is also not a new issue, and there are many areas of the network that are regularly constrained, so some storage asset owners have had significant numbers of bids accepted in constraint periods for years, which is why there is a lot of industry discussion on the topic. The amount of storage connected to the grid, and actions required by NESO to manage constraints, continues to grow. Aside from storage asset growth, there has also been a significant growth in renewable energy systems connected to the grid. Because of this growth, the transmission network around Great Britain has many areas that regularly get congested. This includes north-to-south power flows, export constraints in east England, import constraints in south England, and in north Scotland where there are many wind farms.

The company reported its first-ever positive adjusted gross profit of $1.7 million, a substantial improvement from a $6.2 million loss the previous year. American Battery Technology Co (NASDAQ:ABAT) reduced cash spend on operations by 16% despite increasing throughput, showcasing operational efficiencies. The company has a strong financial position with $49.5 million in cash and zero long-term outstanding debt as of the end of fiscal year 2026. American Battery Technology Co (NASDAQ:ABAT) received certification from the Bureau of Land Management for its plan of operations at the Tonopah Flats Lithium project, advancing the permitting process. Negative Points The Department of Commerce directive banning black mass exports has forced American Battery Technology Co (NASDAQ:ABAT) to store black mass on-site, with no formal response to its exception request yet. Despite revenue growth, the company's cost of goods sold increased by 67%, indicating ongoing cost pressures. American Battery Technology Co (NASDAQ:ABAT) had a Department of Energy grant canceled and had to appeal to reverse the termination, highlighting potential regulatory risks. The company is still in the pre-NEPA phase for its Tonopah project, with full permitting and construction yet to be completed. American Battery Technology Co (NASDAQ:ABAT) relies heavily on government grants and partnerships, which may be subject to political and budgetary uncertainties. Q: What drove the over 400% revenue increase to $21.7 million in fiscal year 2026? He noted that while revenue rose over 400%, cost of goods sold increased only about 67%, and cash spend on operations actually decreased by about 16% despite higher throughput. Q: How did American Battery Technology achieve its first annual adjusted profit? A: CEO and CTO Ryan Melsert explained that higher capacity utilization at the first recycling plant and operational efficiencies led to an adjusted gross profit of about $1.7 million for the year, compared to a $6.2 million loss in the prior year. This marked the company's first-ever positive gross margin on an adjusted basis. Q: What is the status of the Department of Commerce directive banning black mass exports? A: CEO and CTO Ryan Melsert stated that the Department of Commerce issued a directive effectively banning black mass exports unless an exception is obtained. The company has submitted an exception request and responded to follow-up questions, but no formal response has been received. The company received BLM certification accepting its plan of operations, moving it into the full NEPA process. The project was also selected as a priority project by the National Energy Dominance Council and FAST-41 Permitting Council for streamlined federal permitting. Q: What is the status of the second recycling plant and DOE grants? A: CEO and CTO Ryan Melsert said the second recycling plant in the Southeast US is designed to process about 100,000 tonnes per year, supported by a $150 million DOE grant. Additionally, a $10 million DOE grant is being used to commercialize next-generation recycling technologies. One DOE grant for the claystone project was initially canceled but was fully reinstated after a successful appeal. Q: How strong is the company's balance sheet at the end of fiscal year 2026? A: CEO and CTO Ryan Melsert highlighted that the company increased its cash balance to about $49.5 million as of the end of June, grew its total asset base to approximately $133 million, and has zero long-term outstanding debt. He described these as the strongest financial results in the company's history as an operating company. Q: What partnerships support the recycling business? A: CEO and CTO Ryan Melsert noted a partnership with The Battery Network (formerly Call2Recycle), a leading consumer battery collection company, to collect and recycle batteries nationwide. The company was also selected for one of the largest lithium-ion battery cleanup projects in US history, processing grid-scale batteries that have been through incidents. Q: What are the key sources of feedstock for the recycling plant? A: CEO and CTO Ryan Melsert explained that feedstock comes from a wide variety of sources, including grid-scale battery energy storage systems supporting data centers and AI training models, electric vehicles, battery cell manufacturing, and the consumer electronics market. Q: What is the significance of the DOE leadership visit? A: CEO and CTO Ryan Melsert stated that DOE leadership toured the operating battery recycling plant and the integrated demonstration facility for converting Nevada claystone into battery-grade lithium hydroxide. The visit showcased the company's progress from R&D and bench scale through pilot plants to operating commercial-scale facilities. Q: What are the next steps for the company? A: CEO and CTO Ryan Melsert said the company will hold its formal Annual Shareholder Meeting in November to discuss more details of the past year and steps ahead. The webinar will cover three main topics: - How expanding data center infrastructure and electricity transmission lines affect local farmland and farming operations. - The intersection of hyperscale computing, artificial intelligence energy requirements, and rural electrical grids. - Basic frameworks governing land use, transmission siting, and community considerations in Pennsylvania in the legal and regulatory context. This is part of the Understanding Agricultural Law Educational Series co-presented by the Pennsylvania Department of Agriculture’s (PDA) Agricultural Business Development Center (ABDC). The series is designed to develop subject matter literacy and competence in issues of agricultural law for attorneys and business advisors but is open to the public. It’s free to register here. https://psu.zoom.us/webinar/register/2217822390166/WN_7vFIY0h7SKOAQ1IFyH3v4w#/registration With all the concerns about data centers and their power and water usage, and the power grid and transmission line impacts, this webinar could provide valuable information for citizens and government decision makers alike. artigo.texto: A expansão da infraestrutura para inteligência artificial está levando os operadores de data centers a rever uma atividade que durante anos foi baseada em cronogramas fixos: a manutenção dos equipamentos. Segundo um white paper da IDC, o aumento da escala das instalações, a concentração de cargas de IA e a diversidade de fabricantes estão tornando o modelo tradicional de manutenção menos adequado para a complexidade atual da infraestrutura. CONTEÚDO RELACIONADO – Entidades pedem ao Confaz redução de ICMS para equipamentos de data centers O estudo The Self-Aware Datacenter: How Condition-Based Maintenance Turns Fragmented Multivendor Datacenters into Predictable Infrastructure and System Intelligence, aponta a manutenção baseada na condição dos ativos (condition-based maintenance, ou CBM) como uma alternativa para acompanhar essa transformação. O trabalho é assinado pelos analistas Luis Fernandes e Mary Johnston Turner e patrocinado pela Schneider Electric. A mudança acontece em um momento em que a demanda por capacidade de data centers passa a ser medida em gigawatts. De acordo com a IDC, campi de hyperscalers com 300 MW a 500 MW já são comuns, enquanto alguns clientes solicitam capacidades superiores a 1 GW. A capacidade global de data centers deverá ultrapassar 100 GW entre 2026 e 2030. O avanço da IA é um dos principais motores desse crescimento. A IDC estima que o CAPEX dos hyperscalers em data centers deverá superar US$ 600 bilhões até o final de 2026. Ao mesmo tempo, a densidade de potência passou de cerca de 15 kW por rack em instalações convencionais para entre 300 kW e 600 kW em zonas de computação intensiva em IA. Infraestrutura mais densa e mais complexa A mudança na densidade de potência altera também as exigências de operação. Segundo a IDC, as chamadas AI factories possuem características arquitetônicas diferentes das instalações tradicionais, incluindo novas exigências de alimentação elétrica e refrigeração. Muitos desses projetos também não têm histórico operacional suficiente para estabelecer parâmetros tradicionais de manutenção. A disponibilidade de energia tornou-se outro fator determinante para a expansão. O estudo cita que, em mercados estabelecidos como Northern Virginia, nos Estados Unidos, o prazo entre a solicitação de conexão à rede e a ativação pode chegar a sete a dez anos. Com a restrição de energia, operadores estão recorrendo a instalações existentes, geração local, campi distribuídos e aquisições de empresas e estruturas já conectadas à rede. A consequência é o aumento da heterogeneidade dos ativos que precisam ser administrados. Em vez de uma infraestrutura construída integralmente com equipamentos de um mesmo fornecedor, operações resultantes de expansão e aquisições podem reunir ativos de diferentes fabricantes e gerações. A IDC afirma que ambientes multivendor são a norma nos grandes data centers, com três a seis fornecedores principais frequentemente envolvidos nas categorias críticas de infraestrutura. Por que o calendário deixa de ser suficiente A manutenção baseada em calendário estabelece intervalos fixos para inspeções e intervenções, independentemente da condição efetiva do equipamento. Para a IDC, esse modelo não considera adequadamente fatores como utilização, carga, condições ambientais e nível de estresse do ativo. Isso pode resultar tanto em intervenções desnecessárias quanto na identificação tardia de problemas que já estão se desenvolvendo. O problema se agrava quando equipamentos de diferentes fornecedores são administrados por plataformas distintas. Segundo o estudo, a análise de causa raiz em ambientes multivendor continua sendo um dos principais desafios. Mesmo operadores com ampla utilização de sistemas de gerenciamento de manutenção encontram dificuldades para relacionar uma falha em um equipamento a alarmes registrados em outros sistemas. A fragmentação se estende às ferramentas de gestão. CMMS, DCIM e SCADA normalmente operam em plataformas separadas e nem sempre possuem integração nativa. Para a IDC, acrescentar novas ferramentas sem resolver essa fragmentação pode aumentar a complexidade operacional. Em instalações de escala gigawatt, o problema chega a uma dimensão prática: o volume de ativos torna fisicamente inviável executar toda a manutenção tradicional de forma manual. Manutenção passa a acompanhar a condição do ativo É nesse ponto que entra a manutenção baseada em condição. Em vez de determinar previamente quando um equipamento deverá receber intervenção, o modelo monitora seu comportamento e utiliza os dados para identificar sinais de degradação ou alteração. A IDC descreve uma arquitetura que combina monitoramento remoto, acompanhamento contínuo da saúde dos ativos e análise preditiva de falhas. A proposta é que esse conjunto funcione como um serviço gerenciado, com uma camada de especialistas responsável pela interpretação dos dados. Um requisito considerado importante é a capacidade de monitorar equipamentos de diferentes fabricantes. A plataforma precisa reunir dados provenientes de SCADA, DCIM, sistemas de gerenciamento predial, sensores de terceiros e data lakes do próprio cliente. A ideia é construir uma visão do sistema como um todo, e não apenas acompanhar cada equipamento isoladamente. IA ajuda a identificar falhas antes do problema A diferença entre um sistema tradicional de alarmes e a manutenção baseada em condição está no momento da intervenção. Um alarme normalmente é acionado quando determinado limite já foi ultrapassado. A CBM procura identificar a trajetória do equipamento antes que ele alcance esse limite e, potencialmente, apresente uma falha. O modelo pode utilizar sensores de temperatura e umidade, sensores térmicos e sensores de gases e partículas. Eles permitem identificar, por exemplo, alterações ambientais, pontos de aquecimento em conexões elétricas e sinais de deterioração antes que ocorram danos mais graves. A análise também pode cruzar informações de diferentes partes da infraestrutura. Uma

artigo.texto: New Hampshire’s Republican majority will pursue a moratorium on AI data centers, marking a policy shift after two new data centers were proposed in the capital region in recent weeks. Senate President Sharon Carson, a Londonderry Republican, announced on Thursday that the Senate would explore legislation to “protect New Hampshire taxpayers from shouldering the costly demands of data center development and ensure our communities are not left to pay the price.” She echoed recent sentiments from Gov. Kelly Ayotte, who said this summer that she supports a moratorium after public opposition to data center proposals continued to grow across the state. “Large scale facilities can place significant demands on electricity and water, create noise and environmental impacts and require substantial infrastructure,” Carson said in a statement on Thursday. “While we can embrace technological innovation, we agree with Governor Ayotte that it cannot be at the expense of Granite State families.” Two proposed data centers are on New Hampshire’s radar right now: one at the former Merrimack Station power plant in Bow and one at a vacant lot in East Concord. An unofficial plan for a data center in Nottingham was withdrawn in May after widespread public opposition. Resistance to AI data centers is largely bipartisan, according to a recent UNH Survey Center poll, which found that 67% of New Hampshire residents either strongly or somewhat oppose local construction of data centers. New Hampshire already has several data centers, though none are in the capital region. Earlier this year, Republicans watered down a Democratic bill that would have imposed design and noise requirements on data centers and codified towns’ ability to adopt their own regulations. The bill, SB 439, ultimately did not pass. “Republicans in the State House took that bill and gutted it, handing that power to developers instead of the people who actually live next to these projects. I watched them do it,” state Sen. Debra Altschiller, the Stratham Democrat who proposed that bill, said in a statement. “Now, eight months later and weeks before an election, they want credit for caring about the exact thing they tried to take away.” New Hampshire’s next legislative session begins in January 2027.

artigo.texto: Next Upcoming Canary Live Bay Area By Canary Media It’s already hard to build grid batteries in New York City. But now, an increasingly hostile dispute between the utility Con Edison and energy-storage developers is making it even harder. The two sides agree that “community-scale battery projects” — bigger than those that back up a home but smaller than most grid-scale installations — could seriously improve reliability and affordability for New Yorkers. But they disagree on how those batteries should be managed, and on how the financial rewards for the services they provide to the grid should be parceled out. Private energy-storage developers who have been cut off from plugging into Con Ed’s grid for the past year say the utility is unfairly tilting the playing field in its own favor. In August 2025, Con Ed abruptly changed the rules for nearly 600 megawatts of third-party battery projects seeking to interconnect to its grid. Then in November, the utility issued a new interconnection policy that developers say dramatically raised the costs they would have to pay to interconnect, by as much as fourteenfold in some cases. That’s according to a petition filed in March with the New York Public Service Commission from the New York Battery and Energy Storage Technology Consortium (NY-BEST) and the New York Solar Energy Industries Association (NYSEIA). The groups say Con Ed’s changes have effectively made it impossible to move ahead with roughly $1.5 billion in battery-project investment. They also accuse the utility of circumventing proper regulatory procedure to impose these restrictions and are asking the commission to force the utility to revert to its former rules. “It’s just unacceptable for a regulated utility to operate like this,” said New York City Council member James Gennaro, a Democrat who chairs its Committee on Environmental Protection and Waterfronts. “We’re looking to get to the bottom of this because we want battery storage to progress. This is good for the grid, it’s good to reduce our dependence on peaker plants, it’s good for everyone.” In a March letter, environmental groups and city and state elected officials, including Gennaro, called on the commission to force Con Ed to “roll back these unilateral and unwarranted changes.” Con Ed says the changes are about preserving grid reliability and preventing a flood of third-party batteries operating outside of utility control from driving up costs to its customers. It is asking regulators to approve a plan that it says will better align the way that these batteries charge and discharge with the needs of its increasingly strained grid. “We think storage is important for the clean energy transition,” said Raghu Sudhakara, Con Ed’s vice president for distributed resource integration. “But it has to be sited in the right location, it has to come online at the right time, and it has to operate under the right operating conditions.” The dispute is creating roadblocks just when New York City needs all the resources it can get to meet peak electricity demand during heat waves. In fact, the utility’s latest reliability contingency plan, filed with regulators in July, identified the need for 125 MW of “clean and non-emitting” capacity in New York City by 2033. That plan “named energy storage as a primary resource,” said Claudia Villar-Leeman, NY-BEST’s senior director of policy and regulatory affairs. Environmental justice groups are also pushing for batteries to help replace fossil-fueled power plants that are polluting low-income neighborhoods. In light of those pressures, Con Ed’s actions to block battery developers are “frustrating, because batteries should be able to avoid the need for these infrastructure upgrades rather than causing them,” she said. Con Ed argues that its new rules and interconnection charges are needed to prevent third-party batteries from overwhelming its grid. In the past two years, the number of interconnection requests for battery projects of 5 MW or less have increased about threefold, and now add up to nearly 2.5 gigawatts, Sudhakara said. If all those batteries are allowed to plug in and start charging at once, they could pull more power than sections of Con Ed’s grid can handle, the utility warned. And because it doesn’t directly control these third-party batteries, Con Ed argues that it has no way to prevent that from happening. But battery developers and trade groups say Con Ed’s argument relies on worst-case scenarios and ignores the flexibility of energy storage systems. “We have utility planners taking our most flexible resource and treating them as if they’re completely inflexible,” said Noah Ginsburg, NYSEIA’s executive director. “If your starting point is false assumptions about the flexibility of the resource you’re dealing with, you’re not going to get a positive outcome.” Those assumptions bother Adam Cohen, chief technology officer and co-founder of NineDot Energy, a community battery developer that runs six community battery sites and has more than two dozen others in development in New York City. Con Ed’s analysis “assumes batteries will charge in an inflexible manner, from midnight to 8 a.m., with no day-by-day variation, and at a fixed charging rate,” Cohen said. If all those batteries did charge that way, they could indeed overload certain parts of the grid, he said. But batteries can be controlled to avoid these kinds of problems, Cohen said. An April study by analysis firm Danovo Energy Solutions, commissioned by NineDot, found that Con Ed could use technical approaches now available to its grid operators to nearly double hosting capacity. A similar study published in May from NYSEIA, NY-BEST, and the Electric Power Research Institute, a prominent utility research organization, found that active management could significantly increase capacity for community-scale battery projects on Con Ed’s grid. artigo.texto: RN aprova regras para licenciamento ambiental de data centers O Conselho Estadual do Meio Ambiente (Conema) aprovou, na segunda-feira (21), uma resolução que estabelece regras para o licenciamento ambiental de data centers no Rio Grande do Norte. A proposta foi apresentada pelo Instituto de Desenvolvimento Sustentável e Meio Ambiente do RN (Idema). A resolução cria critérios para padronizar os procedimentos administrativos, técnicos e ambientais aplicados aos empreendimentos Um dos principais critérios para definir o tipo de licenciamento será a capacidade elétrica instalada. Os empreendimentos serão divididos em cinco categorias: - Micro: até 20 MW; - Pequeno: acima de 20 MW até 50 MW; - Médio: acima de 50 MW até 100 MW; - Grande: acima de 100 MW até 500 MW; - Excepcional: acima de 500 MW. A potência considerada inclui os equipamentos de tecnologia da informação e os sistemas de refrigeração. Consumo de água A modalidade de licenciamento e os estudos ambientais exigidos também vão variar conforme o porte e o sistema de refrigeração utilizado. Nos sistemas fechados, a água usada para resfriar os equipamentos circula em um circuito e é reaproveitada, sem necessidade de reposição constante em grandes volumes. Já os sistemas abertos, que utilizam torres de refrigeração, podem apresentar maior consumo de água. Segundo o diretor-geral do Idema, Werner Farkatt, essa diferença foi um dos pontos considerados na elaboração da resolução, especialmente diante da escassez hídrica no semiárido. “A resolução estabelece um licenciamento mais simplificado para sistemas fechados, enquanto os empreendimentos de grande e excepcional porte e com sistemas abertos estarão sujeitos a estudos ambientais mais complexos”, explicou. Localização também será considerada Independentemente do porte ou do sistema de refrigeração, os data centers serão considerados de significativo impacto ambiental quando estiverem em áreas como unidades de conservação e áreas de preservação permanente. Outra regra determina que dois ou mais data centers do mesmo empreendedor, localizados a até 500 metros de distância um do outro, sejam considerados como um único empreendimento para a avaliação dos impactos ambientais. Caberá ao Idema analisar tecnicamente os processos, realizar vistorias, definir medidas mitigadoras e compensatórias e estabelecer condicionantes específicas. O órgão também poderá solicitar complementações aos estudos apresentados. g1 RN

artigo.texto: Developers are building data centers with or without public support, and writer Elijah Bosslet argues they need to be held accountable. My business ethics class took a survey on our attitude toward AI a couple of weeks ago. As I finished sifting through the initial questions, the room was silent apart from the clicking of touchpads and a few yawns. I assumed the “create your own statement” section at the end would be an afterthought. It wasn’t. Slowly, mouse clicking turned to keyboard clacking. Responses started rolling in, and students began to vote on their peers’ opinions. As the survey went on, one issue came up repeatedly — the environmental impact of AI. When most people talk about AI affecting the environment, they’re talking about the immense water and energy demands that manifest as ugly, huge, invasive buildings known as data centers. It’s not AI itself killing the planet and driving up America’s energy bill. It’s the infrastructure behind it. Nationally, resistance to data center development has become a bipartisan issue. According to a recent study by Absecon Group, there are 717 individual candidate campaigns — on all levels and in both parties — running ads mentioning data centers, with 636 in clear opposition or advocating for restrictions. A University of Massachusetts Amherst poll found that only one in nine Americans support the construction of data centers in their community. While my in-class survey was small — only 36 students — the results followed a rhetorical trend I’ve noticed. It feels like almost every argument against data centers starts and ends with some combination of “AI is taking our jobs” and “AI is killing the planet.” Aligning with my experience, a recent poll by Gallup News found the five most common anti-data center development topics are water and energy use, utility costs, the environment and AI replacing human jobs. Unfortunately, if a state enacts a one-year ban on data center construction, AI development only slows by five to 10 hours. Although it may seem counterintuitive, AI development, as currently regulated, is inevitable with or without more data centers. For those interested in slowing AI to keep their jobs, arguing against data centers is futile. Opposition to the environmental impact of data centers has a stronger argument. There’s no doubt these monstrous temples of tech infrastructure have dire water and energy usage consequences. My concern is the job loss and environmental arguments are too broad and easily swept aside by developers. Sustainability pledges and job creation promises are initiatives developers have had lots of experience with, similar to the fossil fuel industry. When pitching to public officials, developers promise tax revenue, economic stimulus and creation of jobs in exchange for approval. They frame these deals as good for communities, though their negotiation tactics say otherwise. Use of NDAs is a common method. In Janesville,Wis. — a city of about 64,000 people — officials spent a full year in talks with a data center developer under an NDA before residents even knew a deal existed. If the deal was mutually beneficial, there would be no reason to negotiate with such a shady approach. Saline, Mich., provides a wonderful example of how I believe public focus needs to shift. In August 2025, an OpenAI and Oracle development partner, Related Digital, attempted to rezone agricultural land for a data center. Saline Township’s Board of Trustees voted no four to one. Instead of backing down, Related Digital sued the township. Saline is home to just 3,000 residents. They couldn’t afford to fight the lawsuit and were forced to settle for $14 million. Today, there is a 250-acre data center built on a 1,000 acre compound in Saline. Saline didn’t need an NDA to get taken advantage of. When its board tried to offer Related Digital the minimum allowable tax break, they were threatened with a second lawsuit, and the township was forced to cave with a 12-year, 50% tax abatement. The reshaping, both physically and fiscally, of unwilling communities by these giant corporations is frustrating. Constituents are against development, the board votes no, then it’s built anyway. The current system is being taken advantage of. Cities that approve development are banking on the promise they’ll reap significant tax income and create jobs in the future. Data centers underdeliver on both. Tax benefits are completely reliant on the deal the municipality negotiates with these corporations. As seen in Saline, developers cherry-pick easy targets and negotiate huge tax abatements. The number of jobs created is below what is promised by developers. A study conducted by the Brookings Institution suggests that data centers create fewer employment opportunities than what the industry claims. On average, a new data center creates only 20 to 50 permanent jobs. Additionally, these communities are often forced to expand local utilities infrastructure to provide enough electricity and water. If the AI bubble pops before tax abatements expire, this expansion in infrastructure will force taxpayers to fully support infrastructure upgrades for a data center they never wanted to begin with. Communities will be left with no jobs created, no tax benefit and a giant brownfield for the community to clean up or sell. AI is shaping our world. No ban or protest will stop that. What isn’t decided yet is how it happens to these communities, whether a city council gets a fair negotiation or a lawsuit, a public debate or a year of silence under NDA. Saline lost because Related Digital sued instead of argued. Janesville nearly lost before residents even knew there was a fight to have. Inevitable shouldn’t mean unaccountable. If data centers are coming either way, it’s time to start talking about how communities can actually benefit.

artigo.texto: XIAMEN, China, Sept. 22, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- At its "Powered Day in, Day out" launch event, HiTHIUM unveiled the ∞Power N4.0MWh, a 4 MWh sodium-ion battery energy storage system equipped with its new ∞Cell N785Ah cell. Designed for a 30-year service life, the solution is scheduled to enter full-scale production and delivery in 2027. HiTHIUM said the ∞Cell N785Ah was developed through integrated innovation in materials and manufacturing processes. It uses a polyanionic chemistry based on an NFPP cathode, hard-carbon anode and customized electrolyte, together with ultra-thick electrodes and long-life structural components. Wide-format stacking makes the cell compatible with HiTHIUM's existing kAh-class lithium-ion manufacturing platform, supporting production scale-up. The cell is designed for 20,000 cycles at 70% state of health and supports storage durations from two to eight hours. At system level, a stacked-cell architecture reduces station footprint by 30%, while PCS rated-power utilization is more than 20% higher than in HiTHIUM's previous-generation sodium-ion system. HiTHIUM also reports 24-hour comprehensive efficiency above 88%, with operating and standby auxiliary power consumption reduced by 30% and 50%, respectively. The system is designed to align its operating life with a 30-year power-station cycle. "30 years means 10,950 days of validation—a long-term commitment to our customers," said Dr. Aileen Wang, Director of HiTHIUM's Battery Research Institute. The product advances support HiTHIUM's goal of accelerating sodium-ion industrialization. Dr. Nazar Yi, Chief Technology Officer of HiTHIUM, identified affordability and long-term resource availability as the two main requirements for large-scale deployment. HiTHIUM positions the new solution as part of an effort to treat electrochemical storage as long-life energy infrastructure and move levelized storage costs toward RMB 0.1 per kWh. The company views sodium-ion as complementary to lithium-ion rather than a replacement. It will initially target utility-scale storage before expanding into commercial and industrial, residential and broader energy-access applications. HiTHIUM also launched the ∞Edge Pioneer Program to test cells and systems in extreme environments and disclose progress over the next three years. About HiTHIUM Founded in 2019, HiTHIUM specializes in integrated energy storage solutions centered on battery and system technologies. Its capabilities span R&D, manufacturing, delivery, operation and maintenance, with operations across more than 40 countries and regions.

artigo.texto: Panasonic Energy Raises Maximum Temperature of Its All-Solid-State Battery from 125°C to 150°C, Creates Smaller Prismatic Cell, and Prepares Samples for October to December 2026, Targeting Sensors and Machinery. Panasonic Energy has advanced its solid-state battery to operate at temperatures up to 150°C, while also creating a new small prismatic design to facilitate installation in industrial equipment and automotive sensors. This new development was revealed by the company’s Chief Technology Officer, Shoichiro Watanabe, during an industry conference in Japan. Until now, the all-solid-state batteries being developed by Panasonic operated with a limit of approximately 125°C. The new design expands this range by 25°C and prepares the technology for environments where high heat reduces the lifespan of conventional batteries. The advancement comes with another significant change: in addition to the coin-shaped cells already tested by the company, Panasonic has developed a small prismatic cell. The rectangular design allows for better fitting within products and systems where internal space needs to be utilized more freely. - Motorola Unveils Signature 27 with 200 MP Camera, Next-Gen Snapdragon, and Diamond Cooling - NASA Captures Earth’s Shifting Views Throughout the Year, Highlighting Continent Positions Due to the Planet’s 23.5° Tilt - Brazilian Rocket Launches from Rio Grande do Norte, Sends Experiments to 92 km Altitude, and Returns Scientific Payload via Parachute - Archaeologists Discover 6,500-Year-Old Beer Production Remnants with Sprouted Grains Used for Malting in Bulgaria Samples Set to Be Released Between October and December 2026 Panasonic plans to begin shipping samples between October and December 2026. This phase will put the battery in the hands of customers and partners for testing under real conditions prior to larger-scale production. The initial focus is on industrial machinery and vehicle sensors, two markets where high temperatures and maintenance challenges make a heat-resistant battery especially valuable. In factories, for example, motors and robots work at a high pace and can raise the internal temperature of sensors and controllers. In vehicles, systems installed near wheels, engines, or components exposed to heat face similar conditions. Panasonic also cites applications related to medical equipment sterilization, where high temperatures are a normal part of the operating process. The commercial goal is to start in niches where thermal resistance provides a clear benefit. Panasonic has been advocating this strategy: launching all-solid-state batteries first in challenging applications for liquid systems, rather than trying to immediately enter massive volume markets like that of electric vehicles. Prismatic Format Aims to Solve a Practical Integration Challenge The new prismatic format addresses a simple engineering limitation. Round or coin-shaped cells may be efficient for certain functions but limit the internal arrangement of compact sensors and equipment. A small rectangular cell can be positioned more flexibly alongside plates, motors, electronic modules, and other components. According to Watanabe, this change could facilitate the final design of the products that will use the battery. The company intends to offer different shapes based on application needs while continuing tests with coin-type cells. All-solid-state technology replaces the liquid electrolyte with a solid material. This type of construction can enhance stability at high temperatures and reduce limitations seen in conventional batteries when operating in very hot environments. Panasonic emphasizes that development relies on precisely controlling the contact between electrodes and the solid electrolyte. In a liquid battery, the electrolyte spreads and adheres to the surface of the electrode. In a solid battery, any loss of contact can hinder ion flow and reduce performance. Mass production is planned for one to two years after sample deliveries If customer testing progresses as expected, Panasonic aims to begin mass production one to two years after the start of sample shipments. This timeframe will be used to assess performance, product integration, and stability under various usage conditions. The company also recently strengthened its research infrastructure in Japan with the Energy Innovation Square in Osaka. This center integrates material development, cell design, prototyping, and analysis, bringing together stages that were previously distributed among different facilities. This concentration of engineering helps to reduce the time between laboratory research and production. Panasonic wants to expedite the transition of new chemistries and cell formats to lines capable of producing samples and, later, commercial volumes. In addition to small solid batteries, Watanabe stated that the company also aims to accelerate the development of cylindrical batteries for humanoid robots. The cylindrical shape can better fit into arms, joints, and curved structures, where available space is limited. The new battery rated for 150°C indicates that the race for solid-state batteries is already advancing in industrial applications. Panasonic is aiming to penetrate markets first where heat, maintenance, and internal space create significant challenges. If the samples confirm performance in sensors, machines, and sterilization environments, the technology could hit the market for industrial applications before making its way into passenger vehicles. artigo.texto: O Dia das Emissões Zero, celebrado globalmente em 21 de setembro, propõe uma reflexão profunda sobre o impacto ambiental das atividades econômicas e funciona como um chamado para a descarbonização. No entanto, no dia a dia do setor corporativo, alcançar a neutralidade total é um desafio complexo. Muitas indústrias enfrentam o chamado paradoxo das emissões inevitáveis: mesmo otimizando processos, adotando tecnologias modernas e reduzindo desperdícios, a própria natureza da atividade produtiva acaba gerando resíduos gasosos que não podem ser eliminados por completo. Ciente dessa realidade, a Enel Trading atua como uma facilitadora estratégica no mercado de energia e sustentabilidade. A companhia desenvolve soluções sob medida para que empresas de diferentes portes transformem suas metas ambientais em resultados práticos, oferecendo os instrumentos necessários para mitigar e compensar de forma segura as emissões que o processo industrial ainda não consegue evitar por conta própria. Desmistificando o AIREQ e a rastreabilidade da energia limpa Quando o assunto é a energia elétrica que abastece escritórios, galpões e indústrias, a principal ferramenta de descarbonização é o AIREQ (Certificado de Energia Renovável baseado no sistema global I-REC). O foco desse instrumento está diretamente atrelado ao consumo de eletricidade das empresas, o chamado Escopo 2 dos inventários de sustentabilidade. Na prática, o certificado funciona como uma garantia oficial e auditada de que a energia utilizada pela companhia provém de fontes estritamente limpas, como usinas eólicas, solares ou hídricas. A dinâmica do AIREQ destaca-se pela simplicidade e precisão matemática, operando na proporção direta de um para um: para cada megawatt-hora (MWh) consumido pelo cliente, a Enel Trading comercializa um certificado correspondente. Nosso diferencial está na nossa operação, que conta com 34 usinas próprias integralmente certificadas pelo sistema. Isso assegura ao comprador total rastreabilidade e a tranquilidade institucional de que sua matriz de consumo elétrico é ambientalmente limpa. A abrangência dos créditos de carbono no ecossistema corporativo Embora a eletrificação limpa resolva o desafio do consumo elétrico, muitas organizações possuem demandas que vão muito além da tomada. É o caso de frotas logísticas, processos de aquecimento industrial ou cadeias de distribuição que dependem do uso de combustíveis fósseis, como o óleo diesel. Para cobrir essas lacunas e atuar de forma transversal nos Escopos 1 (emissões diretas) e 3 (emissões indiretas), a Enel Trading disponibiliza os Créditos de Carbono ao mercado. Baseados no conceito de emissões evitadas, em que projetos sustentáveis evitam que gases poluentes cheguem à atmosfera , cada crédito comercializado tem o poder de neutralizar exatamente uma tonelada de CO₂ equivalente a emitida pelo cliente. Para assegurar a máxima governança e afastar riscos de dupla comercialização, todo o volume gerado pela Enel Trading fica sob custódia direta em contas oficiais da Organização das Nações Unidas (ONU). Trata-se de um mecanismo rígido de segurança que garante a legitimidade da compensação ambiental do início ao fim do processo. Da teoria à prática: o inventário e o sucesso em grandes eventos A aplicação conjunta dessas duas ferramentas de mercado permite desenhar estratégias de sustentabilidade completas, mesmo para operações de alta complexidade. Um exemplo prático e real dessa sinergia institucional foi o festival Enel Por Você, planejado para ser um evento 100% carbono neutro. Durante a iniciativa, todo o consumo de eletricidade da estrutura recebeu o selo de energia renovável, enquanto os impactos logísticos inevitáveis gerados pelo transporte e pelos geradores de suporte foram integralmente mitigados via créditos de carbono. Para as empresas que desejam iniciar essa jornada, o caminho ideal começa com a elaboração de um inventário de emissões detalhado, desenvolvido por consultorias especializadas e fundamentado em metodologias internacionais reconhecidas. Esse diagnóstico aponta com exatidão a pegada de carbono da operação e permite que a Enel Trading faça estimativas precisas para indicar o volume ideal de certificados ou créditos necessários para neutralizar o negócio. Neste Dia das Emissões Zero, o mercado cobra ações transparentes e auditáveis. Com o suporte técnico da Enel Trading, sua empresa encontra os caminhos mais eficientes para alcançar o status de carbono neutro, fortalecendo sua reputação e garantindo um papel de liderança ativa na transição energética global. Quer entender melhor como aplicar essas soluções na sua empresa? We are proud to back a team with such an impressive track record as they scale into the next phase of growth,” CAI managing partner Bill Green said in the release. artigo.texto: Baltimore County Council unanimously extends data center moratorium until 2027 The Baltimore County Council voted unanimously Tuesday evening to extend the moratorium on building new data centers in the county until December 2027. Several councilmembers said concerns from residents about the environmental and resource impacts of data centers influenced their decision. | BILL TEXT: Read the Baltimore County Council bill extending the moratorium "I went from one end of Baltimore County to the other, and it's clear to me that the citizens have some very legitimate concerns about energy, water, air quality, noise, so they've made it clear to me that they're not interested in data centers," Councilman Julian Jones, D-District 4, said. Jones, who is a candidate for County Executive, said that while he was initially open to the idea of data centers during his campaign, conversations with residents have changed his stance. | GET THE FACTS: More data centers are popping up across the U.S. What are they? "The public has made it clear to me as I continue to campaign around Baltimore County that they're not interested, and therefore I stand with the people," Jones said. In February, the Council voted to impose a moratorium on data centers while the planning board conducted a report on their impacts. Last week, the planning board approved the report and forwarded it to the council. Baltimore County is among several jurisdictions in the Baltimore metro area that have implemented moratoriums on data center construction. "They don't create jobs, they use up enormous amounts of county resources," Councilman Izzy Patoka, D-District 2, said. "Personally, I think we should hit the pause button for a long, long time." Jones reiterated his position, saying, "I do want to see what the state does, I do want to see what other opportunities come about, but to make a long story short, I stand with the people." Governor Wes Moore is expected to sign an executive order on data centers Wednesday to "protect Marylanders."

artigo.texto: Maui battery storage project reaches milestone KAHULUI (HawaiiNewsNow) - Hawaiian Electric’s battery energy storage project on Maui reached a new milestone. HECO’s Waena Battery Energy Storage System project’s first six Tesla Megapacks arrived and have been installed at the project site along Pūlehu Road in Central Maui. The project will be the island’s first standalone load-shifting battery energy storage system, part of HECO’s commitment to transitioning to renewable energy. When the project is complete, the system will be used during periods of increased energy demand. The batteries, which are each about the size of a 40-foot shipping container, were delivered by semi-truck and lifted into place with a crane in late August. The project was approved by the Public Utilities Commission in 2023. This first battery storage project developed by Hawaiian Electric is part of the company’s goal to reduce carbon emissions and to use renewable resources to generate 100% of electricity by 2045. About 41% of Maui County’s electricity comes from renewable sources, including more than 18,000 customer solar systems. This new battery storage project will incorporate grid-forming technology, which can help maintain grid stability as the island uses more types of energy, like wind and solar. Once in service, the battery system will store excess energy and deliver it back to the grid when needed. The batteries do not generate electricity. They are used to store energy generated through solar and wind, which are typically abundant during daylight hours, to save power for nighttime. “This project has been years in the making, and seeing the batteries arrive on site brings us one step closer to providing Maui with a more renewable electric grid,” said Shelley Takasato, manager of Generation Project Development for Hawaiian Electric. The rest of the batteries will arrive in phases as construction continues. The project is expected to enter service in 2027. Copyright 2026 Hawaii News Now. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Com a sanção do Governo Federal, o Redata, regime especial de tributação que prevê incentivos fiscais para o setor de data centers, passa a criar condições mais competitivas para a instalação e expansão desses empreendimentos no Brasil. A medida busca reduzir barreiras para investimentos de grande porte, ampliar a atratividade do país para investidores internacionais e acelerar a construção da infraestrutura necessária para sustentar o avanço da economia digital. CONTEÚDO RELACIONADO – Redata pode favorecer data center de IA ligado à estratégia de soberania digital do governo Para Fernando Palamone, CEO da RT-One, desenvolvedora de uma das maiores plataformas de infraestrutura para inteligência artificial da América Latina e responsável pela implantação de parques tecnológicos voltados para IA, o Redata contribui para tornar o setor nacional mais competitivo para novos projetos. “Segundo o relatório aprovado no Senado, o regime pode reduzir em até 30% o investimento inicial de um empreendimento. Na prática, isso pode significar maior capacidade de atração de capital, estímulo à expansão da infraestrutura digital e melhores condições para que empresas que dependem de processamento de alta capacidade escolham o Brasil como base para suas operações”, comenta o CEO. Ao redor da infraestrutura necessária para a construção de data centers podem surgir novos negócios, parcerias com universidades, centros de pesquisa e empresas de tecnologia, destravando um ecossistema econômico formado a partir do Redata. Mas, mesmo com a nova política, Palamone acredita que ainda há desafios para o Brasil no setor. “Haverá energia disponível? Em quanto tempo? A que custo? Haverá conectividade suficiente? O licenciamento será previsível? Existirá mão de obra qualificada? Essas respostas serão determinantes para transformar interesse em investimento efetivo. O Redata deve ser entendido como ponto de partida, e não como ponto de chegada”, pontua Fernando. Outro efeito econômico relevante gerado pelo novo regime é o desenvolvimento de polos de tecnologia e infraestrutura fora dos grandes centros tradicionais, expandindo a economia digital para novas regiões. Perante a crescente demanda por IAs, a RT-One planeja a construção de dois parques tecnológicos de data centers na América Latina, um Minas Gerais e outro no Paraná. “Projetos dessa natureza movimentam fornecedores, demandam profissionais especializados, criam oportunidades de qualificação, aproximam empresas de universidades e centros de pesquisa, e podem contribuir para a atração de novos negócios”, opina Palamone. artigo.texto: Califórnia endurece regras para data centers Data centers estão obrigados a divulgar informações sobre o uso de eletricidade, consumo de água, ocupação do solo e necessidades de mão de obra. O governador da Califórnia, Gavin Newsom, sancionou nesta segunda-feira, 21/9, sete projetos de lei destinados a regular o setor de data centers. A legislação exige que os data centers divulguem informações sobre o uso de eletricidade, consumo de água, ocupação do solo e necessidades de mão de obra, ao mesmo tempo em que fornece às comunidades locais mais dados para avaliar projetos propostos. As medidas visam impedir que os custos de nova geração de energia e de atualizações na rede elétrica — necessários para atender aos data centers — sejam repassados a outros consumidores. “Com essas leis, garantimos que os californianos mantenham o controle da situação — e que aqueles que lucram com os data centers não o façam às nossas custas”, afirmou Newsom em um comunicado. O estado da Califórnia informou que a legislação exigirá que os data centers cumpram as normas estaduais de aquisição de energia e ajudem a incorporar novas fontes de energia limpa à rede elétrica. O endurecimento das exigências acontece quando há uma preocupação crescente em todo os Estados Unidos sobre o impacto dos data centers na demanda por eletricidade, nos recursos hídricos e na infraestrutura local, à medida que empresas de tecnologia correm para expandir suas capacidades de inteligência artificial. A rápida expansão dos data centers voltados para Inteligência Artificial tem gerado resistência na Califórnia e em outras regiões, com moradores e grupos de defesa de interesses levantando preocupações sobre as contas de luz e a poluição associadas a essas instalações. Entidades ligadas ao segmento de data center afirmam que medidas mais duras vão fazer os projetos abandonarem a Califórnia e transferirem seus investimentos para outros estados.

artigo.texto: Manifesto conjunto pede aprovação de convênio no Confaz para reduzir a tributação estadual sobre bens e equipamentos destinados à implantação, ampliação e modernização de data centers A Confederação Assespro e outras treze entidades representativas dos setores de tecnologia, telecomunicações, indústria e serviços divulgaram um manifesto conjunto em defesa da aprovação, no Conselho Nacional de Política Fazendária (Confaz), de um convênio para redução do Imposto sobre Circulação de Mercadorias e Serviços (ICMS) incidente sobre bens e equipamentos destinados à implantação, ampliação e modernização de data centers. Intitulado “O Redata é uma realidade, e o Convênio do Confaz é uma necessidade”, o documento destaca que a aprovação do Redata estabeleceu uma base para a atração de investimentos em infraestrutura computacional e sinalizou a intenção do BRASIL de ampliar sua participação na economia de dados, computação em nuvem, inteligência artificial e processamento de alta capacidade. Segundo o manifesto, os data centers exercem papel essencial no funcionamento de serviços digitais, sistemas financeiros, telecomunicações, pesquisa, saúde, educação e governo digital. As entidades também ressaltam que a implantação dessas estruturas movimenta áreas como construção civil, energia, conectividade, equipamentos e serviços especializados, além de contribuir para a formação de profissionais e para o desenvolvimento de polos regionais de inovação. Entidades apontam peso do ICMS nos investimentos O documento argumenta que, embora o Redata tenha reduzido impostos federais, a tributação estadual continua sendo um fator relevante para a competitividade do setor. De acordo com os dados apresentados pelas entidades, o ICMS representa 64% da carga tributária incidente sobre os investimentos de capital (CAPEX) de um data center. Na avaliação apresentada no manifesto, um convênio nacional poderia reduzir diferenças tributárias entre os Estados, ampliar a segurança jurídica e oferecer maior previsibilidade aos investidores, evitando uma competição fiscal descoordenada. As entidades defendem ainda que uma política articulada entre União, Estados e municípios pode favorecer investimentos, geração de renda, inovação, capacidade produtiva e arrecadação de longo prazo. O manifesto também chama atenção para o cenário internacional de expansão dos investimentos em inteligência artificial e infraestrutura digital. Para as organizações signatárias, decisões relacionadas à competitividade tributária ganham relevância diante da disputa global por novos projetos no segmento. Manifesto pede atuação dos Estados e do Distrito Federal Diante desse cenário, as entidades solicitam aos Estados e ao Distrito Federal, reunidos no Confaz, a aprovação de um convênio que permita a redução do ICMS sobre bens e equipamentos utilizados na implantação, ampliação e modernização de data centers. Segundo o documento, a medida daria coerência à estratégia nacional para o setor e ampliaria as condições para o BRASIL disputar investimentos em infraestrutura digital e economia de dados. Além da Confederação Assespro, assinam o manifesto ABEP-TIC, ABES, ABDC, BD30+, Brasscom, CNI, Conexis, dig.ia, Fecomercio SP, Fenainfo, Firjan, Associação NEO e TelComp, reunindo representantes de diferentes segmentos ligados à transformação digital e ao ambiente produtivo nacional. A participação da Confederação Assespro no documento insere a entidade em uma articulação conjunta do setor em torno da infraestrutura digital e das condições tributárias para novos investimentos em data centers no BRASIL.

artigo.texto: CATL has begun trial production of battery cells at its new factory in Debrecen, Hungary, marking a key step toward supplying European automakers from a local manufacturing base. The Chinese battery maker said on September 22 that the plant had secured the permits and met the regulatory requirements needed to start trial operations. The first two production lines are now being tested as CATL prepares the facility for series production. The company has not provided a date for full-scale manufacturing. First cell lines enter trial operations Trial production will allow CATL to set up, optimize, and validate the equipment and manufacturing processes before series production begins. The company said the Debrecen facility had met all conditions required to begin the trial run. The firm received the plant’s occupancy permit in August 2026. It then obtained the remaining relevant permits and completed the requirements under its Integrated Pollution Prevention and Control (IPPC) permit. Local authorities carried out regular inspections before granting the occupancy permit. The inspections followed up on earlier issues that had caused concerns among local residents. Authorities confirmed that the deficiencies identified during the permitting process had been addressed. Factory targets European automakers CATL announced the Debrecen project in August 2022 as its second European battery plant after its facility in Germany. The company said the project is intended to strengthen its position in Europe’s automotive and electric mobility supply chain. More from Energy See All Construction of the first cell building began in summer 2023, while production equipment installation was completed by spring 2026. The factory reportedly uses flexible production lines designed to meet the requirements of its customers. The facility has already been producing battery modules since autumn 2024. The battery maker said it has produced 537,000 modules at the Hungarian site so far. 100 GWh capacity planned Once all planned facilities are ready, the Debrecen site is expected to become CATL’s largest manufacturing base outside China. The company has put its planned capacity at 100 gigawatt-hours (GWh). The factory is positioned near Hungary’s growing electric vehicle manufacturing sector. CATL said it will supply major European automakers that have established significant EV production capacity in the country. The start of cell trials comes after an earlier target for production. According to reports in September 2025, CATL’s European general manager Matt Shen informed that the company had been aiming to start production in late 2025 or early 2026. CATL steps up European battery production The firm said it will continue working with the Hungarian government and regulatory authorities throughout the trial period. The company will monitor employee health, safety, and environmental indicators and proactively submit the results to regulators. CATL is the world’s largest EV battery maker by installations. Data from South Korean market researcher SNE Research showed that the battery maker recorded 289.6 GWh of global battery installations from January through July 2026, up 26.6 percent from the same period a year earlier. Its global market share increased to 39.9 percent during the period, compared with 38.0 percent a year earlier. The Debrecen plant adds another major manufacturing location as CATL expands its production footprint closer to European vehicle manufacturers.

artigo.texto: - A majority of Utahns and Americans say it isn’t worth building data centers near residential areas even if competition against China or jobs are at stake. - Experts say the U.S. is racing to “gobble up space” for data centers to maintain its AI lead over China, but Utahns — and Americans broadly — aren’t persuaded that this urgency justifies building near their communities. - The political fight over data centers is intensifying, with 66% of Utahns opposing the Stratos Project in Box Elder County and candidates like Peter Crosby making local control a campaign issue. It’s no secret that Utahns vocally oppose data centers: From Mona’s mega center to Box Elder County’s Stratos project, rural residents rush to community meetings to make their opinions known. Americans across the country feel pretty much the same way, as vulnerable candidates in this year’s midterm elections line up to denounce the continued construction of the centers. But what’s fueling the opposition? In a new Deseret News/Hinckley Institute of Politics poll fielded this month, Americans and Utahns showed most voters are resistant to arguments made by the pro-data center crowd — that they will bring jobs and help the United States maintain its AI edge. When asked to choose between two alternatives — building data centers to compete with China even if some are built near residential communities, or to protect communities from data centers “even if it slows America’s progress in competing with China” — 67% chose the latter. Opposition softened slightly — but only to 59% — when the question was reframed around economic growth. Nationally, a slightly larger percentage supported data centers in both questions, though the majority still opposed. The national poll was fielded among 2,102 registered U.S. voters from Sept. 10 to Sept. 14, and has a margin of error of +/- 2 percentage points. The Utah poll reached 744 registered voters from Sept. 10 to Sept. 15, and has a margin of error of +/- 4 percentage points. Both polls were conducted by Morning Consult. The race to dominate artificial intelligence Aaron Starks, president and CEO of 47G, an aerospace and defense organization, said the four major areas of AI capability are chips, data centers, electricity and talent. “China does energy and electricity very, very well,” he said. “Eighty percent of China is undeveloped. They have a lot of land. This is a top-down authoritarian regime that can build and electrify at their own pace.” The United States, on the other hand, doesn’t have that capability. “But what we do have is we have tremendous data compute capabilities,” Starks added. To catch up, he said the U.S. is trying to “gobble up space” wherever possible to build more data centers — increasingly depending on the Department of Energy to scope out future sites. Zach Boyd, director of the Office of Artificial Intelligence for the State of Utah, agreed that the U.S. does have a “lead” over China — depending on how you measure the race — and the nation should be able to maintain it for some time. Even still, he said: “I think it should be on people’s radar.” Boyd explained Utah’s part: Gov. Spencer Cox has called on the federal government to create more regulatory policy, though the state is considering creating additional legislation itself. “As these agents become more powerful, I think we are going to see definite benefits for society,” Boyd said, “but also the cases where they get out of hand will become more and more serious just because the AI agents are more powerful.” Data centers and AI are not just a consumer or economic development challenge, Starks said, it’s a national priority. “And so it’s not really just about Utah, it’s about our national interests as a whole and whether or not Congress can properly determine and prioritize things, which they can’t,” he said. “They haven’t for many years.” The promise of a better economy In the Deseret News poll, opposition to data center construction eased slightly when the question shifted to economic growth — though a majority of Americans and Utahns still said no. “Things are rough right now for a lot of people,” said Peter Crosby, Democratic nominee for Utah’s 2nd Congressional District. “So, if you tell me that this kind of economic development project is going to bring jobs, then I’m probably going to be more likely to say yes.” Also according to the Deseret News poll, young residents ages 18–34 were more likely to support data centers for job growth (33%) than those ages 35–44 (25%) — which might not come as a surprise, as the Harvard Institute of Politics found nearly half of young Americans say they are personally affected “a lot” by inflation (50%) in a study earlier this year. Another 45% say they are struggling to make ends meet or getting by with little financial security. “Especially right now with the state of the current economy, anything that suggests that it might give somebody a job is probably going to have a slightly more positive response,” Crosby added. The Governor’s Office of Economic Development projected the Creekstone Energy data center in Millard County — which is currently under construction — will produce 106 full-time jobs, averaging $160,000 per job. But not everyone buys those numbers. “Typically, you see a job buildout for about a year or two while the construction actually happens. But that may be a local workforce — it may not,” said Crosby. “But once the center itself is set up, it takes a caretaker crew — you’re looking at 25, 50 folks maybe, because it’s just a warehouse with server banks.” The next steps for Utah politicians Crosby is the Democratic nominee for Utah’s 2nd Congressional District — which includes Box Elder County, where the controversial Stratos Project launched. Limited (CATL), the world’s largest Chinese battery manufacturer, began test operations on September 22, 2026, at its newly constructed cell manufacturing facility in the eastern Hungarian city of Debrecen. After successfully meeting all regulatory requirements, the first two production lines at the new facility are now up and running. The goal of the test phase is to precisely configure, optimize, validate, and verify the highly complex manufacturing equipment and process chains before regular mass production begins. With the start of cell production, the major project announced in August 2022 has reached its most important milestone to date. The Hungarian factory is the Chinese battery group’s second European site and is designed to integrate directly into the continent’s automotive supply chains. German and European automakers in particular—many of which, for instance, BMW, Mercedes-Benz, and Audi, already have extensive in-house electric vehicle production capacities in Hungary—are expected to benefit from short transport routes and customized deliveries. In addition to cell production, CATL has been manufacturing battery modules in Debrecen since fall 2024. Since then, 537,000 modules have been produced on site. Once all phases of construction are fully completed, the Debrecen plant—with a planned annual capacity of 100 gigawatt-hours (GWh)—will be CATL’s largest production site outside of China. The construction of the plant had been accompanied by intense debate and environmental concerns among the local population. To address these concerns, the permitting process was subject to strict regulatory oversight. Prior to the issuance of the final operating permit in August 2026, the relevant Hajdú-Bihar County government agency conducted regular on-site inspections. Representatives of the regulatory authorities confirmed that the company had rectified all deficiencies and risk points identified in advance as part of the IPPC (Integrated Pollution Prevention and Control) process. Even during the test phase that has now begun, occupational safety, employee health, and environmental parameters are continuously monitored. CATL proactively submits the resulting measurement data to the Hungarian environmental and labor authorities. The company emphasized that it remains committed to maximum transparency and welcomes visits from regulatory agencies at any time. This billion-forint project is considered one of the most significant industrial investments in Hungary’s history. It not only strengthens the regional economy around Debrecen by creating new jobs and expanding local infrastructure, but also solidifies the country’s position as a European heavyweight in the manufacturing of electric vehicles and key components. For the European e-mobility supply chain, the launch in Debrecen represents a decisive step toward supply security and scalability. Via Press Release; Featured photo: Facebook/Joó István

artigo.texto: - Li Auto has several solid-state battery projects underway and has validated prototypes in eyewear products. - A company executive said mature mass production for vehicles would take another 5 years, with lifespan, charging performance and cost still posing challenges. Li Auto (NASDAQ: LI) is expected to have solid-state batteries ready for limited vehicle deployment in 2027 or 2028, though mature mass production for automotive use remains further away. Chinese media outlet Cailian reported the timeline on Tuesday, citing a Li Auto insider, offering a clearer indication of when the company's solid-state battery research could translate into vehicle applications. Li Auto has several solid-state battery projects under development and has validated prototypes in eyewear products as it continues to invest in the technology, Liu Zhimin, the company's senior director of power batteries, said, according to Cailian. However, achieving mature mass production for vehicles while ensuring a consistent and reliable user experience is expected to take another 5 years, Liu said. "Challenges remain in simultaneously meeting requirements for lifespan, charging performance and cost with solid-state batteries," he said. Limited vehicle deployment and mature mass production represent different stages. Being ready for limited deployment in 2027 or 2028 would not mean the batteries could be widely used in production models by then. Li Auto launched its Livis smart glasses in December 2025, though it did not highlight the device's use of solid-state batteries at the time. The solid-state battery work is part of Li Auto's broader push to expand in-house battery development. The company said on September 7 that its in-house developed batteries were already used in the Li L8, Li L6 and Li i8, with deployment set to gradually extend across its lineup. Li Auto said it began developing battery cells in-house in 2020, with its work covering 5C cells, battery packs and battery management systems (BMS). The batteries are produced by a joint venture established in 2025 with Sunwoda (SZSE: 300207), in which each company holds a 50% stake. Li Auto is also strengthening its financial ties with its battery manufacturing partner. Sunwoda disclosed on September 4 that Li Auto planned to invest in Sunwoda Electric Vehicle Battery Co Ltd (Sunwoda EVB), giving it a direct 8.79% stake upon completion and making it the company's second-largest single shareholder. Several Chinese automakers and battery manufacturers have set milestones around 2027 for solid-state battery development, though gaps remain between vehicle validation, limited deployment and large-scale commercialization. Chery Auto (HKEX: 9973) said on September 3 that it planned to begin vehicle validation of all-solid-state batteries in 2027, with solid-liquid hybrid batteries scheduled for vehicle installation in the fourth quarter of 2026 as a transitional solution. CATL (HKEX: 3750) chief scientist Wu Kai said in 2024 that the company aimed to reach the technical readiness required for small-batch production of all-solid-state batteries in 2027, though large-scale production would still face challenges including cost. CATL chairman Robin Zeng said in June this year that solid-state battery technology was only at level 4 on a scale from level 1 to level 9, with level 9 representing readiness for mass production.

artigo.texto: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore announced he has signed an executive order to codify statewide guardrails for “transparent and accountable data center development” in Maryland. The new order will also establish a Data Center Task Force that will be responsible for reviewing projects for large data centers, maintaining a public dashboard and supporting local governments. The group, composed of members from the Maryland Energy Administration and the departments of Commerce, Labor, Environment, Natural Resources, Agriculture, and Planning. “By signing this executive order, we are establishing clear safeguards to ensure Marylanders do not foot the bill, our people benefit, community voices are heard, and our environment is protected â all while centering transparency and accountability throughout the process,” Moore said in a news release. The task force will review proposed large data centers that required more than 25 megawatts. The review process will occur when projects request a state permit, incentive or letter of support. Projects will be considered in terms of five principles, including ratepayer and grid protection, economic benefits for Marylanders, community voice, environmental protections, and transparency and accountability. Following the review process, projects will be qualified as: aligned, conditionally aligned or not aligned. The Governor’s Office said Moore will also seek to repeal a 2020 tax exemption that allowed certain data centers to be exempt from paying sales and use tax with the condition the centers would create at least five net new jobs for the duration of the benefit. The 2020 program was intended to incentivize data center investment and job creation in the state. What’s the state of data centers in Maryland? According to the National Conference of State Legislatures, lawmakers in 16 states, including Maryland, Virginia, Pennsylvania and Delaware, are considering moratoriums or bans on data centers. Last year, four Republican delegates, including Baltimore’s Kathy Szeliga, introduced House Bill 120 to prohibit the construction of data centers in the state. The bill was discussed in a January hearing, but was not taken to a vote. In the Baltimore metro area, multiple counties have passed moratoriums on data centers until 2027. On Tuesday, Baltimore County voted to extend the county’s current data center moratorium through December 2027. Last month, the Baltimore City Planning Commission discussed a new bill that lays out proposed new rules and restrictions for data centers in the city. Harford County is the only county in the state to permanently ban data centers. According to the Governor’s Office, a new statewide dashboard will show the location of new projects. The website will also disclose the developer, the projected power demand and water use and “every State action the project has requested and its status.”

artigo.texto: Caminhões em frente ao Polo Suíço de Farmacêutica Kuehne+Nagel (Foto: Divulgação) A Kuehne+Nagel anunciou uma parceria estratégica de longo prazo com a Amazon, que inclui serviços logísticos para a infraestrutura de data centers da Amazon Web Services (AWS). O acordo amplia o relacionamento entre as empresas e abrange atividades relacionadas à construção, instalação de equipamentos, manutenção e expansão da infraestrutura de nuvem da Amazon em diferentes países. A colaboração prevê o atendimento às necessidades logísticas da AWS durante todo o ciclo de vida da infraestrutura, desde a construção e implantação de equipamentos até a manutenção, atualização e ampliação das instalações. O objetivo é aumentar a capacidade operacional e a eficiência da cadeia de suprimentos, acompanhando a expansão global dos serviços de nuvem da Amazon. Segundo o CEO da Kuehne+Nagel International AG, Stefan Paul, o acordo permitirá ampliar a atuação da companhia no atendimento à Amazon, utilizando sua rede global, seus recursos digitais e sua experiência em gestão da cadeia de suprimentos. ACORDO PREVÊ OPÇÃO DE COMPRA DE AÇÕES A parceria também inclui uma opção de compra de ações já existentes da Kuehne+Nagel pela Amazon. O direito de aquisição está condicionado ao cumprimento de metas comerciais e de prestação de serviços ao longo de um período de até sete anos. O acordo prevê liquidação financeira ou, a critério da Amazon, entrega de ações. Para viabilizar a operação, a Kuehne+Nagel contratou uma instituição financeira terceirizada para realizar operações de proteção (hedge) envolvendo ações da companhia.
