artigo.texto: Republican Tom Tiffany and Democrat David Crowley are staking out positions on artificial intelligence as the technology reshapes government, the economy, and the state's energy landscape. Artificial intelligence is driving demand for hyperscale AI data centers — including one in Port Washington — and has become a major flashpoint in the Wisconsin governor's race. TMJ4 News reporter Charles Brenson has more on how each candidate is tackling the issue in Wisconsin: Republicans have criticized Crowley for suggesting Wisconsin could become a "global hub" for data centers, even as his campaign ads call for accountability from the industry. "Hold data centers accountable and make them pay," a Crowley campaign commercial said. Democrats have criticized Tiffany for voting on a House bill to fast-track data centers, but the SPEED Act stalled in the Senate. He also supported a proposed 10-year moratorium that would have blocked state efforts to restrict AI data centers. The Senate later removed that provision. Tiffany's campaign ads push back on the industry as well. "Stop Wall Street from buying our homes — big data from bulldozing our farms," a Tiffany campaign commercial said. The next governor will have to navigate Wisconsin through the fast-changing world of artificial intelligence and determine how it can be used across state government. State agencies are currently allowed to use AI to "leverage their capabilities in gaining unique insights, problem solving, and enhancing productivity," according to the state's website. Employees are asked to be "vigilant in using generative AI tools" and are "prohibited from sharing Non-Public Information with any generative AI platform that has not been authorized." The state also directs employees to "exercise critical judgment and verify the completeness and accuracy of all information from any AI platform." Tiffany said he sees a need for privacy protections and a measured approach to the technology's expansion. "Certainly have concerns. There needs to be guardrails. I think we need to make sure we protect people's privacy. We need to make sure people's data is not being sent to, especially adversaries, including communist China, who's always trying to harvest our data," Tiffany said. "So I think there needs to be some guardrails around this that we need to take a, a bit of a go slow approach." He said the technology carries both promise and risk. "I think it's like any technology. There are benefits to it, but there's also risks, and that's what we need to do is that assessment," Tiffany said. Crowley said AI should serve as a tool for workers, not a replacement for human decision-making. "I think that artificial intelligence, it can be used as a tool, but it should not replace human judgment. It shouldn't be the end all, be all. And I believe that we need to have strict guardrails here in the state of Wisconsin," Crowley said. Crowley said protecting jobs and personal data would guide his approach to deploying AI in state government. "Well, one, I don't think artificial intelligence should be replacing our jobs. I wanted to increase and enhance our efficiencies and be able to assist all of our workers within a state government," Crowley said. "But again, we have to make sure those protections are there, making sure there aren't any personal identifiers out there, that the privacy, the accountability, but also the public knows exactly how we're utilize." artigo.texto: O debate promovido pelo g1 nesta segunda-feira (21) entre candidatos ao Senador pelo Ceará foi marcado por concordância com a instalação de data centers no estado e discussões sobre a melhor forma de empregar as emendas parlamentares e de medidas para fomentar o trabalho e o emprego. Os candidatos também discutiram medidas para o combate às facções criminosas e à violência contra a mulher, além de discutirem a relação entre os Poderes (veja, mais abaixo, vídeos de cada tema). Participaram do encontro os candidatos Cid Gomes (PSB) e Luizianne Lins (Rede). Alcides Fernandes (PL) e Capitão Wagner (União) também foram convidados para o debate, mas não compareceram. O debate foi transmitido ao vivo, de Fortaleza, pelo site e pelos perfis do g1 no YouTube, Tiktok e Instagram. Foram convidados os candidatos de partidos e federações com representação mínima de cinco parlamentares no Congresso, ou que alcançaram ao menos 5% de intenções de voto na última pesquisa Quaest. Seis temas foram previamente definidos e comunicados às campanhas antes do debate. A ordem dos assuntos foi sorteada antes do início do encontro, bem como a posição das cadeiras durante o encontro e a ordem das considerações finais. Os participantes tiveram 15 minutos de tempo de fala para administrar ao longo da discussão, com intervenções de até 1 minuto e 30 segundos por vez. Ao final, todos tiveram direito a um minuto para as considerações finais. Confira o que falaram os candidatos sobre os temas estabelecidos: Cid Gomes (PSB) e Luizianne Lins (Rede) já estão posicionados para o debate do g1, às 14h. — Foto: Ismael Soares. LEIA TAMBÉM: Primeiro tema: data centers e recursos naturais No primeiro tema, os candidatos do Senado pelo Ceará discutiram sobre as oportunidades de empregos que podem surgir com a chegada de equipamentos tecnológicos como o Data Center do TikTok instalado no Ceará. Cid Gomes destacou as oportunidades que os equipamentos podem criar do estado. O candidato lembrou que, historicamente, no estado, as estruturas são construídas antes de começar as atividades empresariais. Citou o Porto do Pecem, a rede de fibra ótica, a primeira Zona de Processamento de Exportação (ZPE) do Brasil e como os equipamentos tornaram o estado forte na concorrência internacional dos países que pleiteavam o Data Center do TikTok. Cid citou ainda as centenas de pessoas que já trabalham na construção do Data Center. Por fim, o candidato do PSB destacou o uso e a produção de energias renováveis para esses equipamentos. Luizianne falou que é favorável ao estado receber grandes equipamentos de infraestrutura digital. Ela lembrou da legislação que aprovou, durante sua gestão na prefeitura de Fortaleza, as atividades de parques tecnológicos na cidade. A candidata da Rede destacou ainda a participação dela sobre as discussões da soberania digital e tecnológica no Brasil no Congresso, durante os mandatos como deputada federal. Segundo tema: emendas parlamentares No segundo tema, os candidatos discutiram emendas parlamentares, sua distribuição a municípios e a atribuição dos parlamentares na construção do Orçamento da União. Luizianne Lins destacou que as emendas são provenientes de dinheiro público e que, portanto, devem chegar diretamente à população. A candidata defendeu que metade de todas as emendas parlamentares deveriam ir para a área de saúde pública. A candidata pela Rede também afirmou que as emendas deveriam priorizar regiões que têm mais dificuldade de acesso a investimentos e afirmou que, como deputada federal, prioriza emendas para o interior, em áreas como saúde, educação e agricultura familiar. Cid Gomes disse ser favorável à participação de parlamentares na indicação de recursos no Orçamento da União, mas disse que esse processo deve ser feito com parcimônia. Cid defendeu que o Poder Executivo tenha preferência na indicação de recursos do Orçamento, uma vez que é o responsável pela arrecadação. O candidato à reeleição pelo PSB também defendeu o envio de emendas a pequenas cidades e maior fiscalização na aplicação do dinheiro. Terceiro tema: trabalho e emprego No terceiro tema, os candidatos discutiram sobre trabalho e emprego. Cid e Luizianne defenderam iniciativas dos governos Lula (PT) e Elmano de Freitas (PT), além de propor novas medidas para a área. Cid destacou que educação e trabalho são duas áreas prioritárias para quem está no Poder Público. O candidato disse ainda que é preciso garantir as condições de infraestrutura para que o país tenha capacidade de competir de igual para igual com os demais países dentro do mercado global. Cid afirmou que o Ceará se prepara para isso e citou obras do governo do presidente Lula no estado, como a ferrovia Transnordestina. Ele também citou que o Ceará se destaca pela capacidade de produção de energia, dispondo de três vezes mais do que consome internamente. Luizianne relembrou iniciativas da sua gestão quando prefeita de Fortaleza e disse que a capital gerou 180 mil empregos entre os anos de 2005 e 2010. Ela mencionou ações como o acesso ao crédito, aumento de obras públicas e investimento maior em turismo, mencionando a criação de uma secretaria específica e a implantação da festa do Reveillon de Fortaleza. Cid também defendeu ações dos governos Lula e Elmano, destacando a implantação do Polo Automotivo do Ceará, em Horizonte. Luizianne afirmou que pretende atuar nesse tema caso seja eleito senadora e citou a criação de um projeto chamado "Crédito Lilás", para financiar o acesso a crédito para mulheres. Quarto tema: combate às facções criminosas No quarto tema, os candidatos debateram as estratégias para combater o crime organizado e impedir que a juventude seja cooptada por facções criminosas. artigo.texto: BEIJING — Shares of CATL, the world's largest battery maker, have lost nearly a quarter of their value in the past month on concerns that automaker clients are moving away from the Chinese company. Worries have grown that CATL's market dominance could weaken as Chinese automakers diversify their battery supply chains to defend profitability. On the Shenzhen Stock Exchange, CATL closed at 297.10 yuan on the 21st, down 1.61% from the previous session. The stock narrowly avoided a 52-week low of 295.55 yuan, having tumbled 24.04% in September alone and 36.5% from its early-May peak this year. The decline stems from major automaker clients reducing their reliance on CATL. Li Auto recently invested 2.65 billion yuan to become the second-largest shareholder in Sunwoda, a Shenzhen-based battery maker, and fitted its latest model with Sunwoda batteries instead of CATL's. Xiaomi, which had used CATL batteries in its main models, said it would jointly develop batteries with CALB and cooperate across the entire supply chain. Xpeng has also expanded the share of batteries it sources from EVE Energy. Profitability pressure is cited as the reason Chinese automakers have turned to supply chain diversification. Amid weak domestic demand and intensifying price competition, profits at Chinese automakers fell 20% in the January-July period. CATL, by contrast, has thrived on a market share of close to 50% in China. Its total net profit in the first half of this year, at 43.28 billion yuan, was double the 21.05 billion yuan posted by 15 major listed Chinese automakers over the same period. Automakers also want a stronger voice in product development and price negotiations. Unlike CATL, the overwhelming market leader, latecomers such as CALB and Sunwoda cannot afford to lose a single customer and can therefore work more flexibly with automakers. Li Auto's move to become Sunwoda's second-largest shareholder was aimed at that leverage. Still, analysts largely expect CATL's dominance to hold despite the external pressure, as automakers have been unable to sever ties with the company altogether. CATL has also been broadening its portfolio beyond electric-vehicle batteries into energy storage systems and battery recycling. Energy storage already accounts for about 25% of revenue, and the company expects that to rise to 50% within a few years. Kenny Ng Lai-yin, a strategist at Chinese brokerage Everbright Securities, said CATL's market share would remain stable for some time because the EV battery industry has high entry barriers, requiring enormous capital and technology investment as well as time to build up talent.

artigo.texto: Kim Long launches first battery-powered heavy truck in Vietnam Vietnamese commercial vehicle manufacturer Kim Long Motor has officially launched its K9KEV heavy-duty truck tractor in its domestic market, which the company claims is Vietnam's first domestically branded battery-powered heavy-duty truck to go into production in the country. The K9KEV, produced at the company's manufacturing hub in the Chan May-Lang Co Economic Zone, in Vietnam's Hue Province, is a 6x4 road tractor with a towing capacity of 38 tons. It is powered by a 400 kWh BYD battery pack, driving an electric motor with a maximum power output of 450 kW. It has a driving range of up to 350 km, and the battery can be charged from 20% to 80% in 60 minutes. The K9KEV features dual-circuit pneumatic drum brakes as its primary braking system, combined with an anti-lock braking system (ABS) and electronic stability control (ESC). Additional safety systems include a Forward Collision Warning System (FCWS) and a Lane Departure Warning System (LDWS). In Vietnam, the Kim Long K9KEV is priced at VND 2.78 billion (US$ 107,000), with a special promotional price of VND 2.5 billion available to early customers. artigo.texto: Google data center could generate billions, add jobs, and new households EVANS, Ga. (WRDW/WAGT) - A new study released by the Columbia County Economic Development Authority projects the Google data center campus under construction off Interstate 20 could generate $4 billion over 35 years for the county. The study says money spent on items such as property taxes and spending by people moving to the area for the data center could total $4 billion over 35 years. Deal calls for Google to help pay for Vogtle upgrades Georgia Power struck a deal with Google for the tech giant to help fund upgrades at Plant Vogtle and the state’s other nuclear generating plant. The study also projects the project could create 1,600 new jobs, 472 new local households and 307 new students in the Columbia County School System. The Development Authority said the job and household figures are based on research of other, similar facilities. The data center campus covers 3,358 acres of land off I-20’s exit in Appling. Construction is underway, with full completion still years away. The land currently generates $22,000 a year in taxes for the county and schools. The county’s projected tax revenue from the site is $12 billion. The study was produced by a third party and released by the Development Authority on the County’s data center project website (https://roadtorelief-columbiagagis.hub.arcgis.com). Google has signed a $280 million deal with Columbia County. The money will be paid to the county over seven years and will fund homestead property tax relief for people living in Columbia County before construction finishes. The tax break would start in the first year if voters approve it this November. If approved, homeowners would receive an $18,000 credit for each home. The county is lobbying Georgia lawmakers to amend a cap that would allow a full property tax credit in the future. Copyright 2026 WRDW/WAGT. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: ‘Overwhelmed with misinformation’: What data centers mean for the environment LANSING, Mich. (News 10) - Michigan State University’s Institute for Public Policy and Social Research held a conversation Tuesday to discuss common misconceptions about data centers, including their impact on the state’s electrical grid. Dr. Erik Nordman, director of the Institute of Public Utilities at Michigan State University, said a more reliable electricity system benefits everyone. “If the electricity system is more reliable, we’re all going to benefit from that,” Nordman said. Many people have voiced concerns about water usage, but experts at MSU said developers hear those concerns. “Most data centers that are being built today are trying to conserve water because they see the controversies happening around water and they want to be responsible developers,” said Jean Hardy, associate director of the Quello Center at Michigan State University. However, Hardy said not every facility is being developed that way. “For example, the Google data center being proposed in Van Buren Township is supposed to use, I believe, upwards of two million gallons of water a day,” Hardy said. Across the street from the conversation, at the Capitol, environmental groups held their own conference urging for more transparency and seats at the table. “[We’re hearing] Sam Altman, Elon Musk are saying ‘we need to slow down AI ’; we’re seeing [the Michigan Economic Development Corporation] saying that they’re not going to provide any transparency for these tax breaks. Every week it seems like new information comes out on the dangers of AI technology,” said Marta Johnson, Legislative and Political Organizer at the Sierra Club Michigan. Environmental groups, including the Sierra Club of Michigan and Clean Water Action, said regulation is increasingly needed but isn’t happening. That’s why they say more seats are needed at the table. “Because we listen to the communities that are a part of our network...We’ve been hearing from them for a year and a half now. They’re just really concerned; they’re overwhelmed with misinformation. They don’t know what information to trust,” Amanda Robert, Network Director for Michigan Climate Action Network. They also said they are skeptical of claims that some data center developers are responsible. “If responsible data center owners exist, they shouldn’t be worried about real strong protections that are codified into law, enforceable, hold people accountable, because if they’re already doing that, what’s the problem with having those protections in place?” said Nichole Keway Biber, a Water Justice Manager with Clean Water Action. artigo.texto: Igual geladeira? Europa quer selo de consumo de energia para data centers Classificação de A a G também avaliará eficiência no uso de água; primeiras etiquetas estão previstas para agosto de 2027. Os data centers da União Europeia deverão receber etiquetas com classificações de A a G para a eficiência no uso de energia e água, em um formato que lembra os selos de eletrodomésticos. A Comissão Europeia propôs ontem, 20 de setembro, um regulamento que estabelece o sistema, com emissão das primeiras etiquetas prevista até 15 de agosto de 2027. O ato passará por um período de dois meses de análise do Parlamento Europeu e do Conselho, que poderão apresentar objeções. As etiquetas serão geradas a partir das informações fornecidas pelos operadores à base europeia de data centers, com atualização anual. A iniciativa acompanha a intenção do bloco de triplicar sua capacidade de data centers nos próximos cinco a sete anos. Segundo os dados apresentados pela Comissão, essas instalações consumiram 68 terawatts-hora (TWh) de eletricidade na União Europeia em 2024. A projeção é de 114 TWh em 2030, equivalentes a 3,2% da demanda elétrica do bloco. “Triplicar nossa capacidade de data centers não pode significar triplicar a pressão sobre nossas redes, nossa água e nossas contas de energia”, afirmou Teresa Ribera, vice-presidente executiva da Comissão Europeia, em comunicado. Duas classificações na mesma etiqueta O modelo terá escalas separadas para energia e água. A classificação energética utilizará o PUE, indicador que relaciona o consumo total de energia da instalação ao dos equipamentos de tecnologia da informação. A classe A será destinada a instalações com índice igual ou inferior a 1,15; a G, àquelas acima de 1,9. A eficiência hídrica será avaliada pelo WUE, calculado a partir da entrada de água doce em relação ao consumo energético dos equipamentos de TI. Cada instalação receberá, portanto, uma classificação para cada um dos dois indicadores. Além das notas, a etiqueta apresentará informações sobre as fontes de energia utilizadas, a oferta de serviços de flexibilidade à rede elétrica e a existência de infraestrutura preparada para fornecer calor residual a usuários externos. Também identificará operador, localização, categoria de tamanho e período de referência dos dados. Um documento explicativo acompanhará os selos para contextualizar os resultados. Entre os fatores previstos estão clima, condições locais de escassez de água, idade, tamanho e ocupação das instalações, além da relação entre eficiência energética e hídrica. Consulta pública e acesso às informações As etiquetas ficarão disponíveis eletronicamente na base europeia. Os operadores também deverão fornecê-las a qualquer pessoa ou empresa que as solicitar, podendo indicar um site de acesso gratuito ou a própria base de dados. Instalações com potência instalada de TI inferior a 500 kW poderão aderir voluntariamente. A participação também será permitida a empreendimentos ainda fora de operação, com indicadores projetados. Após o início das atividades, esses operadores deverão informar os dados efetivamente registrados. A primeira revisão do sistema está prevista para até 31 de dezembro de 2028. Entre os pontos a avaliar estão mudanças nas escalas, indicadores sobre o consumo dos equipamentos de TI e eventual certificação ou auditoria dos dados declarados. Em paralelo, a Comissão abriu consulta pública sobre padrões mínimos de desempenho para data centers em operação na Europa. As contribuições poderão ser enviadas até 14 de dezembro de 2026. Essa discussão integra o pacote europeu voltado à eficiência das instalações e à sua integração ao sistema energético.

artigo.texto: The US installed 5.4 GW/18.9 GWh of battery energy storage systems in the second quarter of 2026, setting a new quarterly record in terms of energy capacity. According to the latest US Energy Storage Monitor, released by the American Clean Power Association (ACP) and Wood Mackenzie, GWh deployments increased 17% year-on-year, despite a 7% decline in newly installed power capacity, measured in GW, compared with the same quarter of 2025. The divergence between the two figures largely reflects the deployment of battery systems capable of storing energy for longer periods. The national average duration of newly installed battery storage systems increased from 2.8 hours in Q2 2025 to 3.5 hours a year later, driven by growing resource adequacy needs. Utility-scale storage accounts for 17.6 GWh The utility-scale segment continued to account for the vast majority of new capacity, with 4.7 GW/17.6 GWh deployed during the second quarter. In power terms, utility-scale installations declined 8% year-on-year as some key markets became increasingly saturated. However, deployments during the first half of 2026 were 5% higher than in the same period of 2025. Average project duration continued to increase during the quarter, partly driven by a long-duration storage project in California designed to support state targets and utility-contracted storage assets deployed in Texas. “Battery storage is one of the most important tools we have to meet growing electricity demand,” said John Hensley, Senior Vice President of Markets and Policy Analysis at American Clean Power. Hensley highlighted storage’s ability to be deployed quickly, strengthen grid reliability and enable the power system to make better use of both existing and new generation. Residential storage installs 676 MW The residential segment recorded its fourth-largest quarter on record, with 676 MW installed. This represented a 15% decline from the previous quarter but a 3% increase year-on-year. California, Texas, Puerto Rico, Arizona and Illinois collectively accounted for 88% of residential storage capacity installed in Q2, although all five markets recorded quarter-on-quarter declines. Puerto Rico posted the largest decline in absolute terms, falling from 129 MW in Q1 to 73 MW in Q2. Meanwhile, the national residential solar-plus-storage attachment rate reached 46%, up from 41% in the second quarter of 2025. Despite these figures, ACP and Wood Mackenzie expect the US residential storage market to contract by 4% in 2026, amid the elimination of tax credits, consumer hesitancy and a challenging transition toward third-party ownership models. Commercial and industrial segment installs 48 MW The community, commercial and industrial (CCI) segment deployed 48 MW during the quarter, returning to historical deployment levels following California’s record first quarter, which was driven by the deadline to qualify under the state’s Net Energy Metering 2.0 framework. Overall, the segment declined 2% year-on-year, although above-average growth in Hawaii, New Mexico and Texas helped offset some of the contraction. US storage capacity could reach 207 GW/715 GWh by 2031 The outlook points to strong expansion over the next five years. ACP and Wood Mackenzie expect annual US energy storage installations to grow by more than 50% in MW terms over that period. Under the forecast, cumulative installed storage capacity in the country would reach 207 GW/715 GWh by 2031. One of the main drivers will be rapidly increasing electricity demand from data centers. Wood Mackenzie expects utility-scale storage to grow at an average annual rate of 8% over the next five years. “Data center buildout strengthens the US storage outlook across all sectors,” said Allison Feeney, research analyst at Wood Mackenzie. According to Feeney, as hyperscalers face increasing grid-connection bottlenecks, utility-scale storage can provide faster access to the power capacity required by data centers. The CCI segment is projected to grow 27% between 2026 and 2031, supported by deployment expanding beyond California into emerging markets such as Maryland and Texas. The residential market is also expected to rebound from 2027 and grow at an average annual rate of 9% through 2031. Utility-scale battery system prices fall 2% The report also points to declining costs. Utility-scale battery system prices fell 2% year-on-year to $916/kW in the second quarter of 2026. At the same time, the share of hybrid utility-scale installations declined to 33%, down from 45% in Q2 2025, mainly due to a contraction in the California market. Supply chain dynamics remain a key source of uncertainty. Potential trade restrictions could create near-term bottlenecks and lead to some stagnation in the utility-scale segment during 2026 and 2027. Wood Mackenzie nevertheless expects growth to resume in 2028 and average 11% annually through 2031, supported by the expansion of domestic battery cell manufacturing. Against this backdrop, slowing electric vehicle demand is providing an unexpected boost to stationary storage. Allison Weis, Global Head of Energy Storage at Wood Mackenzie, said manufacturers are repurposing idle EV cell production capacity, helping accelerate the development of the domestic storage supply chain.

artigo.texto: This article was produced by Capital & Main, an award-winning publication that reports from California on economic, political, and social issues. It is co-published here with permission. In January, U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany (R-Wisconsin) called data centers “exciting new technology” and voted for a federal bill to speed their construction. But by May, as he was running for governor of Wisconsin, he was promising to repeal the state tax breaks that lure them. And within a week of the Aug. 11 Democratic primary in the Badger State, Tiffany’s campaign was on the air branding his opponent “Data Center David Crowley”—a Republican attacking a Democrat for being too cozy with Big Tech. The ad focused on a statement Crowley gave at a candidate forum in November 2025 that Wisconsin had the opportunity to become a major artificial intelligence and data center hub “not only for the entire country, but for the entire globe and really sets us apart in making sure that we continue to invest in businesses and companies here.” But early this summer, Crowley began insisting that local communities should have absolute veto power to reject any such project and that data center developers should pay for all grid and infrastructure upgrades. Voters in the battleground state’s most important race could be forgiven for experiencing whiplash. Data centers are now what the Wisconsin Examiner called the biggest issue in the governor’s race, and the public has turned on them faster than on anything the state’s leading pollster has measured in 15 years. And Tiffany has navigated that turn to outflank Crowley with tougher rhetoric, his own reversal notwithstanding. A longtime fossil fuel supporter, Tiffany is also using the unpopularity of data centers in service of a much older fight against renewable sources of energy such as wind and solar. He recently called for the state to not close coal-fired plants, arguing that they “are a backbone of baseload power, and cannot simply be replaced with intermittent generation provided by wind and solar.” Nothing Has Moved This Fast “It’s been one of the fastest changes in public opinion that we’ve seen in Wisconsin,” Charles Franklin, director of the Marquette Law School Poll, told Capital & Main. “We’ve been doing the Marquette poll for 15 years, and in that time nothing else has moved this fast.” When Marquette first asked about data centers last October, 55% of registered voters said the costs of data centers outweighed the benefits. By February it was 70%, and by August 78%. What struck Franklin more was the absence of a partisan split: 54% of Republicans, 55% of independents and 56% of Democrats were all opposed last fall. “Almost nothing we see in Wisconsin shows that small a partisan gap,” Franklin said. That backlash reshaped the Democratic gubernatorial primary. At a Milwaukee town hall the week before the vote, five candidates competed to out-tough one another on the developers dubbed “Big Tech oligarchs” by Francesca Hong, a Democratic state representative who is also a member of the Democratic Socialists of America party and a gubernatorial candidate. Hong made a one-year moratorium on data centers the centerpiece of her campaign, but she lost the primary to Crowley. “Data Center David” Tiffany, who had reportedly hoped to run on economic issues, moved fast to claim the voters Hong had galvanized. He pledged to end the sales tax exemption the state legislature adopted for data centers—a break the Legislative Fiscal Bureau estimated could cost the state more than $2 billion. Crowley countered with accountability framing. “They have to pay their own way,” he said. “They need to pay for their own infrastructure, and they need to bring their own new clean energy.” Behind the ad copy, the two men actually agree on a lot. Neither supports Hong’s proposed moratorium. Both back the same guardrails: a ban on nondisclosure agreements between data center companies and local governments, a local veto over whether a project gets built and protection for residential rates. The general election is a contest over credibility and degree, not direction. What Crowley won’t do is promise to claw back the existing tax breaks, and that is the detail that Tiffany has zeroed in on. Tiffany’s central claim—that Crowley is “funded by the people building” data centers—is easy to misinterpret. The more than $350,000 in campaign contributions that an unnamed Tiffany spokeswoman cited to the Milwaukee Journal-Sentinel came largely from building trades unions whose members would pour the concrete for data centers, not the tech companies that own the buildings. “David Crowley is honored to have the support of thousands of hard-working union members who are suffering from the affordability crisis MAGA extremist Tom Tiffany and Donald Trump created,” an unnamed Crowley spokesperson said in an email to Capital & Main. Tiffany, meanwhile, accepted $5,000 in June from Robert Marchant, a lobbyist for the Wisconsin Data Center Coalition, which fought the nondisclosure agreement ban and lobbied for the same tax exemption that Tiffany now vows to repeal. Campaign finance reports also showed donations to him from lobbyists for OpenAI and Oracle and a donation from Amazon, which is actively building data centers across the country. Capital & Main has reached out to the Tiffany campaign for comment. artigo.texto: Geraldo Campos Jr., da Agência iNFRA Um estudo da Volt Robotics apontou que as usinas hidrelétricas tendem a ser mais beneficiadas pela contratação de baterias no sistema elétrico do que as fontes eólica e solar. O trabalho, apresentado nesta terça-feira (22) durante o evento Encontro Técnico Armazenamento 2030, indicou que 88% da energia a ser usada para carregar as baterias viria de plantas renováveis, sendo a maioria por meio da redução do vertimento turbinável das hídricas. Segundo números apresentados pelo CEO da Volt, Donato Filho, a redução do vertimento turbinável por causa das baterias traria ganhos de 66% para as hidrelétricas, que ainda teriam um incremento da geração da ordem de 18%. Isso reduziria também o risco hidrológico, o que tem efeito sobre os consumidores. Já o efeito projetado das baterias sobre a redução do curtailment de eólicas e solares seria de 16%. Considerando os cortes entre 2024 e 2026, até o primeiro semestre, o ganho com a entrada das baterias seria de R$ 2,7 bilhões para hídricas e renováveis. Durante o evento, realizado em Brasília pela Absae (Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia), Donato Filho explicou que o benefício maior das hídricas se deve ao fato de que a parcela que sofre com o vertimento turbinável é bem maior que a dos cortes de eólica e solar. No entanto, tudo dependerá da ordem de cortes a ser definida pela ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) na CP (Consulta Pública) 45/2019. “Com as baterias sendo carregadas, de manhã vai aumentar a carga. Então vai ter que ter uma decisão sobre quem vai ser cortado menos. Que é a regra para alocar o corte que está em discussão na CP 45”, disse Donato, que continuou: “No estudo, a gente aplicou uma regra proporcional à potência que está sendo disponibilizada pelas fontes, e, como as hídricas são bem maiores, elas acabam sendo mais usadas para alimentar as baterias”. Além disso, o armazenamento poderá reduzir em cerca de R$ 630 milhões por ano o montante de encargos hoje repassados aos consumidores, conforme o estudo. Isso porque os sistemas ajudariam a baixar alguns dos encargos existentes hoje, sobretudo pelo menor uso de térmicas, menor restrição da geração e redução do deslocamento hídrico. Ainda segundo o estudo, a receita fixa das baterias deve ficar de 38% a 64% menor que a média do LRCAP (Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade na forma de Potência) que contratou térmicas, realizado em março. Custeio O estudo abordou ainda o encargo de remuneração das baterias, cujo modelo de pagamento – que conforme a lei, será rateado entre os geradores – está em discussão na ANEEL. De acordo com a Volt, parte do custo pode ser repassada integralmente ao consumidor por causa de uma cláusula existente em contratos de geração do ambiente regulado que prevê que novos tributos e encargos criados após o leilão serão repassados para a tarifa. Donato explicou, no entanto, que parte expressiva da capacidade instalada das fontes com vendas no ambiente regulado tem esse modelo de contrato e, por isso, não pagariam o encargo – repassando ao consumidor integralmente. Pelo estudo, 100% das térmicas do ambiente regulado têm em seus contratos essa cláusula. Nas usinas a biomassa, isso se aplica a 80%. Para eólica, o modelo existe em 60% do parque, e, na solar centralizada, 30%.

artigo.texto: CATL, the world's largest battery maker and long constrained in the U.S. market, has developed a new battery aimed at American pickup trucks. With the Chinese company seen as a possible member of Beijing's economic delegation at the U.S.-China summit on the 24th, attention is turning to whether Chinese batteries and electric vehicles may finally gain entry to the United States. Zhu Lingbo, chief technology officer of CATL's international business division, said on the 20th that the company had developed a "tall battery" tailored for U.S. pickup trucks, the Financial Times reported on the 21st. Zhu added that the battery, designed for the American pickup segment, has already been tested by U.S. automakers. CATL and many other Chinese electric vehicle and battery companies have sought access to the U.S. market for years, but steep tariffs, localization requirements and security rules have effectively blocked formal entry. The U.S. Defense Department last year designated CATL as a company suspected of ties to the Chinese military. The U.S. electric vehicle market itself is retreating sharply after the expiration of tax credits and the Trump administration's rollback of vehicle emissions rules. Despite those barriers, CATL said it could license its technology so that U.S. companies can manufacture locally. That approach is expected to resemble the arrangement CATL struck with Ford and other U.S. automakers. Ford has expanded its partnership with CATL for its energy storage business. Chinese Automakers See Opening Ahead of Summit The announcement drew attention because it came just days before the U.S.-China summit. Hong Kong's South China Morning Post earlier reported, citing sources, that CATL, BYD and Xiaomi may be included in the economic delegation accompanying Chinese President Xi Jinping to the United States. With battery maker CATL under consideration alongside BYD and Xiaomi, which has moved into electric vehicles, the trip is being watched for what it could mean for Chinese EV and battery operations in the U.S. The stakes grew after President Donald Trump recently said it would be "OK" for China to build auto plants in the United States as long as they employ American workers. U.S. automakers have sent a letter to Trump arguing that Chinese vehicle manufacturers and their supply chains should continue to be kept out of the country, according to reports. China, for its part, is keenly interested in gaining access to the U.S. market, because overcapacity remains unresolved even as global battery demand surges. Lithium-ion battery output topped 1,240 gigawatt-hours in the first half of this year, up 44% from a year earlier, according to China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology. Production of key battery materials — cathodes, anodes, separators and electrolytes — each rose more than 50%. Output is set to expand further. More than 100 battery plants cleared approval procedures through July this year, according to the China Industrial Association of Power Sources. Those facilities can produce a combined 2,600 GWh of batteries a year, 48% more than China's 1,755 GWh of battery output last year. Chinese battery makers have been pushing aggressively into Europe and other markets, but that is not enough to absorb the snowballing volume. Chinese authorities have conducted a full survey of battery production capacity and utilization rates, and since May have suspended new approvals for plants making batteries for energy storage systems. China held 70.4% of the global market for electric vehicle batteries last year, a dominant lead. Chinese experts expect that share to come in at 68% to 72% this year before declining, with forecasts of 60% to 68% by 2030.

artigo.texto: CATL has officially begun trial production at its newly built battery cell factory in Debrecen, Hungary, marking a major milestone for the company’s European manufacturing expansion. The trial run started on September 22, 2026, after CATL completed all the required conditions and obtained the necessary permits to begin operations. The initial trial production covers the first two cell manufacturing lines at the facility. The purpose of the trial phase is to set up, optimize and validate the factory’s production equipment and manufacturing processes before series production begins. CATL said it will continue working closely with the Hungarian government and local authorities throughout the trial period, with particular attention to environmental protection, employee health and workplace safety. CATL announced plans for its second European battery plant in Debrecen in August 2022. The facility was designed to strengthen the company’s position in Europe’s automotive and electric mobility supply chain while allowing it to better serve major European automakers. Construction of the first cell manufacturing building began in summer 2023. By spring 2026, the building had been equipped with what CATL describes as advanced manufacturing technology. The company received the facility’s occupancy permit in August 2026 and subsequently completed the remaining requirements associated with its Integrated Pollution Prevention and Control (IPPC) permit. Those steps cleared the way for trial operations to begin on September 22. Before the occupancy permit was issued, the Hajdú-Bihar County Government Office carried out regular inspections at CATL’s facilities. The inspections followed earlier concerns raised during the permitting process. According to the authorities, CATL had addressed the deficiencies previously identified. Once fully operational, the Debrecen facility is expected to become CATL’s largest manufacturing site outside China, with planned annual battery cell production capacity of 100 GWh. The factory is strategically located within Hungary’s growing automotive manufacturing network. Several major automakers have established significant electric vehicle production capacity in the country, creating increasing demand for locally produced batteries. CATL says the Debrecen plant uses flexible production lines designed to accommodate the requirements of its automotive customers. The company has already been producing battery modules at the Debrecen site since autumn 2024. CATL says the facility has produced approximately 537,000 battery modules to date. The transition to cell production represents the next major stage in the development of the Hungarian factory and could further integrate CATL into Europe’s rapidly expanding EV battery supply chain. CATL says environmental protection, employee health and workplace safety will remain key priorities during the trial production phase. The company plans to closely monitor health, safety and environmental factors throughout the initial operations and proactively submit the results to the relevant authorities. CATL also said it remains committed to transparency and welcomes inspections by government and regulatory authorities at the Debrecen site. The start of trial production represents an important step toward full-scale battery cell manufacturing in Hungary. For CATL, the Debrecen facility is intended to strengthen its European production footprint, while for Hungary it further expands the country’s role in the continent’s electric vehicle and battery manufacturing ecosystem. [source: CATL]

artigo.texto: Publicidade NOVA YORK — A reação negativa aos data centers, que vem influenciando debates eleitorais e discussões em todo os Estados Unidos, agora também começa a chegar a Wall Street. Empresas que operam data centers ou fornecem energia e terrenos para sua construção eram vistas como grandes candidatas a liderar o mercado de ofertas públicas iniciais (IPOs) nos próximos meses, impulsionadas pelo apetite aparentemente insaciável dos investidores por tudo o que estivesse relacionado à inteligência artificial. Mas parte do mercado passou a demonstrar crescente ceticismo em relação às expectativas de crescimento do setor e aos riscos associados à expansão desses empreendimentos. O movimento tem levado executivos e banqueiros a recalibrar planos para captar dezenas de bilhões de dólares nos mercados públicos. Continua depois da publicidade A SB Energy, subsidiária do conglomerado japonês SoftBank, que pretende construir em Ohio o maior projeto de data center do mundo, planejava realizar seu IPO ainda neste mês. No entanto, a oferta foi adiada após investidores questionarem a avaliação pretendida pela companhia, superior a US$ 50 bilhões, segundo quatro pessoas familiarizadas com a operação. Até o momento, os bancos coordenadores têm encontrado dificuldades para atrair compradores suficientes dentro da faixa de preço desejada pela empresa. Meta: novo agente de IA Muse recebe ótimas avaliações e ações saltam mais de 11% Na segunda-feira, o Muse era o aplicativo gratuito número 1 nas lojas de aplicativos da Apple Inc. (iOS) e do Google Play nos EUA O que escolher em uma bolsa “amassada” antes das eleições? Veja apostas do mercado Especialistas alertam para exterior mais desafiador, mas com oportunidades diante das eleições e de Selic em queda; Ibovespa “tem muita gordura para subir”, diz gestor As dificuldades da SB Energy surgem em meio a outro revés para o setor. Na semana passada, a Holtec, empresa da indústria nuclear que pretende fornecer energia para aplicações de IA, anunciou a suspensão por tempo indeterminado de seu IPO, citando fatores que “comprometeram a confiança dos investidores no mercado de novas ofertas públicas”. Continua depois da publicidade A companhia apontou a “incerteza em torno do desenvolvimento de data centers” como o principal motivo para o adiamento. A Holtec Nuclear opera uma usina nuclear e desenvolve pequenos reatores que podem ser utilizados para abastecer data centers. A empresa pretendia estrear na Nasdaq na semana passada e buscava levantar até US$ 900 milhões, em uma avaliação de até US$ 10 bilhões. Outra empresa que desacelerou os preparativos para abrir capital é a geradora de energia Aggreko, segundo três fontes a par do assunto. A companhia atende data centers de IA, além de eventos ao vivo e projetos de mineração, mas vinha destacando os clientes do setor tecnológico como responsáveis por um salto expressivo em sua receita ao longo do último ano. Continua depois da publicidade Embora o IPO ainda possa ocorrer no próximo mês, a empresa reduziu o ritmo do processo não apenas pelas incertezas envolvendo data centers, mas também pela alta dos juros e pelo ambiente econômico mais desafiador. Os adiamentos representam um raro contratempo para a indústria de IA, que nos últimos anos desfrutou de entusiasmo quase irrestrito dos investidores. A oposição pública aos data centers vem crescendo há meses. Comunidades em várias regiões dos Estados Unidos, especialmente em áreas rurais, têm contestado a expansão dessas instalações, conhecidas pelo alto consumo de energia e pela grande ocupação territorial. Continua depois da publicidade À medida que o país se aproxima das eleições legislativas de meio de mandato, os data centers se transformaram em um tema incomum de convergência política, enfrentando resistência de eleitores dos dois principais partidos. Para muitos americanos, eles passaram a simbolizar preocupações sobre uma economia cada vez mais dominada pela inteligência artificial. Na última semana, os receios em relação à IA ganharam ainda mais força após executivos do setor alertarem para potenciais riscos da tecnologia e sugerirem uma desaceleração no ritmo de desenvolvimento dos sistemas mais avançados. Alguns estados americanos também começaram a adotar medidas para restringir novos projetos de data centers, criando obstáculos adicionais para empresas que buscam recursos junto ao mercado de capitais. Apesar da cautela recente dos investidores, a demanda por capacidade computacional continua enorme. Alguns banqueiros avaliam que o momento representa apenas um soluço temporário. Gestoras como a PIMCO estimam que serão necessários mais de US$ 5 trilhões em investimentos até 2030 para construir toda a infraestrutura exigida pelo boom da inteligência artificial. Além disso, uma das ofertas públicas mais aguardadas do ano, a da Anthropic, que depende fortemente de capacidade de processamento em data centers, continua prevista para ocorrer ainda neste semestre. Atualmente, existem apenas duas empresas listadas em Bolsa com foco exclusivo em data centers: Equinix e Digital Realty Trust. As ações de ambas acumulam queda entre 1% e 2% neste mês. Segundo entrevistas com banqueiros, advogados e investidores, as empresas ligadas ao setor de data centers eram apontadas como responsáveis por cerca de um terço dos IPOs previstos para o restante de 2026. Enquanto isso, gigantes da tecnologia como Meta, Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft e Oracle já se comprometeram a investir mais de US$ 1 trilhão em projetos próprios de infraestrutura. Para muitos investidores, os desenvolvedores de data centers inevitavelmente precisarão recorrer ao mercado acionário para financiar essa expansão. “O tamanho do que essas empresas estão tentando construir é simplesmente gigantesco. Por isso, elas precisam acessar todas as principais fontes de capital disponíveis”, afirmou Tomasz Tunguz, sócio da gestora Theory Ventures e investidor do setor. c.2026 The New York Times Company

artigo.texto: A carbon-credit land rush is hollowing out New Zealand farm country Pongaroa, Sept 21 - At the start of lambing season, Fiona Ramsden's farm near the New Zealand village of Pongaroa is a picture of rural life: newborn lambs trailing their mothers across steep pasture, fields dotted with spiky native palm trees, and a pretty white homestead that dates back about a century. But pine trees are closing in. On neighboring land once grazed by sheep and cattle, young Monterey pines — also known as radiata pines — carpet the hills, planted to earn carbon credits under the country’s emissions trading scheme. "You're connected to the land and that's why it's quite depressing to see good farmland — and to sheep and beef, good country — going into pine trees," Ramsden said. For almost 20 years, New Zealand has pioneered one of the world’s most ambitious tree-planting programs, approving nearly 9,000 square kilometers of carbon-credit forest. That’s about 11 times the land area of New York City. The emissions trading scheme (ETS) has turned forestry into a potentially more lucrative long-term investment than livestock farming, the traditional mainstay of the rural economy. Under the ETS, owners of forests established after 1989 can earn carbon credits for greenhouse gases as their trees grow. Forest owners — companies, indigenous tribal organizations and family farmers with a small slice of land in trees — can sell those carbon credits to companies that need them to offset emissions, creating an income stream long before the forest is harvested. Yet the boom in carbon forestry — and tradable carbon credits — has also driven competition for sheep and beef farming land. The rapid expansion of forest land in traditional beef and sheep country is straining rural communities and prompting the government’s climate advisers to warn that New Zealand is avoiding harder cuts elsewhere in the economy and risks missing its emissions targets. The government counters that forestry remains only one part of its emissions-reduction strategy. Ramsden, 50, returned to take over the family farm in 2012 after a career in fashion and interior design in the capital, Wellington, and elsewhere. From her 1,215-hectare property, the tradeoffs of carbon farming feel personal. Pine forests surround her from all sides, barring one block of land. Bright yellow gorse bushes — an invasive plant in New Zealand — tumble toward the fences. Feral goats dart from the forest and onto pasture intended for her 3,500 sheep and 350 cows. Wild pigs tear up patches of ground, problems she says have grown as forest owners do little to control the population. She pointed out a power pole leaning into the pines, noting that she is experiencing more frequent power cuts as trees encroach on powerlines. WHY TREES BEAT SHEEP Just over half of New Zealand's greenhouse gas emissions come from agriculture, mainly methane and nitrous oxide. Agricultural emissions are excluded from the ETS, which primarily targets carbon dioxide and emissions from heavy industry. Farmers say that, even so, the ETS has transformed rural land markets. Forestry investors, buoyed by carbon-credit revenue, have been able to outbid sheep and beef producers for grazing land, raising concerns from farm industry groups about the future of traditional beef and sheep farming. Since 2017, about 3,300 square kilometers of sheep and beef farmland have been sold for conversion to forestry, according to industry group Beef + Lamb New Zealand. That's enough land to feed more than 2 million sheep, equivalent to nearly 9% of the country's flock. As forestry investors chased carbon credits, grazing land prices rose 9.7%, according to Real Estate Institute of New Zealand data. Dairy land, because it’s generally more expensive, has largely escaped forestry conversion and seen price rises of just 3.7%. Foreign investors have acquired more than 1,000 square kilometers of farmland for conversion to forestry since 2017, according to data from the government’s Overseas Investment Office. Ingka Investments, the investment arm of the company that operates most IKEA stores worldwide, owns 430 square kilometers of forest in New Zealand, some of which is in the ETS. Ingka says its rationale is long-term timber, not carbon-credit income. "The heart of our core investment is more in the timber," said Dylan Foster, forestland operations manager at Ingka Investments. CHEAP CREDITS, HARDER EMISSIONS CUTS Supporters of the ETS say forestry is essential to reaching New Zealand’s climate targets. Climate Change Minister Simon Watts called it a “cost-effective way” to reduce net emissions, because of the country’s established forestry sector and favorable growing conditions. The Climate Change Commission, an independent advisory body, expects ETS forests to deliver a quarter of the emissions reductions needed for New Zealand's 2026-2030 target, and nearly half of those needed for its 2031-2035 target. But critics say the scheme relies too heavily on offsets, rather than direct emissions cuts. Because planting and maintaining forests is relatively cheap, they say polluters can buy credits rather than make the costlier investments required to transition to cleaner fuels or technology. Climate Change Commission chief executive Jo Hendy said the ETS is essentially “functioning as an offsetting scheme.” The government says New Zealand is on track to meet its near-term climate goals. "Forestry is not the whole plan," Watts said in response to emailed questions from Reuters. Late last year, the government tightened the ETS rules for non-native species, including pine, on more productive land. Preliminary data released by Beef + Lamb New Zealand last month showed purchases for wholesale conversions had slowed to nearly 160 square kilometers, less than half of the total the year before. However, the industry group said the total could rise once data is finalized. FEWER ANIMALS, FEWER JOBS, THINNER COMMUNITIES For farmer D

artigo.texto: Positivo dobra negócios de servidores e vê espaço para expansão com ReData Unidade registra alta de 107% no segundo trimestre e amplia produção em 38%, puxada por demanda de nuvem híbrida e IA. A Positivo Servers & Solutions, unidade da Positivo Tecnologia voltada à infraestrutura computacional, registrou crescimento de 107% nos negócios de servidores no segundo trimestre de 2026, na comparação com o mesmo período do ano passado. No mesmo intervalo, a produção de servidores aumentou 38%. A empresa atribui o avanço à maior demanda de clientes corporativos por nuvem híbrida, processamento de dados e infraestrutura para aplicações de IA. O crescimento ocorreu antes da implementação do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center, o ReData, e antecede os efeitos que a companhia espera do novo regime sobre projetos de infraestrutura digital. Empresa espera efeito do ReData sobre novos projetos Na avaliação da Positivo, o ReData pode favorecer novos investimentos em data centers e ampliar a demanda por capacidade de processamento no País. O regime prevê incentivos tributários para projetos de data centers, mas sua implementação ainda depende de regulamentação e de definições complementares. Por isso, os impactos sobre produção local, contratação de equipamentos e novos projetos ainda não podem ser medidos. Silvio Ferraz de Campos, CEO da Positivo Servers & Solutions, relaciona a expansão da demanda ao aumento das necessidades de processamento, armazenamento e eficiência energética em empresas que ampliam o uso de aplicações de inteligência artificial. Produção local acompanha aumento da demanda A Positivo Servers & Solutions fabrica servidores no Brasil e mantém parceria com a Supermicro, da qual é concessionária exclusiva no País. A produção local de soluções da fabricante ocorre desde 2008. A unidade atua com servidores, sistemas de armazenamento e equipamentos de computação de alto desempenho destinados a data centers, ambientes de nuvem e aplicações corporativas. A companhia também oferece soluções on-premises de inteligência artificial no modelo Hardware as a Service, com infraestrutura instalada no ambiente do cliente. Com a alta de 107% nos negócios e de 38% na produção no segundo trimestre, a unidade entra na fase de implementação do ReData já operando em um mercado aquecido por demanda de nuvem híbrida, processamento de dados e aplicações de IA.

artigo.texto: Lower Chichester Township commissioners assured residents Monday night that their voices will be heard as concern about a possible data center ripples through the community. At the monthly board meeting, officials spoke to residents about a proposed 443,000-square-foot project along Ridge Road, mostly in Trainer but with a potion in Lower Chichester. The property being marketed by Link Logistics is in the area of the Congoleum facility. On Sept. 12, Leonard B. Altieri, the attorney for the property, posted a legal notice in the Daily Times stating the developer had been given a favorable preliminary opinion for a data center in the Trainer portion of the development. Lower Chichester has issued a zoning decision that a data center is not a permitted use in the township Limited Industrial District because the township does not yet have enough information about the project. A July letter from the township zoning officer to Altieri reads that a preliminary opinion on the project at 4401 Ridge Road could not be given because “data center” is not a permitted use in the Limited Industrial District. Developers of the proposed facility are promising to engage with the community as the company explores options. Trainer officials have not publicly discussed any plans. On Friday, borough Zoning Officer Charles Remaley said “no comment” when asked about the proposed facility. The developer, Link Logistics, has not applied for a building permit in either municipality but was happy with Trainer’s preliminary opinion. “We are pleased to have received a favorable Preliminary Opinion from Trainer Borough,” a spokesperson for Link Logistics wrote Monday afternoon. “This is not a building permit; any project, should we decide to pursue, will require an application and Borough approvals.” “We regularly evaluate opportunities to enhance the property in ways that support the region’s industrial and economic growth. We appreciate the feedback we are hearing from the community, and if plans for the property move forward, transparent community engagement will be an essential part of the planning process, including engaging residents and stakeholders throughout the Borough’s full review process.” At Monday night’s meeting, residents complained of a lack of information from Trainer, with Lower Chichester officials advising them to go to that municipality to ask for the zoning report. Officials said that typically after a public announcement of a decision there is a 30-day period to appeal the decision. “We don’t have any more information than they do,” said Francis J. Catania, township solicitor. “We have no separate line of communication with Trainer borough, no plan, no conversation, no document, nothing. We don’t know, even though the property is partially in Lower Chichester Township,” he said. “Believe me we are going to be involved if this goes forward. Part of it is in Lower Chichester Township, maybe only 10 percent … and the residents who are most affected by this are all from Lower Chichester. We’ll make sure their voices are heard.” Residents also had questions about the state’s part in data centers, with Amazon investment in two data centers, one in Salem Township in northeastern Pennsylvania, and the other in Falls Township, Bucks County, along with Gov. Josh Shapiro’s executive order setting out tougher statewide requirements for data center development, called the GRID regulations. Activists are planning a public meeting to discuss the possible data center. On Wednesday night, Chester Residents Concerned for Quality Living (CRCQL), an environmental activist group, will hold a public meeting from 6 to 9 p.m. at 1405 Meetinghouse Road in Boothwyn to discuss the project and potential impacts to the community, and what residents can do. Physicians for Social Responsibility, Pennsylvania will also be speaking at the public meeting. Shapiro’s Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development, GRID, standards set out these conditions: • Requiring developers to bear the cost of all new energy infrastructure that would not have been needed “but for” the data center project. • Commitment to sourcing nearly one-third of power consumption from — or at least making equivalent investments in — “clean” energy by 2035. • New transparency standards that require identification of a project’s end user, plus key information about energy and water usage and overall project scale, plus “engagement with local residents and leaders… early enough in the process to allow meaningful public input on major design decisions.” • Community Benefit Agreements for data center host communities that go above and beyond tax revenues • Commitments to meeting certain job creation and salary benchmarks.

artigo.texto: Sustainable investment manager Mirova has committed €65m to launch its Nordic Storage Platform (NSP) alongside developer Ingrid Capacity, targeting utility-scale battery energy storage systems (BESS) across the Nordic region. The Natixis Investment Managers affiliate is investing in a two-project portfolio in Finland and Sweden totaling 145MW of power capacity and 290MWh of storage capacity. Under the partnership, Ingrid Capacity will manage development, construction, technical operations and commerclial optimisation across the platform. Antoine Blayau, investment director at Mirova, said: “Battery storage is becoming a critical component of Europe’s energy infrastructure, enhancing grid flexibility, supporting renewable integration and strengthening security of supply. “This initial portfolio is underpinned by attractive market fundamentals and a resilient risk-return profile, including an offtake agreement for the Pedersöre project. We look forward to scaling the platform and supporting the development of more resilient energy systems across the Nordic region.” Axel Holmberg, CEO of Ingrid Capacity, said: “We are pleased to be Mirova’s first BESS partner in the Nordics. Strong partnerships are essential when creating value for the long term and our two institutions share the same sense of responsibility in doing so. “Both companies understand the critical role for BESS in building a better grid and European resilience. Our mission is to build Europe’s leading integrated flexibility platform. Trusted partners like French Mirova are key to that growth journey.” To read the latest IPE Real Assets magazine click here.

artigo.texto: While local governments are increasingly strapped for cash under Senate Enrolled Act 1, the city of Hobart is swimming in funds as a result of an Amazon data center project still under construction. Speaking to the Post-Tribune this week, Mayor Josh Huddlestun detailed Hobart’s financial windfall and how the “economic impact payments” are being doled out for the benefit of the local community while beefing up city coffers. The city initially received $47 million, with another $10 million arriving last week, according to Huddleston. He expects another $45 million in-hand by the end of 2026, with a $43 million payment scheduled to arrived in 2027. Under the agreement, the city will receive approximately $40 million in both 2028 and 2029 and approximately $52 million in 2030 when the 723-acre project is expected to be completed. The payments from Amazon effectively double the city’s general fund budget year over year, according to Huddlestun. He said that Hobart will receive approximately $52 million per year over the next 35 years. He explained that the city negotiated a plan for direct payments, thus granting Amazon a 35-year tax abatement on personal property (equipment on site) and a 10-year abatement on real property (buildings). Huddlestun sees direct payments from Amazon as a better long term deal for the city, explaining that tax assessments and the resulting proceeds can vary over time. He noted that there is no tax abatement on land, describing a “negligible” assessment. Because the development falls within a Tax Increment Financing (TIF) district, any tax proceeds would have been delegated to improvements within that legally defined area, though Indiana has widened the scope of acceptable TIF uses to include public safety. The data center encompasses a 555-acre parcel located south of 61st Avenue, east of Colorado Street and north of 69th Avenue, known as Hobart Tech Park, which is owned by Amazon Web Services. The other parcel, described as the Ewen Farm property, encompasses 168 acres and is located southeast of 61st and Arizona Street. The data center facility will have 26 buildings spread out across the two sites, with six at the 61st Avenue location and 20 at the Colorado Street location. Spending has already started Hobart homeowners are already realizing the benefits from Amazon’s payments to the city through a new program establishing $10,000 50/50 matching grants for residential exterior home improvements. Another 50/50 matching grant program provides homeowners with $5,000 for energy improvements, such as the purchase of more efficient furnaces and central air conditioning units. The Hobart City Council will appropriate the funds, including $16 million earmarked for improvements to Festival Park. Huddlestun said the city is making funding available to struggling nonprofit groups and has established a $500,000 revolving loan fund to support improvements for downtown businesses. Hobart’s general fund will enable long overdue infrastructure projects involving road repairs, mitigating drainage issues and replacing sidewalks, and the city is shopping for a new fire truck and two ambulances. Huddlestun termed the influx of funding as “generational” wealth, but cautioned that the city will be measured with how the money is spent. “We want to make sure is that this is beneficial to our city and are trying to touch as many of the community members as we can,” he said. “I think this puts us in position to really soar in the next chapter of Hobart’s life, be able to give back to the community and deliver on good projects while being very selective on about the developments that come into our city. Hobart’s future is drastically positive.” Hurdles still exist Continued public opposition to the project aside, one remaining critical issue involves an air permit application, which the Ramboll Engineering firm filed with Indiana Department of Environmental Management on Amazon’s behalf on July 24. According to the permit application, the facility would host 808 fuel storage tanks, storing more than 5.46 million gallons of diesel fuel. At the 61st Avenue location, Amazon plans to build 170 emergency backup diesel generators, while 612 emergency backup generators will be installed at the Colorado Street facility. the total power capacity combined for both sites is 2,119 megawatts. On September 4, the Hobart Plan Commission tabled action until October on final plat approval of the development, requesting that Amazon make minor revisions to requested site improvements. According to Hobart City Engineer Alex Metz, the revisions include recording a legal description for a dedicated of a right-of-way involving a new pedestrian walkway around of the perimeter of the development, primarily along 61st Avenue and connecting to the local neighborhood. Jim Masters is a freelance reporter for the Post-Tribune.

artigo.texto: Designing Layered Drone Defenses for Data Centers Drone threats to data centers are rising and real. Operators should adopt layered defenses – physical hardening, detection systems, redundancy, and regulatory coordination – to build resilience. Drone activity around critical infrastructure is rising, and data centers are not immune. Until recently, few operators considered drones a serious risk. That’s changing fast. The threat is no longer theoretical. In spring 2026, drone strikes disrupted operations at AWS facilities in the Persian Gulf. While that incident occurred months ago, it continues to underscore an evolving risk landscape for operators. How should the industry respond? The most effective response favors resilience, lawful defensive measures, and operational readiness over attempts at interdiction. Why Drone Risks Are Increasing for Data Centers Consumer-grade drones are inexpensive, widely available, and increasingly capable. Their accessibility means more devices in the sky near more facilities on the ground, elevating both intentional and accidental risks. Even small drones can damage exposed mechanical systems or interfere with critical cooling and power infrastructure. While military-grade platforms pose the highest risk in conflict zones, non-state actors and lone individuals could still cause localized disruption. Layered Physical and Detection Controls A layered defense blends practical hardening with multi-sensor detection and clear operational workflows. 1. Physical Drone Defenses Physical hardening should prioritize airflow-safe protection and impact mitigation: - Install protective cages or netting on roofs or around critical components to create a physical buffer against drones. - Deploy radar or other detection systems that trigger physical protection measures. - Where feasible, relocate vulnerable components, such as cooling towers, from prominent rooftops to ground-level areas behind barriers and fencing. - Apply materials for thermal and infrared signature management to help reduce long-range target identification. Any such treatments must remain compliant with building codes and equipment performance requirements. 2. Redundancy and Resilience Planning Even the best defenses can’t guarantee prevention. Treat drones like any other external disruption and design to limit the blast radius. - Intra-site redundancy. Within a site, build multiple cooling and power subsystems so the facility can continue running if one is damaged. - Inter-site failover. Across sites, maintain tested failover runbooks to quickly and safely shift workloads or traffic to other data centers. - Recovery procedures. Include maintaining and regularly rehearsing incident response and disaster recovery plans that specifically account for drone-related disruptions. 3. Location Strategy and Regulatory Environment Site selection should now explicitly consider drone risks alongside traditional criteria. - Conflict-prone regions. Areas vulnerable to military activity carry elevated risks of military-grade threats and may warrant additional protective measures. - Local sentiment and governance. Jurisdictions with strong support for critical infrastructure protections and effective law enforcement coordination can reduce non-military threats. - Regulatory maturity. Regulatory maturity is increasingly important: consider the availability of U-space/UTM services, prevalence of Remote ID compliance, and responsiveness of aviation and public safety agencies. - Terrain and concealment. Hilly, vegetated sites can limit sightlines and complicate the low-altitude approach path, while still preserving necessary detection coverage. Reduce nearby public vantage points and easy launch locations that have clear sightlines to exposed plant, and ensure property boundaries discourage unauthorized drone operations. Airspace Restrictions and Community Coordination Only national aviation authorities can establish enforceable airspace restrictions. Rather than seeking informal “no-fly zones,” operators should collaborate with authorities to raise awareness of critical infrastructure and improve response coordination. Publish site advisories, update perimeter signage, and engage with drone service providers and UTM platforms to increase geofencing awareness around sensitive areas. Build local relationships so that law enforcement and emergency management teams understand the facility’s risk profile. Conclusion Drones introduce low-cost, high-disruption risks that data center operators must plan for as part of business-as-usual resilience. The strongest posture is layered: harden exposed infrastructure, deploy multi-sensor detection, formalize detection-to-response operations, and design for redundancy and failover. Combine these measures with location awareness and regulatory coordination. The industry has clear evidence that drone disruptions are not hypothetical. By focusing on resilience, operators can reduce both the likelihood and impact of drone-related incidents.

Limited (CATL) World's largest battery maker System integrator Fluence and lithium-ion battery manufacturer Eve Energy have agreed a 206GWh battery supply framework spanning 2027 to 2031, a deal the companies describe as among the largest of its kind. According to Energy-Storage.news, the arrangement commits 16GWh of capacity in 2027, with the remaining 190GWh reserved for the 2028 to 2031 period, as disclosed by Eve Energy in a filing on the Shenzhen stock exchange on 18 September. The China-based battery maker indicated it could not yet estimate the financial benefit the agreement would deliver, though its share price rose sharply by 6 to 7 percent when the announcement was made. Eve Energy also noted that the framework remains subject to change, including through industry policies or market conditions that could prevent the cooperation from proceeding as anticipated. The disclosure came a few days after Fluence lowered its fiscal year 2026 guidance, cutting forecast revenues by US$600 million and widening its expected EBITDA loss from US$10 million to approximately US$200 million. The company mainly attributed the revision to delays in its US manufacturing ramp-up. Fluence has treated its US manufacturing ecosystem as central to delivering US battery energy storage projects, following several years of increased tariffs on Chinese batteries and new Foreign Entity of Concern rules under which projects using Chinese battery technology cannot access clean energy tax credits. The company has positioned itself as an early mover in securing a fully FEOC-compliant battery and storage supply chain. Fluence has not communicated anything to the market about the Eve Energy deal, so nothing is certain, but the agreement would therefore presumably cover projects outside the US. While the company has increasingly focused on the US, it retains substantial business elsewhere, including two projects totalling 1.1GW/4.4GWh on which it recently began construction for power firm LEAG in Germany. Eve Energy mainly manufactures in China, and its only non-China facilities to date serve the electric vehicle market. The firm is one of the more recent entrants to the battery energy storage space, but it has aggressively moved into the top three battery energy storage cell suppliers in the past few years, according to Benchmark Mineral Intelligence.
