artigo.texto: Manaus, 21 de setembro de 2026 – O Amazonas entrou no radar da expansão dos grandes data centers, com planos tanto do senador e candidato ao governo Omar Aziz (PSD) quanto pelo atual, Roberto Cidade (União Brasil). Enquanto o plano de governo de Aziz prevê a criação de um polo de data centers de grande escala e um centro estadual para armazenar dados considerados críticos, Cidade já vem defendendo, junto ao governo federal, regras específicas para essas instalações. Embora sejam associados a serviços digitais e atividades econômicas de baixo impacto aparente, data centers são grandes infraestruturas físicas e consumidoras intensivas de recursos naturais. Para funcionar continuamente, precisam de enormes quantidades de eletricidade, sistemas permanentes de refrigeração, água em determinadas tecnologias, equipamentos de segurança e redes de transmissão de dados, além de estruturas redundantes para evitar interrupções. As duas frentes aparecem em documentos de 2025 e 2026 analisados pelo Vocativo, em meio à expansão nacional do setor e à criação de incentivos fiscais federais para novos centros de processamento de dados. Em setembro de 2026, o Senado aprovou o projeto que institui o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), com suspensão de tributos federais sobre equipamentos e exigências de sustentabilidade, eficiência hídrica e fornecimento de energia. A proposta de Aziz está registrada no Plano Estratégico de Desenvolvimento do Estado do Amazonas 2027–2037, no programa “Amazonas Digital e Inovador 2027–2037”, elaborado em 2026 e entregue à Justiça Eleitoral como parte do conjunto de propostas do candidato. O documento estima R$ 6,8 bilhões em investimentos e prevê, entre outras medidas, a articulação para instalação de estruturas de processamento de dados de hiperescala, além de um Data Center Estadual Soberano Tier III. No caso de Cidade, a articulação ocorre a partir da máquina pública. O governo estadual passou a defender a posição do Amazonas na regulamentação do Redata e, em documento encaminhado à Presidência da República em setembro, sustentou que o Estado não deveria ser impedido de utilizar gás natural na geração de energia para data centers, desde que os projetos atendam aos critérios ambientais e de eficiência estabelecidos pelo governo federal. A defesa ocorre enquanto o Estado busca se apresentar como território apto a receber empreendimentos de elevado consumo elétrico. O plano de Omar e a estrutura que o Estado pretende construir No Eixo 7 do programa Amazonas Digital e Inovador, o plano de Aziz estabelece como meta a articulação política e institucional para atrair estruturas de processamento de dados de hiperescala. São instalações muito maiores que os data centers convencionais, voltadas ao processamento e armazenamento de grandes volumes de informações, inclusive para aplicações de computação em nuvem e inteligência artificial. O documento apresenta como vantagens competitivas do Amazonas a disponibilidade de energia, a posição geográfica e o clima. O cronograma coloca a consolidação desse polo na Fase 3, chamada de Maturidade e Inovação, prevista para 2033 a 2037. A proposta, portanto, envolve não apenas infraestrutura pública, mas a criação das condições para atrair empreendimentos privados de grande porte. No Eixo 9, o mesmo plano prevê a construção de um Data Center Estadual Soberano Tier III, destinado à hospedagem de informações consideradas críticas pelo governo. Entre os dados citados estão registros das áreas de saúde, segurança pública, educação e assistência social, acompanhados por um Centro de Operações de Segurança (SOC) para monitoramento permanente dos sistemas. A execução técnica e operacional é atribuída à PRODAM — Processamento de Dados Amazonas S.A.. Para financiar o programa, o documento menciona recursos ordinários do Estado, programas federais, incluindo Norte Conectado e SUS Digital, financiamentos de organismos multilaterais, como Banco Interamericano de Desenvolvimento (BID), Banco Mundial e CAF, além de possíveis parcerias público-privadas (PPPs). Durante a administração de Wilson Lima (União Brasil), o Estado já havia criado mecanismos de incentivo para atividades relacionadas à infraestrutura de data centers. O Decreto nº 45.942/2022, por exemplo, concedeu incentivo fiscal para a fabricação de “Contêineres Metálicos (Data Center)”, enquanto deliberações posteriores do CODAM mantiveram a atividade dentro da política estadual de incentivos. Em dezembro de 2025, na 317ª Reunião Ordinária do CODAM, documentos estaduais passaram a registrar de forma ainda mais explícita o interesse estratégico em data centers. Um decreto publicado em janeiro de 2026 menciona o Amazonas como “polo potencial para a instalação de Data Centers soberanos e sustentáveis”, relacionando essa possibilidade à disponibilidade de energia firme. O ato foi assinado por Wilson Lima, então governador. A transição de governo ocorreu meses depois. Wilson Lima e o vice Tadeu de Souza renunciaram em abril de 2026 para disputar outros cargos, e Roberto Cidade assumiu interinamente o Executivo. Em 4 de maio, a Assembleia Legislativa o elegeu governador em eleição indireta, com Serafim Corrêa como vice, para o mandato-tampão. Cidade leva o gás natural para dentro da disputa pelo Redata A atuação de Roberto Cidade acrescentou uma dimensão energética à política de atração de data centers. Em setembro de 2026, o governador encaminhou à Presidência da República o Ofício nº 429/2026-GE, no qual defende que a regulamentação do Redata preserve a possibilidade de utilização do gás natural por empreendimentos instalados no Amazonas. artigo.texto: The nationwide backlash against the AI buildout promises to play a decisive role in a handful of Senate races this year, and could in turn determine who will control Congress for the second half of Donald Trump’s presidency. Evidence is mixed when it comes to which party voters trust on the issue, though Democrats seem to be maintaining a slight advantage. Recent NBC News polling found that they held a 12-point lead when it came to “dealing with data centers”—32 percent to 20 percent—though 19 percent said both parties were “about the same” and a quarter responded that neither could be trusted. Republicans, however, had a two-point edge on the more general matter of artificial intelligence in a New York Times/Siena poll published last week—within its margin of error. But among voters, opposition to their construction has emerged as one of the only positions drawing bipartisan support this cycle. In June, 64 percent of respondents told a Reuters/Ipsos survey that they disagreed with constructing data centers at scale and pace, and the latest NBC News poll found that the same share of registered voters would be less likely to support a candidate who backs building these facilities in their community. The sleeper issue has become a potentially election-deciding matter, formerly pro-development politicians are now vocal skeptics of an unchecked development push, and campaigns for the House and Senate increasingly read like competitions for who can appear more anti-AI, with Republican strategists telling Newsweek candidates are now “fleeing” from their initial stances on the buildings given alarming levels of local opposition. “Frankly, any incumbent, Republican or Democrat, should be concerned about being tagged as pro-data center,” political strategist Pete Seat told Newsweek. “The loudest voices are being heard, and policy is being made with those voices leading the charge," he said, adding that this trend he says will continue “until the pro-development side can marshal a grassroots army of its own.” Where Data Centers Could Decide Senate Races Jaymie Scotto Cutaia, founder and CEO of the data center PR firm JSA, told Newsweek that voter concerns about grid capacity, water usage and local community impacts were “resonating with voters across party lines," which in turn "creates an incentive for candidates to adopt increasingly aggressive positions, particularly in closely contested races.” And veteran GOP strategist John Thomas said that, while not nationally a priority on the same level as immigration and the economy, data centers’ political implications appeared to correlate with the presence and scale of a local buildout. Given this, Newsweek charted the tight Senate races that are taking place in states with significant numbers of planned data centers. According to the nonpartisan Cook Political Report’s latest update, seven races are currently considered “toss ups,” with two that “lean Democrat” meaning a total of nine could be considered close. Of these, the power-infrastructure tracking website Cleanview.co shows that eight have at least one planned data center—i.e., formally proposed or documented in records but not yet operational. This includes closely watched contests like Maine, where the incumbent Republican Susan Collins is taking on the Democrat Troy Jackson, and where three data center projects are currently planned. Alongside Virginia, Texas is leading the data center development push—with over 300 data centers in the works, per Cleanview. And this has now shown signs of becoming a key attack line in the contest between Democratic State Representative James Talarico and his Republican rival, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. "Ken Paxton has taken nearly half a million linked to the data center industry,” Talarico said in a recent CBS News interview, in which he called Paxton “bought and paid for” by the industry and bragged that he himself receives no center-linked campaign donations. And in Ohio, where 155 data centers are currently planned, Senate candidate Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, recently began running ads which hail the incumbent Senator Jon Husted as the “face of data centers” Republicans ‘Fleeing’ From Data Centers Ahead of Midterms A memo first published by Axios last month revealed that Republican leadership were concerned that data centers—and the party’s apparent proximity to the industry—were becoming a burden for GOP candidates in the midterms. The memo made specific mention of the Ohio race and Brown’s AI-focused strategy. “If [Husted] loses and data centers get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice—and they will not go near the next one,” the National Republican Senatorial Committee wrote. “This has become a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle.” Experts share this sentiment, though they have expressed doubt that either party had yet secured an advantage in painting themselves as less pro-data center. “I don't think it's a partisan issue,” Douglas Heye, a senior adviser to the Iowa Republican Party, told Newsweek. He pointed to the fact that the Republican governor of Texas, Greg Abbott, has been among the most notable buildout skeptics both rhetorically and legislatively in 2026. However, Republican political consultant Mike Madrid said that examples like Texas show that Republicans are “fleeing from early support of data centers”—a pivot perhaps delayed by Trump’s overt backing of a rapid and nationwide development push. And the party itself has now tried to cast Democrats as, if not more pro-data center, at least less committed to protecting voters from the cost of these facilities. “Republicans are building the AI infrastructure America needs while ensuring companies are paying their own way, shielding families from higher utility bills, and safeguarding local water and natural resources,” Natalie Baldassarre, national press secretary for the Republican National Committee, told Newsweek. artigo.texto: ADM is entering the voluntary carbon removal market, with a project supported by its Columbus, Nebraska facility, which can capture more than 800,000 tons of CO2 per year, the company shared in a press release. The commodity company is working with Puro.earth to certify and issue carbon dioxide removal credits for its corn processing facility in Columbus, using global crediting company’s Geologically Stored Carbon methodology. These initial carbon credits will be available by the end of the year, and ADM will issue certifications for a 15-year crediting period, the company stated. This announcement is built on ADM’s previous partnership with energy infrastructure company Tallgrass in 2025, which captures biogenic CO2 from ethanol fermentation and stores it at Tallgrass’ Eastern Wyoming Sequestration Hub. This hub houses underground carbon capture and sequestration wells that are regulated through the Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality Class VI permit. “Certifying carbon removal at this scale demands real rigor, and we believe ADM has approached every stage – from measurement and data collection through to third-party audit – with the discipline and transparency that an investment-grade market requires. The audit process has run exceptionally smoothly, which is testament to the team ADM has built around this asset, and the hard work of the Puro.earth team coordinating with them. That partnership is what turns one of the world’s largest bioethanol carbon capture facilities into verified, investable carbon removal, and it sets a replicable benchmark for this sector worldwide,” Jan-Willem Bode, president of Puro.earth, said in the press release. ADM’s decarbonization efforts pay off This announcement comes less than a week since ADM released its 2025 regen ag report, with the company reporting that it has cut nearly a million metric tons of CO2 emissions through sustainable farming practices. “Our growth strategy is predicated on smart investments that build on our world-class footprint, and carbon capture is a great example of that. More broadly, we view agriculture as a powerful engine to lower carbon, and our capabilities uniquely position us to help deliver for stakeholders across value chains,” Kris Lutt, VP of innovation and growth at ADM. He added, “ADM has more than a decade of experience supporting carbon capture and geologic storage, including operating Class VI wells at our Decatur, Illinois, facility. That experience, together with Tallgrass’ CO2 transportation and sequestration system and the capabilities of other project participants, positions us to connect agricultural production with growing carbon removal markets at scale.”

artigo.texto: Com a sanção do Governo Federal, o Redata, regime especial de tributação que prevê incentivos fiscais para o setor de Data Centers, passa a criar condições mais competitivas para a instalação e expansão desses empreendimentos no Brasil. A medida busca reduzir barreiras para investimentos de grande porte, ampliar a atratividade do País para investidores internacionais e acelerar a construção da infraestrutura necessária para sustentar o avanço da economia digital. Para Fernando Palamone, CEO da RT-One, desenvolvedora de uma das maiores plataformas de infraestrutura para Inteligência Artificial da América Latina e responsável pela implementação de parques tecnológicos voltados para IA, o Redata contribui para tornar o setor nacional mais competitivo para novos projetos. “Segundo o relatório aprovado no Senado, o regime pode reduzir em até 30% o investimento inicial de um empreendimento. Na prática, isso pode significar maior capacidade de atração de capital, estímulo à expansão da infraestrutura digital e melhores condições para que empresas que dependem de processamento de alta capacidade escolham o Brasil como base para suas operações”, comenta o CEO. Ao redor da infraestrutura necessária para a construção de data centers podem surgir novos negócios, parcerias com universidades, centros de pesquisa e empresas de tecnologia, destravando um ecossistema econômico formado a partir do Redata. Mas, mesmo com a nova política, Palamone acredita que ainda há desafios para o Brasil no setor. “Haverá energia disponível? Em quanto tempo? A que custo? Haverá conectividade suficiente? O licenciamento será previsível? Existirá mão de obra qualificada? Essas respostas serão determinantes para transformar interesse em investimento efetivo. O Redata deve ser entendido como ponto de partida, e não como ponto de chegada”, pontua Fernando. Outro efeito econômico relevante gerado pelo novo regime é o desenvolvimento de polos de tecnologia e infraestrutura fora dos grandes centros tradicionais, expandindo a economia digital para novas regiões. Perante a crescente demanda por IAs, a RT-One planeja a construção de dois parques tecnológicos de data centers na América Latina, um Minas Gerais e outro no Paraná. “Projetos dessa natureza movimentam fornecedores, demandam profissionais especializados, criam oportunidades de qualificação, aproximam empresas de universidades e centros de pesquisa, e podem contribuir para a atração de novos negócios”, opina Palamone. artigo.texto: By Siddarth Sivaraman Voters in 18 Ohio municipalities and townships will decide the future of data centers in their communities this Election Day. The deadline to file charter amendment petitions with Ohio’s city councils in time to make the Nov. 3 ballot passed Sept. 4. Registered voters in charter cities can file charter amendment petitions at any time, but if the next regular election is less than 60 days or more than 120 days away, a special election is held instead. Nine petitions — in Conneaut, Defiance, Granville, Oregon, Pataskala, Piqua, Sunbury, Trenton, and Upper Sandusky — mirror a statewide effort to ban data centers that draw over 25 megawatts of energy per month. Organizers with Conserve Ohio are hoping the statewide petition will make the 2027 ballot after missing a signature deadline in July. “Conserve Ohio is continuing to organize with many more communities across Ohio to enact local data center bans and to create local government structures that are by the people and for the people,” the group said in a statement Tuesday. Piqua petition organizer Alisha Lange said she became politically engaged in 2023, when a battery plant approved by the city gave her and others living nearby long-term health issues. She pleaded with politicians who represented Piqua, including U.S. Rep. Mike Carey, with little success. Now, she says those private meetings are a waste of time. After Meta announced plans for a data center in Piqua that would demand around 1,400 megawatts of power, she gathered enough signatures for a petition to recall Piqua’s mayor and two city commissioners, she said. Two more petitions filed Monday would change the city’s signature requirements for recalls to match state law and strike down a city agreement to power the data center. “When we’re out getting signatures, people come up, and they all want to share something. They’re all upset,” she said. “It’s like some fellowship … Even though the data centers are driving us apart, the petitions are bringing us together.” Ohio has the fourth-most operational data centers in the country, according to an analysis by Pew Research Center published in April, and tech giants and data center developers want to build dozens more across the state. 14 of the 18 communities with petitions filed for the November election have received formal proposals for new data center projects. A Gallup poll in May found that over 70% of Americans oppose data center construction in their area, and a Bowling Green State University poll found that a similar percentage of Ohioans support a data center moratorium. Opponents list a variety of grievances, like rising utility bills, negative effects on the environment, or concerns about artificial intelligence. Different petitions tackle the issue in different ways. While gathering signatures for the 25-megawatt petition, many Piqua residents told Lange they would rather ban data centers entirely. That became another petition, and it now has enough signatures for a special election, she said. Urbana voters will decide on a charter amendment to ban data centers that draw over 7.5 megawatts of power, and Hubbard is the only Ohio city that will vote on a full ban this November. Pleasant Township resident Jen Belt lives within two miles of a proposed data center in Grove City. She was part of a petition drive to make any new heavy industrial project in Grove City — not just data centers — subject to a citywide vote. While she signed the statewide Conserve Ohio petition, Belt said Grove City organizers decided against advocating for a local data center ban because they were worried about litigation. “If the state would just ban these hyperscale facilities in general, that would be awesome,” she said. “ … I just feel like they need to sell it to us and come here responsibly.” Two Adams County townships located on the Ohio River will vote on zoning plans meant to preserve their “rural and agricultural character” in response to a potential data center that would use more than 20 times as much power as the county itself. Two counties over, Wilmington residents proposed a 33-page zoning ordinance after Amazon Web Services announced plans for a $4 billion data center on land next to a local subdivision. Residents have filed multiple federal lawsuits over the city’s handling of the project, and four referendums on Wilmington’s November ballot would strike down zoning ordinances passed by the city. The city’s alternative zoning ordinance is the fourth ballot measure related to data centers to go in front of the Ohio Supreme Court in the last month. A referendum against a proposed data center in Ashville and a 25-megawatt data center ban in Trenton will be on the general election ballot after legal battles, and a trio of Sidney petitions related to data centers will likely become a special election after the state’s highest court ruled that the city clerk illegally blocked them. The Clinton County Board of Elections rejected Wilmington residents’ petition to put the zoning ordinance on the ballot after determining that it would create new ways for residents to sue, which would go beyond Wilmington’s municipal power. If the court rules against residents in their lawsuit challenging the board of elections’ decision, Koger Kidd said he plans to circulate new petitions without the clause. artigo.texto: Craig Thompson is co-founder of Austin, Texas-based specialty executive recruitment firm Allegiance Search, which focuses on digital infrastructure, energy and advanced manufacturing teams. Opinions are the author’s own. Power has been the defining barrier to the data center industry growth for years. But in August, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott gave the industry a very public reminder that access to power is not the only thing developers need to worry about. Abbott temporarily halted approvals for new data center projects within Texas’ grid interconnection process and ordered an audit of pending developments amid concerns over grid reliability and the extraordinary volume of proposed new electricity demand. It was reported that around 90% of the 474 GW of proposed new load requests in the state were linked to data centers. For anyone working in digital infrastructure, let alone Texas developments, this is a bit of a jaw-dropper. Texas is one of the most pro-development states in the country and expected to become one of the most important data center markets in the world. Yet the state is now effectively saying that expansion has to happen on terms that protect the existing grid and the communities already relying on it. I think that points to the next major development challenge for this industry. On top of powered land and capital, developers need public support. The residents pushing back have a point It’s easy for us to characterize community opposition as people failing to understand the economic opportunity data centers create. I think that would be a mistake. Let’s look at the development through the eyes of someone living in one of the smaller communities where these projects are often being built. They are not thinking about artificial intelligence compute demand or the long-term value of hyperscale infrastructure. They are thinking about what has changed outside their front door: construction traffic, noise pollution, open land suddenly becoming a construction site and, of course, energy costs. If residents believe a huge new user of electricity is contributing to higher costs or putting additional strain on the infrastructure they already depend on, telling them the project will ultimately be good for the local economy is not going to win them over. Abbott’s intervention is important precisely because those concerns have moved beyond local protest and into state-level infrastructure policy. Texas is now scrutinizing whether proposed data center demand is realistic and whether the grid can support it without placing an unreasonable burden on existing customers. That is a significant change in the conversation. The benefits are real, but they arrive later There is obviously the other side to this — and for the record, the side I believe really matters. Data centers bring substantial economic benefits to the communities where they are developed. The construction phase creates thousands of jobs. Once operational, the projects provide permanent employment and can generate significant local tax revenue. Over time, that money contributes to roads, public services and wider infrastructure improvements. The problem is that the costs and benefits arrive on completely different timelines. The disruption begins as soon as construction starts. The larger economic benefits might take years to materialize. That gap is where developers risk losing people. If your commute gets worse this month, your electricity costs increase and the landscape around your town changes dramatically, it is understandable that the promise of better infrastructure five or 10 years from now does not immediately feel like much of a win. Community relations as a development function This hurdle has given rise to community relations as a genuine leadership function. At scale, more developers are hiring senior people specifically to manage the relationship between projects and the communities around them. The title varies. In some businesses it sits under community relations, while elsewhere it falls closer to external affairs. The purpose is the same. These people are the link between the developer and the community. Their job is to explain what is being built, why it is being built and what the long-term benefits could be. Just as importantly, they need to understand local concerns early and make sure those concerns reach the people making decisions inside the business. That is why I think the role is moving well beyond traditional public relations. When projects create visible disruption before the benefits arrive, somebody has to own that communication. Developers need people who can engage credibly with local leaders and residents while also giving the internal team a much clearer understanding of how the project is being received — before the cardboard signs come out. As data center projects become more politically and publicly visible, community relations is moving closer to the core of how those projects are developed, and I expect that to continue. Over the next few years, I think we will see community relations professionals become a much bigger board-level priority, particularly for those building at scale across multiple markets. The companies that recognize that early will be better prepared for the next phase of data center growth.

artigo.texto: Dive Brief: - California Gov. Gavin Newsom on Monday signed seven bills aimed at giving communities more information about proposed data centers’ energy, water, workforce and land use to help weigh their economic costs and benefits. - The new laws require data centers “pay their fair share of grid update costs,” disclose water use to local governments and give up eligibility for blanket environmental exemptions, according to the governor’s office. - They come on the heels of Los Angeles County’s planning director ordering a temporary ban on development of large-scale AI data centers in unincorporated areas of California’s most populous county, according to multiple news reports. Dive Insight: California is home to 296 data centers, the third highest number in the U.S., according to Data Center Map. “Communities are left to deal with the consequences — higher electricity demand, grid constraints, water use, and pollution,” Newsom said in a statement. “With these laws, we are ensuring that Californians remain in the driver’s seat — and that those profiting from data centers aren’t doing so at our expense.” The bills Newsom signed Monday include: SB 1168: Directs the California Public Utilities Commission to examine data centers’ energy use and ensure they pay for transmission and distribution upgrades and load increases. “Californians’ utility bills are already among the highest in the nation, and the rapid growth of data centers is threatening to send rates through the roof,” state Sen. Jerry McNerney, the bill’s sponsor, said in a statement. SB 886 and SB 887: Require data centers to pay all infrastructure upgrade and generation costs, bear a larger share of wildfire mitigation and liability costs, and undergo environmental review. The bills will also ensure local communities have a say in data center projects, according to a news release from state Sen. Steve Padilla, the bills’ sponsor. “These are some of the nation’s strongest data center ratepayer protections — stopping Big Tech from sticking California families with the bill for their data centers,” Padilla said in a statement. AB 1577: Requires monthly reporting of data centers’ energy consumption and efficiency metrics to the California Energy Commission and estimated energy usage to local agencies as part of permitting. AB 2383: Incentivizes data centers to use onsite clean energy resources to help California “responsibly plan for the future of our electrical grid while keeping electricity costs down for consumers,” the bill’s sponsor, Assemblyman Rick Chavez Zbur, said in a statement. AB 2469 and AB 2619: Strengthen oversight of data center water use by requiring potential data center developers to complete a water supply assessment and develop a water scarcity plan during permitting and establishing a statewide water reporting requirement to obtain and renew business licenses. “Every drop counts,” Assemblymember Diane Papan, chair of the Assembly Water Committee and sponsor of the bills, said in a statement. “We cannot manage what we do not measure.”

artigo.texto: Why this conservative Maine town is trying to ban data centers DOVER-FOXCROFT — Dover-Foxcroft is the latest town in rural Maine that may pass a ban on building large-scale data centers as backlash against big tech sweeps the state. Developers are unlikely to build such a project in the town, which has limited infrastructure and ordinances already on the books to regulate development. But with support from a statewide environmental group, the rural community’s Select Board is on track to pass a six-month ban on large-scale data center development by the end of September. It’s another in a string of small, conservative towns backing temporary bans of data centers, a movement that sprouted up on the left but has quickly become more bipartisan. Maine has few data centers, the warehouse-like facilities that provide computing power for a variety of uses, including AI. News stories from away have Mainers concerned that such centers may crop up and use significant amounts of water and electricity, driving up utility prices. Since Gov. Janet Mills vetoed legislation that would have created a statewide moratorium on some new data center projects this spring, towns are taking up the issue themselves. Dover-Foxcroft is no exception. Select Board Chair Stephen Grammont said despite the low odds of a data center being built in town, jitters about the projects are “not a make-believe concern.” “We’re not high up on the mega data center list of places to locate,” Grammont said. “I think what’s concerned a lot of people is that there have been some surprises.” It wouldn’t be the first Maine town to be surprised by plans for a data center; officials in Jay only found out about a proposed project after the plan was well underway and reported on by the Bangor Daily News. Dover-Foxcroft’s proposed ban was pushed in part by Carole Boothroyd, chair of the town’s Climate Action Advisory Committee and wife of a Democratic candidate for state Legislature. Boothroyd sought and received advice from Maine Conservation Voters, an environmental group, as she drafted the proposed ordinance. The group worked closely with legislators during the last session to pass the statewide moratorium that Mills ultimately vetoed in the spring. As towns began weighing moratoriums this summer, the group posted on its social media accounts asking local officials to contact them if they needed advice drafting policy. “We were very, very disappointed by the governor’s veto of that bill, because we know that we need time to understand the impacts of these large-scale data centers,” Maggie Somers, the group’s outreach director, said. “That’s really when this got kicked into high gear, and I started working closely with these communities to see how we could help.” Boothroyd and Somers said Dover-Foxcroft’s proposed ban, which could be extended beyond six months, is meant to give the town cover while the state’s Data Center Advisory Council studies ways to regulate the projects, a process Maine Conservation Voters is involved in. “We’re already gearing up for this next [legislative] session and making sure that we have legislation prepared,” Somers said. Whatever bills on data centers are passed will not have to go through Mills, who is retiring. Those running to replace her, Republican Bobby Charles, Democrat Hannah Pingree and independent Rick Bennett, have all said they would sign data center moratoriums. In Dover-Foxcroft, Grammont said it isn’t just Boothroyd and the conservationists who are supportive of a local ban. “I think it’s across the board,” he said. “We want to make sure that we, the town’s people, don’t get screwed.” Daniel O’Connor is a Report for America corps member who covers rural government as part of the partnership between the Bangor Daily News and The Maine Monitor, with additional support from BDN and Monitor readers.

artigo.texto: CHESTERFIELD COUNTY, Va. — Chesterfield County residents are speaking out about how the county should spend revenue expected from three approved Google data center campuses, as the Board of Supervisors prepares to vote on a proposal that would use that money to lower the car tax. The local NAACP chapter hosted a roundtable Tuesday night, bringing together neighbors, faith leaders and civic organizers from communities closest to the three sites where Google is already approved to build data center campuses. Representatives from Google were invited but backed out, according to the NAACP. "So what I want them to do is go back to the drawing board and actually see like this is not about capitalism, this is not about your stakeholders. This is about the people and we will hold the fort for the people," one attendee said. "I believe that once the community speaks up, that's when change happens. And if we can get consistent community engagement and education, then the community is going to do what needs to be done," another attendee said. Chesterfield officials say they are not accepting any new data center proposals, but the three Google campuses, that include a total of nine buildings, are already approved and set to open in about a decade. The three projects are: - Project Peanut at 2100 Bermuda Hundred Road - Project Loch at 750 Watkins Center Parkway - Project Skye at 4201 Moseley Road Once finished, Google will be the largest commercial taxpayer in the county. Google is projecting revenue of $300 to $500 million per building. County leaders say that level of revenue would reduce the $3.25 car tax rate to about $1.79. The allocation of data center-derived tax revenue is on the Board of Supervisors' agenda today. During August's board meeting, supervisors tabled the car tax vote and spent the month meeting with residents in their respective districts to hear their thoughts on where they want the money directed. "I'm just simply saying that I just think that there's a lot of better ways that would cover things that we should be paying for or making available as resources in the county, and is reducing a personal property tax the best way to do that?" board member Jessica Schneider said during August's board meeting. The Board of Supervisors meeting starts at 6 p.m. in the Public Meeting Room at 10001 Iron Bridge Road. The board will also celebrate 21 residents who are 100 years of age or older during the meeting, in conjunction with National Centenarian's Day, observed annually on Sept. 22. AGÊNCIA DE COMUNICAÇÃO Conteúdo de responsabilidade da empresa 22 de setembro de 2026 XANGAI, 22 de setembro de 2026 /PRNewswire/ — A DoGo Power realizou o evento “Formando o Futuro da Energia” – Estratégia e Lançamento de Novos Produtos, lançando globalmente sua estratégia “Orientada a Cenários + Formação de Redes + IA”, juntamente com soluções inteligentes de armazenamento de energia para formação de redes para cenários comerciais e industriais (C&I) de grande e médio porte e em escala de serviços públicos. Robin Zhu, fundador e CEO da DoGo Power, afirmou: “Após uma rápida expansão em escala, o setor de armazenamento de energia entrou em uma fase de desenvolvimento de alta qualidade.” A adaptação de cenários, a formação de redes e a IA tornaram-se elementos essenciais da competitividade. O armazenamento de energia precisa deixar de ser uma “unidade de custo” e se tornar uma “unidade criadora de valor”. A DoGo Power concentra-se no armazenamento de energia em escala de rede para formação de redes elétricas, com o objetivo de ser líder em tecnologia de ponta para o novo tipo de sistema de energia. Buscamos cooperar com parceiros globais para fomentar um novo crescimento industrial através da inovação tecnológica.” A DoGo Power estabeleceu três centros de P&D e dois centros de simulação e testes na China, reunindo 19 grupos de especialistas interdisciplinares liderados por doutores, com mais de 60% da equipe dedicada à P&D. Seus três centros de produção globais oferecem uma capacidade de produção de 10 GWh na primeira fase. Apoiada por uma rede de vendas e serviços que abrange mais de 30 países e regiões, a DoGo evoluiu da exportação de produtos para a operação localizada. Orientação estratégica: Da industrialização da energia renovável à transformação das indústrias tradicionais pelas energias renováveis. A DoGo Power identifica um caminho de evolução em quatro estágios para um novo tipo de sistema de energia: 1-Expansão de P&D, da indústria e das tecnologias, 2-Formação de Grade para Estabilização, 3-IA para Maior Receita e 4-Integração Inteligente Holística. O setor encontra-se atualmente na Fase 2. Com base nisso, a DoGo desenvolve uma solução para a Etapa 3 e implementa negócios globais rumo à Etapa 4 sob dois pilares principais: - Definição de soluções baseada em cenários reais de clientes, desafios práticos e valor comercial mensurável. - A plataforma tecnológica 4S, desenvolvida internamente, impulsionada duplamente pela formação de redes e pela IA, possibilita um sistema de energia definido por algoritmo. Integrando EMS, PMS, PCS e BMS, a plataforma 4S constrói estações de armazenamento de energia inteligentes capazes de análise, otimização, tomada de decisões e atualização iterativa. Com o respaldo dessa base técnica, a DoGo fornece soluções em escala de rede adequadas para diversos cenários, requisitos de múltiplas energias e múltiplas escalas temporais em todo o mundo. Soluções de Novos Produtos Baseadas em Cenários Duas soluções emblemáticas de sistemas de armazenamento de energia (ESS) para formação de redes inteligentes foram lançadas para cenários comerciais e industriais (C&I) e de grande escala para concessionárias de serviços públicos. 1.Solução C&I Smart GFM ESS Adotando um design compacto do tipo “1 ESS substitui 8 gabinetes”, esta unidade de 3 metros consolida as funções de seis gabinetes ESS de 260 kWh+, um gabinete combinador, um gabinete on/off-grid e um transformador de isolamento. Isso reduz o CAPEX inicial em 1,2 centavos de dólar por Wh, diminui a ocupação de terras em 35% e encurta a entrega do projeto em 5 a 7 dias. Com suporte para acesso a múltiplas fontes, como painéis fotovoltaicos, geradores a diesel, pontos de recarga, rede elétrica e sistemas de gerenciamento, o sistema permite a comutação perfeita entre conexão e desconexão da rede em ?20ms, atendendo de forma confiável cargas sensíveis e de alta potência e concretizando o conceito de “1 contêiner equivale a 1 microrrede”. A capacidade de dimensionamento flexível suporta a implantação mista de diferentes séries e a compatibilidade com inversores de terceiros para maximizar a utilização dos ativos existentes. 2.Solução de armazenamento de energia GFM inteligente em escala de utilidade pública Desenvolvido para projetos com terrenos complexos e restrições de transporte, o contêiner pesa menos de 22 toneladas, dobrando as rotas de transporte viáveis em comparação com os contêineres convencionais de 20 pés e reduzindo os custos de logística marítima e terrestre. Seu design sem cabos elimina a necessidade de escavações e montagem de cabos no local, com o pré-comissionamento completo do sistema realizado na fábrica. Aproveitando a arquitetura dinâmica de taxa C, os clientes podem começar com uma implementação de duração de 2 horas para controlar o CAPEX e expandir por meio de gabinetes de expansão de data center para ajustar suavemente as taxas C e as durações de backup para corresponder aos modelos de negócios em evolução. Grade-Formando o Núcleo: Arquitetura de Coordenação de 3 Camadas Para equilibrar a estabilidade do sistema e os benefícios econômicos, a DoGo Power adota uma arquitetura de 3 camadas: - Camada de controle formadora de grade estável inferior: Atende às demandas de estabilidade em nível de milissegundos, incluindo a resposta inercial. - Camada intermediária de controle de coordenação eficiente: Executa funções de nível de centenas de milissegundos, como regulação secundária de frequência e tensão e partida a frio rápida. - Camada superior de despacho de otimização inteligente: Oferece previsão e otimização globais para maximizar os retornos econômicos em condições de operação estáveis. artigo.texto: Philippines to strengthen carbon market readiness, Article 6 implementation Manila, Philippines As the Philippines advances its carbon market development and strengthens its climate policy framework, national government agencies, private sector, civil society organizations, and international organizations convened for a country workshop on carbon pricing in Mandaluyong City on 18 September 2026. The workshop discusses the Philippines’ institutional and regulatory readiness for carbon market development. It also probed into how the country can better situate itself within the evolving carbon market landscape in Asia and the Pacific, particularly under Article 6 implementation. “We are encouraged by the Philippines’ commitment to climate action through updating of the Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC), which will be a fantastic roadmap for all of us. Today’s discussions are an important contribution to [equipping us with] more tools to help move faster in the right direction, towards a low-carbon economy. This is not just a climate agenda, but also an economic agenda, a social agenda, a fiscal agenda,” said Arnaud Peral, United Nations Resident Coordinator in the Philippines. In February 2026, the Philippines adopted the Roadmap to Readiness in the Voluntary Forest Carbon Market to strategically position the country as a high-integrity investment destination for forest carbon. This was followed by the signing of the Philippines and Singapore’s first bilateral implementation of Article 6 during the ASEAN Climate Week in Manila in April 2026, opening pathways for international carbon finance and emissions reduction projects. Despite these developments, the Philippines remains at the early stages of its carbon markets journey. “Carbon prices, sectoral coverage, exemptions, and revenue use differ widely. For the Philippines, the first question is not how to build a carbon market. It is what policy problem a carbon price is expected to solve, and whether carbon pricing is the appropriate instrument designed around national development priorities and our NDC," said Secretary Robert E.A. Borje, Vice Chairperson and Executive Director of the Climate Change Commission (CCC), in his opening remarks. Secretary Borje further emphasized that carbon pricing is one instrument within a wider policy package, and is not a replacement to climate finance, technology development and transfer, and capacity building. The effectiveness of carbon markets in the Philippines will also depend on the country’s existing policies, infrastructure, institutions, and investment environment. “The relevant test is not whether a carbon market can generate trade. It is whether the chosen instrument can reduce emissions cost-effectively, distribute burdens fairly, and support Philippine development and implementation of our NDC.” “With a climate crisis that is threatening to render us extinct, reimagining and reinventing the way we live and do business are a moral and a categorical imperative. Indeed, we do not have a moment to lose—we have to be part of the solution,” said Hon. Rep. Anna Victoria Veloso-Tuazon, Chair of the Committee on Climate Change of the House of Representatives, as she highlighted developments in Philippine climate policies such as the Low Carbon Economy Investment Bill and Climate Accountability Bill. The workshop is organized by the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (ESCAP), together with the Institute for Climate and Sustainable Cities (ICSC), the Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI), the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA), and the Asia Society for Social Improvement and Sustainable Transformation (ASSIST). Its findings will feed into a policy paper jointly being developed by UN ESCAP, GGGI, IEEFA and the Southeast Asia Energy Transition Partnership (ETP) to be launched at COP31 in Turkiye. It is a joint publication on forward-looking recommendations and policy signals on carbon pricing in the region, informed by country snapshots of China, Thailand, the Philippines, Republic of Korea, Japan, Indonesia, and Vietnam. About the Organizers The Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (ESCAP) is the most inclusive intergovernmental platform in the Asia-Pacific region. The Commission promotes cooperation among members in pursuit of solutions to sustainable development challenges. ESCAP is one of the five regional commissions of the United Nations. The Institute for Climate and Sustainable Cities is a Philippine-based non-governmental organization that advances climate, energy, and low-carbon solutions to enable fair and climate-resilient development at the national and international levels. The Global Green Growth Institute is a treaty-based international, inter-governmental organization dedicated to supporting and promoting strong, inclusive and sustainable economic growth in developing countries and emerging economies. The Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis provides independent, evidence-based financial analysis of global energy markets, investment trends, and policies. IEEFA’s work helps investors, policymakers, regulators, communities and the media better understand risks, opportunities and market dynamics shaping the energy transition. The Asia Society for Social Improvement and Sustainable Transformation is an international capacity building NGO that aims to achieve and witness meaningful changes to and for our planet and the people. It works towards the development and protection of the economic, social and environmental conditions.

artigo.texto: Clear answers remain elusive regarding the fire suppression systems currently installed at the Cove Hollow battery energy storage system — or BESS — in East Hampton During an appearance before the East Hampton Town Board last week, representatives from the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) deferred questions on the fire suppression mechanisms to the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA). “NYSERDA is currently reviewing information about fire suppression systems used across New York’s battery storage portfolio, obtained by the Inter-agency Fire Safety Working Group (FSWG) during inspections conducted in 2024/25, and will be considering changes to our program rules going forward to address concerns raised by the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation’s report,” the authority said in a statement. “For information about this specific project please contact NextEra.” NextEra Energy did not return multiple requests for information sent to its press office regarding the facility’s fire suppression mechanics. Calls for a shutdown of the BESS facility have swelled since contaminated water was detected in two Suffolk County Water Authority wells about a quarter-mile south of the plant. Suffolk County Executive Ed Romaine was among the first to advocate for closure, with East Hampton Village Mayor Jerry Larsen soon following suit. East Hampton Town officials have not yet joined those calls. Asked about the town’s stance on a shutdown following the DEC’s presentation at the Town Board meeting, town spokesman Patrick Derenze said only that officials are assessing their options. The BESS plant was previously equipped with a gaseous fire suppression system called NOVEC 1230. During a May 2023 fire, the chemical reportedly mixed with water, broke down into a so-called “forever chemical” called PFPrA, and seeped into the groundwater. Testing samples collected by the State DEC showed contaminant levels as high as 10,000 parts per billion, dwarfing the referential 3 parts per billion site specific screening value previously set by the state. The lack of concrete information on the facility’s current fire suppression setup remains a major concern for nearby residents and the East Hampton Village fire administrator — one of the few officials on scene during the May 2023 fire linked to the contamination.

artigo.texto: Politics & Government Calls Intensify For AI Data Center Ban In Newark, Local Groups Push For Moratorium Data centers will make an already heavy environmental burden worse, while offering little benefit to the people who live there, critics say. NEWARK, NJ — Calls for a temporary ban on artificial intelligence data centers continue to grow louder in New Jersey’s largest city. Two local advocacy groups – the South Ward Environmental Alliance (SWEA) and the Ironbound Community Corporation (ICC) – are asking for a one‑year moratorium on AI data center development in Newark. Supporters of data centers say they’re needed to keep the state competitive in the rapidly growing artificial intelligence industry. But critics allege that they consume too much power and water – jacking up utility bills for local residents. Find out what's happening in Newarkfor free with the latest updates from Patch. The campaign from advocates comes as the Newark City Council moves towards a possible ban. Earlier this month, the city council voted in favor of a resolution that supports a 12-month moratorium on the development or expansion of data centers in Newark. For now, the resolution doesn’t make any changes to city code, which would have to be approved through a local ordinance. READ MORE: Newark City Council Takes Stance On Data Centers With New Resolution Find out what's happening in Newarkfor free with the latest updates from Patch. The move was a step in the right direction, advocates said. According to the SWEA and ICC, a temporary ban would allow time for more research into the potential impact on the local community. It would also give the public a chance to give feedback, and for the city to roll out “clear, protective standards” for any future data center proposals. Here’s why advocates are calling for a ban, they said: “AI data centers–particularly large‑scale, AI‑focused facilities–pose significant risks to overburdened communities. These facilities consume enormous amounts of electricity and water, generate substantial air and noise pollution, and often operate with limited transparency. Newark’s frontline neighborhoods, including the South Ward and Ironbound, already face some of the nation’s worst cumulative environmental burdens, including elevated asthma rates, cardiovascular illness, and chronic exposure to industrial emissions.” “Newark’s frontline neighborhoods have long been asked to absorb the harms of polluting industries,” said Leah Owens, ports and policy analyst at the SWEA. “AI data centers threaten to intensify those burdens while offering little benefit to the people who live here,” Owens said. Alejandra Torres, assistant director of advocacy and organizing at the ICC, said a moratorium is essential for studying the potential added environmental harms on already overburdened communities. “Industrial development that exposes our communities to more pollution must be seriously contended with to ensure it does not sacrifice our communities’ health,” Torres said. South Ward Councilman Patrick Council – a supporter of the city council’s resolution – said he stands with the two groups in their fight to temporarily put the brakes on data centers in Newark. “This moratorium is an essential step toward protecting Newark residents, our environment, and the future of our neighborhoods while we fully examine the potential impacts of data centers,” he said. Newark wouldn’t be the first New Jersey city to pass a local law prohibiting data centers. Dozens of municipalities in New Jersey have passed full or partial bans in the past year, including Jersey City and Union. Send local news tips and correction requests to eric.kiefer@patch.com. artigo.texto: By — Matt Loffman Matt Loffman Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/voters-dont-like-data-centers-they-really-dont-like-them-close-to-home Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Voters don't like data centers. They really don't like them close to home Politics Sep 23, 2026 5:00 AM EDT Voters share an opposition to data centers that scrambles usual party lines, according to the latest poll from PBS News, NPR and Marist. Public opposition especially hardens when people are asked about construction in their own communities. Fifty-eight percent of U.S. voters say the construction of new data centers by companies like Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI will mostly have a negative effect on the country. And 65% of voters oppose construction in their communities, including 43% who are strongly opposed. A quarter of voters say they support data center construction. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The opposition barely follows party or geography. It runs above 60% in big cities, suburbs, small towns and rural areas alike. More than 80% of Democrats oppose local construction. Republicans overall are close to evenly split, with 46% in favor and 44% opposed. The president's core supporters are an exception. More than half of self-identified MAGA supporters are in favor of data centers in their own communities, the only group that favors construction. MORE: Why communities are revolting against data centers The intense opposition to data centers has had far-reaching effects this year. At least 75 data center projects worth roughly $130 billion were blocked or delayed in the first three months of 2026, according to Data Center Watch, a research project tracking opposition efforts. The National Republican Senatorial Committee warned in an August memo obtained by Axios that data centers had become a "sleeper issue" for the entire cycle. And candidates in both parties have featured ads on the issue. WATCH: How data centers became a major issue in the midterms What to do about data centers is another issue entirely as lawmakers scramble for solutions. Last week, the House overwhelmingly passed bipartisan legislation that would require state energy regulators to consider requiring data centers to pay for electrical upgrades in their communities. Trump, however, remains on the side of data centers. Communities that oppose construction will be "backwards and poor," he wrote on social media last month. "China could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement." The split leaves Republicans in districts with angry constituents choosing between them and him. "I understand the balancing act that Donald Trump is doing," despite public concern and rising energy costs, Republican strategist Melik Abdul said. "From Donald Trump's perspective, it should just be a wild, wild west because he doesn't want the regulations." Trump, Abdul argued, is worried that more government oversight would lead to a competitive advantage for China, which has fewer regulations. WATCH: Sen. Mark Warner says U.S. can strengthen AI safety without losing race to China Democratic strategist Joel Payne said the president is trying to pull his party along with him. "He is essentially trying to make it a litmus test for Republicans," he said. "I don't believe that has been met with the success that he intends for it to." The president is "out there on his own on this one," said Lee Miringoff, director of the Marist Institute for Public Opinion. He added that the anxiety increasingly runs through a broader fear of artificial intelligence. Neither party, Payne argued, can afford non-answers on this issue. "From a political standpoint, there is no nuance. The public has no nuance within how they think about AI and data centers." More from this poll Democrats lead in new poll as Trump looms over midterms Voters trust local election officials. They're less sure about the mail PBS News, NPR and Marist Poll conducted a survey from Sept. 14 to 15, 2026, that polled 1,280 registered voters by phone, text and online with a margin of error of 3.8 percentage points. For Democrats, the margin of error is 6.5 percentage points; Republicans, 6.8 percentage points; independents, 7.2 percentage points. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. artigo.texto: Americans have grown more negative toward the possible environmental and economic effects of data centers since the beginning of the year. And a majority say they’d be uncomfortable if a new data center started operating in their area, according to a new Pew Research Center survey. The survey comes as protests against new data center construction have spread, and as some state and local politicians have spoken out against data centers. Meanwhile, President Donald Trump has been a vocal supporter of data centers. More than half of Americans (54%) now say data centers are mostly bad for the environment, up from 39% in January. Half say they are mostly bad for home energy costs, up from 38%. And 49% say they are mostly bad for people’s quality of life nearby, up from 30%. The new survey was conducted from July 20 to Aug. 9 among 10,548 U.S. adults. Just 4% of Americans think data centers have a mostly good impact in each of these areas. Views on how data centers impact local tax revenue and jobs are mixed. Similar shares (between 21% and 24%) say data centers are mostly good and mostly bad for these things. Since January, there have been increases of 9 percentage points in the shares of Americans who say data centers are mostly bad for local jobs (from 15% to 24%) and local tax revenue (from 12% to 21%). Many Americans are still unsure or unfamiliar with data centers altogether. Shares ranging from 18% to 32% say they are not sure how data centers impact the five things we asked about. And overall, 12% say they haven’t heard of data centers. Jump to the following sections for more: - Views of data centers have become more negative across groups - Changing partisan views on data centers’ impact on local jobs and tax revenue - A majority of Americans would be uncomfortable with a new local data center - Awareness of data centers continues to grow Views of data centers have become more negative across groups Americans in a variety of demographic and partisan subgroups have become more negative in their views of data centers. Men and women alike, as well as adults across age groups and education levels, have become more likely since January to say data centers have a mostly bad impact on the things we asked about. For example, rural Americans have become more likely to say data centers are mostly bad for the environment (from 32% in January to 50% in August), home energy costs (32% to 46%) and the quality of people living nearby (28% to 45%). Most data centers currently being planned or under development will be in rural areas. Americans in urban and suburban areas have also become more likely to say data centers areas are mostly bad for these things. As was the case earlier this year, Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents are more likely than Republicans and Republican leaners to view the impacts of data centers negatively. Still, Republicans’ views have also turned more negative: In the new survey, for example, 42% say the facilities are mostly bad for the quality of life of people nearby, up from 24% in January. Republican elected officials have staked out varying positions on data centers. While Trump has consistently supported their construction in his second term, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott previously supported expansion but issued a statewide moratorium on new data centers in August. Some Democrats, such as Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, have also recently shifted their positions to support additional rules and oversight on data center construction and operation. Changing partisan views about impact on local jobs and tax revenue Among Democrats and Republicans alike, views on the effects of data centers on local jobs and tax revenue are somewhat more negative than they were at the start of the year. But many people in both partisan groups either say that they’re not sure or that the effects are neither good nor bad. More Democrats now say the effects of data centers in these two areas are mostly bad than mostly good. Liberal Democrats have primarily driven this shift: For example, 34% of liberals now say data centers are mostly bad for local tax revenue, up from 19% in January. More Republicans continue to say the effects of data centers on local jobs and tax revenue are mostly good than mostly bad. Still, Republicans are now 7 percentage points more likely than in January to say the effects in both areas are mostly bad. A majority of Americans would be uncomfortable with a new local data center The new survey also finds that 60% of Americans say they would be not too or at all comfortable with a new data center operating in their area. Much smaller shares say they would be somewhat comfortable (19%) or extremely or very comfortable (7%) with this. Just over half of Republicans (54%) and about two-thirds of Democrats (68%) say they’d be not too or not at all comfortable with a new local data center. Liberal Democrats stand out, with 81% saying they’d be uncomfortable. Majorities of urban, suburban and rural Americans say they would be not too or not at all comfortable with a new data center in their area. Awareness of data centers continues to grow Americans are more aware of data centers than they were earlier in the year. The share of Americans who say they have heard or read a lot about them has increased from 25% in January to 35% today. About nine-in-ten adults (88%) have now heard at least a little about data centers. As was the case in January, awareness of data centers is higher among men than women, and higher among people with at least a bachelor’s degree than those with less education. artigo.texto: Estimated read time: 2-3 minutes - Eagle Mountain's rezoning for a potential data center faced minimal opposition. - Only two residents commented during the Planning Commission meeting on the proposal. - The commission unanimously recommended approval; City Council will consider it next month. EAGLE MOUNTAIN — While proposed data centers have sparked heated debates in communities across Utah and the country, a public hearing in Eagle Mountain drew little public interest Tuesday night. Only two residents offered public comment during a planning commission meeting on a rezoning request that could eventually make way for another data center near existing facilities already operating in the city. South of Eagle Mountain, surrounded by open land, two major data center projects already dominate the area. Meta has operated its Eagle Mountain data center for about five years and employs roughly 1,200 people. Another facility, QTS Data Centers, is expected to be completed in the coming months and is projected to bring about 2,000 jobs to the area. City leaders said residents have become familiar with how data centers operate and the economic benefits they can provide. "What's happening here is very new, different technology than what's happening across the U.S.," said Eagle Mountain Economic Development Director Abby Ivory. "This is going in an area that really can't be used or developed for anything else." She believes the city's approach to educating residents and working closely with data center operators has helped build public trust. The discussion centered on a request from property owner Reagan Peck, who owns 41 acres adjacent to the Meta and QTS sites. Related: Peck told the commission the request is simply to change the property's zoning and does not guarantee a data center will be built there. "It doesn't mean it's going to be a data center," Peck said. "We don't have a buyer right now; we don't have a builder. We want to make sure we have this development agreement, this zoning in place so that if we were to advertise it, we could control how we did it." However, the zoning change would allow the property to be marketed for that use in the future if the owner chooses to sell. When the public comment period opened, only two residents addressed the commission. One urged city leaders to move cautiously. "If there is no need, don't do it," said Elbamara Perez. "We really need to figure out what's going on in the city we are living in." Another resident encouraged commissioners to carefully consider the long-term impact of the decision. "Consider carefully what you are opening up and what your making possible when you do this," said Teresa Edwards. Despite those concerns, the planning commission unanimously voted to recommend approval of the zoning change and forward it to the City Council for final consideration. The rezoning proposal is expected to go before the Eagle Mountain City Council next month, where members of the public will have another opportunity to comment.

artigo.texto: CATL Begins Trial Production at Debrecen Battery Cell Plant on 22 September 2026 CATL has started trial production at its newly constructed battery cell factory in Debrecen, Hungary, effective 22 September 2026, according to a company press release. The company stated that all preconditions needed to begin the trial run had been satisfied before operations commenced. The trial phase is intended to set up, optimise and validate production equipment and manufacturing processes before series production begins. The company said its Debrecen operation continues to work closely with the government and authorities to maintain high environmental standards and protect employee health and safety. CATL announced the Debrecen plant, its second European battery facility, in August 2022, with the goal of joining the European automotive and e-mobility supply chain and serving leading European automakers. Construction of the first cell building began in summer 2023, and by spring 2026 the building had been fitted with advanced technology. After receiving the occupancy permit in August 2026, the company secured all relevant permits and completed the preconditions tied to its IPPC permit, allowing trial operations to start on 22 September on the first two production lines of the cell manufacturing facility. Before the occupancy permit was issued, the Hajdú-Bihar County Government Office conducted regular on-site inspections at CATL facilities to follow up on earlier issues that had raised serious concerns among local residents. Authority representatives confirmed that the company had resolved all deficiencies identified during the permitting process. CATL described the Debrecen site as a strategic manufacturing hub that will supply well-known European automakers, which have already built substantial electric vehicle production capacity in Hungary in recent years. The company said it installed advanced, flexible production lines in Debrecen to meet client needs. CATL has been manufacturing battery modules in Debrecen since autumn 2024 and has produced 537,000 modules since then. Once all facilities are complete, the Hungarian plant will be CATL's largest manufacturing base outside China, with a capacity of 100 GWH. Beyond obtaining permits and completing preconditions for trial operations, CATL Debrecen said it remains committed to working closely with the government and authorities, prioritising employee health and safety. Employee health, safety and environmental factors will be thoroughly monitored during trial operation, with results submitted proactively to the authority. The company said its investment is important not only for Debrecen and its region but also for the Hungarian economy and the European e-mobility supply chain. CATL stated it is committed to transparency and welcomes authorities to visit its site at any time. - 1. artigo.texto: Fundo Imobiliário de data centers da AZ Quest capta R$ 482 milhões O fundo imobiliário de data centers da AZ Quest captou R$ 482 milhões na primeira emissão de cotas e reuniu mais de 7 mil investidores, segundo informações da gestora divulgadas em entrevista ao Estadão. O valor corresponde ao teto da oferta. O AZ Quest Panorama Data Centers FII teve o registro concedido pela CVM em 3 de julho de 2026, pelo rito automático. A oferta previa a emissão de 4,82 milhões de cotas a R$ 100 cada, com captação mínima condicionada a R$ 291 milhões. Quer conferir notícias de finanças em tempo real, direto do seu WhatsApp, de maneira gratuita? Clique e confira a nova comunidade de notícias da Status Invest. Pela classificação ANBIMA, o fundo é de tijolo, com gestão ativa e subclassificação de renda. A administração é do Banco Daycoval e a gestão, da AZ Quest Panorama. Quatro ativos da Scala, com projeção de retorno equivalente a IPCA + 9,5% Os recursos foram destinados à compra de quatro imóveis da Scala Data Centers: o data center de Fortaleza (CE) e sua subestação elétrica, além de duas subestações em Tamboré (SP) e Jundiaí (SP). O ativo cearense e sua subestação respondem por cerca de 60% do valor econômico da operação, de acordo com o estudo de viabilidade da oferta. O empreendimento fica na Praia do Futuro, região por onde chega a maior parte dos cabos de fibra óptica internacionais que conectam o país. A estrutura é de sale and leaseback: a Scala vendeu os imóveis, recebeu os recursos e segue como locatária, com contrato de dez anos. O fundo tem prazo de duração equivalente, prorrogável por mais 18 meses, e o contrato prevê três janelas de recompra pela Scala — no 36º mês, com prêmio de 9% sobre o cap rate de entrada; no 72º, com 5%; e no 120º, sem prêmio. Os documentos da oferta projetam rentabilidade líquida equivalente a IPCA + 9,5% ao ano no cenário de captação máxima, já considerando a recompra ao fim do contrato. Trata-se de projeção do estudo de viabilidade, sem garantia de retorno. O fundo imobiliário aproveita o crescimento do setor A operação ocorre em um ciclo de expansão da infraestrutura digital no Brasil. A Associação Brasileira de Data Centers (ABDC) estima investimentos de R$ 500 bilhões no país até 2030, com a capacidade instalada saindo de 730 MW para 3,2 GW. Fundada em 2020, a Scala opera 13 unidades no Brasil, com cerca de 200 MW instalados, e é controlada pela DigitalBridge. A companhia atende grandes empresas de tecnologia e já era conhecida da gestora: em maio de 2024, o AZIN11 alocou R$ 50 milhões em debêntures da SDC Participações, holding do grupo. A AZ Quest tem R$ 36,7 bilhões sob gestão, dos quais R$ 1,1 bilhão em estratégias imobiliárias. Com a conclusão da oferta, o FII de data centers passa a integrar a prateleira de ativos alternativos que a casa vem ampliando desde 2022.

artigo.texto: Insight and analysis on the data center space from industry thought leaders. Same Roof, 10 Different Gases: What a Data Center Is Quietly Holding Data centers’ reliability equipment – UPS batteries, refrigerants, and generators – creates hidden gas hazards that cause both safety incidents and costly outages. A year ago this month, during maintenance at South Korea’s National Information Resource Services (NIRS) in Daejeon, a UPS battery failure triggered a fire. The fire destroyed 384 lithium-ion batteries and took 647 government systems offline. Recovery was projected to take four weeks. Nothing about a facility like that would have told you it was dangerous: filtered air, locked doors, no flare stack – nothing that looks remotely like a process plant. Yet the very equipment that makes a data center dependable also makes it hazardous. UPS strings, chillers, standby generators, switchgear, suppression, and the water treatment skid are all essential; together, they introduce something close to 10 gas and chemical hazards hidden behind doors that mostly stay shut. Batteries, Then Everything Else Nine times out of 10, when an operator asks me about “gas,” they are asking about the batteries. Lead-acid on float can evolve hydrogen, and flammable concentrations begin at just 4% by volume. Hydrogen is invisible and odorless, and it migrates through gaps you did not know existed. Lithium-ion removes the hydrogen risk, but it introduces another: thermal runaway can vent flammable and toxic gases within minutes, often adjacent to live DC equipment. Refrigerant is typically the largest chemical volume on site, sitting behind more joints than anyone has counted. Because most refrigerants are heavier than air, leaks settle into plant rooms and pits, and when they do, they can take your cooling with them. Generator exhaust goes where the wind and the building let it. With short stacks, nearby intakes, and still air, exhaust can re-enter “fresh air” systems. Every test or run of a standby generator puts carbon monoxide and nitrogen dioxide somewhere. Sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) is an asphyxiant; under arcing, it decomposes into hazardous byproducts that accumulate in low, poorly ventilated areas. Clean-agent and inert-gas suppression systems require concentrations for occupied spaces, which limits tactics when people may be present. In Daejeon, responders used gas-based suppressants such as carbon dioxide rather than water to protect critical state infrastructure. Even so, the fire’s intensity meant it took firefighters 22 hours to extinguish it completely. Water treatment adds its own risks. Chlorine is a familiar one, and at an Apple data center in Maiden, North Carolina, in 2015, a spilled cooling-system cleaning chemical put five people in the hospital. Underneath many of these scenarios is the same mechanism: oxygen depletion. Why There’s More Than There Used to Be Data center capacity is on course to go from 103 GW to 200 GW this decade, according to JLL’s 2026 Data Center Outlook report. The gases have not changed. There is simply more of everything now, and it arrives faster than it used to. Lower-GWP blends, some of which are mildly flammable, are being retrofitted into plants designed for something else. Liquid cooling, unusual five years ago, is now assumed, which means a great many more joints right beside servers. The building itself can work against you. Data centers are sealed, secure, and pressure-managed for the equipment’s benefit, and this containment slows leaks rather than letting them dissipate. In a room nobody visits, a leak can sit for a week. The person who opens that door may be the first to encounter the hazard. The Uptime Argument Uptime Institute lists power and cooling as the leading causes of significant outages, with cooling alone responsible for 19% of outages; more than half of serious incidents cost over $100,000. Daejeon was both a safety incident and an availability incident. No one separates the two afterward because, in practice, they are one and the same. What I’d Check First Nobody has a single list of what is in the building. The battery data lives with the UPS vendor. Refrigerant quantities are stamped on the chiller. Suppression information is in a fire file somewhere. Dosing chemicals are handled by a contractor who turns up once a month. Consolidating that information is a dull afternoon’s work, and it can go out of date the moment a contract changes. Mounting height is the first thing I would look at. Too often, detectors end up at head height because installers can reach that easily. Hydrogen does not stop at head height. These incidents above occurred during planned work, not because of equipment “breakdowns.” The Daejeon event happened during a job to make the site safer. The Maiden case was scheduled maintenance. It pays to know who is on the schedule next month and what substances and procedures they bring. And buy detectors you can actually access for routine maintenance. If a sensor requires a permit, an escort, and a scheduled access time, calibration will slip. Eight years later, it can read several percent off, with the paperwork still in order. Notably, the Daejeon batteries reportedly passed an inspection in June of that year. Finally, treat rooms for what they are, not for the roof they share. A switch room and a chiller hall pose different questions, require different detection strategies, and entail different failure consequences. They just happen to be in the same building.
