artigo.texto: Two decades after the housing boom reshaped, then tanked, the U.S. economy, the AI boom is similarly transforming the drivers of growth. Hyperscalers have poured so much money into building as much AI infrastructure as possible—and as quickly as possible—that investment from a handful of companies is expected to reach $1 trillion a year soon. Meanwhile, the housing market has been largely frozen since the COVID-era boom ended in 2022, when the Federal Reserve embarked on an aggressive rate-hiking campaign to rein in inflation. “We’re seeing a pivotal shift in the US economy: investment is shifting away from residential investment and towards computers,” Adam Shapiro, vice president at the San Francisco Fed, posted on LinkedIn recently. He pointed out that inflation-adjusted spending on information processing equipment, which includes data centers and computer hardware, now exceeds residential investment. According to data from the Bureau of Economic Analysis, real private residential fixed investment was $748 billion in the second quarter, down 18% from an early 2021 peak. During that same span, spending on information processing equipment has soared 51% to $752 billion. “The AI investment boom is massive,” Shapiro added. He also noted that residential investment is more sensitive to borrowing costs, which have gone up alongside Treasury yields. The benchmark 30-year mortgage rate is nearly 7% as the 10-year bond yield has hit the highest level since 2007. By contrast, AI investment has been less sensitive to interest rates, even as hyperscalers have started issuing more debt to supplement drawdowns of their cash piles. Google parent Alphabet, for example, even reported negative cash flow earlier this year. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has also highlighted the eagerness with which AI companies are offering debt—no matter the cost of borrowing. “We are also seeing big corporate issuance. And a lot of that corporate issuance, I would say, is almost yield-agnostic, because the build-out for AI, the returns on that, the companies believe they’re going to be so high. They don’t really care what they’re paying,” he said recently. The onslaught of AI spending is expected to keep ramping up. S&P Global estimated last month that capital expenditures from Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, Oracle, and SpaceX will exceed $1.3 trillion in 2027, up from a projected $870 billion in 2026 and $470 billion in 2025. The ratings firm added that the industry’s capex is growing faster than revenue, warning that the aggressive build-out could lead to overcapacity if future demand doesn’t pan out as expected. S&P sees 2028 as an inflection point, with revenue accelerating and capex flattening. Until then, however, operating cash flow from the six hyperscalers will collectively be negative in 2026 and 2027, it added. The breakneck speed of AI development has also generated immense political backlash that’s rippling through the midterm election season. A new NBC News poll found that 64% of registered voters said they’d be less likely to support a candidate who’s in favor of building a data center in their community. AI has also fed into the cost-of-living crisis as consumers grapple with higher electricity bills and prices for new smartphones and PCs. That’s added to angst with home prices remaining out of reach for many Americans. While increased housing supply would ease pressure on prices, availability has been limited. The supply of existing homes has been constrained by the “lock-in” effect of homeowners with low mortgage rates reluctant to give them up amid today’s high rates. And new construction has been weak as high rates weigh on demand while building costs grow. Housing starts fell 2.6% in August to an annualized pace of 1.275 million, led by a drop in multifamily projects. While single-family homes rose, permits fell, signaling muted activity in the future. Meanwhile, the National Association of Home Builders reported builder sentiment fell to its lowest level in a year. “The big picture remains that elevated and rising borrowing costs are holding developers back, supporting our view that the downward trend in housing starts has further to run,” Capital Economics said in a recent note.

artigo.texto: CATL has started trial production at its newly built battery cell manufacturing facility in Debrecen, Hungary, after completing the preconditions required to begin operations. The trial run is aimed at setting up, optimising and validating production equipment and manufacturing processes ahead of the start of series production. CATL Debrecen said it will continue working closely with the Hungarian government and relevant authorities to maintain environmental, health and safety standards during the trial phase. CATL announced its second European battery plant in Debrecen in August 2022, with the objective of integrating into the European automotive and e-mobility supply chain and serving European automakers. Construction of the first cell production building began in summer 2023. By spring 2026, the facility had been equipped with advanced production technology. Following the issuance of the occupancy permit in August 2026, CATL obtained the relevant permits and completed the preconditions required under its IPPC permit to begin trial operations. Trial operations on the first two production lines of the cell manufacturing facility began on September 22. Before issuing the occupancy permit, the Hajdú-Bihar County Government Office conducted regular on-site inspections at CATL's facilities, including follow-up inspections related to issues that had raised concerns among local residents. According to CATL, the authorities confirmed that the deficiencies identified earlier in the permitting process had been addressed. 100 GWh Capacity Planned CATL's Debrecen facility is intended to become a strategic manufacturing hub supplying European automakers that have established significant electric vehicle production capacity in Hungary. The company said it has deployed advanced and flexible production lines at the plant to meet the requirements of its customers. CATL has already been manufacturing battery modules at the Debrecen site since autumn 2024 and has produced 537,000 modules to date. Once fully operational, the Hungarian facility is expected to have a 100 GWh annual production capacity, making it CATL's largest manufacturing base outside China. Trial Operation Phase During the trial operation phase, CATL said employee health and safety and environmental factors will be closely monitored, with the results to be submitted proactively to the relevant authorities. The company said the investment is expected to play a role in Debrecen and the surrounding region, as well as in Hungary's economy and the broader European e-mobility supply chain. CATL also said it remains committed to transparency and will allow authorities to visit the facility.

artigo.texto: Chinese automaker Li Auto will begin small-batch vehicle integration of solid-state battery technology in 2027 or 2028. However, the mature mass production of such packs for vehicles is expected to take another five years. On September 22, Cls reported that sources within Li Auto have revealed that the company’s solid-state battery (SSB) technology is expected to be ready for small-batch vehicle integration by 2027 or 2028. Senior director of traction batteries at Li Auto, Liu Zhimin, shared that the company is “actively laying the groundwork” for solid-state battery technology. Li Auto currently runs multiple related projects. The prototype validation has already been conducted using smart glasses that the company also sells in China. However, the sources shared that achieving mature mass production for vehicles while ensuring a “consistent user experience” is expected to take another five years. This means the mass-produced Li Auto vehicles with SSB technology will enter the market in 2032 or 2033. Liu Zhimin shared that the core challenges of making solid-state batteries include requirements for lifespan, charging performance, and cost. Previously, Li Auto revealed that its entire lineup will adopt in-house developed batteries. It will allow the brand to control the supply chain, potentially making its products more cost-effective. Li Auto-branded packs have already been deployed in the Li Auto L6, the Li Auto L8, and the Li Auto i8. According to a previous report from 36kr, Li Auto has launched a business unit dedicated to supplying its in-house developed tech to third-party companies. It focuses on Mach M100 autonomous driving chips with a computing power of 1,280 TOPS, SiC power modules, and EREV powertrain systems. However, the company’s batteries weren’t being considered for supply to other automakers. As it comes from China EV DataTracker, Li Auto delivered 259,930 units domestically from January to August 2025, down 1.2% Year-Over-Year. Its current bestseller is the Li Auto i6 electric SUV with a price range from 249,800 to 269,800 yuan (37,310 – 40,300 USD). It sold 152,842 cars in the first eight months of 2026.

artigo.texto: A discussão sobre mecanismos de mercado para redução de emissões é anterior ao que hoje se conhece por créditos de carbono. O Protocolo de Kyoto, de 1997, foi o primeiro marco internacional a estruturar mecanismos formais de mercado para a redução de emissões, com metas obrigatórias para países desenvolvidos e os primeiros instrumentos de comércio de créditos entre nações. O Acordo de Paris, de 2015, ampliou o compromisso para praticamente todos os países e estabeleceu as bases para mecanismos de cooperação internacional em torno do mercado de carbono. Diante deste cenário, os créditos de carbono deixaram de ser um tema de nicho ambiental para ocupar espaço central na agenda econômica. Cada crédito representa, em regra, uma tonelada de dióxido de carbono equivalente (tCO₂e) reduzida, removida ou evitada, conforme metodologia aplicável, podendo ser negociado entre empresas e governos que buscam compensar suas próprias emissões. Com o avanço de metas públicas de descarbonização e a pressão por compromissos ambientais mensuráveis, o mercado de carbono cresceu rapidamente nos últimos anos. Foi nesse contexto que o Brasil instituiu, por meio da Lei nº 15.042/2024, o Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa (SBCE), criando as bases regulatórias para o mercado de carbono no país. Entre suas disposições, o artigo 56 chamou atenção do setor segurador: o dispositivo determinava que seguradoras, entidades abertas de previdência complementar, sociedades de capitalização e resseguradores locais destinassem, anualmente, ao menos 0,5% de suas reservas técnicas e provisões à aquisição de créditos de carbono ou cotas de fundos desses ativos. Na prática, a norma transformava essas instituições em investidoras compulsórias de um mercado ainda em maturação. O Supremo Tribunal Federal, na Ação Direta de Inconstitucionalidade nº 7.795, declarou esse dispositivo inconstitucional. O Tribunal concluiu que não havia conexão entre o fim pretendido pela norma (a redução de emissões de gases de efeito estufa) e o meio escolhido, já que seguradoras e entidades correlatas não figuram entre os grandes emissores. Para a Corte, o critério usado para eleger os destinatários da obrigação relacionava-se apenas à disponibilidade de capital dessas instituições, o que violaria os princípios da isonomia, da livre iniciativa, da livre concorrência e do poluidor-pagador, além de comprometer a segurança jurídica das entidades. Importante destacar, contudo, que o Supremo Tribunal Federal não afastou a legitimidade da política ambiental nem a relevância do mercado de créditos de carbono. O que se reputou incompatível com a Constituição foi a opção legislativa de impor a determinados agentes privados o financiamento obrigatório desse sistema, sem que houvesse relação material entre a obrigação instituída e a atividade econômica por eles desenvolvida. A decisão, no entanto, não afasta o setor segurador do mercado de créditos de carbono, apenas redefine o papel que ele deve ocupar nesse mercado. Enquanto a atuação como investidor compulsório foi encerrada, cresce a oferta de seguros estruturados para proteger os próprios créditos de carbono, uma frente ainda emergente, mas com potencial expressivo. Entre as coberturas que vêm sendo discutidas ou desenvolvidas para esse segmento destacam-se: risco de reversão, que oferece cobertura para a perda do carbono armazenado por eventos como incêndios, secas, pragas ou desmatamento ilegal, especialmente relevante em projetos baseados em soluções naturais;risco de invalidação, que confere proteção para o cancelamento retroativo do crédito por erro metodológico, fraude ou revisão de critérios pelo órgão certificador;e risco de entrega e desempenho, que tem por objeto o descumprimento de contratos de compra antecipada, quando o projeto atrasa, tem desempenho abaixo do esperado ou não conclui a verificação no prazo combinado. Além de transferir riscos, o seguro agrega valor econômico ao mercado de créditos de carbono. Isso porque a subscrição pressupõe uma análise técnica da qualidade do projeto, de sua metodologia e dos riscos capazes de comprometer a geração ou a validade dos créditos. Na prática, esse processo funciona como um mecanismo privado de diligência, reduzindo assimetrias de informação e aumentando a confiança de investidores e compradores. Nesse modelo, o seguro funciona como um selo adicional de credibilidade: quando uma seguradora aceita subscrever o risco de um projeto, isso reforça a confiança de investidores e compradores na integridade do crédito negociado. Para o Brasil, esse movimento representa uma oportunidade concreta, pois o país reúne condições favoráveis para a geração de créditos de alta qualidade e a maturidade regulatória do SBCE tende a atrair a estruturação de coberturas específicas para projetos nacionais. Do ponto de vista do mercado segurador, a elucidação trazida na ADI 7.795 não é de afastamento do tema climático, mas de reposicionamento. Em vez de financiador compulsório de ativos ambientais, o setor ganha espaço para se consolidar como parceiro técnico do mercado de carbono, oferecendo produtos que mitiguem os riscos reais da cadeia, papel compatível com a expertise seguradora e com potencial de expansão nos próximos anos. Portanto, do Protocolo de Kyoto à ADI 7.795, a trajetória dos créditos de carbono é, no fundo, a busca por credibilidade e segurança jurídica para um ativo ambiental cada vez mais estratégico. Se o desafio de ontem era criar as regras desse mercado, o de hoje é fazer com que ele funcione com previsibilidade para quem nele investe. E é justamente nesse ponto que o mercado de seguros tende a deixar de ser mero coadjuvante regulatório para se firmar como peça-chave: não mais como investidor compulsório, mas como o agente que garante, na prática, que o crédito negociado vale o que realmente promete valer. *Por Ana Carolina Fuerbringer dos Santos, advogada do escritório Poletto & Possamai Sociedade de Advogados.

artigo.texto: A Companhia Energética de Minas Gerais (Cemig) e a Federação das Indústrias do Estado (Fiemg) estão entre as organizações que participaram da consulta pública organizada pela Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) sobre os leilões de baterias marcados para dezembro deste ano. O período de coleta de sugestões se encerrou na semana passada. Em sua contribuição, a Fiemg defendeu que as baterias a serem contratadas no certame sejam custeadas apenas por agentes de geração. Para isso, pede para que não seja admitido o repasse direto ou indireto desses custos aos consumidores finais por meio das tarifas de energia elétrica. A organização empresarial também solicitou que o mecanismo de rateio das tarifas seja objetivo, transparente, previsível e previamente conhecido pelos agentes do mercado. O pleito da Fiemg está inserido em uma das principais discussões do setor elétrico atualmente, sobretudo em torno dos leilões de baterias. Isso porque uma lei aprovada pelo Congresso Nacional e sancionada no final do ano passado pelo presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) estipula que os custos de baterias contratadas em leilões de reserva de capacidade “serão rateados apenas entre os geradores de energia”. O trecho aprovado, no entanto, depende da regulamentação da Aneel, a quem cabe definir, por exemplo, quais geradores ficarão sujeitos ao rateio – se apenas proprietários de plantas intermitentes, como solares e eólicas, ou de hidrelétricas e termelétricas também. Uma definição rápida sobre o tema é vista pelo mercado como fundamental para que o certame tenha êxito. Além disso, geradores tentam apoio no Congresso para aprovar um projeto de lei que retira a obrigação prevista no texto aprovado no ano passado. A proposição, de autoria do deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania- SP), ainda aguarda despacho do presidente da Câmara dos Deputados, Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB). Ainda na consulta pública, o Conselho de Cidadãos Consumidores de Energia Elétrica de Poços de Caldas (CONCCEL), organização formada para avaliar os serviços da DME Distribuição na cidade do Sul de Minas, seguiu linha semelhante e defendeu que os custos das baterias sejam arcados apenas por geradoras. Cemig Já a Cemig pleiteou que as usinas hidrelétricas reversíveis (UHR) também sejam consideradas um produto de armazenamento de energia. Essas instalações são destinadas a atender o sistema em momentos de estresse, principalmente no começo da noite, quando a demanda elétrica sobe, e nas tardes ensolaradas, em que a geração costuma ser superior à demanda. “Embora o certame ora proposto restrinja se, por força das diretrizes, ao armazenamento em baterias químicas, é oportuno destacar que a UHR constitui, ela própria, solução consolidada de armazenamento de energia, capaz de prestar ao SIN (Sistema Interligado Nacional) serviços de deslocamento temporal de energia, de reserva de capacidade e de suporte à confiabilidade operativa, com atributos de longa duração, elevada vida útil e maturidade tecnológica que a distinguem das demais alternativas”, argumenta a energética. A estatal, por outro lado, reconhece que o prazo de suprimento fixado ao certame de baterias — com início em agosto de 2028 — dificilmente seria compatível com o ciclo de desenvolvimento e implantação de uma UHR.

artigo.texto: O Rio Grande do Norte deu o primeiro passo regulatório para entrar na disputa por investimentos em grandes centros de processamento de dados. O Conselho Estadual do Meio Ambiente (Conema) aprovou nesta segunda-feira 21 uma resolução específica para o licenciamento ambiental de data centers, encerrando uma discussão que se estendeu por mais de um ano e que era apontada como uma das barreiras à chegada desses projetos ao Estado. A norma cria cinco categorias de empreendimentos de acordo com a potência demandada, estabelece procedimentos diferenciados conforme o sistema de refrigeração e permite que o Instituto de Desenvolvimento Sustentável e Meio Ambiente (Idema) comece a analisar formalmente os projetos após a publicação da resolução, prevista para esta semana. A mudança ocorre no momento em que a expansão da inteligência artificial, da computação em nuvem e dos serviços digitais aumenta a procura por infraestrutura de processamento e armazenamento de dados. Para o Nordeste, a disputa envolve principalmente Estados com elevada disponibilidade de geração renovável e infraestrutura de telecomunicações. No caso potiguar, a aposta está na combinação entre produção de energia eólica e solar, localização geográfica, conectividade e disponibilidade de áreas para novos empreendimentos. A Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) já inclui o Rio Grande do Norte entre os Estados nordestinos com perspectiva de receber grandes cargas eletrointensivas, categoria na qual estão os data centers e projetos de produção de hidrogênio por eletrólise. Até agora, porém, a falta de uma classificação ambiental específica impedia que essa vantagem energética se traduzisse em um processo definido de licenciamento. Com a aprovação, o governo estadual considera removida essa primeira barreira. “Nós abrimos aí um novo horizonte de possibilidades de desenvolvimento para o RN, trabalhando com agilidade e segurança ambiental”, afirmou o presidente do Conema e secretário estadual de Meio Ambiente e Recursos Hídricos, Paulo Varella. A resolução divide os projetos em cinco grupos conforme o consumo de energia. Data centers com demanda de até 20 megawatts (MW) serão classificados como de microporte. Entre mais de 20 MW e 50 MW, entram como pequeno porte; acima de 50 MW e até 100 MW, médio porte; acima de 100 MW e até 500 MW, grande porte; e aqueles com potência superior a 500 MW serão considerados de porte excepcional. A classificação é relevante porque a demanda elétrica está entre os principais fatores considerados na implantação de grandes centros de dados. São empreendimentos que precisam funcionar de forma contínua e podem representar cargas de centenas de megawatts. Estudos recentes da EPE mostram a dimensão dessa nova demanda sobre o sistema elétrico. Em junho, a estatal apresentou uma proposta de expansão da transmissão para permitir a conexão de até 4 gigawatts (GW) adicionais de cargas eletrointensivas nas regiões de Pecém, no Ceará, e Parnaíba, no Piauí, a partir de 2032. O RN também aparece nos estudos da empresa sobre a preparação da rede para essas cargas. A chegada dos empreendimentos, portanto, não depende apenas da existência de geração renovável, mas também da capacidade do sistema de transmissão de entregar grandes volumes de energia de forma contínua. Para o governo potiguar, a produção de energia é uma das principais vantagens do Estado. A disponibilidade hídrica, por outro lado, exigiu tratamento específico durante a elaboração da resolução. “O RN, apesar de estar no semiárido, tem uma produção de energia muito grande e tem uma carência hídrica. Todavia, a tecnologia hoje permite que os data centers já não precisem mais usar muita água, quase nada, porque trabalha em um circuito fechado”, afirmou Varella. Refrigeração define exigência ambiental e inicia avanço A utilização da água esteve no centro das discussões que antecederam a aprovação da norma. Data centers precisam retirar o calor produzido por servidores e outros equipamentos, mas o volume de água necessário varia de acordo com a tecnologia adotada. A resolução diferencia sistemas abertos e fechados de refrigeração. Nos circuitos fechados, a água ou outro fluido circula continuamente pelo sistema, diminuindo a necessidade de reposição. Nos sistemas abertos, especialmente aqueles associados a torres de resfriamento, o consumo pode ser maior. Segundo o diretor-geral do Idema, Werner Farkatt, os investidores que procuraram o Estado até agora apresentaram interesse principalmente pela primeira tecnologia. “Aqui no RN, até o momento, o que tem sido procurado são os sistemas fechados”, afirmou. A distinção foi incorporada ao licenciamento. Como regra, os data centers poderão ser analisados por meio de Relatório Ambiental Simplificado (RAS), independentemente do porte. “Isso dará também velocidade ao processo”, disse Farkatt. A simplificação, entretanto, não será aplicada de maneira uniforme quando houver maior pressão sobre os recursos hídricos. Projetos classificados como de grande porte ou porte excepcional que utilizarem sistemas abertos de refrigeração terão de apresentar estudos ambientais mais completos, incluindo Estudo de Impacto Ambiental e Relatório de Impacto Ambiental (EIA-Rima). A solução tenta conciliar dois interesses presentes desde o início da discussão: evitar que uma norma excessivamente restritiva retire competitividade do Estado e, ao mesmo tempo, aumentar as exigências para empreendimentos que apresentem maior impacto potencial sobre a água. Durante a elaboração da regulamentação, entidades do setor produtivo cobraram parâmetros que aproximassem o RN das regras existentes em outros Estados. Levantamento divulgado pela Comissão Temática de Energias Renováveis da Fiern chegou a estimar um potencial de até R$ 232,6 bilhões em investimentos associados a grandes projetos de data centers e sistemas de armazenamento de energia, além de 53,6 mil empregos diretos e indiretos. artigo.texto: A flurry of project completions, financings and supplier deals for large-scale BESS across the Central and Eastern Europe (CEE) region, from Greenvolt, Renovatio & CATL, Eurowind, Renalfa, MOL Group, Tavion, MetaWealth and Enexus & Longi. The announcements come with the Energy Storage Summit Central and Eastern Europe 2026 right around the corner, taking place on 6-7 October in Warsaw, Poland. Renovatio Solar and CATL to deploy 918MWh Romania BESS for Greenvolt Construction is underway on a 918MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) project in Romania, one of the country’s largest. The owner is IPP Greenvolt, while Renovatio Solar is providing EPC services and lithium-ion giant CATL will provide the BESS technology. The project will reportedly be completed within 12 months. Eurowind completes 120MWh project in Romania IPP Eurowind Energy Romania, through vehicle Teiuș Solar SRL, has completed and commissioned its 120MWh BESS in Teiuș, Alba County. It started building the project in March this year, with a total investment of €21 million (US$24 million). The companies have collaborated on solar PV projects previously, but the 15MWh and 35MWh BESS projects in Dâmbovița County mark the first storage collaboration between them. Longi only recently entered the BESS space, with the acquisition of system integrator PotisEdge late last year. MetaWealth finances first Romanian BESS Real estate investment platform MetaWealth has completed a €19 million financing structure for its first BESS, a 50MW/100MWh project, also in Romania. It comprises €10 million from CEC bank, €5.5 million from the founding Topolinski family, and €3.5 million from its securitisation and bond platform, which an executive explained to us in a recent interview. Renalfa IPP repowers, adds BESS to Bulgaria solar plant Renalfa IPP has completed the repowering and hybridisation of its Devnya PV plant in Northeastern Bulgaria. It has increased the plant’s capacity from 5MWp to 65MWp and added a BESS totalling 60MW/165MWh. Solarpro was the EPC contractor. Bulgaria is now the most battery-heavy electricity market in the world, explained one of the Energy Storage Summit Central and Eastern Europe event’s speakers in a recent Q&A with us. MOL Group completes solar-plus-storage in Hungary Industrial firm MOL Group has completed a 37.4MWp solar, 20MW/40MWh BESS project in Hungary, called Algyő. The project benefitted from funds under Hungary’s EU-backed capex grant scheme for storage, head of communications Ambrus Halász said in a video on LinkedIn (image below). Tavion raises €50 million for Polish BESS projects BESS owner-operator Tavion has raised €50 million in a fundraise and debt raise, which will go towards completing three projects in Poland totalling a combined 69MW. Leitmotif and Oberon Capital led the fundraise, which totalled €34 million, and construction will start on the first two projects this month. They are part of a 184MW portfolio Tavion intends to deploy in Poland.

artigo.texto: By Kathiann M. Kowalski Ohio has emerged as one of the top states for data center developers, with roughly 100 of the facilities already up and running and nearly 150 more on the way. Many of those planned facilities may never get built, but their projected electricity needs will drive up energy bills for Ohioans anyway. Utilities base their grid investments on demand projections. In Ohio, those forecasts are now through the roof. The state’s largest regulated electric utility is American Electric Power’s Ohio Power Co., which anticipates demand will nearly triple over the next decade, largely due to expected data center projects. Critics question the validity of these forecasts — and the wisdom of using them to justify costly investments that utility customers will end up on the hook for if the numbers don’t pan out. Forecasts from utilities in Ohio and elsewhere generally presume trends will continue along the same paths as in recent years, said Jonathan Koomey, a researcher who runs the firm Koomey Analytics and focuses on issues related to data centers, computing, and climate solutions. But in fact “there is deep uncertainty,” Koomey said. Computing generally has gotten more efficient over time, and so future data centers might be less energy-intensive. There’s also the question of whether demand for AI services will be able to support the ambitious plans developers are pursuing today. Plus, developers often shop projects in multiple locations to look for the best deal. Ohioans are already facing rising power bills — and more increases are now likely based on sky-high demand forecasts. “We have watched projected demand become the justification for enormous spending, record capacity costs, and increasingly urgent claims about grid reliability,” Brad Belden, board chair of the Ohio Manufacturers’ Association Energy Group, said at its annual energy conference on Aug. 27. “‘Reliability’ cannot become the magic word that ends every conversation about cost.” So far, regional grid operator PJM Interconnection hasn’t been persuaded by those challenging the extent to which energy needs will actually grow. PJM serves Ohio and all or parts of a dozen other states, overseeing the procurement of generation and transmission. “The Ohio Manufacturers’ Association has been saying that, effectively, load growth is not real. I think that is both naive and irresponsible,” said Asim Haque, PJM’s executive vice president for government and member services. Mounting costs Data center forecasts can drive up electricity costs in two key ways: by increasing capacity prices and by prompting utilities to build new power lines in anticipation of future demand. Capacity prices pay for power plant operators to be available to meet spikes in demand. In PJM territory, those charges have surged more than tenfold since May 2025. That’s because PJM lacks the total generation necessary to meet the deluge of demand it expects from data centers. Meeting that need, which analysts like Koomey say may be inflated, will likely lead to a jump in fossil-fueled electricity. Between 2025 and 2027, added generation from fossil-fueled plants in the region will be 2.5 times the extra electricity supplied by solar and wind, reported Dennis Wamsted, an energy analyst for the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis. Analysts have criticized PJM in general and Ohio in particular for making it difficult to build inexpensive solar, wind, and battery projects in recent years — all of which could have helped cushion rising costs now and alleviate projected capacity problems in the future. Projections by utilities and the grid operator also drive plans for expanded infrastructure, because utilities map out those investments today on the basis of what they expect customers will need in the future. “If these data centers don’t show up …, you’re going to pay the costs,” said John Seryak, CEO and founder of the energy consulting firm RunnerStone. In Ohio, both manufacturing and consumer advocates worry that plans to build transmission and other infrastructure are not being met with enough scrutiny. Although large-scale projects are overseen by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, lower-level “supplemental” transmission is up to the states, PJM’s Haque said. Those projects are necessary to meet growing demand, including that from data centers, especially where developers won’t bring their own power or nonetheless want to tie into the grid for backup. Supplemental transmission projects can add up to billions of dollars, though. And in Ohio, no one is independently examining their prudence or cost-effectiveness, Maureen Willis, agency director for the Office of the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel, said at the OMA conference. A 2025 Ohio law calls for utilities and state regulators to consider grid-enhancing technologies as a more cost-effective alternative to building traditional transmission projects. But it’s unclear how that provision and cost recovery will work together. A new rule limiting the time to question company witnesses about customer charges will make it even harder to challenge costs. The Ohio Consumers’ Counsel filed a complaint with FERC in 2023, asking it to require scrutiny of the costs for supplemental transmission, but the agency has not yet acted. Last month the agency asked the commission to speed up its review. “OCC’s consumer-protection complaint has been collecting dust at FERC for nearly three years while billions more in transmission projects continue to be added,” Willis said. “Consumers deserve answers, accountability, and protection from unjustified costs.” In Ohio, the largest projected overall growth in demand is the tripling expected by AEP Ohio, Koomey said at the OMA event. As of February, that AEP Ohio load forecast reflected signed contracts for 17.8 gigawatts of data-center demand planned to come online at various points through 2035, down from its earlier estimate in 2025. artigo.texto: Nearly 21GWh of grid-scale BESS came online globally last month, of which around a fifth was in Saudi Arabia while the majority was in China. The latest figures are out from Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, which we report as part of a monthly series for ESN Premium. They show that grid-scale battery energy storage systems (BESS) entered commercial operation last month globally totalling 6,516MW/20,855MWh of capacity. Some 61% of that was in China, 19% was in Saudi Arabia, 11% was in Europe while just under 5% was in South and Central America. See a full table of the figures further down. Europe in particular has ramped up its activity, commissioning three times the amount of capacity that it did in the same eight-month period in 2025: 18.2GWh. In August, 914MW/2,290MWh came online, including a 150MW/600MWh project from EDF in Belgium and a 500MW/1GWh project from CIP in Scotland. Saudi Arabia’s figure was made up of two 500MW/2GWh projects (the Tabuk and Ha’il projects) supplied by China-based Hithium. The South and Central America figures meanwhile are made up of projects that Engie brought online during the month. North America had its quietest month of the year by far, with only 100MW/400MWh coming online, mainly comprising EDP’s Sandrini project in California. China meanwhile deployed 4,131MW/12,757MWh of capacity. The largest of these were two in inner Mongolia (the Inner Mongolia Xilingol Dongsu Energy Storage Project sub-project I & 2, 500MW/2GWh each with StarCharge as integrator) and one in Hebei (a 300MW/1.2GWh project with Sungrow as integrator).

artigo.texto: A third planning commission vote on expanding a zone in Salem Twp. to accommodate two additional data center campuses is scheduled for Thursday, as land deals totaling around $1.4 billion for property owners hang in the balance. 4-3 Glennbrook Group and principal Jack Sordoni applied to add 4,466 acres to the Special Data Center Overlay District, which initially included about 1,200 acres for the Amazon Web Services Salem Township Innovation Campus where three data centers are completed and 17 more are planned, and the township later added about 1,700 acres for the QTS Salem data center campus. Moores 109 LLC had also applied to include 185 acres surrounded by the Glennbrook Group parcels for a fourth data center campus within the overlay district. The planning commission initially approved the applications at a meeting on July 23, but a group of citizens sued the township, claiming that some residents were unfairly locked out of the meeting in violation of the Pennsylvania Sunshine Act. Luzerne County Judge Lesa S. Gelb ruled at an Aug. 25 hearing that the planning commission had to hold another hearing on the applications, which the commissioners did on Aug. 27. The commissioners again approved the applications. But, following that meeting, township officials were provided with Gelb’s written order, in which she ordered a stay on any data center overlay district action at an Aug. 26 public hearing on the issue followed by a township supervisors meeting, as well as the planning commission meeting that had been scheduled for Aug. 27. Township officials had not seen that written order prior to the Aug. 27 meeting. The planning commission will meet at 5:30 p.m. Thursday at Berwick Assembly of God Church, 801 E. 5th St. Public comment will be allowed from township residents and taxpayers.

artigo.texto: BYD’s flagship luxury marque, Yangwang, has released official teasers for its upcoming luxury sedan. It recalls Rolls-Royce offerings, with an overall silhouette strikingly similar to the Phantom sedan. The new sedan will also feature rear-hinged coach doors, a first for BYD. The sedan was previously spied at BYD’s facilities, along with a luxury SUV that is expected to take on the Rolls-Royce Cullinan. This marks the first confirmation from BYD and Yangwang that its new flagship sedan is now under development. The new flagship could also become BYD’s first vehicle to feature solid-state batteries. Exterior The latest teasers provide more detail on the new sedan’s styling. Its front end continues with Yangwang’s “ding” (鼎) design theme, with a fascia similar to the U8 and U8L SUVs. Its headlamps are also visible, with a close-up shot showing multiple LED elements, along with an engraved “Yangwang” logo. The sedan’s overall shape remains largely unchanged from the previous spy shots, though BYD has covered the rear taillights in the latest shots. Its door handles are now clearly visible, and their placement confirms the presence of rear-hinged coach doors. Without interior images, it is still unclear whether the new sedan will feature a pillar-less chassis design, which would provide more space for entry and exit when both doors open on each side. Yangwang is expected to offer self-opening power doors, in line with other luxury NEVs in China. The roof-mounted LiDAR unit is still present, though a vehicle at this price point is expected to have additional side-mounted LiDARs for assisted driving. As a BYD flagship product, it’s expected to feature BYD’s DiPilot 600 assisted driving system, also known as God’s Eye in China. Possible SSB pioneer Chinese sources claim the new Yangwang sedan will be BYD’s first vehicle equipped with solid-state batteries (SSB). CarNewsChina previously reported on the automaker’s planned rollout of SSBs, with vice executive Stella Li announcing plans to launch an SSB-equipped vehicle in 2027. As a flagship model, the new sedan’s high price and positioning would make it well-suited to serve as a launch vehicle for BYD’s SSBs. One spy shot shows the sedan parked in front of a Flash Charging station, hinting that the new battery will also support megawatt rapid charging. Yangwang’s other models have often served as BYD’s tech demonstrators, with the U8 SUV becoming the first model on the e4 quad-motor platform. The U9 Xtreme supercar is also poised to attempt breaking the 500 km/h barrier in November. SSB development is rapidly heating up among Chinese battery brands and automakers. Most firms are still aiming for trial production in 2027, with limited vehicle trials planned for later. For Yangwang’s new sedan, SSB-equipped trims may be offered at a high price with limited supply, while “normal” trims with BYD’s LFP “Blade Battery 2.0” will be sold alongside at a lower price. This would align with BYD’s scheduled roadmap for SSB commercialisation, with the automaker’s Chief Scientist, Lian Yubo, stating that liquid lithium-ion batteries and all-solid-state systems could coexist for 15 to 20 years. artigo.texto: 4 Common Direct-to-Chip Cooling Challenges and How to Solve Them As AI workloads drive higher rack densities, engineers must overcome corrosion, contamination, retrofit and monitoring challenges in direct-to-chip cooling. September 23, 2026 Sponsored by Schneider Electric Traditional cooling architectures are no match for the blistering growth of AI workloads. AFCOM’s 2026 State of the Data Center Report found that 72% of operators expect AI workloads to increase data center capacity requirements, while average rack density has climbed from 16 kW to 27 kW in just one year, a staggering increase that represents the largest year-over-year jump in AFCOM’s 10 years of research. Engineering direct-to-chip liquid cooling environments at scale requires a reimagining of the entire cooling stack, from coolant distribution and facility water systems to monitoring and operational resilience. Here we identify some of the challenges operators and engineers face when moving to direct-to-chip liquid cooling, with practical guidance to overcome them. Material Compatibility and Corrosion A primary risk in integrated cooling systems is galvanic corrosion, which occurs when incompatible metals are connected in the presence of a fluid. This process causes metal ions to migrate, leading to material degradation and the formation of debris. For example, if a system uses copper cold plates, using aluminum piping creates a large electrochemical potential difference that triggers rapid corrosion. To solve this, engineers use the Anodic Index to select noble metals with similar potential, such as using brass or stainless steel alongside copper components to minimize the risk of erosion. Maintaining a registry of all wetted materials, including seals, valves, and connectors, is essential to prevent debris from clogging the tiny microchannels within a server’s cold plate. Managing Contamination and Installation The complexity of the installation phase is significantly higher for DLC than for traditional water systems. Contamination can enter the loop through machining shavings, incompatible thread sealants, or even biological growth if fluid remains stagnant in lines for too long. A practical solution is a modular approach, limiting the size of the TCS loop so that a contamination event only affects a small number of servers. Best practices include welding junctions to reduce dissimilar material couplings, applying passivation treatments to heated joints, and thoroughly flushing the entire loop before the first IT equipment is ever connected. Retrofitting Existing Facilities Integrating high-density AI clusters into existing “brownfield” facilities presents a unique set of engineering constraints. Most legacy halls were designed for power densities and cooling methodologies that are fundamentally challenged by the requirements of modern AI accelerators. Modernization, therefore, is not a simple hardware replacement but a strategic physical and thermal integration. Modernizing a brownfield site requires a modular execution model to overcome legacy constraints. Traditional facilities often face fixed-rack layouts, floor-loading limits, and power distribution systems sized for lower densities. To navigate these, engineers can leverage a rack-by-rack deployment strategy. This phased approach enables hybrid air and liquid environments to coexist during the transition, protecting existing workloads while scaling AI capacity. Successful retrofits depend on localized heat rejection strategies that minimize disruption to the central plant: - Rear-Door Heat Exchangers: Systems stabilize rack temperatures even under peak AI workloads, making them an ideal server cooling option for GPUs. - Liquid-to-Air Exchangers: For facilities where water access is limited, heat dissipation units (HDUs) can remove heat from AI servers and reject it directly into the room air, eliminating the need to route facility water to the rack. - Localized Scaling: Direct-to-chip liquid cooling at the rack level allows for staged upgrades, preventing major central plant overhauls and making the modernization of smaller, constrained sites more feasible. This modernization framework turns underleveraged assets into growth drivers. By syncing power distribution, cooling controls, and DCIM monitoring tools, facility engineers can safely evolve their power and cooling systems together. This approach ensures the performance envelope of the existing facility is maximized to support the densification required by modern AI. Monitoring and the Intelligence Layer The complexity introduced by liquid cooling reinforces the need for data centers to have granular monitoring to minimize risk. Traditional building management systems are often too slow to detect the subtle pressure drops that precede a component failure. Utilizing an integrated Data Center Infrastructure Management (DCIM) platform allows for real-time telemetry that correlates pump speed with workload intensity. This enables predictive leak detection. By monitoring the differential pressure across the CDU and comparing it to flow rates, the software can identify a breach based on anomalies. This is often more effective than traditional rope-style sensors, as it can alert the operator the moment fluid escapes the loop. In a high-scale AI environment, where downtime costs are massive, this predictive visibility is the ultimate tool for risk reduction. Overcoming Direct-to-Chip Cooling Challenges As AI workloads continue to push rack densities higher, direct-to-chip cooling will become increasingly essential. Success depends on treating cooling as an integrated system, including materials, installation, facility infrastructure and monitoring. By addressing these challenges early, operators can build resilient cooling environments that support AI growth without compromising reliability. artigo.texto: Covenergo and Delta Capacity have begun construction on AKKU One, a standalone 125MW/300MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) in Lapinlahti, Finland, with commissioning targeted for the fourth quarter of 2027. Covenergo, a renewable energy services provider, holds majority ownership of the project and is responsible for project finance and long-term asset value creation. Delta Capacity, a Swiss-based developer and operator of utility-scale battery storage systems, is acting as engineering, procurement, construction and management (EPCM) contractor, taking responsibility for securing offtake, construction and long-term asset management. AKKU One was acquired as a ready-to-build asset from Helios Nordic Energy. The project marks Delta Capacity’s second battery storage project in Finland, and it also completed the 70MW/160MWh Ånge BESS in Sweden earlier this year. Patrik Hes, CEO of Delta Capacity, said the project builds on the company’s track record in the region. “We’re proud to bring the same speed and execution that delivered Ånge to our new project in Finland,” Hes said. A Nordic delivery team is supporting construction. Rejlers, a Nordic engineering consultancy, is providing technical project support throughout construction, while NYAB is delivering balance-of-plant works and Ampner is carrying out grid connection studies and compliance verification. Sungrow will supply the project’s battery system, under a 1GWh framework agreement it signed with Delta Capacity earlier this year. GreenPowerMonitor, a DNV company, will provide energy management and SCADA systems for real-time monitoring once the project is operational. Once operational, AKKU One will provide flexibility to Finland’s power system, supporting frequency regulation and balancing services as the country integrates growing volumes of wind and solar generation. Delta Capacity’s Nordic pipeline extends beyond AKKU One AKKU One is one of several projects Delta Capacity has under way in the region. The company has entered into a partial tolling agreement with Centrica Energy for the 125MW/300MWh Karppio project in Teuva, Finland, also acquired from Helios Nordic Energy, this time alongside family investment office Strioga Family Foundation. Centrica Energy already trades output from Delta Capacity’s Ånge project, which the developer has described as the largest battery storage facility in the Nordics. Delta Capacity brought the Ånge project online in June, completing it from procurement to commercial operation within 15 months, a joint venture with Czech investment bank WOOD & Company’s Renewables Sub-Fund. Delta Capacity has said it has nearly 1GWh of battery storage under construction and is targeting more than 6GWh of flexible assets in operation across the Nordics by 2030. Grid-forming compliance has emerged as a defining engineering requirement for large-scale Nordic battery projects. Hitachi Energy, which is supplying the power conversion system for a separate 125MW/250MWh BESS under construction in Haapajärvi, Finland, has said projects in the region must be built to withstand low temperatures, high humidity, snow and ice, while meeting increasingly stringent grid code requirements set by Finland’s transmission system operator, Fingrid. Hitachi Energy’s head of power conversion solutions, Alberto Prieto, has said the exact revenue mix available to Finnish battery storage projects is still evolving, spanning ancillary services, wholesale arbitrage and cross-border balancing within the shared Nordic electricity market.

artigo.texto: Executive Roundtable: AI Infrastructure Under Pressure At Data Center Frontier, we rely on industry leaders not only to help us understand the most urgent challenges reshaping digital infrastructure, but also to illuminate the broader technological, operational and market forces driving the industry’s evolution. In the third quarter of 2026, those forces are increasingly converging. Power constraints, unprecedented compute densities and pressure to bring capacity online faster are no longer separate problems. They are interacting across the entire data center infrastructure stack. AI is pushing facilities into operating conditions that would have been exceptional only a few years ago. Higher rack densities are concentrating risk. Scarce power is changing decisions about architecture and redundancy. Accelerated deployment schedules are putting greater pressure on integration, commissioning and supply chains. At the same time, increasingly interconnected electrical, thermal, storage and control systems mean that resilience can no longer be considered solely at the level of an individual component. The result is a moment when some of the industry’s most durable assumptions deserve another look. For our Q3 Executive Roundtable, Data Center Frontier asks industry leaders what AI-scale infrastructure is revealing about traditional data center design, where the boundaries of critical infrastructure are expanding, and how operators can pursue speed without sacrificing the rigor required for reliability. As AI infrastructure moves from exceptional deployment to an increasingly important part of the industry’s baseline, the question is no longer simply how much capacity can be built, but whether the underlying infrastructure can evolve fast enough to support it reliably. Our distinguished Executive Roundtable panelists for Q3 of 2026 include: - Chrissy Olsen, Vice President of Critical Power Solutions, MPI Energy - David Shepard, Global Head of Data Center Business, Chemelex-Raychem - Pierre-Adrien Bel, Product Manager, EMEA, Rehlko Today, we’ll explore What AI Is Exposing: As rack densities rise and infrastructure is pushed harder, AI is bringing long-standing design assumptions into sharper focus. Practices that proved sufficient in lower-density environments may offer less margin at AI scale, forcing operators and designers to reexamine where redundancy is truly needed, how much failure tolerance remains, and which once-secondary infrastructure considerations now deserve to be treated as critical. In coming days, we’ll also explore: - Redefining Critical Infrastructure: How rising density, tighter power constraints and increasingly interconnected systems are expanding what operators must treat as mission-critical — and why the handoffs between power, storage, cooling and controls may deserve as much attention as the systems themselves. - Speed Without Compromise: How the push for faster deployment is changing the balance between speed and rigor, including where schedules can be compressed safely and where commissioning, testing and operational visibility need to become even more exacting. And now, onto our first Executive Roundtable question for Q3 of 2026. Data Center Frontier: What is AI infrastructure exposing that the data center industry could get away with overlooking at lower densities — and which traditional design or redundancy assumptions now need to be reconsidered? Chrissy Olsen, MPI Energy: AI is showing us where we have relied too heavily on extra capacity and traditional ways of thinking. At lower densities, individual systems could be designed and managed somewhat separately. That does not work as well at AI scale, where power, cooling and backup systems are much more dependent on one another. We also have to look beyond simply adding more redundancy. Having backup equipment is important, but real resilience comes from knowing that all of those systems will work together when something goes wrong. The question is no longer just, “Do we have enough backup?” It is, “Can we respond, recover and keep the most critical workloads operating?” David Shepard, Chemelex-Raychem: The deployment and rapid adoption of AI infrastructure is beginning to expose a few areas of risk that were previously not top of mind with operators. Holding aside the “new normal” of extended supply chain issues, deploying IT infrastructure that is, say, 10 times more dense and 10 times more expensive puts a lot of pressure on operators to mitigate this new level of risk and protect these now far more expensive assets. As a for instance, we do leak detection in the white space. Leak detection SOP 5 years ago was ropes or point sensors on the floor, or under the raised floor. With AI infrastructures, those individual racks run between $2-7M per rack. That means traditional leak detection is simply not good enough, and “in rack, in CDU, in server” has become necessary. Pierre-Adrien Bel, Rehlko: AI is exposing that traditional redundancy models can look sufficient on paper while still leaving gaps in dynamic system performance. Conventional generator systems were designed around relatively stable loads and isolated transient events, with time to stabilize and recover between disturbances. Large AI training clusters change that operating profile because thousands of GPUs may ramp power demand in synchronized, repetitive cycles, significantly reducing or eliminating those recovery windows. That means installed megawatts and redundancy alone do not fully define resilience. Operators also need to understand voltage stability, frequency control, dynamic response time and available operating margin under sustained stress. artigo.texto: GK Energy Secures 150 MW Battery Storage Project From MSEDCL With ₹42.84 Crore Annual Revenue GK Energy has bagged a long-term domestic contract from MSEDCL to establish a 150 MW / 300 MWh battery storage project in Maharashtra. The utility contract features a fixed tariff of ₹2.38 lakh per MW per month, locking in predictable annual revenues of ₹42.84 crore (excluding GST) for a period of 15 years. Market snapshot: GK Energy Limited has secured a Letter of Award (LoA) from the Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Limited (MSEDCL) to develop a 150 MW / 300 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) in Maharashtra. Backed by Viability Gap Funding (VGF) support, the project is scheduled for commissioning within 18 months from the signing of the Battery Energy Storage Purchase Agreement (BESPA). Data Snapshot - Awarded a letter of award for setting up a 150 MW / 300 MWh Battery Energy Storage System in Maharashtra under Viability Gap Funding. - Fixed tariff rate of ₹2.38 lakh per MW per month, providing stable annual revenue of ₹42.84 crore excluding GST over 15 years. - Reported Q1 FY27 standalone revenue growth of 71% year-on-year to ₹505.19 crore, alongside a standalone net profit increase of 61.55% year-on-year to ₹59.67 crore. What's Changed - Order Book Diversification: GK Energy is expanding its portfolio into large-scale Battery Energy Storage Systems, moving beyond its traditional core of decentralized solar pumps and rooftop solar solutions. - Extended Revenue Visibility: The 15-year contractual agreement locks in an annual recurring cash flow stream of ₹42.84 crore, enhancing long-term operational predictability. Key Takeaways - Structural Shift in Portfolio: Entering the high-growth utility-scale storage sector opens up new, larger addressable markets as India accelerates its renewable grid integration. - Predictable Long-Term Cash Flows: The monthly fixed-tariff payment model mitigates standard merchant power risk, ensuring predictable annuity-style revenues. - Robust Order Book Inflows: Coupled with the recent rooftop solar empanelment, GK Energy continues to scale up its outstanding order pipeline significantly in FY27. SAHI Perspective The award of this 150 MW / 300 MWh BESS project marks a strategic evolution for GK Energy. Historically focused on retail and agricultural solar execution, the transition to utility-scale grid infrastructure validates the company's scalability. Additionally, the project is structured with Viability Gap Funding support, which substantially de-risks the capital outlay required for high-capacity battery installations, ensuring healthy project IRRs. Market Implications The project underscores the accelerating momentum in India's battery energy storage segment. Large discoms like MSEDCL are aggressively building storage capacity to balance high-penetration renewable grids, creating multi-gigawatt opportunities for specialized clean energy EPC players like GK Energy. Trading Signals Market Bias: Bullish The BESS award establishes a high-margin, long-term annuity revenue stream of ₹42.84 crore annually for 15 years, complementing GK Energy's record-high Q1 FY27 standalone revenue growth of 71% year-on-year to ₹505.19 crore. Overweight: Renewable Energy, Power Infrastructure, Energy Storage Trigger Factors: - Timely signing of the formal BESPA agreement with MSEDCL within prescribed timelines. - Successful grid integration and commissioning of the BESS system within the 18-month execution window. - Working capital efficiency as the company handles multiple large-scale solar and storage projects simultaneously. Time Horizon: Medium-term (3-12 months) Industry Context As India scales up its non-fossil fuel capacity toward the 500 GW target by 2030, battery storage infrastructure is turning critical for grid stability. Standard discom frameworks are rapidly incorporating BESS bids under regulatory guidelines to bridge solar-generation peaks and evening consumption surges. Key Risks to Watch - Execution timeline pressure, as the contract mandates completion within 18 months from the date of the BESPA signing. - Fluctuations in global battery cell chemistry prices, which could impact technology procurement margins during construction. - Risk of counterparty payment delays from state distribution utilities, although MSEDCL has historically managed disciplined payment cycles. Recent Developments In August 2026, GK Energy secured a ₹454.5 crore letter of empanelment to deploy 100 MW of rooftop solar systems across 1 lakh households. Earlier in July 2026, the company also bagged a ₹235.92 crore order from MSEDCL for 10,000 off-grid solar-powered water pumping systems. Closing Insight GK Energy's pivot to battery energy storage with the 150 MW MSEDCL win establishes a critical base of long-term recurring cash flows, indicating a successful diversification that pairs well with its massive solar pump and rooftop order book. artigo.texto: Como é trabalhar em um data center de inteligência artificial Alimentar a gigantesca expansão da inteligência artificial exige caminhar muito, procurar cheiro de queimado e monitorar estragos causados por pássaros As rondas do homem de 33 anos incluem farejar equipamentos queimados que possam indicar superaquecimento, apalpar tubos à procura de rachaduras e verificar lâmpadas defeituosas ou transformadores de energia quebrados. Engenheiro-chefe da unidade, Waddy supervisiona dezenas de outros engenheiros que fazem o mesmo e chama a si próprio de “O General”. “Não ouço nenhum ruído”, disse ele enquanto caminhava sobre um piso elevado, acima de uma câmara que faz o ar circular para resfriar os servidores. “Não sinto cheiro de nada. Está tudo funcionando direito.” Os data centers estão sob intenso escrutínio à medida que os americanos ficam cada vez mais desconfiados da IA e dos possíveis riscos da tecnologia. Eles também permanecem um tanto misteriosos para além de suas fachadas geralmente quadradas e sem características marcantes: o que há lá dentro e o que os funcionários fazem? A instalação onde Waddy trabalha, pertencente à empresa de data centers Digital Realty, é cheia de corredores com eco, tão compridos que alguns técnicos usam patinetes para se deslocar. Há gaiolas altas repletas de fios. Também existem camas e chuveiros para os técnicos que eventualmente precisem permanecer no local durante eventos climáticos extremos a fim de manter os servidores funcionando. Mesmo com até 120 pessoas no local em determinados momentos — a unidade emprega cerca de 50, mas seguranças terceirizados e funcionários enviados pelos clientes também trabalham ali —, o tamanho enorme do prédio fazia com que muitas salas estivessem vazias em um dia de semana recente. Os funcionários de data centers exercem uma atividade em alta demanda, responsável por sustentar o gigantesco investimento do país em inteligência artificial. Data centers não exigem equipes numerosas — as estimativas variam de algumas dezenas a algumas centenas de funcionários permanentes para operar uma unidade, dependendo da instalação —, mas a dimensão da expansão nos Estados Unidos pode se traduzir em dezenas de milhares de trabalhadores. Já existem cerca de 2.700 instalações de data centers em operação nos Estados Unidos, segundo a provedora de dados do setor Data Center Map. Entre elas está a unidade de nove anos onde Waddy trabalha, situada em uma densa concentração conhecida como Data Center Alley, a cerca de uma hora de Washington. Quase 400 outras unidades estão em construção no país, enquanto pelo menos 1.500 se encontram em fase de planejamento, segundo estimativa da Data Center Map. Mais de 1 milhão de candidatos a emprego procuraram vagas em data centers no site de recrutamento Indeed neste ano. Em agosto, o volume de buscas era oito vezes maior que no início de 2022. Pesquisas do site de empregos constataram que, entre os trabalhadores horistas responsáveis por manutenção e instalação, os data centers oferecem salários cerca de 42% maiores do que funções semelhantes em outros tipos de empresa. Segundo o Indeed, um gerente de projetos em um data center ganha por volta de US$ 115 mil por ano — cerca de R$ 591 mil pela cotação de R$ 5,14 por dólar. A Digital Realty afirmou que engenheiros iniciantes em suas instalações podem ganhar aproximadamente US$ 66 mil por ano, ou cerca de R$ 339 mil, enquanto a remuneração média pode superar US$ 120 mil, o equivalente a cerca de R$ 617 mil, para profissionais mais experientes. Profissionais com conhecimento em sistemas elétricos, engenharia de redes e sistemas de refrigeração são muito procurados, disse Brandi Galvin Morandi, diretora de recursos humanos da operadora de data centers Equinix. Grandes empresas de tecnologia, entre elas a Meta Platforms, investiram na formação de mão de obra especializada para construir essas instalações. Na Virgínia, onde há uma grande concentração de data centers, o Northern Virginia Community College lançou, com a ajuda do setor privado, um programa de capacitação para o trabalho nessas unidades. “Essas são instalações essenciais, que operam 24 horas por dia, e isso exige uma combinação específica de formação técnica, disciplina de segurança e experiência prática — algo que está em falta diante da velocidade com que o setor cresce”, disse Cindy Fiedelman, diretora de recursos humanos da Digital Realty. A empresa opera mais de 300 data centers em seis continentes. Em unidades como a de Ashburn, a Digital Realty aluga espaço para grandes empresas de tecnologia que precisam de capacidade computacional. Entre seus clientes estão Oracle, Meta e IBM. A Digital Realty também enfrenta a reação pública cada vez mais intensa contra a construção de data centers. Em Atlanta, a companhia busca uma exceção a uma proibição local de data centers perto de terminais de transporte enquanto tenta construir na cidade uma unidade de US$ 500 milhões — cerca de R$ 2,57 bilhões. Moradores se opuseram ao projeto, que atualmente se encontra num impasse. Um porta-voz da Digital Realty afirmou que o projeto criaria empregos bem remunerados e que a empresa estava “comprometida em chegar lá da maneira correta”, em parceria com a comunidade. A unidade de Ashburn reúne trabalhadores administrativos e operacionais. Entre eles estão seguranças, técnicos que cuidam da estrutura de cabos dos clientes, profissionais da cadeia de suprimentos que buscam materiais e engenheiros que monitoram possíveis problemas. As funções são semelhantes em outros data centers pelo país. A parte mais importante do trabalho é manter os centros em funcionamento. A Digital Realty estima que seus data centers ficam operacionais durante 99,999% do tempo, mas agora busca alcançar 99,9999%. A diferença parece pequena, mas equivale a reduzir o tempo de interrupção de seis minutos para 30 segundos por ano. artigo.texto: Conema aprova regras para data centers e abre caminho a novos projetos no RN Norma define regras para projetos de diferentes portes, prevê licenciamento simplificado e estabelece exigências ambientais mais rigorosas para grandes estruturas. Cláudio Oliveira Repórter O Rio Grande do Norte deu nesta segunda-feira (21) um passo para entrar na disputa pela instalação de data centers no Nordeste. O Conselho Estadual do Meio Ambiente (Conema) aprovou a minuta de resolução que estabelece diretrizes, critérios e procedimentos para o licenciamento ambiental desses empreendimentos no Estado. A medida cria, pela primeira vez, um regramento específico para a atividade e, após a publicação, que deverá ocorrer nesta semana, permitirá ao Instituto de Desenvolvimento Sustentável e Meio Ambiente (Idema) iniciar o licenciamento dos projetos. O presidente do Conema e secretário estadual de Meio Ambiente e Recursos Hídricos, Paulo Varella, explica que a resolução busca conciliar a proteção ambiental com a criação de condições para novos investimentos. O documento foi construído ao longo de mais de um ano e procura estabelecer segurança para os empreendedores e para o órgão ambiental. “Nós abrimos aí um novo horizonte de possibilidades de desenvolvimento para o RN, trabalhando com agilidade e segurança ambiental”, afirmou. O regramento estabelece cinco categorias de porte dos data centers, conforme a demanda de energia: empreendimentos de até 20 megawatts (MW) serão classificados como de microporte; acima de 20 MW até 50 MW, pequeno porte; acima de 50 MW até 100 MW, médio porte; acima de 100 MW até 500 MW, grande porte; e acima de 500 MW, porte excepcional. Um dos principais pontos discutidos durante a elaboração da norma foi a diferença entre sistemas fechados e abertos de refrigeração. O diretor-geral do Idema, Werner Farkatt, explica que nos sistemas fechados a água ou o fluido utilizado para resfriamento desloca-se em um circuito, reduzindo significativamente a necessidade de reposição. Já os sistemas abertos, associados a grandes torres de resfriamento, podem demandar volumes maiores de água. “Aqui no RN, até o momento, o que tem sido procurado são os sistemas fechados.” A resolução prevê que o licenciamento dos data centers será feito por meio de Relatório Ambiental Simplificado (RAS), independentemente do porte. “Isso dará também velocidade ao processo”, diz o diretor. Para projetos de grande porte e excepcionais que utilizem sistemas abertos de refrigeração, entretanto, serão exigidos estudos ambientais mais complexos, incluindo Relatório de Impacto Ambiental (EIA-Rima), em razão do potencial impacto sobre os recursos hídricos. A regulamentação também altera a posição do RN diante de investidores interessados em instalar grandes estruturas de processamento e armazenamento de dados. Para o relator da proposta no Conema, Kepler Brito, representante da OAB/RN, um dos principais avanços foi estabelecer regras específicas para os diferentes sistemas de refrigeração. Kepler avalia que a norma coloca o RN em condições semelhantes às de estados que já disputam esses investimentos. “Acredito que o Rio Grande do Norte entrou aí no mercado e a gente permite hoje sistemas fechados de refrigeração com regras parecidas com nossas principais concorrentes, o Ceará e a Paraíba”, declarou. Preocupação ambiental Para o presidente do Conema, Paulo Varella, a segurança jurídica é necessária para que o desenvolvimento da atividade ocorra sem afastar a preocupação ambiental. “Demos toda a importância que a proteção ambiental merece. Por outro lado, nós temos potenciais no nosso Estado que precisam ser desenvolvidos”, disse. O secretário citou a disponibilidade de energia como uma das vantagens do RN, mas reconheceu que a questão hídrica precisa ser considerada. “O RN, apesar de estar no semiárido, tem uma produção de energia muito grande e tem uma carência hídrica. Todavia, a tecnologia hoje permite que os data centers já não precisem mais usar muita água, quase nada, porque trabalha em um circuito fechado”, disse Varella”. A aprovação da regra estadual ocorre poucos dias depois de o Governo Federal sancionar a Lei nº 15.504, de 15 de setembro, que instituiu o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata). O programa criou incentivos fiscais para a instalação e ampliação de data centers e estabeleceu contrapartidas relacionadas a pesquisa, desenvolvimento, eficiência hídrica e sustentabilidade. O Redata também prevê incentivos regionais: empreendimentos instalados nas regiões Norte, Nordeste e Centro-Oeste têm redução de 20% em duas das principais contrapartidas previstas no programa. A legislação considera ainda vantagens brasileiras para a atividade, como disponibilidade de energia renovável e infraestrutura de comunicação por cabos submarinos. No RN, permanece em discussão outro componente da competitividade: a possibilidade de redução do ICMS sobre equipamentos de infraestrutura de tecnologia da informação destinados aos data centers. A proposta depende de análise do Conselho Nacional de Política Fazendária (Confaz).

artigo.texto: Sunwoda joins China’s flash charging race with battery system promising 10%-97% in 9 minutes Sunwoda Electric Vehicle Battery Co Ltd (Sunwoda EVB) has unveiled a 15C smart flash charging battery system and aims for 10,000 megawatt charging stations by the end of 2027, joining China’s intensifying race in ultrafast charging. The Chinese battery maker announced the plan on September 17. The system debuted at a battery industry conference held September 16-17 in Zaozhuang, Shandong province. The launch comes as Chinese automakers and battery makers step up their push into flash charging. After BYD (HKEX: 1211) introduced its second-generation Blade Battery and new flash chargers in March, Hongqi, Dongfeng and Xpeng (NYSE: XPEV) announced advances in batteries or ultrafast charging infrastructure. Data Sunwoda presented at the conference showed that the new battery system can charge from 10% to 70% in 5 minutes and from 10% to 97% in 9 minutes at room temperature. A 1-minute charge can add 100 kilometers of range. The charging times for both intervals match the room-temperature figures BYD announced when it unveiled its second–generation Blade Battery in March. At minus 20°C, Sunwoda’s new system takes 15 minutes to charge from 10% to 97%. The company said the system can support a driving range of more than 700 kilometers. Sunwoda also said the system can meet warranty requirements of 10 years or 300,000 kilometers, with no limit on ultrafast charging sessions for vehicles not used commercially, seeking to address concerns that high-rate charging could shorten battery life. Beyond charging speed, Sunwoda made smart monitoring a focus of the upgrade. The system integrates smart battery cells 3.0, an energy domain controller and an AI cloud-control platform to improve battery monitoring and early fault detection. The system can provide warnings for more than 20 types of faults 2 to 10 days in advance, with an accuracy rate of 99.77%, the company said in the statement. An open ecosystem platform combining solar power, energy storage and flash charging, unveiled alongside the battery system, extends the company’s offering into charging infrastructure. The platform integrates flash charging EV batteries, energy storage systems, megawatt charging units, high-power liquid-cooled charging terminals and an AI cloud-control platform. It supports vehicles from multiple brands and different partnership models. Sunwoda expects its flash charging ecosystem to include 10,000 megawatt charging stations by the end of 2027. The statement did not disclose station locations, investment plans, the first vehicle models to use the new battery or a mass-production timetable. Competition in China’s flash charging market has moved from technology launches to network expansion. BYD announced the completion of its 10,000th flash charging station in China on August 28, reiterating its target of 20,000 stations by the end of 2026. Other domestic automakers are also advancing the technology. Test results Hongqi released in July showed that a battery jointly developed with China Automotive New Energy Battery Technology (CNET) could charge from 10% to 70% in 3 minutes and 41 seconds at 25°C. The brand did not disclose a mass-production timetable at the time. Dongfeng rolled out a prototype of its independently developed ultrafast charger on July 29. Its peak output of 1,500 kW per charging connector matches that of BYD’s new flash charger unveiled in March. Xpeng announced on September 15 that its first X-Energy megawatt charging station had begun operating in Hong Kong. Jointly built with local charging provider Halo, the station is open to drivers of all vehicle brands. The station has a peak output of 1 megawatt and is equipped with 400 kWh of energy storage. That figure represents the station’s output capacity; actual vehicle charging power still depends on the vehicle’s battery and charging capabilities. De acordo com os familiares, eles possuem 66 acres e dizem que cumpriram uma série de exigências antes de receber novas restrições para seguir com o projeto. A principal reclamação envolve a exigência de reservar 44,2 acres da área, o equivalente a cerca de dois terços do terreno. O casal compara a situação com a estrutura da Microsoft, construída a aproximadamente 16 quilômetros do local. De acordo com o The Times of India, a família comprou três lotes em 2021, em uma área com zoneamento residencial, acesso à energia, água e estradas. A intenção era construir uma casa e um galpão, além de deixar espaço para futuros projetos. Dessa forma, antes das obras, o casal realizou estudos geológicos, de solo, levantamento do terreno e engenharia. Na sequência, o Condado de Chelan autorizou o avanço do projeto. Entretanto, a situação mudou após uma troca na direção do setor de Desenvolvimento Comunitário do local. O órgão passou a exigir novos documentos e análises ambientais e geotécnicas. Segundo os familiares, a família gastou quase US$ 300 mil para atender às solicitações. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC A disputa entre a família e o condado aumentou quando as autoridades exigiram que os familiares destinassem 44,2 acres de terra como área de mitigação. O proprietário questiona a medida e compara seu caso com o data center da Microsoft, localizado nas proximidades. Os envolvidos afirmam que a Microsoft movimentou uma quantidade muito maior de terra no empreendimento, mas recebeu uma exigência menor de reserva de área. Vale destacar que as informações não comprovam tratamento diferente por parte das autoridades, nem estabelecem relação entre os dois projetos. Além dos impasses com as autoridades, a disputa trouxe impacto financeiro para os proprietários. Os familiares afirmam que ainda pagam cerca de US$ 3 mil por mês (R$ 15,4 mil) pelo financiamento da construção. Com isso, a família pretende continuar contestando as restrições e mantém o plano de construir uma casa no terreno. artigo.texto: Laredo City Council to discuss Flock cameras, school property purchase, and data center rules LAREDO, Tex. (KGNS) - The Laredo City Council meets Monday at 5:30 p.m. at City Hall to discuss key issues affecting the community. One item up for discussion is whether voters should decide the future of the city’s Flock Safety cameras through a non-binding referendum, following Gov. Greg Abbott’s decision to pause state funding for the technology. Council members are also considering whether to buy the recently closed Matias De Llano Elementary School from United ISD, launching a study into purchase and renovation costs to see if the building could be converted into a community center, library, or recreation space with help from Webb County partners. Finally, leaders will get an update on potential changes to the city’s land development rules aimed at protecting neighborhoods from any adverse effects tied to data center developments.
