artigo.texto: Here's Why You Should Add BYD Company Stock to Your Portfolio BYD Company Limited BYDDY is principally engaged in the research, development, manufacture and distribution of automobiles, secondary rechargeable batteries and mobile phone components. It is poised to benefit from advanced electrification through its European commercial vehicle lineup, intelligent driving systems and FLASH Charging technology and investment in ADAS and next-generation Blade Battery technology. Let’s dig deeper and see why you should consider including this Zacks Rank #2 (Buy) stock in your portfolio. Advanced European Portfolio & Investment in R&D to Aid BYD BYD Commercial Vehicles recently unveiled its most advanced European product portfolio, covering electric solutions for urban distribution, municipal operations, regional logistics and long-haul transport. The flagship ETT 44 is built on a dedicated electric architecture, combining high performance, ultra-fast charging of up to 1.5MW, advanced battery technology, driver-focused ergonomics and safety features. Its charging capability can add more than 400 kilometers of range in 20 minutes. The portfolio also includes rigid trucks such as the T020 and T028, vocational vehicles for last-mile delivery and municipal applications, and fully electric yard tractors. These models share common technology and ecosystem foundations. BYD supports customers with in-house expertise spanning vehicle development, batteries, charging infrastructure, energy storage and energy management. With the ETT 44 launch and dedicated commercial-vehicle sales and technical teams, BYD aims to strengthen its position as a comprehensive electrification partner in Europe. In May 2026, BYD introduced Full Damage Coverage for its Urban Navigate on Autopilot function under the God's Eye driver assistance system in China. Following its Intelligent Parking coverage, the move made BYD the first automaker to offer dual coverage for advanced driver assistance features. As part of its “Intelligent Driving for All” strategy, BYD also made its God's Eye LiDAR version available as an option across its entire vehicle lineup. The company aims to reduce traffic accidents, enable ADAS to function as a “Super Driver” and use AI as a “Super Personal Assistant.” BYD plans to invest more than RMB 100 billion in intelligent driving R&D. Building on the safety-focused approach behind its Blade Battery, the company is seeking to increase consumer confidence in ADAS through coverage programs while advancing proprietary technologies, including the XUANJI A3 chip and God's Eye system. In March 2026, BYD introduced its self-developed FLASH Charging technology, capable of delivering up to 1,500kW through a single connector, alongside the second-generation Blade Battery. Developed over six years, the new battery underpins BYD's latest charging breakthrough and addresses a longstanding trade-off between charging speed and energy density. The second-generation Blade Battery increases energy density by 5% while substantially improving charging performance. BYD achieved these improvements while maintaining the safety and durability associated with its lithium iron phosphate battery technology. Central to the breakthrough is the company's proprietary “FlashPass” Ion Transport System, designed to accelerate ion movement within the battery and improve charging efficiency. By combining higher energy density with significantly faster charging, BYD aims to reduce charging-related barriers to EV adoption. The FLASH Charging system and upgraded Blade Battery therefore represent key elements of the company's strategy to advance EV performance, convenience and broader market adoption. BYD reported an 18% year-over-year increase in global sales to 440,293 units in August 2026, marking its fourth consecutive month of growth after eight months of declines, driven by a 134% surge in overseas sales to 189,466 vehicles. Price Performance, Valuation and Estimates BYD has underperformed the Zacks Automotive - Foreign industry in the last six months. Its shares have lost 22.4% compared to the industry’s decline of 9.7%. From a valuation perspective, BYD appears overvalued. Going by its price/sales ratio, the company is trading at a forward sales multiple of 0.66, higher than the industry’s 0.57. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for BYDDY’s 2026 EPS has remained the same in the past 90 days, while for 2027 it has moved up by 3 cents in the past 60 days. Other Stocks to Consider Some other top-ranked stocks in the auto space are Garrett Motion Inc. GTX and China Yuchai International Limited CYD. While GTX sports a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy), CYD has a Zacks Rank #2 at present. You can see the complete list of today’s Zacks #1 Rank stocks here. artigo.texto: China's battery company CATL is reported to have developed a dedicated battery targeting the U.S. electric pickup truck market. U.S. automakers have already begun testing the battery, raising interest in CATL's prospects for entering the U.S. market. InsideEVs reported on Sept. 21 local time that CATL designed a taller-shaped battery to match the body structure and cargo demands of U.S. pickup trucks. CATL is reviewing ways to enter the market by licensing its technology to U.S. manufacturers rather than building its own production facilities. A feature of the development is that CATL has made large pickup trucks, rather than the U.S. passenger electric vehicle market, a separate target. Pickup trucks are larger than passenger cars and have wider cargo space, requiring a different design for battery packaging. Liangbo Zhu (주링보), chief technology officer for CATL's international business unit, said in an interview with the Financial Times that U.S. automakers have already tested the battery. He did not disclose the names of the companies. He said the U.S. market is in a geopolitically intense environment but still offers huge business opportunities. Many steps remain before actual commercialization. CATL has not disclosed the battery's chemical composition or specific size, performance or mass-production timing. No U.S. automaker that has decided to adopt it has been confirmed. For now, it is closer to a stage where CATL has shown its willingness to enter the U.S. pickup truck market than one where a specific supply contract has been signed. Technology licensing premised on local production is widely cited as the likely route to the U.S. market. Zhu also mentioned that transferring technology to U.S. manufacturers could be one path to entry. Examples already exist of battery production in the United States using CATL technology. Ford's next-generation electric pickup truck, the "Fathom", is set to use LFP battery cells produced in Michigan, and those cells are made based on CATL technology. It has not been confirmed whether that battery is in the same family as the pickup-specific design disclosed this time. Even so, it is an example showing that CATL technology can be applied to pickup trucks in the form of batteries produced locally in the United States. This is not the first time CATL has outlined plans to enter the U.S. market. CATL Chairman Robin Zeng previously said the company could build a local plant if it were allowed in the United States. Tesla also has a precedent in Nevada of using a license structure similar to CATL's LFP-related production technology. That production was limited to cells for energy storage systems, not vehicle batteries. The biggest variable blocking CATL's entry into the United States is politics and regulation rather than technological competitiveness. The United States applies high tariffs and strict localization requirements to Chinese-made products, and the possibility of national security-related regulation targeting Chinese companies remains. The U.S. government included CATL in January 2025 among targets of suspected military links. CATL strongly denied the allegation and previously said it could take legal action if necessary. Even if production takes place locally in the United States, debate could continue over the fact that the origin of the battery technology is China. Even so, CATL's move to design a separate battery for U.S. pickup trucks is interpreted as a signal it still sees strong growth potential in the local market. With pickup trucks accounting for a large share of the U.S. auto market, competition over the battery supply chain could intensify further if the electric pickup market expands. Whether it is actually adopted is expected to be decided by U.S. automakers, along with local production structures, trade policy and the stance on regulation targeting China. If CATL enters via technology licensing, it can highlight the benefits of U.S. production and job creation, but political backlash over dependence on Chinese technology remains a variable.

artigo.texto: ANNAPOLIS — Governor Wes Moore is implementing new rules for large data centers in Maryland while also pushing to end the industry's tax break. The executive order creates a Maryland Data Center Task Force aimed at protecting ratepayers, communities and the environment while increasing transparency around data center development. The task force will review projects based on five principles: ratepayer and grid protection, economic benefits for Marylanders, community input, environmental protections, and transparency and accountability. The new process applies to data centers using 25 megawatts or more once they seek state action, including a permit, incentive or letter of support. The task force will review those projects, support local governments and work with neighboring states. Each project will receive a public determination of Aligned, Conditionally Aligned or Not Aligned. The order also creates a public Data Center Dashboard that will be updated monthly. It will include information such as a project's location, developer, parent company, projected power demand and water use, along with state actions requested and decisions made. Moore also says he will work with the General Assembly during the upcoming legislative session to repeal the Data Center Sales and Use Tax Exemption enacted in 2020. artigo.texto: Centralized AI vs. Distributed AI vs. Edge AI: What’s the Difference? Choose an AI architecture based on your latency, cost, and compliance needs. The tech industry loves buzzwords, so it’s no surprise that a swarm of terms has emerged to describe AI infrastructure strategies. Centralized AI, distributed AI, and edge AI sound distinct at first glance, but in practice, their meanings overlap – and the lines between them can blur quickly. This overview clarifies what each term typically means, how they intersect, and what the practical implications are for data centers and enterprise deployments. Centralized AI: One Site, Many Nodes Centralized AI refers to hosting AI workloads in a single location. In modern practice, that usually means a single data center (or cloud region) running a cluster of servers. Although “centralized” might imply a single machine, today’s large-scale AI workloads, especially training and serving large language models (LLMs), almost always span multiple servers or GPUs due to high compute and memory demands. Local or on-device models that run on a single workstation do exist, but they are exceptions in enterprise contexts. In short, centralized AI concentrates resources and operations in one facility (or region), even if those workloads are distributed across many nodes within that one site. Distributed AI: Multisite by Design Distributed AI spreads AI workloads across multiple servers and, frequently, multiple sites. This is where confusion with centralized AI can creep in: both can involve multi-node clusters. The distinction is primarily about geography and site count. In enterprises, distributed AI often means deploying across multiple distinct data centers or cloud regions to serve different user populations, improve resilience, reduce latency for geographically dispersed users, or meet regulatory and data residency requirements. The operative idea is a multisite footprint by design. Edge AI: Compute Near Users and Data Edge AI places AI workloads near the network edge – close to end users, devices, or local data sources – to reduce latency, trim data transfer costs, or avoid round trips to a core data center. Organizations implement edge AI in several ways: compact edge data centers near users, regional or micro data centers for inference, or models pushed directly onto devices. Depending on the setup, these architectures may also qualify as distributed AI, underscoring the overlap in terminology. Think of “edge” as a location property (near users or data) and “distributed” as a topology property (multisite). Where These Approaches Actually Differ Because the terms overlap, it’s helpful to focus on what truly differentiates them in practice: Number and Placement of Sites Centralized AI typically uses a single data center or cloud region. Distributed AI spans multiple facilities, often in different regions or countries. Edge AI may also involve multiple sites, especially when using micro or regional data centers or on-device deployments. Performance and Cost Goals Distributed and edge strategies often target lower latency, locality, or lower egress costs by placing compute closer to users and data. Centralized AI prioritizes consolidation, capacity pooling, and operational simplicity over geographic optimization. Implementation and Operations Centralized AI is generally easier to set up, govern, and monitor because everything lives in one place. Distributed and edge architectures increase complexity, from orchestration and observability to data synchronization, failover design, and compliance. How Should You Decide? Rather than getting stuck on labels, align infrastructure with goals and constraints. If you have a single facility or region and need to quickly stand up capabilities, centralization offers a straightforward path. If you serve users in multiple geographies, must meet data residency mandates, or want to reduce latency and egress costs, a distributed footprint makes sense. Where ultra-low latency, intermittent connectivity, or bandwidth constraints dominate, edge deployments – potentially including on-device inference – will be compelling. Many enterprises ultimately blend these patterns: centralized training plus distributed or edge inference, tuned by workload criticality, latency budgets, and cost.

artigo.texto: O debate sobre Data Centers no Brasil entrou em uma nova fase. Em 15 de setembro, foi sancionada a Lei nº 15.504/2026, que instituiu o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata). O programa cria incentivos tributários para projetos de instalação, modernização ou ampliação dessas estruturas no país, incluindo ambientes destinados à computação em Nuvem, processamento de alto desempenho e treinamento e operação de modelos de Inteligência Artificial (IA). Até aqui, parte importante da discussão estava concentrada em tornar o Brasil mais competitivo para receber investimentos de grande porte. Com o Redata, surge outra questão: a infraestrutura brasileira conseguirá acompanhar a velocidade da expansão da capacidade computacional? Um Data Center não depende apenas dos servidores instalados dentro de um prédio. Para operar continuamente e em escala, precisa de energia disponível e confiável, capacidade de transmissão, conectividade, refrigeração e arquitetura adequada. Reduzir o custo de equipamentos pode melhorar a viabilidade econômica de um projeto, mas não elimina essas outras necessidades. A própria legislação mostra a dimensão desse desafio ao vincular os benefícios do Redata a compromissos como destinação de parte da capacidade ao mercado interno, critérios de sustentabilidade e atendimento da demanda de energia elétrica por fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão. Na minha visão, é aí que começa a próxima etapa. Atrair projetos é uma parte do caminho; transformá-los em capacidade efetivamente disponível exige que energia, conectividade e infraestrutura digital avancem de forma coordenada. Isso se torna ainda mais relevante com a expansão da IA. Quanto maior a demanda por processamento, mais estratégicas se tornam as condições para alimentar, conectar, resfriar e operar esses ambientes com segurança e previsibilidade. Também será necessário avaliar onde esses projetos poderão ser instalados e quanto tempo cada região levará para oferecer a estrutura necessária. Há ainda uma oportunidade importante: o Redata não contempla apenas novas instalações, mas projetos de modernização e ampliação. Isso abre espaço para aumentar a eficiência e aproveitar melhor a capacidade já existente, sem concentrar toda a discussão na chegada de novos empreendimentos. Claro, a nova legislação resolve uma parte relevante da equação ao criar um ambiente tributário específico para o setor, mas o próximo passo é garantir que atração de investimentos, energia, conectividade, sustentabilidade e planejamento tecnológico avancem como partes de uma mesma estratégia. O Brasil já sinalizou que pretende ampliar sua participação na expansão global dos Data Centers. Agora, o desafio é transformar esse interesse em infraestrutura capaz de sustentar, de fato, a demanda das empresas e o avanço da Inteligência Artificial. Por Eliézer Mota, CEO da Genux Consult

artigo.texto: Can Cars And Data Centers Carry Qualcomm Stock Past Apple? Qualcomm (QCOM) stock is up about 37% over the past six months, even after falling 21% over the past three. The case for the next leg rests outside phones, where management expects growth fast enough to cover a shrinking Apple business. The first real test arrives in the December quarter, when management expects its two custom data center wins to start producing revenue. Qualcomm stock has moved fast before. It has gained more than 30% in under two months 12 times since 2010, most recently in 2026. It is up 9.8% over the past year and sits about 29% below its 52-week high. Where Is Qualcomm Already Growing Outside Phones? Cars are the proof so far. Automotive sales rose 61% year over year in fiscal Q3 2026, another record quarter. In April management expected to leave fiscal 2026 at an annual run rate above $6 billion. By July it had raised that to about $7 billion. Part of the growth comes from more silicon in each car. BMW chose Qualcomm as its lead compute silicon provider for its next-generation ADAS and digital cockpit. And management said in July that the fifth-generation Snapdragon digital chassis, which it calls the largest content jump between generations in Qualcomm’s history, would start ramping in September. Can That Growth Cover What Apple Takes Away? Apple is leaving faster than planned, and Qualcomm’s own supply limits are part of the reason. The company now expects its share of Apple’s new iPhone launch to fall materially below the 20% it had assumed. Management forecasts Apple product revenue falling about 50% from the September quarter to the December quarter. For that quarter it expects Android growth to significantly offset the drop. The non-handset business is the fiscal 2027 answer, and management expects its growth to replace all of Apple’s fiscal 2026 product revenue. Management’s answer is the rest of the business. Qualcomm expects non-handset revenue growth over the prior year to jump from 24% in fiscal 2026 to more than 60% in fiscal 2027, growth it says will replace all of Apple’s fiscal 2026 product revenue. Data centers are the new part of that plan. Qualcomm has two custom silicon wins at global-scale hyperscalers, holds purchase orders, and has begun wafer production. The customer count has grown across two calls. In April management described one custom silicon engagement with a leading hyperscaler. By July there were two. Management sizes data center revenue at $5 billion in fiscal 2027 and $15 billion in fiscal 2029. Both sit inside a non-handset target of $40 billion by fiscal 2029, nearly double its earlier goal. Trailing revenue is $44.07 billion, so the target is close to the size of today’s whole company. For a company this large, a goal that size is not incremental. What Would Prove Qualcomm’s Data Center Plan Works? The doubt is execution. The CEO concedes the data center business is just starting and that investors want proof a new entrant can deliver. artigo.texto: By Mitch Perry, The Florida Phoenix David Jolly has already made it clear he’s a critic of large-scale data centers, for which Floridians continue to express disapproval up and down the state. The Democratic gubernatorial candidate had already said that if elected in November, he’d issue a one-year moratorium on construction of these facilities. But after visiting a region of Northern Virginia this week with the highest density of data centers in the country, he says he’s seen first-hand the economic and public health disruption they inflict on communities and that it’s not what he wants to see in the Sunshine State. “I visited a family with a home, you open the door and you’re hit with the noise pollution,” he said Friday after attending an event with Habitat for Humanity in Pinellas County. “You walk outside, you see the turbines that are fueling the energy. Down the street, there were four kids who developed respiratory conditions who had to seek medical help.” Data centers also are deflating real estate prices in their communities, Jolly said. He learned of a home near a massive data center that sat on the market for nearly a year and ended up selling for $80,000 below list price. “Let’s be honest about what’s happening in Florida,” he said. “Big tech, big data, the utilities are rushing into a relatively unregulated environment, or at least a favorably regulated environment. And that’s why you’re seeing voters who feel like they don’t have the economic or political power to push back, stand up, and say, ‘Please don’t do this.’ Local communities in Florida continue to say they don’t want data centers. This week, the Orange County Commission advanced a plan to temporarily ban data center development. Commissioners reached a consensus for a 6-to-18 month moratorium, depending on how long county staff need to research the potential harms, according to Orlando Weekly. Three local governments in Florida have permanently banned construction of data centers, and 19 are pausing such development, according to FloridaDataCenters.org. Already operating However, 12 data centers are already operating in Florida and another eight are planned, according to Cleanview, a marketing intelligence company. The Florida Legislature approved and Gov. Ron DeSantis signed legislation earlier this year that bans public utilities from passing the electricity costs of data centers onto residential and small business customers. It also preserved local authority over zoning, permitting, and land use for such centers, and gives local governments authority to set strict standards or deny projects. Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds has expressed support for letting local governments decide whether they want to construct data centers. He has dismissed Jolly’s one-year moratorium as “politics.” And Donalds said in Tampa earlier this month that construction of data centers would not resemble what Jolly visited this week. “In Northern Virginia, they built them next to apartment complexes and residential neighborhoods,” he said. “We’re not going to allow that in Florida. … If you’re going to do it, just do it a couple of miles down the road. Don’t do it in residential neighborhoods.” Advocates for data centers say they are needed in the United States, lest this country lose the race for AI superiority to China. The strongest advocate for that position is President Donald Trump. The Bureau of Land Management is reviewing data center-related proposals covering at least 17,600 acres of public land across six states — Arizona, Idaho, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, and Wyoming, the Washington Sun reported Friday. Jolly says he’s perfectly fine if the other 49 states build data centers — just not Florida. “There is no long-term economic impact from the data centers. There is the upfront construction jobs, but that there’s not the legacy economic impact that actually justifies the disruption of a community,” he said. “Look I do think that our national policymakers do need to work through some things to the extent that it’s a national security strategy. Let the White House and the Congress figure it out. But as Florida and Florida voters, we’re saying don’t build them here, let the other 49 states build them. It doesn’t hurt our national security strategy to say no to data centers in Florida.” The Donalds campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

artigo.texto: Envision Energy has energised Morocco’s first large-scale lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery energy storage system, but the 25 MW/125 MWh project at OCP Green Energy’s Benguerir mining site is designed for a role that goes beyond conventional grid-scale storage. The five-hour BESS is being deployed as an industrial energy-management system, integrating with the mining site's solar generation, grid conditions and electricity consumption profile. The system will store surplus solar power generated during the day and discharge it during peak consumption hours, with Envision expecting it to reduce OCP's peak-hour electricity bill by approximately 25%. The project, supplied and commissioned by Envision under a contract signed in late 2025, is currently undergoing testing before commercial operation. Five hours of storage changes the use case At 125 MWh, the system has five hours of storage duration at its 25 MW power rating. This allows the battery to shift a significant amount of daytime solar generation into periods when the industrial facility's electricity demand is higher. That makes the economic proposition different from a short-duration BESS primarily deployed for grid balancing or ancillary services. For OCP, the value of the battery is tied directly to how much renewable electricity can be shifted and how much peak-hour power costs can be avoided. Envision said the system is designed for a 25-year lifetime with daily charge-discharge cycles. The project has received $20 million from the Clean Technology Fund, managed through the African Development Bank Group. “The successful energisation of Morocco's first large-scale battery storage project demonstrates the reliability, flexibility and cost-effectiveness of integrated renewable-plus-storage solutions in industrial applications,” said John Lee, General Manager of Envision Energy for the Middle East and Africa. Storage becomes an extension of OCP's renewable strategy For OCP Green Energy, the battery is intended to address one of the central challenges of renewable power: solar generation does not necessarily coincide with industrial electricity demand. Omar Kadir, CEO of OCP Green Energy, described storage as the “natural extension” of the company's energy strategy, saying it allows the company to reconcile variable renewable generation with the continuous electricity requirements of its industrial operations. The project is therefore less about simply adding 125 MWh of battery capacity and more about connecting renewable generation with an industrial load that requires power beyond daylight hours. The company also sees storage as having implications beyond its own operations, with Kadir saying the technology could support greater integration of renewable energy into Morocco's national power system by adding flexibility and resilience. A potential model for industrial decarbonisation The Benguerir project could serve as a reference point for the use of long-duration storage at energy-intensive industrial facilities, particularly where companies are increasing their reliance on renewable electricity but still face a mismatch between generation and consumption. Morocco is targeting 52% of installed electricity capacity from renewable sources by 2030, making the ability to manage variable renewable generation increasingly important. For Envision, the project also provides an opportunity to demonstrate its storage technology in an industrial environment in the Middle East and Africa. The immediate commercial objective, however, remains specific: use solar power when it is generated, store the surplus and deploy it when the mine needs it most. That makes the Benguerir BESS not just a grid battery, but a tool for managing the economics and reliability of renewable power at one of Morocco's major industrial sites.

artigo.texto: Gov. Wes Moore laid out a data center policy plan Wednesday aimed at protecting Marylanders’ wallets and the environment, even as he steered clear of the statewide pauses enacted by some other state executives. Moore’s proposal, made by executive order, outlines uniform standards for reviewing data centers, establishes a task force within the governor’s office to help steer the state’s data center decision-making, and creates a dashboard for tracking projects across the state. Moore also pledged to work with lawmakers to repeal a broad tax exemption for data centers, approved by the General Assembly in 2020. According to a recent report from the watchdog group Good Jobs First, that exemption cost Maryland $22 million in forgone revenues in 2026 alone. The announcement comes as concerns about data center growth and the artificial intelligence industry they power have become a top political issue across Maryland and the country while federal officials have yet to take action. “By signing this executive order, we are establishing clear safeguards to ensure Marylanders do not foot the bill, our people benefit, community voices are heard, and our environment is protected — all while centering transparency and accountability throughout the process,” Moore said in a statement on the order. Moore, a Democrat, made data centers part of his plan to boost Maryland’s economy and reduce the state’s reliance on jobs in the federal government, healthcare and education. Moore has cautioned against giving data center companies “free rein” to write their own rules and has urged local say-so over projects. Still, many data center critics hope to keep the massive server farms out of Maryland for good, and Moore’s plan stops short of the statewide pause that some advocates have called for. The announcement comes days after Moore told political news site Punchbowl that if the legislature approves a statewide moratorium or ban, he will “absolutely” sign it. The General Assembly instituted guardrails for data center developers earlier this year, but since then calls for a pause have grown louder, and lawmakers are expected to weigh various moratorium bills in the upcoming session. For some local leaders, large data center developments promise jobs and property tax windfalls, but others have already moved to slow new data center expansion. Counties from the deep-blue Washington, D.C., suburbs to the conservative Eastern Shore have enacted data center moratoriums of varying lengths, while Republican-led Harford County approved the state’s first indefinite ban in June. Wednesday’s executive order also comes as governors across the country have raced to outline stricter data center policies in recent months. Some of those governors have enacted sweeping development stoppages: In July, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signed a one-year pause on hyperscale data centers. And on Tuesday, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott paused reviews of all data center permits. Others have chosen a softer approach. Last week, Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger issued an executive order aimed at tightening policies around data center development, while California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a slate of bills cracking down on the industry’s usage of land, water and energy. Unlike those two states, which each house hundreds of data centers, the industry remains in its infancy in Maryland. Frederick County has the state’s only approved hyperscale project. On Tuesday, Moore announced a series of proposals to regulate the artificial intelligence industry in the state as existential fears over unbridled AI have compounded data center anxieties.

artigo.texto: A Evos, empresa do Grupo Interjato especializada em conectividade e segurança no transporte de dados, está ampliando sua infraestrutura de fibra óptica no Rio Grande do Norte para atender ao crescimento da demanda por conectividade de alta capacidade e resiliência associada a datacenters, supercomputação e aplicações de Inteligência Artificial. CONTEÚDO RELACIONADO – Redata pode favorecer data center de IA ligado à estratégia de soberania digital do governo Atualmente, a empresa possui 1.441 quilômetros de fibra óptica no Rio Grande do Norte e está implantando 410 quilômetros de rede subterrânea, modelo que reduz a exposição da infraestrutura a ocorrências em redes aéreas e aumenta a proteção das rotas físicas. Para os próximos seis meses, estão planejados mais 245 quilômetros de fibra, expansão que permitirá à Evos chegar a Fortaleza (CE) com infraestrutura própria. Com as duas etapas, a malha da companhia passará dos 2,1 mil quilômetros de fibra óptica. O movimento ocorre em um momento de expansão da infraestrutura computacional no estado. Em agosto, o Governo Federal anunciou a implantação, no Parque Científico e Tecnológico Augusto Severo (PAX), em Macaíba, de um novo supercomputador de alto desempenho voltado à Inteligência Artificial. Conduzido tecnicamente pelo Laboratório Nacional de Computação Científica (LNCC/MCTI), o projeto integra o Plano Brasileiro de Inteligência Artificial (PBIA) e deverá ampliar a capacidade nacional para desenvolvimento, treinamento e utilização de modelos avançados de IA. Para a Evos, a chegada de uma infraestrutura computacional desse porte evidencia uma nova categoria de demanda para o Rio Grande do Norte: além de energia e capacidade computacional, operações críticas de IA e data centers dependem de redes de alta capacidade, disponibilidade, redundância e diversidade física de rotas. A infraestrutura da empresa foi concebida para permitir interconexão com múltiplos carriers e rotas fisicamente distintas, reduzindo pontos únicos de falha e ampliando a resiliência necessária a operações que precisam permanecer disponíveis de forma contínua. Segundo Erich Rodrigues, CEO do Grupo Interjato, o anúncio do supercomputador eleva o patamar da discussão sobre infraestrutura digital no estado. “O Rio Grande do Norte começa a reunir componentes que podem colocá-lo em uma nova posição no mapa da infraestrutura digital brasileira. Energia renovável é uma vantagem importante, mas aplicações críticas de Inteligência Artificial precisam também de conectividade de alta capacidade, redundância e rotas fisicamente independentes. É nessa camada que estamos investindo”, afirma. O estado possui mais de 98% de sua potência instalada de geração elétrica proveniente de fontes renováveis, principalmente eólica e solar. Na avaliação do Grupo Interjato, essa disponibilidade cria uma vantagem competitiva para projetos de infraestrutura digital intensivos em energia, desde que acompanhada por avanços em transmissão elétrica, conectividade, licenciamento e segurança operacional. A expansão da Evos faz parte dessa estratégia. Além de reforçar a infraestrutura dentro do Rio Grande do Norte, a chegada a Fortaleza por fibra própria amplia as alternativas de conexão interestadual e aproxima a rede de um dos principais pontos de conectividade internacional do país. “Nossa visão é contribuir para que o Rio Grande do Norte transforme sua vantagem energética em uma vantagem também digital. Para isso, não basta ter geração de energia ou terrenos disponíveis. É preciso construir uma infraestrutura capaz de dar previsibilidade e segurança a quem pretende instalar operações críticas no estado. A nossa contribuição é entregar a camada de conectividade necessária para que esses projetos possam operar e crescer”, acrescenta Rodrigues. A expansão anunciada é a primeira etapa de uma estratégia da Evos direcionada a infraestruturas digitais de missão crítica. A companhia pretende aprofundar, nos próximos meses, iniciativas envolvendo diversidade de rotas, interconexão com carriers, redundância, conectividade interestadual e atendimento às novas demandas de data centers e computação de alto desempenho. A Evos é uma empresa do Grupo Interjato especializada em conectividade, SD-WAN e segurança no transporte de dados para empresas privadas e instituições públicas. Integra um grupo com mais de 30 anos de atuação em tecnologia e conectividade e possui certificações ISO/IEC 20000 e ISO/IEC 27001. artigo.texto: CATL Achieves 2025 Core Operation Carbon Neutrality Target, Sets Path to 2035 Value-Chain Goal NINGDE, China, Aug. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — CATL today announced it had achieved its 2025 target of carbon neutrality across core operations as scheduled, with all 20 battery plants certified as carbon neutral, and unveiled its action roadmap toward full value-chain carbon neutrality by 2035. This signals that decarbonization has evolved from a corporate social responsibility to a core growth driver for CATL. At a launch event held in Ningde on Monday, the company also called on global partners to accelerate decarbonization across the battery value chain. It announced procurement guidelines that require suppliers to provide carbon footprint data from 2027, and offers favorable terms to suppliers with better carbon emission performance. Robin Zeng, Chairman and CEO of CATL, said: Before contributing to global carbon rules and standards, CATL must first prove what is possible through our own industrial practice, “As the world ramps up efforts toward net-zero, zero-carbon batteries will not be a choice but a necessity in the near future. We are ready to share our technologies and experience with partners across the industry, helping to shape global carbon standards and advance industry-wide decarbonization.” 2025 Carbon Neutrality Target for Core Operations Delivered as Planned Since the commissioning of our first battery factory in 2012, CATL has been exploring and validating every aspect of zero-carbon manufacturing. This has become an integral part of CATL. Jiang Li, Vice President, Board Secretary and Head of Corporate Sustainable Development Management Committee of CATL, said, “Carbon neutrality cannot be built on estimates alone. It requires reliable data, clear boundaries and systematic execution.” To build this data foundation, CATL independently developed the CATL Carbon Chain Management System (CCMS) in 2022 to monitor and calculate carbon emissions at its plants and production lines. To date, CATL CCMS has covered carbon data across battery production operations and core upstream suppliers, generating more than 1,000 product and raw material models. Based on this data system, CATL embeds decarbonization efforts across process and equipment optimization, battery design, green energy consumption, raw‑material sourcing and recycling. In 2025, zero-carbon electricity accounted for 100% of electricity consumption in its core operations, with more than 18 billion kWh of zero-carbon power consumed cumulatively since 2023. Energy consumption per unit of product at its battery manufacturing bases decreased by 28% compared with 2022, below the industry average. Its carbon emission intensity decreased by approximately 77% compared with 2022. From 2023 to 2025, CATL delivered a cumulative carbon reduction of over 10 million tons of CO₂ equivalent, comparable to Brunei’s total national carbon emissions in 2025. The milestone not only marks CATL’s first fulfilled carbon neutrality commitment, but also sets a new benchmark for carbon neutrality practices in the lithium-ion battery industry. Advancing Toward Full Value-Chain Carbon Neutrality by 2035 More than 80% of carbon emissions across CATL’s product lifecycle stem from its supply chain, with total value-chain emissions exceeding five times those generated in core operations. Bryan Huang, Head of Procurement Center at CATL, said: CATL will advance value-chain decarbonization across key areas including material innovation, material manufacturing, green logistics, and battery recycling. This requires collaboration across the entire battery value chain In terms of data management, baseline carbon data has been established for more than 100 core Tier 1 suppliers, and CATL aims to progressively achieve 100% data coverage across key upstream links. For emissions reductions, CATL will pursue decarbonization in four pillars: material and process innovation, manufacturing, green logistics and battery recycling. - Material innovation: CATL is focusing on green material innovation and low-carbon process upgrades. For example, for anodes, the company is promoting the adoption of low‑carbon materials such as raw petroleum coke with lower moisture and volatile content. - Material manufacturing: Given the energy-intensive nature of upstream raw material production, CATL has launched a green power coverage plan, targeting 100% green electricity usage across the value chain by 2035. - Green logistics: Leveraging its advanced battery technology and battery swapping network, CATL is promoting 100% zero-carbon logistics solutions across the industry chain. - Battery Recycling: CATL will continue to accelerate the development of a global battery recycling network through Brunp Recycling. To support supplier decarbonization, CATL will issue its Green Procurement Guidelines requiring new suppliers to provide product carbon footprint data and incorporating renewable electricity usage and energy efficiency into annual supplier reviews. Under comparable conditions, suppliers with stronger low-carbon performance may be prioritized in order allocation and supported through long-term agreements. CATL will also launch its Zero-Carbon Supply Chain Empowerment Initiative, launching in-depth joint decarbonization initiatives with an initial cohort of 30 core suppliers. The economics of zero-carbon opens substantial new growth opportunities. CATL is making strong efforts in zero-carbon mobility, zero-carbon power, and the electrification of industries, with several application scenarios already implemented. Together with global partners, CATL aims to expand the zero-carbon economy, accelerate the global clean energy transition, and help create a more sustainable future. artigo.texto: Data centers drawing 25 megawatts or more of electricity are no longer allowed on Allegheny County-owned property. County Council voted unanimously Tuesday to prohibit the construction, operation or establishment of large-scale data centers — and the infrastructure built specifically to support them — on county-owned land and in county-owned buildings. The measure does not restrict data centers on privately owned property, leaving those land-use decisions to individual municipalities. The ordinance had broad support ahead of Tuesday’s votes, with council’s Sustainability and Green Initiatives Committee unanimously advancing it last week. Sponsors of the bill include President Michelle Naccarati-Chapkis, D-Plum; Dan Grzybek, D-Bethel Park; Kathleen Madonna-Emmerling, D-Moon; Lissa Geiger Shulman, D-Hampton; Pat Catena, D-Carnegie; Paul Klein, D-Pittsburgh; Jordan Botta, D-Bloomfield; and at-large members Bethany Hallam, D-North Side, and Alex Rose, I-Squirrel Hill. On Tuesday, Rose, who chairs the Sustainability and Green Initiatives Committee, explained to the council that the committee adopted an amendment to help avoid accidentally banning servers from “existing on Allegheny property” and avoid unintended impacts on facilities such as county server operations and the 911 center. Under the bill, infrastructure associated with data centers, including generators, utility lines, cooling water and wastewater treatment facilities, water-holding facilities, pump stations, water towers and other environmental controls are prohibited. Also, county property can no longer be used for data center ancillary use or secondary structures such as administrative, logistical, fiber optic, storage and security buildings or structures. The council opted not to impose a countywide land-use ban because, under Pennsylvania law, zoning and land-use decisions involving private property are made by individual municipalities rather than the county. Private developers could still potentially propose a data center in a municipality subject to that municipality’s zoning and other applicable laws. Some municipalities in Allegheny County already host existing smaller data centers or have larger projects proposed. In Springdale, a major planned data center would stand 75 feet tall and stretch over 652,000 square feet. Several boroughs and townships, including East Deer, Oakmont, Tarentum, Upper Burrell, Murrysville and Gilpin, have adopted or are in the process of implementing ordinances similar to the county in an effort to regulate data center development.

artigo.texto: BALTIMORE COUNTY, Md. — Data centers have been up for debate in Baltimore County for quite some time. Currently, there's a moratorium on data center developments until January 1st. On Tuesday, Baltimore County Council will decide whether or not to extend that pause to December 2027. "The public needs much more of an opportunity to comment on data centers," said Councilman David Marks, "This is a very complex issue that involved land use, taxation, water use, and we don't want to rush judgment on any of these issues." At a council meeting last week, many neighbors agreed but urged members to take it a step further. "Extend the moratorium and change "am" to "or" and seriously consider whether they should be there at all. It's our land, our home, and we have carried enough on the east side," one resident said. However, another man asked for an amendment to allow the moratorium to end early once appropriate regulations are adopted. "Data centers can provide significant income and economic opportunities for Baltimore County including good family sustaining union jobs that means opportunities not only for experienced trades people, but also new workers," he told council members. President and CEO of the Maryland Tech Council, Kelly Schulz is also against the pause. She previously told WMAR-2 News that the county could risk missing out on opportunities for growth. "I think this is a way to look at a way to advance our innovation and our technology industries," Schulz said. The vote is scheduled for Tuesday at 6 p.m. This is a developing story, so check back with WMAR2News.com for updates. Email the WMAR-2 Newsroom if you have info, photos or videos to share. artigo.texto: 'We don't know how to be proactive': Data center fight intensifying in central Wisconsin "UPFRONT' recap: Inside the proposed data center controversy in Wisconsin Rapids Wisconsin Rapids Mayor Matt Zacher said he backs a one-year moratorium on data center construction amid growing controversy in the city surrounding a proposed data center on the city's old paper mill site. "The problem I see in this situation is that we are acting reactively," Zacher said on WISN 12's "UPFRONT" which is produced in partnership with WisPolitics. "We don't know how to be proactive necessarily because nobody's really ever done; there's no playbook on this." Last week, the city's plan commission unanimously rejected a conditional use permit from New York-based PNK Group, which is proposing the 200-acre data center on the city's old paper mill site. The recommendation is now before the full city council alongside a separate proposal for a one-year data center moratorium. "They kind of throw it in our lap," Zacher said. "They know that we're unqualified. I'm not saying, you know, I'm doing pretty well, if I do say so myself, trying to juggle all of these things. But am I really qualified for this high level of a situation and negotiation and trying to figure this stuff out? And I think if the data centers were really being super real and fair about what's happening, they would back off. They would give us some time." The city's plan commission heard more than three hours of public comment last week on the proposal, a majority opposing the data center, including GOP State Rep. Scott Krug, who represents Wisconsin Rapids. "It's nothing against anybody in the trades," Krug said. "There will be other projects, and we will get a chance to use that local labor and make sure that the IBEW and the electric workers and pipefitters and the steamfitters and all the guys who lost their jobs at the mill are going to have a chance in Wisconsin Rapids again, but it's not going to be this one." GOP State Sen. Patrick Testin said four key state Senate races ahead of November are "tight" and "statistical toss-ups" in the battle for control of the chamber. "That's why we keep telling all of our staff that are up in these key races, we keep telling the candidates keep working, keep knocking doors and getting their message out there," said Testin, who leads the Committee to Elect a Republican Senate. The four key districts include the 5th between Republican Mike Roberts and Democrat Robyn Vining, the 21st featuring Republican Jim Croft and Democrat Trevor Jung, the 17th featuring GOP State Sen. Howard Marklein and Democrat Jenna Jacobson and the 31st featuring Democrat State Sen. Jeff Smith and Republican Michele Magadance Skinner. "We affectionately call them the core four," Testin said. "When you look at the odds in the math, we have to win two out of those four to come back in the majority. And I believe that we are going to, at least, not win all of them, but I feel good with where we're at." When asked if Republicans are urging candidates to distance themselves from President Donald Trump, Testin said, "Well, look, we can't control what happens in D.C. We can't control the cost of gas. What we can control is things like income taxes, property taxes and do what we can to make things more affordable." "I think despite the fact that there are some national headwinds," Testin added. "I think we are well positioned to come back in the majority." Watch: WisPolitics Editor JR Ross has the latest analysis on key state Senate races.

artigo.texto: Anne Arundel County is backing away from a proposed ban on new data centers and instead considering a temporary pause on new development while officials decide how to regulate the facilities. The County Council unanimously approved an amendment to Bill 63-26 that would replace the proposed ban with a moratorium lasting until January 31, 2028, or until the county adopts comprehensive data center legislation, whichever comes first. During the moratorium, the county would establish a work group to study data center development and recommend regulations to the county executive and council. The group would consider issues including energy and water use, utility infrastructure, climate and environmental impacts, air quality, noise and economic development. Projects already in the development process would generally be allowed to continue. The amendment also includes future phases of existing data centers on adjacent or adjoining properties. The original bill drew concerns from residents about the potential impact of data centers on electricity demand, water use, noise and the environment. Others argued a countywide ban could hurt Anne Arundel County's technology and cybersecurity sector, particularly around Fort Meade, NSA and U.S. Cyber Command. Microsoft, which is developing a data center campus at Annapolis Junction Business Park, testified against the original ban. A company representative said Microsoft has completed two buildings at the site and plans additional phases. The company said it supports data center regulations and a work group but wants existing campuses to continue development. The amendment also calls for repealing a personal property tax assessment reduction for data storage centers. The County Council approved the amendment 7-0. The amended bill is scheduled to come back before the council on October 5. This is a developing story, so check back with WMAR2News.com for updates. artigo.texto: The Eugene City Council returned Sept. 14 from their summer break to a room packed full of residents. All members of the council, barring Ward 3 councilor Alan Zelenka, were in attendance. Mayor Kaarin Knudson expressed her appreciation for those in attendance, who would later share their thoughts during public comment. Mayor Knudson’s proclamations Knudson then moved on to acknowledge the Fiesta Cultural and Cascade Chorus Barbershop Harmony Day events, which took place earlier this month. Knudson also highlighted the Society for the Legitimization of the Ubiquitous Gastropod Queen Celebration Week, which will take place Sept. 20 through 26. Following these proclamations, council members were given the opportunity to speak on items of personal interest. These comments largely regarded the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks in New York City on Sept. 11, 2001. Ward 2 councilor Matt Keating read the words of a plaque he visited this summer at the United States Capitol building, which honors United Airlines Flight 93 and said, “May we never forget.” Randy Groves, councilor representing Ward 8, highlighted the annual stair climb hosted by local firefighters, which takes place in remembrance of those lost at Autzen Stadium each year. He spoke to his personal experience on that day as a former local firefighter and fire chief of Eugene Springfield Fire. “Our first priority, of course, was always to protect this community,” Groves said. Knudson closed by encouraging community members to reflect on their personal experiences regarding that tragedy. “It is important to think about what we do when we feel afraid and how we decide to walk into the future with courage and compassion,” Knudson said. Dozens of public commentators speak to council Approximately 72 individuals were signed up to give public comments, while more spectated. The public comment period is restricted to 90 minutes or ending at 10 p.m., whichever comes first. Only 43 of those 72 were able to address the council before time expired. The majority of public comment was in response to a recent proposal to use the former Hynix site for a data center. Residents expressed everything from environmental concerns to personal beliefs as reasons for councilors to bar this land purchase or construction. Many called for a moratorium, a legally authorized period of delay, which could allow for further public discussion and regulations to be put in place. However, Knudson revealed that this action would not be necessary since the construction of a data center at this site is already not allowed under city zoning regulations. In a Sept. 8 letter, the city outlined that the site is within an E-1 or Campus Employment zone, which does not currently list data centers as a permitted use for the land. Additionally, a city council work session is currently scheduled for Dec. 14 to discuss data centers in more detail. This letter’s content and city action were acknowledged by numerous public commentators as a “step in the right direction,” however, they still advocated that there is far more work to be done. Theo Milligan, a resident of Ward 5, explained that Eugene’s nature and greenery are among its defining characteristics and appeals. Milligan expressed their belief that “a data center would be the antithesis of our entire community.” With the Willow Creek Preserve nearby the proposed site, they worry that a data center would poison the land, saying “We cannot let this happen.” Later on in the public comment, Ellen Bridges, a lifelong resident of the Pacific Northwest, sang a song for the councilors. “I am going to sing out for the love of clean water, … of clean air, (and) the freedom of silence,” Bridges said. They explained their belief that while data centers are not necessary, these things are for the health of a city. Finally, Bridges thanked the council and urged them to set a good example, ending their statement with, “The only data center that I want is a library.” Nate Rhoads, during their comments, cited National Public Radio, which said that despite political polarization both the Democratic and Republican parties can agree on two things. “One: Dolly Parton was a saint. And two: the majority of voters … opposed data centers in their communities,” Rhoads said. They went on to explain that as a constituent and a taxpayer, they are “somehow (the) boss” of council members, with Rhoads stating, “As one of your many bosses, I am telling you, just say no to large-scale data centers.” In addition to comments regarding data centers, residents also raised concerns about public safety and policing in Eugene. One resident shared the effects that losing the CAHOOTS program has caused. Jacob Trewe of Ward 1 said, “There is a clear and evident gap in public safety that needs addressing.” True went on to cite a study by the Rohlfs Lab at the University of Oregon that showed that of the 235 calls that CAHOOTS used to cover, now 126 calls per week are being unaddressed. Board President Lisa Levsen of Neighbors Feeding Neighbors in Eugene spoke out regarding the policing in Washington Jefferson Park, where meals are served. “We have people who are afraid to come for meals because they don’t want to be arrested,” Levsen said. Levsen went on to urge councilors to create further conversation and positive change to “take care of our most fragile citizens.” The next Eugene City Council meeting will be held Monday, Sept. 28.

artigo.texto: Local leaders in Tucson and Cedar Rapids share different approaches to one of the country’s fastest-growing development issues WASHINGTON — As demand for Artificial Intelligence (AI) and cloud computing drives rapid data center development across the country, local governments are confronting complex decisions about water and energy use, infrastructure, economic development and community impact. More than 3,000 data centers currently operate in the United States, and more than half of the world’s hyperscale or AI data centers are located here. NLC research has found that at least 120 communities have adopted moratoria on data centers and 60 have passed new zoning regulations this year. In a new episode of the National League of Cities’ CitiesSpeak podcast, Kate Stoll, project director at the American Association for the Advancement of Science Center for Scientific Evidence in Public Issues; Tucson, Ariz. Councilmember Nikki Lee; and Cedar Rapids, Iowa Mayor Tiffany O’Donnell examine the choices communities face as data center proposals expand nationwide. What Local Leaders Should Know The Scale of a Project Matters Data centers vary significantly in their demand for local resources. Stoll explains that a 100-megawatt hyperscale facility can use roughly as much electricity as 80,000 U.S. households, while a large facility’s peak water use can reach between one and eight million gallons per day. She recommends that communities evaluate energy, water, air quality, infrastructure costs, jobs and tax revenue before making development decisions. NLC and the AAAS EPI Center developed the Key Questions to Ask When Considering a Data Center in Your Community resource to help local leaders evaluate these considerations and better understand the potential benefits and impacts of proposed projects. “These are questions you could ask of data center developers to get a real handle on what will be the impacts of the data centers, what will be the positive benefits, what will be the drawbacks, with the ultimate goal of bringing more clarity and transparency for communities so that they can make informed decisions for their communities.” — Kate Stoll, Project Director, AAAS EPI Center Tucson Chose Stronger Guardrails After Rejecting a Hyperscale Proposal After significant community concern contributed to the city’s decision not to move forward with annexation for the proposed $3.6 billion Project Blue, Tucson spent nearly a year developing new regulations with input from a 13-member technical advisory committee and the public. Councilmember Lee says the process reinforced the importance of considering the full system of water, energy, infrastructure and environmental impacts, and engaging residents early. “You really have to look at the whole system and not just, for example, water. What does the water meter at the site say? We have to look at the whole picture on what resources are actually necessary to power and operate these facilities.” — Councilmember Nikki Lee, Tucson, Ariz. Cedar Rapids Has Taken a Different Path The city is welcoming two hyperscale facilities after years of planning and due diligence around infrastructure capacity. Mayor O’Donnell says development agreements are expected to generate significant property tax revenue and include investments in water, wastewater and other infrastructure, as well as community betterment funding. “Ask for what you need, know what you need. Do your due diligence, good relationships and communicate with the public. The public has to know all that’s going on if you want the project to have any shot at being successful.” — Mayor Tiffany O’Donnell, Cedar Rapids, Iowa The conversation underscores that there is no single approach to data center development for every community. Local leaders are weighing different economic opportunities, infrastructure capacities, environmental considerations and resident concerns as they determine what, and under what conditions, makes sense locally. Listen to the full conversation, also available on Apple Podcasts, Spotify and YouTube. About CitiesSpeak Each episode of NLC’s podcast, CitiesSpeak with Clarence Anthony, dives into a critical issue facing local leaders today, featuring conversations with elected leaders and policy experts from across the country. The podcast is a relaxed and entertaining resource for local policymakers looking for ideas and information to bring back to their communities. The podcast is hosted by NLC CEO and Executive Director Clarence Anthony, who previously served as mayor of South Bay, Florida, for more than two decades. New episodes of CitiesSpeak are available on all major podcasting platforms and on YouTube. If you have feedback for the show or ideas for future guests, email us. Happy listening!

Summary As AI workloads drive unprecedented growth in data center capacity and density, cooling infrastructure has become an increasingly critical factor in getting facilities online quickly and reliably. Traditional piping methods such as welding, brazing and grooving can introduce labor-intensive processes, sequential work dependencies and skilled labor constraints that make it difficult to keep pace with aggressive construction schedules. This webinar explores how modern press technology can help data center owners, engineers and contractors rethink the design and installation of cooling and fluid systems. Viewers will learn how eliminating hot work and reducing installation time can support parallel construction workflows, accelerate commissioning and create a more scalable approach to high-density data center development. The session will also examine opportunities to improve consistency, quality and sustainability across cooling infrastructure while maintaining the standards and performance required for mission-critical environments. Key Takeaways: - Understand the mechanical infrastructure challenges affecting AI data center speed-to-market. - Learn how press technology can significantly reduce piping installation time. - Explore how eliminating hot work enables safer, more parallel construction workflows. - Discover ways to improve consistency, commissioning efficiency and system quality at scale. - See how press systems support chilled water, cooling loops and other critical data center applications.

artigo.texto: Jørgensen urged tech companies to view EU efforts to regulate their environmental impact as an "opportunity" that could help them win over a skeptical public. | EP BRUSSELS — Brussels on Monday unveiled an environmental rating scheme for data centers that power artificial intelligence, a move the EU's energy chief described as the first step in pressuring tech giants into aligning with the continent’s climate efforts. The new rules, which will apply from August 2027, oblige big data centers to display a label grading them on their energy efficiency, water usage and clean power uptake on a scale of A to G, much like the EU's influential appliances ranking. “This will add a lot of transparency and hopefully provide the incentives for these data centers to be as sustainable as possible,” said Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen in an interview with POLITICO ahead of the label's presentation. Advertisement The new label is optional for smaller data centers, “but later we are also going to introduce minimum performance standards which, of course, will put more pressure on those who may not voluntarily wish to be as sustainable as we want them to,” he added. While Australia and Singapore already have schemes rating the energy efficiency of data centers, the Commission's new label would be the most comprehensive worldwide — asking tech companies to be transparent not only about their power use but also their impact on the local and global environment via information on how much water they consume, how clean their electricity is, whether they reuse the heat they generate and more. The EU executive's performance standards, which the Commission wants to present in spring 2027, are expected to tighten the screws by setting mandatory sustainability thresholds for newly built or retrofitted data centers. Those two initiatives are an attempt at ensuring the European Union can compete in the artificial intelligence race without sacrificing its commitment to climate neutrality in 2050, Jørgensen said. “We need to deal with this in a way that data centers in the future are not something that will hurt our energy systems, and thereby our competitiveness and capabilities of decarbonizing and making sure we have security of supply for our citizens,” he said. “If we do not make sure that these big power consumers are indeed in line with our overall objectives… then they will risk undermining our ability to live up to our own targets,” Jørgensen warned. Data centers are already hoovering up 2.5% of the bloc’s electricity use, a share expected to double in the coming years, he noted. “We’re looking at a huge change.” Advertisement Monday's announcement is a delegated regulation, meaning that it can take effect without the input of EU governments and the European Parliament. The two institutions have two months to object to the regulation, however. The label will be generated automatically each year from figures companies are already required to report under the bloc's energy efficiency rules, though an accompanying Commission report acknowledges that compliance with those rules is low: Only 36% of sites in the EU disclose required data. Go green, get popular Data center operators have lobbied against the Commission's plans. The European Data Center Association in April warned that the requirements would kill investment and in June insisted that the bloc must prioritize AI ambitions over its climate goals. Earlier this year, a Commission document seen by POLITICO indicated that around 20 percent of Europe’s data centers could land at the bottom of the new rating scheme. But Jørgensen urged tech companies to view EU efforts to regulate their environmental impact as an "opportunity" that could help them win over a skeptical public. In the United States, a backlash is mounting against AI infrastructure, in part over its voracious appetite for energy and water. Similar protests are starting to emerge in Europe. Advertisement “We do see some places where public opinion is maybe turning a little bit against these data centers, we've seen it in some places in Europe and we see it even more so in the United States of America,” said Jørgensen. “So I firmly believe that it's also in the interest of the data centers to be able to show how sustainable they are.” But he indicated that the EU would not impose bloc-wide rules requiring data center operators to provide their own clean energy, something his Commission colleague Teresa Ribera advocated for in a recent interview with POLITICO. “This will always be a national decision,” he said. Still, government efforts such as Spain’s recent move toward forcing data centers to provide a share of their own renewable power are “a part of the solution in many places, because the consumption of these data centers will be so big,” he added. Overall, Jørgensen said, the EU wants to avoid developments such as in the U.S., where data centers are increasing the demand for polluting fossil fuels. “My overall message to the Big Tech sector is: We want AI, of course, we want data centers, we want Europe to be a place for investments, but it's in the interest of them and of the European Union that we do it in a way that is sustainable,” he said. “And we will be setting demands for them.”

artigo.texto: UK energy industry regulator Ofgem said it is minded to approve the introduction of a financial commitment for BESS in an attempt to reduce the oversupply of the projects awaiting a grid connection. There is about 90GW of battery energy storage (BESS) capacity either operational or in the reformed connections queue, almost three times the 29GW that the government is targeting as part of its Clean Power 2030 target. The Oversubscribed Technologies Commitment Fee (OTCF) would require projects to demonstrate a minimum level of financial commitment starting at £3,000 per MW and rising to a maximum £25,000 per MW if the queue remains significantly oversubscribed. Ofgem said that while battery storage has a “vital role” to play in a clean energy system, the scale of the queue “makes it difficult to know which projects are genuinely likely to be built”. This was the issue with the broader grid connection queue before it was reformed to follow a ‘first ready, first connected’ process. artigo.texto: RWE secures 119 MW of onshore wind capacity in latest German auction 18.09.2026 The Moerdijk power station site will be home to a flagship large-scale battery system in the Netherlands. RWE has taken the final investment decision to build a 400 megawatts (MW) and 1100 megawatt-hours (MWh) battery storage system at the site. It will consist of 208 containers with lithium-ion batteries and can deliver its full output for almost three hours. Construction is scheduled to start in due course, commissioning is planned for second quarter of 2028. Nikolaus Valerius, CEO of RWE Generation SE: “This battery marks a major milestone for reliable power supply and grid relief in Noord-Brabant. As one of the largest and most powerful battery systems in the Netherlands, it will be capable of covering the evening peak demand of around 500,000 households for almost three hours. At the same time, it can absorb surplus electricity from the grid within seconds. Battery storage plays a crucial role in building a resilient energy system that can accommodate a growing share of renewables.” Mark Lentjes, Regional Director of TenneT Southern Netherlands: “We are pleased that RWE intends to contribute to a more efficient use of the electricity grid in West Brabant with a large-scale battery that acts as a congestion reliever. RWE’s large-scale battery is located close to the 150,000-volt high-voltage substation at Moerdijk-Noord, where it will help to alleviate the regional bottleneck, which in turn has an impact on congestion across the whole of Noord-Brabant.“ Moerdijk battery to relieve grid congestion The new battery system will make best use of the existing infrastructure: It will be connected to the national grid via the existing substation at the RWE power plant in Moerdijk. Through capacity steering agreements with Transmission System Operator TenneT, the battery will be dispatched to relieve congestion in the Noord-Brabant region. Thanks to this development, space is being created on the grid for parties on the waiting list who wish to purchase electricity. TenneT, together with the regional grid operator Enexis, will be investigating what this means in the coming period. The grid operator will take this development, along with other developments in the region, into account when reviewing the congestion management study in December of 2026. The new battery system will also be equipped to provide advanced grid services such as instantaneous reserve (inertia). The Moerdijk site already hosts the first synthetic inertia battery connected to the continental European grid, with a capacity of 7.5 MW/11 MWh. Matching offshore wind with onshore flexibility RWE and TotalEnergies’ 795 MW offshore wind project off the Dutch coast, is designed to combine offshore wind generation with onshore flexibility solutions that help align renewable power production with electricity demand. At Moerdijk, the battery projects play an important role here by storing electricity when wind output is high and feeding it back into the system when needed, helping to balance fluctuations and optimise the use of renewable power. Together with technologies such as electrolysis, e-boilers and smart charging, it supports OranjeWind’s ambition to integrate offshore wind more effectively into the Dutch energy system. Battery storage at RWE As a driver of the energy transition, RWE develops, builds and operates battery storage systems in the US, Europe and Australia. In the Netherlands, RWE currently operates two battery storage systems. In addition to the existing battery at Moerdijk, RWE operates a 35 MW/41 MWh battery at Eemshaven power plant. Globally, RWE currently operates battery storage systems with a total capacity of around 1.7 gigawatts (GW) and 3 GW are under construction. As an integral part of its growth strategy, RWE plans to significantly expand its battery storage capacities worldwide. artigo.texto: Energy-Storage.news speaks with Nathan Picarsic, co-founder of Horizon Advisory, at the 2026 US Battery Asset Management and Solar and Storage Finance Summits in Garden Grove, California. Changes to traditional tax equity structures and growing geopolitical tensions are fundamentally reshaping how renewable energy projects secure financing in the US, according to Nathan Picarsic, co-founder of Horizon Advisory, a geopolitical and supply chain risk intelligence provider. Picarsic outlines how legislative changes enabling tax credit transferability have opened up renewable energy financing to a much broader pool of capital allocators, whilst mounting US-China tensions are forcing developers to reassess their supply chain strategies. Transferability expands capital access The introduction of tax credit transferability created what Picarsic describes as a “secondary tranche” in renewable energy financing, allowing a more diverse set of capital allocators to participate in the market beyond traditional tax equity investors from major banks. This allows projects that might previously have struggled to secure financing to move forward, whilst creating a more risk-adjusted investment universe. Domestic content versus speed to market Developers now face a complex trade-off between navigating regulatory hurdles to gain domestic content tax credits versus importing components to accelerate project timelines. Picarsic characterised this as “a new type of consideration, a new challenge” for the market. “Developers are ultimately looking at economic return,” he says. “There’s the timeline on which they need to deliver a project and generate liquidity for their upstream capital formation.” Many developers are currently in a “sit and wait situation” seeking maximum certainty before proceeding, though some are moving forward where the economic delta between domestic and imported components justifies faster execution. However, Picarsic suggests the political and regulatory environment is pushing towards models that support domestic manufacturing capacity, pointing to challenges in the data centre space as an early signal of these political realities. “There’s both leadership in US government as well as popular support on economic development, but a certain type of economic development,” he says. “People need electrification to deliver all sorts of common goods that people want across the country, and we need to decrease emissions in all sorts of ways and in all sorts of places across the country.” Credit expiry timelines versus policy direction With solar investment tax credits (ITCs) set to expire at the end of 2027 and storage credits running to 2033, developers face strategic decisions about capital allocation sequencing. Picarsic identifies a current rush to lock in anything that can be safe harboured or imported and put into service as quickly as possible, independent of credit expiry dates. However, he argues that credit timelines are less important than the underlying bipartisan policy push towards stronger domestic and allied supply chains for critical infrastructure. “Investors, developers, suppliers who understand and build their businesses around that logic are likely the ones that are going to win out by the time we’re to 2037. There’s a capex story that you’ll see playing out toward that trajectory that is a little bit indifferent toward the 2027 or 2033 deadlines,” he says. FCC inverter ban and implementation challenges Regarding the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) 28 July equipment bans targeting Chinese inverters and other components, Picarsic emphasises that implementation details will prove critical. He suggestes successful models would pair bans with white lists or approved vendor lists, where suppliers clearly documenting their supply chains and firmware can guarantee compliance upfront, lessening the burden on broader markets dependent on cost-competitive inputs. “You end up in some place where domestic and some whitelisted set of things can substitute for where risks exist,” he says.
