artigo.texto: Compressed air energy storage holds much promise for large-scale, long-duration energy storage (LDES), but so far has struggled to really get off the ground outside of China. Will Hydrostor’s iteration on the technology finally take it to large-scale, commercially viable deployments? CAES and A-CAES technology explained Compressed air energy technology that delivers mechanical power has been around since the 19th century. Compressed air energy storage (CAES) is relatively newer, with the first utility-scale CAES project opening in 1978 at Huntorf in Germany. There have been other CAES projects commissioned since, with the largest to date coming online in Jiangsu Province, China. The Huai’an Salt Cavern CAES project in China has a 600MW power output and a 2,400MWh storage capacity. Even though there are multiple CAES projects live, they are hard to deploy. Hydrostor has been developing a new type of CAES called advanced CAES (A-CAES), that they will hope will make CAES easier to deploy. CAES works by pressurising and directing air into a storage medium. When there is an excess of electricity, be it from the grid or from renewable generation, the electricity is used to compress air. This air is then compressed in a cavern underground and acts as the stored energy (instead of traditional electrochemical stored energy). The heat captured during the compression process is released to the surrounding atmosphere. When the demand for energy is high, the compressed air is expanded and released through a natural gas combustion heating system to drive a turbine generator that produces electricity. A-CAES still compresses air to store energy and releases it via a heating medium, but the technology captures the heat generated during the charging process instead of venting it to the atmosphere. This heat is stored in overground thermal storage tanks and used as the fuel in the discharge heating process, eliminating the need for natural gas. The air in A-CAES is stored slightly differently to CAES. Where CAES stores energy in natural rock salt caverns, A-CAES can store air in different hard rock caverns that have been artificially made into the rock body. Inside these caverns, a water head is used to enhance land density and maintain the system at a constant pressure. When it’s time to discharge the energy, the water head weight is released, and the cavern is flooded with water. This pushes the air to the surface, and it is recombined with the stored heat, expanded, and sent through the turbine to create electricity. When it’s time to charge, the introduction of compressed air to the cavern displaces the water upwards into a surface reservoir (ready for release again when there’s a need to discharge). In essence, the water acts as a kind of piston. So, while the technologies are similar in principle, they actual everyday function is different. The cavern in A-CAES maintains a moderate pressure of 75bar, and the installation of one these systems require a one-time fill of water to create the water head. This requires 150 cubic meters per MWh. For a 500MW, 8-hour A-CAES system, this is about 50 Olympic sized swimming pools worth of water. The other main difference is the cavern itself. CAES uses natural rock salt caverns whereas A-CAES requires the excavation of a cavern at a suitable geological site. Controlled detonations between 0-2,000ft provides the initial 4-foot diameter shaft down to the cavern, which eventually becomes the air shaft. A cavern is then excavated using mining equipment and a second 8-foot diameter shaft is made using a raise bore process back to the surface to act as the water shaft. Why CAES is difficult to deploy The invention of the newer A-CAES process has been driven by the inherent difficulty of developing CAES. Yes, there are some in use, including some that have been around for a long time, but there are also many projects that have been cancelled and companies that have folded because it has been too difficult. For example, Corre Energy developed CAES and has already been liquidated and Bedrock Energy has recently had its 382MW/3,056MWh CAES project in Huron County, Ontario, Canada rejected because it was planned to cover over 100 acres of ‘productive farmland’. There are various technical, economic, and social challenges facing companies looking to deploy CAES. One of the main challenges is a low round-trip efficiency (RTE), as the RTE is often as low as 40% because the majority of the heat produced during air compression is lost. This could make CAES a lot less favourable for grid operators, especially when they have a much lower RTE than BESS. There’s also the challenge of integrating and synchronising CAES technology with the power grid, as the power grid requires assets to be synchronised at specific grid frequency and voltage levels—and it requires a lot of extra ancillary equipment, such as grid-tied inverters, sensors, and smart controllers to connect CAES to the grid. CAES also has slow ramp rates which makes it unsuitable for some energy deployment scenarios that require quicker and more responsive deployment of energy. The last major technical hurdle is that CAES require specific geological structures, such as salt domes, depleted aquifers, and hard rock caverns. These formations are not available everywhere, which limits where the energy storage systems can be sited. A-CAES

artigo.texto: RWE has taken a final investment decision (FID) on 400MW/1.1GWh BESS in the Netherlands with construction to start in due course, while Giga Storage has started building its 2.8GWh Green Turtle project in Belgium. Both are set to be commissioned in early 2028. RWE to build congestion-relieving BESS in Netherlands Power firm RWE has taken FID on the 2.75-hour battery energy storage system (BESS) to be built at the Moerdijk power station site, it said yesterday (21 September). Commissioning is planned for the second quarter of 2028, and it will contribute to the system integration of the 795MW OranjeWind offshore project, which is a joint venture between RWE and TotalEnergies. The BESS will comprise 208 lithium-ion containers (a little over 5MWh each) Mark Lentjes, regional director of grid operator TenneT Southern Netherland said the BESS would act as a congestion reliever. It will do this via ‘steering agreements’ with TenneT, whereby it will be dispatched to relieve congestion in the Noord-Brabant region. That means that space can be created on the grid for parties on the waiting list. Other projects have been given ‘time-dependent transport rights’ (TDTR), similar to a flexible connection agreement (FCA) in Germany The Moerdijk benefits from a location close to the 150,000V high-voltage substation at Moerdijk-Noord, where it will help to alleviate the regional bottleneck, which in turn has an impact on congestion across the whole region, Lentjes said. The project can also provide advanced grid services such as instantaneous reserve (inertia). RWE is highly active in BESS in the Netherlands, its home country of Germany as well as the US and Australia, see all coverage of it here. Giga Storage starts building Belgium’s largest BESS project BESS owner-operator Giga Storage has launched construction on its Green Turtle project, a 700MW/2,800MWh system, one of the largest in Europe. Announced last week (17 September), the start of construction comes a few months after financing was secured and a letter of intent (LOI) was agreed with Tesla to supply the project. Tesla will provide 640 of its lithium iron phosphate-based (LFP) Megapack 3 BESS units under a full EPC wrap contract, while civil works are being carried out by Stadbader Contractors. We did a deep-dive on the Megapack 3 product in a recent ESN Premium article. Commissioning is scheduled for March 2028. Preparatory earthworks and roadworks commenced in mid-August and now the batteries, cabling, and high-voltage installations will begin. Like RWE’s Dutch project, Green Turtle benefits from close proximity to a high-voltage line, the 380kV Van Eyck-Gramme line. Grid operator Elia is building a new high-voltage substation at the site to accommodate the project. Giga Storage, owned by investor InfraVia since 2024, is based in the Netherlands and also is active there, recently launching construction on a 1.2GWh BESS there last year, and it is also building a 1.4GWh one in Germany.

artigo.texto: Acme Solar Holdings hit a fresh all-time high of ₹455.0 on the NSE on September 21, capping a run that has taken the stock up over 100% over eight months and almost 125% from its 52-week low of ₹195.65, touched on January 27. Over just the past six months, the return stands at 76.7%. Set against that: the Nifty 50 spent most of 2026 barely above the record it had already set in September 2024, weighed down by sustained FII selling, while the Nifty Midcap 100 has managed roughly 2% year-to-date and even the more richly rewarded Nifty Smallcap 100 sits at about 13%. Acme Solar's gain isn't just ahead of the market, it is several multiples ahead of even the best-performing broad index. In doing so, it has comprehensively outperformed peers as well, That scale of outperformance has invited scepticism at times, with Acme Solar's own market history showing why: the stock actually slipped on July 30, the day it reported its strongest quarter yet, as investors weighed rich valuation multiples and rapid cash burn against an aggressive expansion plan. What has changed since is not the narrative. The BESS pivot was flagged as early as April 2025, when CEO Nikhil Dhingra called hybrid and FDRE capacity "a critical pivot in our business strategy", but the evidence that the narrative is actually being executed, quarter after quarter and, increasingly, week after week. What the Q1 numbers actually said The July 30 print, unflattering stock reaction notwithstanding, was genuinely strong. Total revenue for Q1 FY27 came in at ₹954 crore, up 63% year-on-year; EBITDA rose 56% to ₹831 crore at an 87% margin; profit after tax jumped 80% to ₹235 crore. Capacity utilisation factors (CUF) hit a record 30.9%, up from 28.5% a year earlier. None of that was BESS alone, but BESS was doing disproportionate work inside those numbers. The company commissioned 2.3 GWh of battery storage in the quarter, taking cumulative commissioned capacity to 3.62 GWh, roughly 40% of all commissioned BESS capacity in India at the time. That capacity alone generated ₹226 crore of the quarter's ₹954 crore in revenue — about a quarter of the total, from a business line that barely existed eighteen months ago. Management also used the call to upgrade full-year guidance, telling analysts the company is now on track for more than 10 GWh of BESS capacity by FY27, pulled forward by nearly three quarters from the original schedule with 70-80% of that target already contracted and locking in more than ₹1,400 crore of near-term revenue at realisations of ₹8-10 per unit through the DEEP portal and HP-TAM markets. Chairman Manoj Upadhyay told the call the company intends to keep 10-12 GWh of BESS capacity available for the short-term market annually over the next five years, even as capex increasingly shifts toward PPA-backed long-term projects. September is where the promise turned into proof If the July call supplied the guidance, September supplied the proof of delivery. On September 16, Acme Solar commissioned 66.68 MW of solar capacity alongside 300 MWh of BESS in Rajasthan. On September 17, a subsidiary commissioned Phase-II of the BESS component of its SJVN-contracted FDRE project in Bikaner — 52.32 MW/209.28 MWh of the eventual 300 MW/1,200 MWh discharge capacity, with commercial operations dated September 19 and the remainder targeted for Q3 FY27. That single subsidiary now has 105.95 MW/423.80 MWh of BESS commissioned. The stock's jump to its record high including the spike on September 18 tracked directly to this run of operational updates, not to any new guidance or analyst upgrade. The market rewarding delivery, essentially in real time. That is the more interesting read on this rally than the headline return itself. Acme Solar isn't being re-rated because the BESS story is new; it's being re-rated because each quarter narrows the gap between what management said it would build and what has actually been switched on and started earning. For a sector where announced capacity and commissioned capacity routinely diverge by years, that gap-closing is, on its own, a data point worth more than the guidance slide it came from. The obvious caveat None of this makes Acme Solar's valuation cheap. At its current price-to-earnings ratio and a market capitalisation heading of over ₹32,000 crore, the stock is pricing in a great deal of future execution alongside the execution already delivered and has outpaced even analyst price targets, which were averaging around ₹428 against a stock now trading near ₹455, suggest the sell-side broadly agrees the easy re-rating has already happened. The next leg of this stock's story depends less on hitting the 10 GWh BESS targetwhich looks very doable, and more on what realisations look like once 10-12 GWh a year is actually competing for space in India's still-developing short-term power and ancillary services markets. Competitors like Adani Green Energy, ReNew and NTPC Green will have noticed, and it remains to be seen how fast they can 'pivot' to a BESS powered strategy yet.

artigo.texto: Battery energy storage systems (BESS) have emerged as a critical piece of the power sector ecosystem – with applications across generation (to help manage resource intermittency and provide firm clean power), and across transmission and distribution (to help improve grid stability, load management and a variety of ancillary services). As the power systems become more complex, reliable and secure industrial networks with efficient connectivity are important for seamless communication between various assets – right from renewables or other power supply source, battery containers, power conversion systems, and energy management systems, to SCADA, substations, and grid operators. The government’s plan is to deploy 80 GW of BESS over the next decade, and this would need significant upgradation and enhancement of reliable and secure industrial connectivity systems for uninterrupted operations of utility-scale and industrial BESS projects. Secure communication infrastructure is vital to leverage real-time data for remote monitoring, predictive maintenance, and operational efficiency, and also protect critical assets from cybersecurity risks. The mission of this webinar on “Connected Energy Storage: Building Reliable and Resilient BESS Infrastructure” was to highlight the critical importance of industrial networking for implementing BESS. The webinar focused on key aspects of BESS communication networks and their applications in enabling real-time monitoring, remote diagnostics, cybersecurity, and scalable integration with the power grid. The webinar brought together power producers, renewables and BESS developers, EPC contractors and system integrators, utilities and grid operators, large C&I consumers as well as energy consultants and digital transformation leaders. The webinar delved into discussions around the following topics: - What are the key challenges being faced across renewable energy projects, commercial and industrial facilities and T&D assets with respect to operation of BESS? How do you expect the challenges to evolve as power systems become smarter and more distributed? - What are the key connectivity challenges faced by BESS installations, including remote locations and network disruptions? What role can real-time connectivity play in improving asset visibility, predictive maintenance, and remote operations across distributed BESS sites? - What connectivity technologies and network architectures are already in use to build scalable and resilient BESS infrastructure in India? What are the key design priorities for organisations with respect to BESS communication networks? - With increasing connectivity comes increasing cyber risk. How should utilities, IPPs, and industrial operators approach cybersecurity for BESS infrastructure? The webinar panel included: - Durgesh Agarwal, DGM, NTPC Green Energy - Nitesh Bhutada, Founder, Newen Systems - Naresh Chandak, Senior Vice -President (New Business and Renewable Energy), IndiGrid - Udyut Goyal, Head Business Development, AmpereHour Energy - Dhaval Makhecha, Senior Solutions Account Manager, Belden India - Gaurav Shanbhag, Solution Consulting (Energy & Transportation), Belden Inc For any questions, please write to ashima.gupta@indiainfrastructure.co.in

artigo.texto: A Apple aumentou o preço para os seus serviços de reparos e outros consertos relacionados aos iPhone 18 Pro em quase R$ 1.000 para determinados procedimentos. O dispositivo com o maior números de aumentos é o próprio iPhone 18 Pro Max, mas o modelo Pro foi o que viu o maior reajuste de preço. A Maçã tem uma longa lista de opções para reparar seus produtos com preços já normalmente altos. No iPhone 18 Pro, a companhia resolveu subir o valor cobrado na categoria de reparos para “Outros danos” em R$ 960. O valor sai dos R$ 7.599 do iPhone 17 Pro (valor aplicado até junho deste ano) para R$ 8.559 no produto mais novo. É interessante notar que a maioria dos serviços ofertados pela Apple tiveram seus preços inalterados, como danos na câmera, tela, vidro traseiro, etc. Apesar disso, trabalhos relacionados à bateria do iPhone 18 Pro ficaram R$ 40 mais caros e agora custam R$ 1.039 para serem realizados pelos técnicos da companhia. Aumentos no iPhone 18 Pro Max Quando o assunto parte para o produto entusiasta da Apple para 2026, as coisas mudam de figura. Esse celular também aumentou o preço de reparos para a tela em R$ 47, saltando de R$ 3.282 no iPhone 17 Pro Max para R$ 3.329 no novo iPhone 18 Pro Max, possivelmente devido aos custos de fabricação mais altos para desenvolver esses displays. A categoria de “Outros danos” segue com um aumento forte, mas ligeiramente menor que no modelo Pro, e agora está R$ 940 mais cara. Quanto aos serviços na bateria, o aumento é o mesmo citado anteriormente, de R$ 40. Danos no vidro e na câmera traseira continuam inalterados pela Maçã. Aliás, é até curioso pensar que a Apple não pontuou aumentos de preço para a câmera traseira dessa linha. Com os iPhones 18 Pro, a Maçã inseriu a tecnologia de abertura variável, que parece bem complexa e difícil de consertar. Seja como for, o preço médio para consertar os iPhones 18 Pro fica perto dos R$ 3.400. O iPhone 18 Pro e o iPhone 18 Pro Max já foram oficialmente lançados no mercado brasileiro, disponíveis nas cores bordô, glacial, prateado e preto. A versão Pro custa a partir de R$ 11.999, mas custa até R$ 20.999, enquanto o Pro Max varia entre R$ 12.999 e R$ 21.999 na variante mais cara. Por falar na Apple, a companhia possui um novo sistema de fotos verificadas para os iPhones, que usa processos de autenticação e assinatura. artigo.texto: Hiring for long-term manufacturing roles starting at $23 per hour RACINE, Wis., Sept. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Modine (NYSE: MOD), a diversified global leader in thermal management technology and solutions, today announced ongoing hiring efforts in southeastern Wisconsin to fill up to 300 positions to support its rapidly growing data center cooling business. The state-of-the-art manufacturing facility at 3303 W. Oakwood Road, Franklin, WI, will host a walk-in hiring fair on Thursday, September 24, to fill these positions across both first and second shifts. The hiring expansion comes amid growing demand for energy-efficient cooling solutions that support the rapidly expanding U.S. data center market. In September 2025, Modine opened a new 153,000-square-foot plant in Franklin, dedicated to manufacturing Airedale™ data center cooling systems. The additional workforce will help ramp up production to meet increasing demand for cooling solutions that optimize data center performance and sustainability. "In 2025, our expansion into Franklin was fueled by customer interest in the advanced thermal management solutions our team builds to cool data centers in the U.S.," said Karen Sutherland, Vice President of Human Resources for Data Centers, Americas at Modine. "We're now at a point where we need a larger, committed workforce that wants to help serve the growing needs of our customers. We provide on-the-job training, with no prior manufacturing experience required for most entry-level positions." The Franklin expansion is part of a broader investment announced by Modine in July 2025 to increase U.S. manufacturing capacity for Airedale data center cooling products across facilities in Franklin, WI; Grand Prairie, TX; Grenada, MS; and Jefferson City, MO. Franklin Facility Hiring Fair Open on September 24 Modine will host a hiring fair Thursday, Sept. 24, from 4–7 p.m. at its Franklin facility, 3303 W. Oakwood Road. The company will have HR professionals and leaders onsite to discuss open positions and conduct on-the-spot interviews. Candidates are encouraged to register in advance using this form: Airedale - Walk-In Interview Event – Form, and walk-ins are welcome. Modine has first and second shift openings, with production assembler positions starting at $23 and an additional $1-per-hour premium for second shift. New employees are eligible to receive health insurance and other benefits beginning on their first day. Modine will continue to hire in the coming months until open roles are filled and will also be promoting the openings through a billboard advertising campaign throughout the Milwaukee area. Below are links to assembler positions posted on Modine's website. Assembler - Assembler Job Details | Modine Manufacturing Company For more information, visit https://airedale.com/careers. About Modine For more than 100 years, Modine has solved the toughest thermal management challenges for mission-critical applications. Our purpose of Engineering a Cleaner, Healthier World™ means we are always evolving our portfolio of technologies to provide the latest heating, cooling, and ventilation solutions. Through the hard work of more than 11,000 employees worldwide, our Climate Solutions and Performance Technologies segments advance our purpose with systems that improve air quality, reduce energy and water consumption, lower harmful emissions, enable cleaner running vehicles, and use environmentally friendly refrigerants. Modine is a global company headquartered in Racine, Wisconsin (U.S.), with operations in North America, South America, Europe, and Asia. For more information about Modine, visit modine.com. artigo.texto: 247 – Data centers têm recorrido às redes de distribuição para se conectar ao sistema elétrico e contornar a disputa por margem de escoamento na transmissão, segundo fontes ouvidas por reportagem da Agência iNFRA. A estratégia também permite que os empreendedores evitem o pagamento de garantias prévias antes de saber se haverá capacidade disponível para seus projetos. O crescimento desses pedidos levou o Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) e a Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) a relatarem a situação à Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (ANEEL). Há, segundo a apuração, preocupação de que parte do movimento tenha caráter especulativo, com reserva de capacidade na distribuição por projetos que ainda não têm garantia de implantação. ONS e EPE defendem que as regras de acesso às distribuidoras sejam compatibilizadas com as normas aplicadas à transmissão. O sistema de transmissão passou a contar, em dezembro de 2025, com a Política Nacional de Acesso ao Sistema de Transmissão (Pnast). Uma eventual integração dos procedimentos exigiria mudanças regulatórias envolvendo o Prodist e atuação da ANEEL. Empresas apontam gargalos da Pnast Representantes do setor de data centers atribuem a busca pelas distribuidoras às condições estabelecidas para conexão pela transmissão. O vice-presidente da Scala Data Center, Luciano Fialho, afirmou que a falta de diálogo na elaboração da política produziu uma “solução que não resolve nada”. Segundo Fialho, dois obstáculos pesam sobre os projetos: a necessidade de aportes milionários como garantia antes da confirmação da conexão e o número limitado de períodos em que os empreendedores podem solicitar acesso, as chamadas temporadas de acesso. A alternativa pela distribuição, porém, não está disponível para qualquer empreendimento. Fialho afirma que ela tende a atender cargas menores. Mesmo nesses casos, a distribuidora pode negar o pedido se o ONS identificar falta de capacidade correspondente na rede de transmissão. O CEO da Thymos, João Carlos Mello, também defendeu maior coordenação entre os agentes do setor. Para ele, “o todo não está bem desenhado”, e a transição entre o modelo anterior e a Pnast foi “muito abrupta”. “Ninguém tem espaço infinito na rede para as cargas entrarem, mas acho que tinha que dar uma melhorada nesse protocolo. O que era antes organizado pelo MME [Ministério de Minas e Energia], ONS, ANEEL e EPE, agora ficou só com o ONS”, afirmou Mello. Capacidade das distribuidoras também tem limites A conexão pela distribuição não elimina a dependência da infraestrutura de transmissão. As concessionárias possuem Contratos de Uso do Sistema de Transmissão (CUSTs) e precisam manter sua demanda dentro dos montantes contratados. O CEO da consultoria PSR, Luiz Barroso, disse à Agência iNFRA que já existem casos em que pedidos de ampliação dessa capacidade foram negados por falta de margem no sistema. Segundo ele, a escolha entre acessar diretamente a distribuição ou a transmissão tem consequências econômicas tanto para os consumidores quanto para o sistema elétrico. Um interlocutor com conhecimento das discussões afirmou ainda que algumas distribuidoras vêm pagando penalidades por ultrapassarem os montantes contratados com as transmissoras à medida que novas cargas são incorporadas. Essa restrição pode resultar na rejeição de solicitações de grandes consumidores interessados em se conectar pela distribuição. ANEEL avalia mudanças regulatórias A ANEEL informou que trabalha em ajustes para oferecer “sinais adequados para que os consumidores optem por determinado sistema de acesso considerando seus diferentes requisitos”. Segundo a agência, as mudanças também devem buscar maior previsibilidade para o planejamento do setor e evitar que a capacidade disponível nas redes seja ocupada por empreendimentos que não venham a ser efetivamente implantados. O assunto integra a Agenda Regulatória 2026-2027 e está sendo analisado em diferentes processos e tomadas de subsídios. A ANEEL destacou que continua avaliando individualmente os pedidos porque o atendimento pelas distribuidoras permanece condicionado a restrições técnicas, normas de conexão e, em determinados casos, à participação financeira do consumidor nas obras necessárias. EPE vê risco de duplicação dos estudos O presidente da EPE, Thiago Prado, afirmou que o volume de solicitações de conexão de data centers na distribuição está se aproximando do registrado no sistema de transmissão. O movimento leva as distribuidoras a pedir novos estudos de expansão à empresa e pode fazer o planejamento avaliar duas vezes demandas relacionadas aos mesmos projetos. “Posso estar trabalhando duas vezes porque vou estar trabalhando para expandir a transmissão, […] mas esses estudos estão concorrendo com os estudos de expansão [solicitados pela] distribuidora, porque ela celebra esses acordos de acesso, mas sem necessariamente ter uma garantia financeira”, afirmou Prado. ❗ Se você tem algum posicionamento a acrescentar nesta matéria ou alguma correção a fazer, entre em contato com [email protected]. ✅ Receba as notícias do Brasil 247 e da TV 247 no Telegram do 247 e no canal do 247 no WhatsApp. Marque o Brasil 247 como fonte preferida no Google: Apoie o jornalismo independente do 247:

artigo.texto: RWE has taken the final investment decision (FID) to build a 400 MW/1,100 MWh battery energy storage system at its Moerdijk power station in the Netherlands as part of the system integration solutions for the 795 MW OranjeWind offshore wind farm being developed with TotalEnergies. The battery will comprise 208 lithium-ion battery containers and will be able to deliver its full 400 MW output for almost three hours. Construction is scheduled to start in due course, with commissioning planned for the second quarter of 2028, RWE said on 21 September. OranjeWind, also known as Hollandse Kust West VII, is being built approximately 53 kilometres off the Dutch coast and will comprise 53 Vestas V236-15.0 MW turbines. Offshore construction has already started, with monopile installation currently underway. Turbine installation is planned for 2027, and the wind farm is scheduled to become operational in 2028. The new battery will be connected to the national grid through the existing substation at RWE’s Moerdijk power plant. Under capacity steering agreements with transmission system operator TenneT, it will be dispatched to relieve grid congestion in Noord-Brabant and create additional capacity for parties currently on the grid connection waiting list. The battery will also provide grid services, including instantaneous reserve. RWE already operates a 7.5 MW/11 MWh battery at Moerdijk, also developed as part of OranjeWind’s system integration package, which entered commercial operation in June 2025. OranjeWind’s system integration package also includes electrolysers, e-boilers and smart charging, as part of the tender requirements for the offshore wind farm site, which RWE secured in 2022.

artigo.texto: The Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission (MERC) has proposed a revised regulatory framework aimed at accelerating the integration of renewable energy and energy storage systems across Maharashtra. the draft signals a shift towards treating storage as an independent and increasingly important component of the state’s power system. The draft Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission (MERC) (Battery Energy Storage System) Regulations, 2026 cover the planning, procurement, development, ownership, operation, scheduling, dispatch, metering and commercial settlement of BESS across the state. The framework applies to generators, transmission and distribution utilities, standalone BESS developers, open-access consumers, captive projects and renewable energy developers. One of the most significant proposals is the recognition of standalone BESS as a distinct asset class. Such projects would be permitted to participate in applications ranging from energy arbitrage and energy banking to ancillary services, demand management, renewable energy optimisation and electricity market participation. The draft also establishes clearer entry thresholds. Standalone BESS would require a minimum capacity of 5 MW for inter-state transmission connectivity and 1 MW for distribution connectivity, with a minimum duration of two hours. Aggregation of smaller systems could be enabled through a designated “Lead ESS”. Importantly, the proposed framework could improve the economics of storage. Electricity drawn for intermediate storage would be exempt from certain transmission, distribution demand, wheeling and surcharge-related charges, provided the stored electricity is subsequently consumed within Maharashtra. At the same time, BESS operators would face significantly greater grid discipline, including separate injection and drawal metering, scheduling, energy accounting, deviation settlement, telemetry, cybersecurity and safety requirements. Overall, the draft marks an important move towards creating a structured market for storage, positioning BESS not merely as an adjunct to renewable generation, but as a dispatchable grid asset capable of providing multiple power-system services. The proposed framework has been released for public consultation as the state looks to manage rising electricity demand alongside increasing solar and wind generation. The commission said demand is also growing from major cities and data centres, which require reliable round-the-clock renewable power. Boost For RE Sources Maharashtra is targeting 50% of its electricity demand from renewable sources by 2030 under initiatives including Mukhyamantri Saur Krishiwahini Yojana 2.0. Renewable generation in the state has increased by 25% over the past year, with solar generation growing 36% and wind generation by 12%, according to the press release. The Maharashtra Renewable Energy and Energy Storage Policy 2035-36 further targets 65% of electricity demand from renewable sources by 2036. It also envisages meeting at least 10% of demand through energy storage technologies such as battery energy storage systems and pumped hydro, requiring 100 GW of renewable capacity and 100 GWh of storage. Long Term Pathway The framework also proposes a long-term pathway for Renewable Purchase Obligation and Energy Storage Obligation, along with related amendments to the State Grid Code. MERC said the proposed changes are expected to facilitate additional solar, wind and storage capacity while strengthening grid reliability and promoting a fair allocation of network and system service costs. The framework also seeks to protect existing contracts under the prevailing regulatory regime, while giving eligible consumers and project developers the option to migrate to the proposed framework. MERC has invited comments and suggestions from consumers, industry stakeholders, renewable energy developers, utilities, experts and members of the public. Stakeholders have 21 days to submit their views, with the deadline set for October 12, 2026. Counter-submissions can be made until October 15.

artigo.texto: European Commission Proposes Energy Efficiency Rating for Data Centers The European Commission has put forward a proposal for a European Union rating scheme to help ensure energy efficiency and minimize resource wastage and emissions at data centers. Concurrently it launched a public consultation on minimum energy efficiency standards for data centers across the 27-member bloc. "In addition to using more energy, an increase of data centers could put extra pressure on electricity grids and the use of natural resources, such as water, and contribute to increase carbon emissions", the Commission said in an online statement. "To limit these impacts, it is essential that data centers are highly energy- and water-efficient and sustainably integrated in the energy system". Covering data centers that exceed 500 kilowatts of capacity, the rating scheme would measure the actual use of energy and water resources. "It will also cover data centers' contribution to the grid such as the reuse of waste heat, the addition of clean energy generation capacities as well as flexibility", the Commission said. "A striking example: reusing around half of all waste heat from European data centers is the equivalent of the total heating demand of four million households in Europe. "Sustainable, flexible and well-designed data centers that can adjust their electricity use to the grids conditions can help lower the overall cost of the electricity system, improve grid stability and integrate more renewable energy". Ratings would be issued by means of electronic labels. Labels would be issued to data centers starting August 2027, valid for one year, according to the delegated regulation published by the Commission. The rating scheme builds on Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364, which already implemented a reporting scheme for data center operators. "The thresholds for each indicator have been set based on analysis of the data submitted by data center operators during the first reporting period and assessment of existing legislation, initiatives, benchmarks and standards", the new proposal document says. "The selected indicators and thresholds will be reviewed and may be revised in the future to accommodate technological progress, improve the effectiveness of the scheme and strive for higher sustainability standards", the proposal says. "This regulation is part of an ongoing effort of simplification and harmonization across EU policies. By leveraging already reported data, it makes sure that no additional burden is put on member states and data center operators", it says. "The rating scheme is intended to harmonize approaches across EU member states and will be used to assess the sustainability of data centers in other EU legislation, including in the Cloud and AI Development Act. It has also been considered in the review of the Climate and Environmental Delegated Acts under the Taxonomy Regulation", it says. Crafted after public consultation, the new delegated regulation is now subject to a two-month scrutiny period by the European Parliament and the European Council before taking effect. Additionally the Commission said it is "following up to the declaration of intent signed in June 2026, working with data center operators, grid operators, energy providers and public authorities towards a tripartite agreement on data centers in the second half of the year". The consultation on minimum energy standards for data centers ends December. "Tripling our data center capacity cannot mean tripling the pressure on our grids, our water and our energy bills. That starts with transparency, rating large data centers depending on their impact on our energy system", said Teresa Ribera, Commission executive vice president for a clean, just and competitive transition. "Efficient, flexible, powered by additional clean energy and reusing waste heat, this is how data centers become an asset for EU's energy transition". On June 3 the Commission proposed the Cloud and AI Development Act, which aims to triple the EU's "data center capacity" over the next five to seven years. artigo.texto: A Casa dos Ventos trabalha em projetos de centro de dados no Sul do país, disse o presidente da TotalEnergies, Patrick Pouyanné, durante painel na ROG.e nesta segunda-feira, 21 de setembro. A TotalEnergies é sócia da Casa dos Ventos desde 2022 e planeja aumentar sua fatia de 34% para 49%. Até o momento, a Casa dos Ventos divulgou projetos de data center em São Paulo e no Ceará. Em agosto, a empresa recebeu aval para a compra de 500 MW em geração eólica no Rio Grande do Sul. Pouyanné observa o aumento na demanda vinda de data centers no país. “Há dois anos, nós estávamos lutando para encontrar clientes [offtakers], para crescer, porque nós temos um enorme portfólio. Agora, no ano passado, nós conseguimos assinar mais de 1 GW de centros de dados, e nós vamos atrair mais”, disse o francês. Ele também destacou o aumento no portfólio da Casa dos Ventos neste período: “Em 2022, quando nos juntamos à Casa dos Ventos, a capacidade era de 1,5 GW. No final deste ano, nós temos 7,5 GW”, declarou. Mas não é apenas na Casa dos Ventos que a TotalEnergies aumenta seu portfólio de geração renovável. Globalmente, a geração da empresa deve passar dos atuais 60 TWh para mais de 100 TWh até o fim da década, disse o líder da empresa. Da mesma forma, a demanda por data centers ocorre em outras regiões: “Nós desenvolvemos, no ano passado, 4 GW de projetos de data center em dois países, os EUA e o Brasil”, declarou Pouyanné. Para ele, o principal gargalo para o setor de centro de dados no Brasil é a conexão de dados entre o Nordeste e o Sul do país. O investimento no Rio Grande do Sul se insere neste contexto. Na ROG.e, Pouyanné participou de sessão com Carlos Pascual, vice-presidente e líder de Geopolítica e Assuntos Internacionais da S&P Global Energy. No painel, Pascual observou o potencial de atrativos do Brasil para data centers, como “a combinação de recursos renováveis, a potencial disponibilidade de gás para a estabilidade e a intermitência, a capacidade técnica neste país e a habilidade de treinar modelos de inteligência artificial”. “Estou feliz que o mundo não saiba [desses atrativos], porque nós sabemos”, comentou Pouyanné, que também declarou não ter problemas em compartilhar o negócio com tanto potencial: “Eu posso fazer isso porque nossos parceiros estão protegendo muitos direitos de conexão”.

artigo.texto: TE Connectivity Leading supplier of filling connector solutions for harsh environments According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Filling Connector Assembly market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global Filling Connector Assembly market is entering a period of accelerated demand expansion, with an estimated compound annual growth rate of 8–12% through 2035. This specialized component market—covering complete units, components and modules, integrated systems, and consumables—is being reshaped by the rapid global build-out of lithium-ion battery gigafactories. Announced battery production capacity is projected to exceed 6 TWh by 2035, implying a tripling of installed filling-equipment lines and a corresponding 2.5–3.5x increase in annual filling connector assembly demand for both new-fit and replacement applications. The market remains structurally import-dependent in Europe and North America, which rely on imports for 50–70% of procurement, while China and Japan maintain concentrated domestic supply bases covering 65–80% of localized demand. Pricing is tiered: standard-grade assemblies trade at $50–$90 per unit, while premium cleanroom-compliant specifications command $150–$220 per unit. Aftermarket replacement accounts for 30–40% of total market volume, with average replacement intervals of 18–24 months under continuous production shifts. Supplier qualification cycles of 8–14 months and raw material cost volatility of ±12–18% year-on-year present persistent challenges, but the overall trajectory remains firmly upward as battery, semiconductor, and industrial automation sectors scale. The baseline scenario for the Filling Connector Assembly market through 2035 assumes continued global investment in lithium-ion battery manufacturing capacity, steady growth in semiconductor and precision manufacturing, and sustained demand from industrial automation and instrumentation. Under this scenario, the market expands at an 8–12% CAGR, with the market index reaching approximately 280 by 2035 (2025=100). The strongest demand driver is the battery gigafactory build-out: announced global capacity exceeding 6 TWh by 2035 implies a tripling of installed filling-equipment lines, directly translating into 2.5–3.5x higher annual demand for filling connector assemblies. Replacement demand, representing 30–40% of total volume, provides a stable baseline that grows with the installed base. Regionally, Asia-Pacific remains the largest market, led by China, while North America and Europe post above-average growth rates as domestic battery supply chains mature. Supply constraints—including 8–14 month supplier qualification cycles and raw material cost swings of ±12–18%—may periodically slow market expansion but are unlikely to alter the long-term growth trajectory. Premium assemblies with integrated sensing and self-diagnostic features are expected to grow at roughly twice the rate of standard configurations, gradually increasing their share of new shipments from 15–20% toward 30% by 2035. Industrial automation and instrumentation represents a foundational demand segment for filling connector assemblies, encompassing applications in process control, fluid handling, and automated filling systems across chemical, food and beverage, pharmaceutical, and general manufacturing. Currently, this segment benefits from steady replacement demand and incremental new installations as factories upgrade to Industry 4.0 standards. Through 2035, demand will be shaped by the integration of smart sensors and self-diagnostic features into connector assemblies, enabling predictive maintenance and reducing downtime. Demand-side indicators to watch include global industrial robot installations, process automation spending, and instrumentation replacement cycles. The segment is less volatile than battery manufacturing but provides a reliable baseline. Growth will be moderate but consistent, with premium assemblies gaining share as end-users seek higher reliability and lower total cost of ownership. Major companies active in this space include Swagelok, Parker Hannifin, and Emerson, which supply a broad range of instrumentation fittings and connectors. Current trend: Steady growth, supported by factory automation and process instrumentation upgrades. Major trends: Integration of smart sensors and IIoT connectivity into filling connector assemblies, Shift toward predictive maintenance and condition monitoring in process industries, Growing demand for leak-proof, high-purity connectors in pharmaceutical and food processing, and Standardization of connector interfaces to reduce inventory complexity. Representative participants: Swagelok Company, Parker Hannifin Corporation, Emerson Electric Co, SMC Corporation, and Festo AG & Co. KG. The electronics and optical systems segment uses filling connector assemblies in precision dispensing, encapsulation, and cooling applications for semiconductors, LEDs, displays, and optical components. Current demand is driven by the need for micro-dispensing of adhesives, thermal interface materials, and optical fluids with high accuracy and repeatability. Through 2035, growth will be supported by the expansion of advanced packaging, 5G infrastructure, and augmented/virtual reality device manufacturing. Demand-side indicators include semiconductor capital expenditure, display panel production, and optical module shipments. The segment demands increasingly miniaturized connectors capable of handling low-viscosity fluids without leakage or contamination. Premium assemblies with integrated flow sensing and cleanroom compatibility are expected to gain share. Key suppliers include Nordson, Graco, and Nitto Kohki, which offer precision dispensing and connector solutions tailored to electronics manufacturing. artigo.texto: Dragonfly Energy Partners with Sphere Energy to Develop Next-Generation AI-Enhanced Battery Technology - Sphere Energy’s proprietary battery AI models will be integrated into Dragonfly Energy’s next-generation battery management system architecture. - The integration is designed to improve state-of-charge and state-of-health accuracy while expanding Dragonfly IntelLigence® into AI-enhanced battery management. - The partnership will leverage Dragonfly Energy’s hundreds of thousands of deployed battery packs, established OEM relationships and vertically integrated engineering capabilities to accelerate data-driven product development. RENO, Nev., Aug. 17, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) — Dragonfly Energy Holdings Corp. (Nasdaq: DFLI) (“Dragonfly Energy” or the “Company”), an industry leader in energy storage, today announced a strategic partnership with Sphere Energy to develop and integrate next-generation AI capabilities into its future battery technologies and integrated power systems. With hundreds of thousands of battery packs deployed across a broad range of applications, Dragonfly Energy has built a substantial base of real-world operating data spanning years of field performance. The partnership will combine that data with Sphere Energy’s battery-specific AI technology, based on its AI platform VETTA®, advancing the Company’s Dragonfly IntelLigence® communications technology beyond battery connectivity and system visibility and creating an AI-driven intelligence layer across future products and systems. Sphere Energy’s proprietary battery AI models will be integrated into Dragonfly Energy’s next-generation battery management system architecture, making Dragonfly Energy the first battery pack manufacturer to place Sphere Energy’s AI-powered state-of-health technology at its core. The integration is designed to improve the accuracy of state-of-charge and state-of-health data while creating a more flexible development platform that can help Dragonfly Energy bring new products and solutions to market faster in response to specific customer needs. Dr. Denis Phares, chief executive officer of Dragonfly Energy, said: Our established product lines, long-standing customer relationships and years of field performance have created a powerful data advantage, “By combining that data advantage with Sphere Energy’s battery-specific AI models, we expect to evolve Dragonfly IntelLigence into a platform capable of delivering more precise, actionable insights across the applications we serve.” Luca Scherrer, co-founder and managing director of Sphere Energy, said: Dragonfly Energy’s vertically integrated capabilities, substantial deployed base and established relationships with leading OEM customers provide a unique foundation for applying battery-specific artificial intelligence at scale, “That combination gives us the opportunity to apply our technology across a broad range of real-world applications and operating conditions, turning battery data into better intelligence, stronger product performance and greater value for customers.” For fleet operators, OEMs and other commercial customers, more accurate battery intelligence is intended to provide greater visibility into battery condition and lifecycle performance, supporting better asset management and operating decisions. The AI-enabled architecture is also designed to create a faster feedback loop between field performance and product development, helping Dragonfly Energy refine existing products and accelerate future solutions. Together, we believe these capabilities can turn Dragonfly Energy’s growing base of field data into a lasting advantage across product performance, development and customer value. artigo.texto: Waena battery storage project hits key milestone, will strengthen Maui grid and support renewables Hawaiian Electric’s Waena Battery Energy Storage System project reached a major construction milestone with the arrival and installation of the project’s first six Tesla Megapacks at the project site along Pūlehu Road in Central Maui. The project will be the island’s first standalone load-shifting battery energy storage system that will enable more renewable energy to be used during periods of peak energy demand. The batteries were delivered by semi-truck and carefully lifted into place by crane in late August. Roughly the size of a 40-foot shipping container, they are the first of 54 units that will make up the 40-megawatt (MW), 160-megawatt-hour (MWh) battery energy storage system, one of the largest in Hawai‘i. Approved by the Public Utilities Commission in 2023, the project is the first battery storage project to be developed by Hawaiian Electric and part of the company’s plans to reduce carbon emissions and to use renewable resources to generate 100% of electricity by 2045. Currently, about 41% of Maui County’s electricity comes from renewables, including more than 18,000 customer solar systems. The system will also incorporate grid-forming technology, which can help maintain grid stability as the island uses more variable energy resources, including wind and solar. As Maui continues its transition to clean energy, battery storage is becoming increasingly important. Once in service, the system will store excess energy and deliver it back to the grid when it is needed most. The battery doesn’t generate electricity but stores it, shifting energy from resources such as solar and wind, which are often abundant during daylight hours, to better align with customer demand at night. “This project has been years in the making, and seeing the batteries arrive on site brings us one step closer to providing Maui with a more renewable electric grid,” said Shelley Takasato, manager of Generation Project Development for Hawaiian Electric. The remaining battery units will arrive in phases over the coming months as construction continues. The project is expected to enter service in 2027. The arrival of the first battery units marks an important step toward a more renewable energy future for Maui.

artigo.texto: The New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection said Sept. 22 that it has fined the DataOne data center in Vineland $1.07 million for violations of the New Jersey Air Pollution Control Act for installing and operating 62 large natural-gas power generators without the requisite DEP permits. The state is calling the action the largest fine ever imposed on a data center in New Jersey. The DEP’s Administrative Order and Notice of Civil Penalty Assessment (AONOCAPA) stems from a July 29 site inspection of the facility, during which the power generators were observed. The power generators were not observed during the DEP’s previous site inspection in December 2025. “This enforcement action – by far the largest ever taken against a data center in New Jersey and possibly one of the largest such actions in the nation – sends a clear message that these facilities will not be constructed or operated with impunity in this state,” said DEP Commissioner Ed Potosnak. “The Sherrill administration demands accountability and corporate responsibility in the construction and operation of data centers and is committed to putting in place legal and regulatory guardrails that protect ratepayers, communities and the environment.” Gov. Mikie Sherrill has made data center expansion in New Jersey a key issue of her administration. She signed legislation on Aug. 27 requiring data centers to self-report their water and energy use every six months to the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities. The measure requires data center owners and operators to submit semi-annual water and energy usage reports to BPU. These actions follow the signing of legislation in July that requires data centers to bring their own clean energy and establishes a separate rate class for these developments to shield other ratepayers from shouldering the costs of data center energy demand. “I said from the beginning that we are going to hold data centers accountable, period. That is exactly why I announced the most comprehensive data center plan in the nation and moved quickly to put those guardrails in place,” said Sherrill. “We are putting power in the hands of the people and ensuring this industry works for us, on our terms – not theirs. Data centers will pay their fair share for energy, be accountable for their water and energy use, protect our environment, create good-paying union jobs, and invest in communities. New Jerseyans have my firm commitment, and today’s action is an example.” The New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) issued this Administrative Order and Notice of Civil Administrative Penalty Assessment following a July 29 inspection of the Vineland facility, during which DEP observed 62 large natural-gas generators that were installed and operating without required DEP permits. Natural gas generators emit carbon dioxide, nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide and other combustion-related pollutants. The civil penalty assessment cites DataOne with violating the Air Pollution Control Act by installing and operating 62 1,982-kilowatt stationary reciprocating generators (known as engines) without first obtaining a preconstruction permit and valid operating certificate. These approvals are required for any generator with 37-kw capacity or higher. The civil penalty assessment orders DataOne to immediately apply for and obtain the required permits or cease operations.

artigo.texto: A Alibaba Group Holding (BABA) está lançando o que diz ser o chip de inteligência artificial (IA) mais potente da China, um acelerador destinado a competir com a Nvidia (NVDA) e a sustentar uma expansão maciça da capacidade dos centros de dados nos próximos anos. A empresa de e-commerce, que agora aspira ao mercado de IA, apresentou na terça-feira (22) um novo acelerador Zhenwu V900 que, segundo ela, triplica o desempenho de seu antecessor. De acordo com o CEO Eddie Wu, o produto, desenvolvido pela divisão T-Head do Alibaba, pode ser combinado em clusters de até 500 mil unidades para viabilizar o treinamento de modelos de ponta. A Alibaba é uma das empresas chinesas líderes que mais investe em IA. Ela se comprometeu a investir mais de US$ 53 bilhões ao longo de um período de três anos para expandir suas capacidades de IA e levantou cerca de US$ 10,2 bilhões em uma oferta de ações adicional realizada em agosto. ⟶ Assine as newsletters da Bloomberg Línea e receba as notícias do dia em primeira mão no e-mail. A empresa de tecnologia de Hangzhou se comprometeu a intensificar o investimento em hardware e infraestrutura de IA, à medida que Wu faz da busca pela inteligência artificial geral o norte da empresa. Na terça-feira (22), o CEO anunciou planos para desenvolver modelos com entre 5 e 10 trilhões de parâmetros — muito maiores do que o comum atualmente — para tarefas mais longas e complexas. Em seguida, ele estabeleceu uma meta de 20 gigawatts de capacidade de data center para o serviço Alibaba Cloud globalmente até 2032 — uma grande expansão que, segundo estimativas do Citigroup, poderia gerar mais de US$ 160 bilhões em receita externa para a divisão em rápido crescimento. Leia também: Por que reunião de rei Charles com líderes de IA pode incentivar regulação no setor Essa velocidade de desenvolvimento contrasta com alertas recentes dos principais laboratórios de IA nos Estados Unidos, depois que o CEO da Anthropic, Dario Amodei, defendeu um ritmo mais lento para lidar melhor com os riscos. A declaração de Wu — na véspera de uma cúpula histórica entre o presidente americano, Donald Trump, e seu homólogo chinês, Xi Jinping — sugere que a Alibaba não tem intenção de desacelerar. Suas ações subiram mais de 5% em Hong Kong, enquanto a Tencent Holdings, operadora do WeChat, registrou alta de mais de 7%. “No ano passado, afirmamos que, quanto mais capaz a IA se tornar, mais poderosa será a humanidade”, disse Wu. “Hoje, continuo firme nessa convicção.” O plano de 20 GW do Alibaba — embora gigantesco para uma empresa chinesa — é relativamente menor do que alguns dos projetos de expansão mais ambiciosos do mundo. O SoftBank Group, por exemplo, prevê um centro de computação com capacidade de 10 gigawatts somente em Ohio. Embora tenha apresentado toda a gama de chips proprietários, serviços em nuvem e modelos de IA da Alibaba, Wu não abordou se a empresa será capaz de produzir silício suficiente no curto prazo para atender à crescente demanda doméstica, especialmente com os chips de ponta da Nvidia restritos na China. Ainda não está claro se a Alibaba está trabalhando com fabricantes de chips nacionais — como a Semiconductor Manufacturing International, que enfrenta restrições de capacidade — mas os controles de exportação dos EUA impedem, em grande parte, que as empresas chinesas utilizem líderes de mercado como a Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing. Leia também: Avanço de agentes de IA abre nova frente de crescimento para cibersegurança, diz BofA O evento da Alibaba ocorre pouco antes do encontro entre Trump e Xi para discutir uma série de questões. Os assuntos relacionados à IA devem ter destaque, já que executivos de alto escalão dos EUA, como o chefe da Nvidia, Jensen Huang, e Satya Nadella, da Microsoft (MSFT), participarão de um jantar de Estado na Casa Branca. As negociações tiveram início esta semana entre o secretário do Tesouro dos EUA, Scott Bessent, e o vice-primeiro-ministro chinês, He Lifeng, ocasião em que ambas as partes concordaram em estabelecer um diálogo sobre IA com o objetivo de chegar a um entendimento comum sobre metas e ameaças. Isso apesar de Washington acusar a Alibaba e outros desenvolvedores líderes, como a DeepSeek, de “acessar ilegalmente” modelos americanos de ponta para ajudar a desenvolver seus próprios produtos. Pequim rejeitou tais acusações como infundadas e prometeu retaliar caso Washington tome medidas contra empresas chinesas de IA. A Alibaba — até recentemente mais conhecida como operadora dos mercados Taobao e T-mall — criou o modelo de IA mais popular do mundo em termos de downloads. Desde então, a empresa expandiu rapidamente sua série Qwen, mantendo preços baixos para atrair usuários. Isso teve um custo, no entanto, já que a empresa viu seu lucro despencar em mais de 75% no último trimestre, após uma onda de gastos de quase US$ 10 bilhões. Leia também: Empresas que adotam IA criam mais vagas, mas reduzem espaço para jovens, diz estudo Os executivos da empresa falaram recentemente sobre como seus investimentos em IA estão cada vez mais rendendo frutos, com a receita anualizada proveniente de produtos relacionados à IA prevista para atingir US$ 10 bilhões no trimestre atual. A Alibaba deve conseguir recuperar seu investimento total em um período de três anos, afirmou a equipe de Wu. A empresa também tem como meta quintuplicar a receita anual com nuvem e IA para US$ 100 bilhões em cinco anos. A Alibaba — que lançou seu mais recente chip de IA em maio — planeja atualizar essa linha de produtos anualmente. Eles foram projetados para operar em clusters gigantes a fim de impulsionar o desempenho, uma estratégia amplamente adotada por fabricantes chineses de chips, desde a Huawei Technologies até a Moore Threads Technology. A T-Head, que busca uma abertura de capital, já entregou 560 mil unidades da família de produtos Zhenwu, e seus processadores foram implantados por mais de 400 clientes externos, informou a Alibaba. --Com a colaboração de Vlad Savov. artigo.texto: Os empreendimentos serão divididos em cinco categorias de potência — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução O Conselho Estadual do Meio Ambiente (Conema) aprovou, na segunda-feira (21), uma resolução que estabelece regras para o licenciamento ambiental de data centers no Rio Grande do Norte. A proposta foi apresentada pelo Instituto de Desenvolvimento Sustentável e Meio Ambiente do RN (Idema). A resolução cria critérios para padronizar os procedimentos administrativos, técnicos e ambientais aplicados aos empreendimentos. 🔎 Data centers são estruturas destinadas ao processamento, armazenamento e comunicação de dados e contam com sistemas de energia, refrigeração, segurança, conectividade e servidores. Um dos principais critérios para definir o tipo de licenciamento será a capacidade elétrica instalada. Os empreendimentos serão divididos em cinco categorias: - Micro: até 20 MW; - Pequeno: acima de 20 MW até 50 MW; - Médio: acima de 50 MW até 100 MW; - Grande: acima de 100 MW até 500 MW; - Excepcional: acima de 500 MW. A potência considerada inclui os equipamentos de tecnologia da informação e os sistemas de refrigeração. LEIA TAMBÉM: Consumo de água A modalidade de licenciamento e os estudos ambientais exigidos também vão variar conforme o porte e o sistema de refrigeração utilizado. Nos sistemas fechados, a água usada para resfriar os equipamentos circula em um circuito e é reaproveitada, sem necessidade de reposição constante em grandes volumes. Já os sistemas abertos, que utilizam torres de refrigeração, podem apresentar maior consumo de água. Segundo o diretor-geral do Idema, Werner Farkatt, essa diferença foi um dos pontos considerados na elaboração da resolução, especialmente diante da escassez hídrica no semiárido. “A resolução estabelece um licenciamento mais simplificado para sistemas fechados, enquanto os empreendimentos de grande e excepcional porte e com sistemas abertos estarão sujeitos a estudos ambientais mais complexos”, explicou. Localização também será considerada Independentemente do porte ou do sistema de refrigeração, os data centers serão considerados de significativo impacto ambiental quando estiverem em áreas como unidades de conservação e áreas de preservação permanente. Outra regra determina que dois ou mais data centers do mesmo empreendedor, localizados a até 500 metros de distância um do outro, sejam considerados como um único empreendimento para a avaliação dos impactos ambientais. Caberá ao Idema analisar tecnicamente os processos, realizar vistorias, definir medidas mitigadoras e compensatórias e estabelecer condicionantes específicas. O órgão também poderá solicitar complementações aos estudos apresentados.

artigo.texto: Are more data centers coming to North Alabama? What local leaders are saying Few development issues are currently as hotly debated as data centers. In North Alabama, questions are intensifying as Huntsville and surrounding communities continue expanding both residentially and commercially. A Gallup poll conducted in March of this year states that 70 percent of Americans are either somewhat or strongly opposed to data center construction in their local area. In Madison County, Alabama, state Sen. Sam Givhan said a recent poll he conducted found that 55 percent of respondents in his district opposed additional data center development. The Huntsville Business Journal spoke with elected officials, residents, and utility representatives about the current and future roles of data centers in North Alabama. Data centers in North Alabama North Alabama is home to two hyperscale data centers built by Meta and Google. Meta’s campus is in north Huntsville near Toney. The company is contracted with the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) for its electricity needs and is a Huntsville Utilities water customer. In June 2022, Meta announced plans to add two buildings, bringing the campus to nearly 3.5 million square feet. Google’s hyperscale data center is in Jackson County in the Bridgeport area near the Tennessee state line. Located at the former TVA Widows Creek coal plant property, the facility also receives electricity through the TVA system. In June, Google announced it plans to expand this location by $1.5 billion in 2026 and 2027. At the time of publication, the Huntsville Business Journal was unable to confirm Google’s water source. Smaller data centers in the region include facilities operated by Simple Helix, DC BLOX, and Scipio Technologies. In Huntsville, Huntsville Utilities Director of External Affairs Joe Gehrdes compared Meta’s water usage with that of another common type of commercial customer. “They use about as much as a big retailer might use,” Gehrdes said. Gehrdes said Meta pays according to the applicable customer classification. “They are a water customer, but they’re like any other water customer in their rate class. They do not consume massive quantities of water,” Gehrdes explained. The long-term picture remains difficult to predict because data center equipment and cooling methods keep evolving. Gehrdes said he recently attended a presentation about data centers where the speaker said technology is changing so rapidly his presentation will be outdated in 30 days. TVA aims to protect customers As data center demand increases, TVA is taking steps to prevent the cost of serving data centers from being shifted to residential customers and other businesses. In August 2026, TVA’s board approved a new rate structure specifically for data centers effective October 1. Data centers are expected to pay approximately 10 percent more for power, with the increase phased in over three years. New or expanding data centers requiring more than five megawatts must also pay a capacity commitment charge (CCC). McClain said the charge allows TVA to collect money before investing in the generation and transmission infrastructure needed to serve a project. “This fee is collected proactively to minimize financial risk for all ratepayers. The capacity commitment charge is about $1.5 million per megawatt,” McClain said. McClain said the policy is intended to keep other customers from paying for infrastructure built for a data center, particularly if the project does not use all the electricity it requested or does not move forward. McClain also said the CCC allows TVA to interrupt data center operations to protect grid reliability while infrastructure updates are completed. Where does this leave the future of data centers in North Alabama? Local leaders weigh in Huntsville City Council President Jennie Robinson said the city should set standards for resource use and community impacts before considering another hyperscale project. “Honestly, the one hyperscale data center we currently have in Huntsville is plenty. Any future proposal should be evaluated under a formal city policy addressing location, power and water consumption, noise, infrastructure costs, environmental effects, job creation, and the overall benefit to residents,” Robinson said. District 4 City Council Member Bill Kling took a more definitive position on additional development. “I am opposed, lock, stock, and barrel, to any additional data centers coming into the city of Huntsville. Period,” Kling said. Kling said he favors discouraging new projects rather than imposing a temporary pause for further study. “I’m not particularly interested in a two-year moratorium to study it. Don’t want to study it. We’re done. We got our energy. Legally, I don’t know if we can prevent them, but we don’t have to give them any inducements. We don’t have to give them any support,” Kling said. Kling said the city should determine what restrictions are legally available. “I would certainly encourage the city attorney’s office to investigate and make sure that we’re doing everything we can to discourage them within the law,” Kling said. Looking ahead to the 2027 legislative session, Givhan said he expects lawmakers to consider additional data center legislation, particularly changes to the state tax incentives offered to qualifying projects. “It’s clear now that they want to come whether they get the incentives or not. So why should we give them incentives? From a tax standpoint, I don’t see any reason to do that,” Givhan said. Givhan said broader restrictions are less likely to gain legislative approval. Instead, he said lawmakers could consider development standards for projects proposed in more rural areas. “I think there is some discussion about out in the county where they don’t have zoning, that there might be minimum acreage requirements,” Givhan said. artigo.texto: At the start of lambing season, Fiona Ramsden's farm near the New Zealand village of Pongaroa is a picture of rural life: newborn lambs trailing their mothers across steep pasture, fields dotted with spiky native palm trees, and a pretty white homestead that dates back about a century. But pine trees are closing in. On neighboring land once grazed by sheep and cattle, young Monterey pines — also known as radiata pines — carpet the hills, planted to earn carbon credits under the country’s emissions trading scheme. "You're connected to the land and that's why it's quite depressing to see good farmland — and to sheep and beef, good country — going into pine trees," Ramsden said. For almost 20 years, New Zealand has pioneered one of the world’s most ambitious tree-planting programs, approving nearly 9,000 square kilometers of carbon-credit forest. That’s about 11 times the land area of New York City. The emissions trading scheme (ETS) has turned forestry into a potentially more lucrative long-term investment than livestock farming, the traditional mainstay of the rural economy. Under the ETS, owners of forests established after 1989 can earn carbon credits for greenhouse gases as their trees grow. Forest owners — companies, indigenous tribal organizations and family farmers with a small slice of land in trees — can sell those carbon credits to companies that need them to offset emissions, creating an income stream long before the forest is harvested. Yet the boom in carbon forestry — and tradable carbon credits — has also driven competition for sheep and beef farming land. The rapid expansion of forest land in traditional beef and sheep country is straining rural communities and prompting the government’s climate advisers to warn that New Zealand is avoiding harder cuts elsewhere in the economy and risks missing its emissions targets. The government counters that forestry remains only one part of its emissions-reduction strategy. Ramsden, 50, returned to take over the family farm in 2012 after a career in fashion and interior design in the capital, Wellington, and elsewhere. From her 1,215-hectare property, the tradeoffs of carbon farming feel personal. Pine forests surround her from all sides, barring one block of land. Bright yellow gorse bushes — an invasive plant in New Zealand — tumble toward the fences. Feral goats dart from the forest and onto pasture intended for her 3,500 sheep and 350 cows. Wild pigs tear up patches of ground, problems she says have grown as forest owners do little to control the population. She pointed out a power pole leaning into the pines, noting that she is experiencing more frequent power cuts as trees encroach on powerlines. WHY TREES BEAT SHEEP Just over half of New Zealand's greenhouse gas emissions come from agriculture, mainly methane and nitrous oxide. Agricultural emissions are excluded from the ETS, which primarily targets carbon dioxide and emissions from heavy industry. Farmers say that, even so, the ETS has transformed rural land markets. Forestry investors, buoyed by carbon-credit revenue, have been able to outbid sheep and beef producers for grazing land, raising concerns from farm industry groups about the future of traditional beef and sheep farming. Since 2017, about 3,300 square kilometers of sheep and beef farmland have been sold for conversion to forestry, according to industry group Beef + Lamb New Zealand. That's enough land to feed more than 2 million sheep, equivalent to nearly 9% of the country's flock. As forestry investors chased carbon credits, grazing land prices rose 9.7%, according to Real Estate Institute of New Zealand data. Dairy land, because it’s generally more expensive, has largely escaped forestry conversion and seen price rises of just 3.7%. Foreign investors have acquired more than 1,000 square kilometers of farmland for conversion to forestry since 2017, according to data from the government’s Overseas Investment Office. Ingka Investments, the investment arm of the company that operates most IKEA stores worldwide, owns 430 square kilometers of forest in New Zealand, some of which is in the ETS. Ingka says its rationale is long-term timber, not carbon-credit income. "The heart of our core investment is more in the timber," said Dylan Foster, forestland operations manager at Ingka Investments. CHEAP CREDITS, HARDER EMISSIONS CUTS Supporters of the ETS say forestry is essential to reaching New Zealand’s climate targets. Climate Change Minister Simon Watts called it a “cost-effective way” to reduce net emissions, because of the country’s established forestry sector and favorable growing conditions. The Climate Change Commission, an independent advisory body, expects ETS forests to deliver a quarter of the emissions reductions needed for New Zealand's 2026-2030 target, and nearly half of those needed for its 2031-2035 target. But critics say the scheme relies too heavily on offsets, rather than direct emissions cuts. Because planting and maintaining forests is relatively cheap, they say polluters can buy credits rather than make the costlier investments required to transition to cleaner fuels or technology. Climate Change Commission chief executive Jo Hendy said the ETS is essentially “functioning as an offsetting scheme.” The government says New Zealand is on track to meet its near-term climate goals. "Forestry is not the whole plan," Watts said in response to emailed questions from Reuters. Late last year, the government tightened the ETS rules for non-native species, including pine, on more productive land. Preliminary data released by Beef + Lamb New Zealand last month showed purchases for wholesale conversions had slowed to nearly 160 square kilometers, less than half of the total the year before. However, the industry group said the total could rise once data is finalized.
